Determine $f(n,r,k,t)$ for all admissible parameters $n,r,k,t$. In particular, determine the order of magnitude of $f(n,r,k,t)$ as $n\to\infty$ for each fixed $r,k,t$.

(Known partial information: it has been shown that $f(n,r,k,1)\le c\, n^{r-2}$ for a constant $c=c(r,k)$, and for $r=3$ asymptotically tight bounds for $f(n,3,k,t)$ are known.)

Setup and definitions. Work in ZFC. For a cardinal λ and a cardinal κ > λ, let cof(λ) denote the class of ordinals of cofinality λ, and for a cardinal κ let κ ∩ cof(λ) = {α < κ : cf(α) = λ}. Given a strictly increasing sequence of regular cardinals ⟨κ_α : α < δ⟩ with sup_{α<δ} κ_α = κ, and a regular cardinal λ < κ_0, a sequence ⟨S_α : α < δ⟩ with each S_α a stationary subset of κ_α ∩ cof(λ) is said to be mutually stationary if the set
  S := { X ∈ [κ]^λ : sup(X ∩ κ_α) ∈ S_α for every α < δ such that sup(X ∩ κ_α) has cofinality λ relevant in S_α }
is stationary in [κ]^λ (i.e., meets every club subset of [κ]^λ).

Let MS(⟨κ_α : α < δ⟩, λ) denote the assertion: for every sequence ⟨S_α : α < δ⟩ with each S_α a stationary subset of κ_α ∩ cof(λ), the sequence is mutually stationary.

Question. Determine the exact consistency strength, measured on the standard large cardinal hierarchy, of the principle
  MS(⟨ω_n : n < ω⟩, ω_1).
Determine also the exact consistency strength of MS(⟨ω_n : n < ω⟩, ω_1) together with the Continuum Hypothesis (CH).

Let r ≥ 2 and k ≥ 2 be integers. An r-uniform hypergraph (r-graph) on a vertex set V is a pair (V, E) where E is a set of r-element subsets of V. Given r-graphs H_1, …, H_k with the same number of edges, a U-decomposition of (H_1, …, H_k) into t parts is a family of partitions

  E(H_i) = E_{i,1} ∪ E_{i,2} ∪ ⋯ ∪ E_{i,t}  (i = 1, …, k),

such that, for every j ∈ {1, …, t}, the r-graphs induced by E_{1,j}, E_{2,j}, …, E_{k,j} are pairwise isomorphic. Define

  U_k(n, r) = max over all k-tuples (H_1, …, H_k) of r-graphs on n vertices having the same number of edges, of the minimum number of parts t in any U-decomposition of (H_1, …, H_k).

It is known that for r = 2 (ordinary graphs),
  (2/3) n − 1/3 < U_2(n, 2) < (2/3) n + c,
and for k ≥ 3,
  (3/4) n − √n − 1 < U_k(n, 2) < (3/4) n + c_k.
For r = 3, it is known that
  c_1 n^{4/3} log log n / log n < U_2(n, 3) < c_2 n^{4/3},
and more generally, for every ε > 0,
  c_3 n^{2 − 2/k − ε} < U_k(n, 3) < c_4 n^{2 − 1/k}.

Determine the asymptotic behaviour of U_k(n, r) as n → ∞. In particular, determine U_2(n, 3) up to a constant factor and, more generally, close the gap between the known lower and upper bounds for U_k(n, r) when r ≥ 3.

Let G = (V, E) be a finite hypergraph (a finite set V of vertices together with a family E of nonempty subsets of V called edges) with n vertices, having no isolated vertices. Define:

- the point covering number α₀(G) to be the smallest cardinality of a subset T ⊆ V such that T ∩ e ≠ ∅ for every edge e ∈ E;
- the line covering number α₁(G) to be the smallest cardinality of a subfamily S ⊆ E such that every vertex of V is contained in at least one edge of S.

For graphs (the 2-uniform case) it is known that
   n − 1 ≤ α₀(G) · α₁(G) ≤ ⌊(n+1)/2⌋ · ⌈(n−1)/2⌉ (or the analogous sharp bound),
and the extremal graphs are characterized.

Problem: Determine, for general finite hypergraphs on n vertices (with no isolated vertices), the maximum and the minimum possible value of the product α₀(G) · α₁(G), and characterize all hypergraphs attaining these extremal values.

For ordinals $\kappa, \alpha, \beta$ and a positive integer $n$, the partition relation $\kappa \to (\alpha, \beta)^n$ means: for every coloring $c : [\kappa]^n \to \{0, 1\}$ of the $n$-element subsets of $\kappa$ with two colors, either there exists $A \subseteq \kappa$ of order type $\alpha$ with $c$ constantly $0$ on $[A]^n$, or there exists $B \subseteq \kappa$ of order type $\beta$ with $c$ constantly $1$ on $[B]^n$.

Let $\omega_1$ denote the first uncountable ordinal. Determine whether the following holds:
$$\omega_1 \to (\alpha, 4)^3 \quad \text{for every countable ordinal } \alpha < \omega_1.$$

That is, decide whether for every countable ordinal $\alpha$ and every 2-coloring of the 3-element subsets of $\omega_1$, there is either a subset of order type $\alpha$ all of whose triples receive color $0$, or a 4-element subset all of whose triples receive color $1$.

$$\omega_1 \to (\alpha, 4)^3 \quad \text{for every countable ordinal } \alpha < \omega_1.$$

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The problem is a longstanding question in the partition calculus of Erdős–Rado. Partial positive results have been established: Milner and Prikry handled countable ordinals up to about $\omega^2+1$; later Schipperus (1999 thesis, and subsequent work) and Jones extended this to countable ordinals whose Cantor normal form has at most two summands. The general case for all countable $\alpha < \omega_1$ does not appear to be settled, so the problem is partially solved.

Using the Erdős–Rado partition arrow notation, for ordinals $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$, write $\alpha \to (\beta, \gamma)^2$ to mean: for every coloring $c: [\alpha]^2 \to \{0,1\}$ of the unordered pairs of elements of $\alpha$ with two colors, either there is a subset $X \subseteq \alpha$ of order type $\beta$ with $c$ constantly $0$ on $[X]^2$, or there is a subset $Y \subseteq \alpha$ of order type $\gamma$ with $c$ constantly $1$ on $[Y]^2$. Here ordinal exponentiation is used, so $\omega_1^2$ denotes the ordinal product $\omega_1 \cdot \omega_1$ (where $\omega_1$ is the least uncountable ordinal).

(a) Decide whether the partition relation
$$\omega_1^2 \to (\omega_1^2,\, 3)^2$$
holds in ZFC. It is known that under the Continuum Hypothesis this relation fails. Determine whether, under the axiom $\mathrm{MA}_{\aleph_1} + 2^{\aleph_0} = \aleph_2$ (Martin's Axiom at $\aleph_1$ together with the continuum being $\aleph_2$), the relation $\omega_1^2 \to (\omega_1^2, 3)^2$ holds.

(b) More generally, characterize the infinite cardinals $\lambda$ for which the partition relation
$$\lambda^2 \to (\lambda^2,\, 3)^2$$

Consider the nonsmooth regularized optimization problem
    minimize over x in R^n   F(x) := f(x) + h(x),
where f : R^n → R is continuously differentiable (with, in standard assumptions, locally Lipschitz-continuous gradient) and h : R^n → R ∪ {+∞} is proper and lower semicontinuous, possibly nonconvex.

A proximal quasi-Newton trust-region method generates iterates x_k by approximately minimizing, within a trust region of radius Δ_k, a model of the form
    m_k(s) = f(x_k) + ⟨∇f(x_k), s⟩ + (1/2) ⟨s, B_k s⟩ + h(x_k + s),
where B_k is a symmetric Hessian or quasi-Newton approximation (e.g., PSB, BFGS, SR1). Standard convergence analyses assume that the family {B_k} is uniformly bounded, i.e., sup_k ‖B_k‖ < ∞, and prove that a suitable first-order stationarity measure tends to zero.

Question: Can the global convergence analysis of such a proximal quasi-Newton trust-region method be extended to allow the sequence {‖B_k‖} to be unbounded, provided the approximations do not deteriorate too fast — for instance, under a controlled growth condition of the form ‖B_k‖ ≤ C (1 + |S_k|)^p for some constants C > 0 and p ∈ [0, 1), where S_k denotes the index set of successful iterations up to iteration k — and still guarantee convergence of a first-order stationarity measure to zero, together with a worst-case iteration complexity bound for reaching ε-approximate stationarity?

Follow-up work has carried out exactly this generalization. Two recent papers in Mathematical Programming establish complexity and convergence results for trust-region methods with potentially unbounded model Hessians, including the nonsmooth regularized setting. Consider the composite optimization problem

where f : ℝ^n → ℝ is continuously differentiable with Lipschitz-continuous gradient and h : ℝ^n → ℝ ∪ {+∞} is proper, lower semicontinuous, and prox-bounded (possibly nonconvex and nonsmooth). A proximal quasi-Newton trust-region method generates iterates x_k by approximately minimizing, over a trust region of radius Δ_k, a model
    m_k(s) = f(x_k) + ⟨∇f(x_k), s⟩ + (1/2)⟨s, B_k s⟩ + h(x_k + s),
where B_k is a symmetric quasi-Newton approximation to ∇^2 f(x_k). The closely related proximal quadratic-regularization variant replaces the trust-region constraint by an added term (σ_k/2)‖s‖^2 in the model, with adaptive σ_k > 0. For both schemes, under standard assumptions on f, h, and {B_k}, global convergence to first-order stationary points (in the sense that a suitable proximal stationarity measure tends to zero) and worst-case iteration complexity bounds of the form O(ε^{-2}) for driving this stationarity measure below ε > 0 are known.

Now consider the cubic regularization analogue, in which the step at iteration k is computed as an approximate minimizer of
    m_k^{cubic}(s) = f(x_k) + ⟨∇f(x_k), s⟩ + (1/2)⟨s, B_k s⟩ + (σ_k/3)‖s‖^3 + h(x_k + s),
with σ_k > 0 updated adaptively according to the achieved-versus-predicted reduction in φ.

Question: Can one establish, for this proximal quasi-Newton cubic-regularization method, global convergence to first-order stationary points together with a worst-case iteration complexity bound (analogous to the O(ε^{-3/2}) bounds known for smooth cubic regularization) for driving the proximal stationarity measure below ε?

  f(n) / g_G(n) → 0  as n → ∞.

Let $d\ge 2$ and let $B\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ denote the open unit ball. For a finite Borel measure $\nu$ with compact support in $B$, define its potential by
$$U^\nu(x)=\int \frac{1}{|x-y|^{d-2}}\,d\nu(y)\quad (d\ge 3),\qquad U^\nu(x)=\int \log\frac{1}{|x-y|}\,d\nu(y)\quad (d=2).$$
Let $\mu$ be a compactly supported probability measure in $B$ such that:
(i) $\operatorname{supp}\mu$ is a smooth $C^1$ submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^d$ (possibly with boundary), and
(ii) $\mu$ has a smooth, strictly positive density with respect to the surface (Lebesgue) measure on $\operatorname{supp}\mu$.

For each positive integer $n$, let $\mu_n$ denote a discrete probability measure of the form $\mu_n=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\delta_{x_j^{(n)}}$ (with $x_j^{(n)}\in \overline{B}$, repetitions allowed; equivalently, supported on at most $n$ points with equal weights) which minimizes
$$\bigl\|U^{\mu_n}-U^\mu\bigr\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^d)}$$
among all such measures. Let $\nu_n=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^n\delta_{x_j^{(n)}}$ be the equal-weight counting measure on the support points of $\mu_n$.

Let $\omega_{\operatorname{supp}\mu,B}$ be the Green equilibrium distribution of $\operatorname{supp}\mu$ relative to $B$, i.e.\ the unique probability measure on $\operatorname{supp}\mu$ minimizing the Green energy $\iint g_B(x,y)\,d\sigma(x)\,d\sigma(y)$, where $g_B$ is the Green function of $B$ with pole at infinity (Dirichlet Green function).

Question: Does $\nu_n\xrightarrow{*} \omega_{\operatorname{supp}\mu,B}$ in the weak-$*$ topology as $n\to\infty$?

Let $G$ be a (simple) graph with infinite chromatic number, and suppose that $G$ contains odd cycles of lengths $n_1 < n_2 < n_3 < \cdots$ (listed without repetition). Must it be the case that
$$\sum_{i \ge 1} \frac{1}{n_i} = \infty?$$
Equivalently, does every graph of infinite chromatic number contain odd cycles whose lengths form a set with divergent reciprocal sum?

Let $G$ be a (simple) graph with infinite chromatic number, and suppose that $G$ contains odd cycles of lengths $n_1 < n_2 < n_3 < \cdots$ (listed without repetition). Must it be the case that

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The problem was resolved affirmatively by Hong Liu and Richard Montgomery (arXiv:2010.15802, 2020). They proved that for a graph of chromatic number k, the sum of reciprocals of its odd cycle lengths is at least (1/2 - o(1)) log k, which is asymptotically tight. This implies the Erdős–Hajnal odd cycle conjecture.

Let $A(z)=\prod_{j=0}^{p}(z-a_j)$ be a polynomial of degree $p+1$ with pairwise distinct complex zeros $a_0,\dots,a_p\in\mathbb{C}$, and let $B(z)$ be a polynomial of degree at most $p$. The generalized Lamé differential equation
$$A(z)\,y''(z)+B(z)\,y'(z)-n(n+	extstyle\sum_{j}ho_j-1)\,V(z)\,y(z)=0,$$
with parameters $ho_j\in\mathbb{C}$ determined by $B/A=\sum_j ho_j/(z-a_j)$, is known (after Heine and Stieltjes) to admit, for suitable choices of the polynomial $V(z)$ of degree $p-1$ (called Van Vleck polynomials), polynomial solutions $y(z)$ of degree $n$. These polynomial solutions $y$ are called Heine-Stieltjes polynomials.

In the classical Jacobi case ($p=1$, with $a_0,a_1\in\mathbb{R}$ and $ho_0,ho_1>0$), Stieltjes proved that the zeros of the Heine-Stieltjes polynomial of degree $n$ are the unique global minimizer, among configurations of $n$ distinct points $x_1,\dots,x_n\in(a_0,a_1)$, of the weighted logarithmic energy
$$E(x_1,\dots,x_n)=-\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}\log|x_i-x_j|-\sum_{j=0}^{p}ho_j\sum_{k=1}^{n}\log|x_k-a_j|.$$

Problem. For general configurations of nodes $a_0,\dots,a_p\in\mathbb{C}$ and parameters $ho_j\in\mathbb{C}$, construct an electrostatic model that characterizes the zeros of every Heine-Stieltjes polynomial as a min-max (saddle-point) configuration of a suitable energy functional. More precisely, give a variational principle of min-max type on an appropriate class of configurations (or measures) in the complex plane whose critical configurations are exactly the zero sets of the Heine-Stieltjes polynomials and which singles out each individual Heine-Stieltjes polynomial of degree $n$ (rather than merely identifying their union as critical points of the discrete logarithmic energy).

Setup. An ordinal graph is a simple graph whose vertex set is an ordinal (with the natural well-order). For subsets A, B of an ordinal, write A < B to mean that every element of A is strictly less than every element of B. A down-up matching in an ordinal graph G is a perfect matching between two disjoint vertex sets A and B of G such that A < B and every matched pair {a, m(a)} (with a ∈ A and m(a) ∈ B) is an edge of G.

Partition notation. For ordinals α, β, γ, write
  α → (β, γ-matching)²
to mean: for every graph G on the ordinal α, either G contains an independent set of order type β, or G contains a down-up matching between some sets A and B with A of order type γ (and A < B).

Known facts. Let j, k be positive integers with k ≥ 2 and let η be a countable limit ordinal. Then
  ω^{η+jk+1} → (ω^{η+j}, ω^k-matching)²,
while
  ω^{η+jk−1} ↛ (ω^{η+j}, ω^k-matching)².

Question. Under the same hypotheses (j, k positive integers with k ≥ 2 and η a countable limit ordinal), is it true that
  ω^{η+jk} → (ω^{η+j}, ω^k-matching)²?

Let π(x) denote the number of primes not exceeding x. Consider the following three questions:

(a) Is it true that for all real x, y ≥ 2,
   π(x + y) ≤ π(x) + π(y) ?

(b) (A weaker form.) Prove or disprove: for every ε > 0 there exists y_ε such that, for all y > y_ε and all x ≥ 0,
   π(x + y) − π(x) < (1 + ε) y / log y .

(c) Define ρ(y) = limsup_{x → ∞} [π(x + y) − π(x)]. Is it true that ρ(y) = 1 for every integer y ≥ 2 (equivalently, is the bound π(x+y) − π(x) ≤ 1 attained infinitely often, but never exceeded asymptotically, for each fixed y)?

Determine the truth of (a), (b), and (c).

(c) Define ρ(y) = limsup_{x → ∞} [π(x + y) − π(x)]. Is it true that ρ(y) = 1 for every integer y ≥ 2 (equivalently, is the bound π(x+y) − π(x) ≤ 1 attained infinitely often, but never exceeded asymptotically, for each fixed y)?

Determine the truth of (a), (b), and (c).

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The inequality π(x+y) ≤ π(x)+π(y) is the second Hardy–Littlewood conjecture, generally regarded as still open. Hensley and Richards (1973) showed it is incompatible with the first Hardy–Littlewood prime k-tuples conjecture, so at most one of the two can hold; most number theorists believe (a) is false but no explicit counterexample is known. The weaker form (b) and the assertion ρ(y)=1 also remain unresolved. A 2021 preprint by Visser claims a proof, but it has not been accepted by the mainstream community, and subsequent papers (e.g., 2025) continue to treat the conjecture as open.

Define the Sobolev inner product
$$\langle f, g \rangle_S \;=\; \int f\,\overline{g}\, d\mu_0 \;+\; \int f'\,\overline{g'}\, d\mu_1,$$
and let $\{Q_n\}_{n\ge 0}$ denote the sequence of monic polynomials orthogonal with respect to $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_S$, so that $Q_n$ has degree $n$ and $\langle Q_n, p \rangle_S = 0$ for every polynomial $p$ of degree less than $n$.

Assume that the supports $\operatorname{supp}(\mu_0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\mu_1)$ are disjoint, or at least noncoincident (i.e. neither is contained in the other). Determine the strong (Szegő-type) asymptotic behavior of $Q_n(z)$ as $n \to \infty$ for $z$ in the appropriate exterior region of the complex plane: namely, find an explicit limit of the form
$$\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{Q_n(z)}{\Phi_n(z)} \;=\; F(z),$$
where $\Phi_n$ is a suitable normalizing sequence (e.g. powers of the conformal map onto the exterior of the relevant support) and $F$ is an explicit analytic function expressible in terms of Szegő functions associated with $\mu_0$ and $\mu_1$.

Let $p_n$ denote the $n$-th prime number, so that $p_1=2, p_2=3, p_3=5,\ldots$, and let $g_n = p_{n+1}-p_n$ denote the $n$-th prime gap.

(a) (Piltz's conjecture) Prove or disprove: for every $\varepsilon > 0$,
$$p_{n+1}-p_n = O(n^{\varepsilon}),$$
i.e., there exists a constant $C_\varepsilon > 0$ such that $p_{n+1}-p_n \le C_\varepsilon\, n^{\varepsilon}$ for all $n \ge 1$.

(b) (Cramér's conjecture) Prove or disprove the stronger assertion
$$p_{n+1}-p_n = O\!\left((\log n)^2\right).$$

(c) (Primes between consecutive squares) Prove or disprove: for every integer $m \ge 1$, there exists a prime $p$ with $m^2 < p < (m+1)^2$.

Determine, more generally, the true order of magnitude of $p_{n+1}-p_n$.

All three questions remain open. Cramér's conjecture $p_{n+1}-p_n = O((\log n)^2)$ is unproven, and probabilistic refinements by Granville and others suggest the constant may need adjustment, but no proof or counterexample exists. Piltz's weaker $O(n^\varepsilon)$ bound is also open: the best unconditional results give $p_{n+1}-p_n \ll p_n^{0.525}$ (Baker–Harman–Pintz), still far from $n^\varepsilon$. Legendre's conjecture that there is a prime between $m^2$ and $(m+1)^2$ remains open and is known to lie beyond the Riemann hypothesis.

each have asymptotic density 1/2, i.e.
   lim_{N→∞} |A ∩ [1,N]| / N = lim_{N→∞} |B ∩ [1,N]| / N = 1/2 ?

(b) Equality question. Are there infinitely many positive integers n such that d_{n+1} = d_n ?

(c) Monotone triples. Are there infinitely many positive integers n such that
   d_{n+2} > d_{n+1} > d_n ,
and are there infinitely many positive integers n such that
   d_{n+2} < d_{n+1} < d_n ?

Let $\Gamma$ be a Jordan arc or Jordan curve in the complex plane, and let $h:U\to\mathbb{C}$ be a function holomorphic in a neighborhood $U$ of $\Gamma$. For each integer $n\geq 0$, suppose there exists a monic polynomial $P_n$ of degree $n$ characterized by the "nonstandard" orthogonality conditions
$$\int_\Gamma P_n(z)\, h(z)^k\, dz \;=\; 0, \qquad k = 0, 1, \dots, n-1,$$
(or an analogous family of orthogonality conditions against powers of the holomorphic function $h$ on $\Gamma$).

Question: Is it possible to characterize the family $\{P_n\}_{n\geq 0}$ as the (1,1)-entry of the solution $Y(z)$ of a matrix Riemann–Hilbert problem? That is, does there exist a contour $\Sigma$ (built from $\Gamma$ and possibly auxiliary arcs), a jump matrix $V(z)$ defined on $\Sigma$, and normalization conditions at infinity such that the unique matrix-valued function $Y:\mathbb{C}\setminus\Sigma\to\mathrm{GL}_m(\mathbb{C})$ (for some $m\geq 2$) satisfying
- $Y$ is holomorphic on $\mathbb{C}\setminus\Sigma$,
- $Y_+(z) = Y_-(z)\,V(z)$ for $z\in\Sigma$,
- $Y(z)\,\mathrm{diag}(z^{-n},z^n,\dots)\to I$ as $z\to\infty$,

encodes the polynomials $P_n$ (and associated Cauchy-type transforms) through its entries, in analogy with the Fokas–Its–Kitaev characterization of classical orthogonal polynomials?

$$d_n := \frac{p_{n+1}-p_n}{\log p_n}, \qquad n=1,2,3,\dots.$$
Let $L \subseteq [0,\infty]$ be the set of limit points of $(d_n)_{n\ge 1}$ in the extended real line.

(b) Does $(d_n)$ possess a limiting distribution function? That is, does there exist a non-decreasing right-continuous function $F:[0,\infty)\to[0,1]$ such that for every continuity point $x\ge 0$ of $F$,
$$\lim_{N\to\infty} \frac{1}{N}\,\#\{n\le N : d_n \le x\} = F(x)?$$

Partial progress has been obtained but the full questions remain open. Goldston–Pintz–Yıldırım (2005) showed $0\in L$; Banks–Freiberg–Maynard (2016) proved that at least 12.5% of $[0,\infty)$ lies in $L$, and subsequent refinements (Pintz; Merikoski) raised this to at least one-third and showed $L$ has bounded gaps. However, density of $(d_n)$ in $[0,\infty)$ (i.e. $L=[0,\infty]$) and existence of a limiting distribution function are still unresolved.

Let $\mu$ be a finite positive Borel measure on $[-1,1]$ with infinite support, and let $(p_n)_{n\ge 0}$ be the associated sequence of orthonormal polynomials, i.e., $p_n$ has degree $n$, positive leading coefficient, and $\int_{-1}^{1} p_n(x) p_m(x)\, d\mu(x) = \delta_{nm}$. The Boltzmann–Shannon entropy of $p_n$ with respect to $\mu$ is defined by
$$E_n(\mu) \;=\; -\int_{-1}^{1} p_n(x)^2 \, \log\bigl(p_n(x)^2\bigr) \, d\mu(x).$$
For the (first-kind) Chebyshev measure $d\mu_T(x) = \pi^{-1}(1-x^2)^{-1/2}\,dx$ the orthonormal polynomials satisfy a known extremal asymptotic behavior of $E_n$ as $n\to\infty$ (namely $E_n(\mu_T)$ attains, in the limit, the extremal value characteristic of the Chebyshev case).

Recall that $\mu$ belongs to the Szegő class on $[-1,1]$ if $\mu$ is absolutely continuous with weight $w(x) = d\mu/dx$ satisfying
$$\int_{-1}^{1} \frac{\log w(x)}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\, dx \;>\; -\infty.$$

Question: Suppose $\mu$ lies in the Szegő class and the sequence $E_n(\mu)$ exhibits the same asymptotic extremal behavior as $E_n(\mu_T)$ for the Chebyshev measure. Does this asymptotic property force $\mu$ to be the Chebyshev measure (up to the standard normalization), i.e., does the asymptotic extremality of the Boltzmann–Shannon entropy characterize the Chebyshev family within the entire Szegő class?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Major progress exists but the problem of determining the true order of $f(k)$ remains open. Shelah (1988) gave the first primitive-recursive upper bound (in the wowzer/tower hierarchy). Gowers (2001), as a consequence of his quantitative Szemerédi theorem, proved $f(k) \le 2^{2^{2^{2^{k+9}}}}}$, a vast improvement. Let $p_1 < p_2 < p_3 < \cdots$ denote the sequence of prime numbers, and let $\varphi$ denote Euler's totient function.

(a) Assuming the Riemann hypothesis, it is known that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a constant $c_\varepsilon$ such that
$$\sum_{p_n < x} (p_{n+1} - p_n)^2 \;<\; c_\varepsilon \, x (\log x)^{3+\varepsilon}$$
for all $x \ge 2$. Determine whether the exponent $3+\varepsilon$ on $\log x$ can be reduced to $1$; that is, prove or disprove the existence of an absolute constant $C$ such that
$$\sum_{p_n < x} (p_{n+1} - p_n)^2 \;<\; C \, x \log x \qquad \text{for all } x \ge 2.$$

(b) For each integer $n \ge 2$, let $1 = a_1 < a_2 < \cdots < a_{\varphi(n)} = n-1$ be the integers in $\{1, 2, \ldots, n-1\}$ that are coprime to $n$. Prove or disprove that there exists an absolute constant $c > 0$ such that
$$\sum_{k=1}^{\varphi(n)-1} (a_{k+1} - a_k)^2 \;<\; \frac{c \, n^2}{\varphi(n)}$$
holds for every integer $n \ge 2$.

Let $w$ be the symmetric Pollaczek weight on the interval $[-1,1]$, namely
$$w(x)=\frac{1}{\pi}\,e^{(2\theta-\pi)a/\sin\theta}\,\bigl|\Gamma\bigl(\lambda+i\,a/\sin\theta\bigr)\bigr|^{2},\qquad x=\cos\theta,\ \theta\in(0,\pi),$$
with parameters $a\ge 0$ and $\lambda\ge 1$, and let $\{p_n\}_{n\ge 0}$ be the sequence of polynomials orthonormal with respect to $w$, so that $\int_{-1}^{1}p_n(x)p_m(x)w(x)\,dx=\delta_{nm}$.

Define the Shannon entropy of $p_n$ by
$$E_n \;=\; -\int_{-1}^{1} p_n(x)^2\,\log\!\bigl(p_n(x)^2\bigr)\,w(x)\,dx.$$

It is known that $w$ lies outside the Szegő class on $[-1,1]$, so the standard Szegő‐class hypotheses under which the asymptotic formula
$$E_n \;=\; \log(2\pi) - 1 - \int_{-1}^{1}\frac{\log w(x)}{\pi\sqrt{1-x^2}}\,dx + o(1)\qquad (n\to\infty) \tag{$\ast$}$$
has been established do not apply, and in fact $E_n\to -\infty$.

Question: Does the asymptotic relation $(\ast)$ — interpreted with its leading terms suitably normalized — nevertheless remain valid for the orthonormal symmetric Pollaczek polynomials, and if so, determine the first two terms in the asymptotic expansion of $E_n$ as $n\to\infty$.

(b) Is $\liminf_{n \to \infty} \dfrac{d_n}{\log n} = 0$?

(c) Is $\limsup_{n \to \infty} \dfrac{\min(d_n,\, d_{n+1},\, d_{n+2})}{\log n} = \infty$?

Let $p_1 < p_2 < p_3 < \cdots$ denote the sequence of prime numbers, and for each $n \ge 1$ set $d_n = p_{n+1} - p_n$. Resolve the following four questions:

(a) Is $\liminf_{n \to \infty} d_n = 2$ (the twin-prime conjecture)?

(b) Is $\liminf_{n \to \infty} \dfrac{d_n}{\log n} = 0$?

(c) Is $\limsup_{n \to \infty} \dfrac{\min(d_n,\, d_{n+1},\, d_{n+2})}{\log n} = \infty$?

(d) Is $\liminf_{n \to \infty} \dfrac{\max(d_n,\, d_{n+1})}{\log n} < 1$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The four sub-questions have different statuses. (a) The twin-prime conjecture $\liminf d_n = 2$ remains open, though Zhang (2013) and Maynard (2013) established that $\liminf d_n$ is finite. (b) $\liminf d_n/\log n = 0$ was proved by Goldston, Pintz and Yıldırım (2009). (c) Large gaps results of Ford–Green–Konyagin–Tao and Maynard (2014/2016), combined with chain-of-large-gaps results (Banks–Freiberg–Maynard and related work), give $\limsup \min(d_n,d_{n+1},d_{n+2})/\log n = \infty$. (d) The question of whether $\liminf \max(d_n,d_{n+1})/\log n < 1$ appears to remain open. Overall the problem is partially solved.

Associated to $Q$ is the (weighted) equilibrium measure $\mu_w$, i.e. the unique Borel probability measure on $\mathbb{R}$ that minimizes the weighted logarithmic energy
$$I_Q(\mu) = \iint \log\frac{1}{|x-y|}\,d\mu(x)\,d\mu(y) + 2\int Q(x)\,d\mu(x),$$
with compact support $S_w := \operatorname{supp}(\mu_w)$.

Define the (differential) entropy of the squared orthonormal polynomial against the varying weight by
$$E_n(w) := -\int_{\mathbb{R}} p_{n,n}^2(x)\, \log\bigl(p_{n,n}^2(x)\bigr)\, e^{-2nQ(x)}\,dx,$$
and let $E(\mu_w)$ denote the corresponding logarithmic entropy functional of the equilibrium measure $\mu_w$ that, under suitable regularity hypotheses, governs the leading-order asymptotics of $E_n(w)$ as $n\to\infty$.

Under the hypothesis that the asymptotic formula
$$E_n(w) = E(\mu_w) + o(1) \quad (n\to\infty)$$
(expressing the entropy asymptotics of the varying-weight orthogonal polynomials through the equilibrium measure in the external field $Q$) is known to hold in some restricted setting, determine whether the same asymptotic remains valid in the more general setting in which the support $S_w$ of the equilibrium measure is assumed only to be a single interval.

Equivalently:

The Erdős distinct subset sums problem is widely regarded as still open. The best known lower bounds for the largest element in a Sidon-type distinct-subset-sum set in {1,...,N} of size n give N ≥ √(2/(πn))·2^n (Elkies–Gleason, with subsequent refinements), but the conjectured bound N ≫ 2^n (equivalently h(x) = log_2 x + O(1)) has not been established. Recent work (e.g., arXiv:2208.12182, arXiv:2006.12988, arXiv:2308.03748) continues to refine bounds without resolving the conjecture.

representations.normalized:
Let $S^{q-1} \subset \mathbb{R}^q$ denote the unit sphere, equipped with its normalized surface measure $\sigma$. For an integer $n \geq 0$, let $\mathcal{P}_n$ be the space of spherical polynomials of degree at most $n$ restricted to $S^{q-1}$, and set $d_n = \dim \mathcal{P}_n$. Given a finite set of nodes $B = \{x_1, \ldots, x_N\} \subset S^{q-1}$, an interpolatory quadrature formula based on $B$ for $\mathcal{P}_n$ is a set of real weights $w_1, \ldots, w_N$ such that
$$\int_{S^{q-1}} p(x)\, d\sigma(x) = \sum_{j=1}^N w_j\, p(x_j) \quad \text{for all } p \in \mathcal{P}_n,$$
where $n$ is chosen as large as possible (typically requiring $N = d_n$). The quadrature is called positive if $w_j > 0$ for all $j$. A node set $B \subset S^{q-1}$ with $|B| = d_n$ is called extremal with respect to an energy functional $E$ (for example a discretized logarithmic or Riesz energy, or a Fekete-type determinant maximization on $\mathcal{P}_n$) if it optimizes $E$ over all $d_n$-point configurations on $S^{q-1}$.

Address the following two questions:

(1) If $B$ is an extremal configuration with respect to some energy problem of the above type, must there exist an interpolatory positive quadrature formula on $B$ that is exact for $\mathcal{P}_n$?

(2) Conversely, if a finite set $B \subset S^{q-1}$ admits an interpolatory positive quadrature formula exact for $\mathcal{P}_n$ with $|B| = d_n$, must $B$ coincide with the extremal configuration for some discretized energy problem?

Work by Sloan and Womersley (and subsequent authors) shows numerically and in special cases that extremal (maximum-determinant / Fekete) point systems on $S^2$ yield interpolatory cubature rules with positive weights, at least up to degree 191. However, a general proof that extremal systems always produce positive interpolatory quadratures, and the converse characterization, do not appear to have been established. The questions as stated remain open.

For a set $A=\{a_i\}$ of nonnegative integers, let $k_A(x)=|\{i:a_i\le x\}|$ denote its counting function.

(a) Suppose $A$ has the property that every natural number $n$ can be written as $n=a_i+2^j$ for some $a_i\in A$ and some nonnegative integer $j$. It is known that there exists such a set with $k_A(x)<c\,x(\log\log x)/\log x$ for some constant $c>0$. Can the factor $\log\log x$ be removed, i.e., does there exist such a set with $k_A(x)=O(x/\log x)$?

(b) Suppose $A$ has the property that every natural number $n$ can be written as $n=a_i+p_j$ where $a_i\in A$ and $p_j$ is prime. It is known that there exists such a set with $k_A(x)<c(\log x)^2$. Can this bound be improved; in particular, can one achieve $k_A(x)=O(\log x)$?

(c) Let $\{a_i\}$ and $\{b_i\}$ be two infinite increasing sequences of nonnegative integers such that every sufficiently large natural number $n$ can be written as $n=a_i+b_j$. Let $A(x)$ and $B(x)$ be the corresponding counting functions. Is it true that
$$\limsup_{x\to\infty}\frac{A(x)B(x)}{x}>1?$$

(c) Let $\{a_i\}$ and $\{b_i\}$ be two infinite increasing sequences of nonnegative integers such that every sufficiently large natural number $n$ can be written as $n=a_i+b_j$. Let $A(x)$ and $B(x)$ be the corresponding counting functions. Is it true that

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Part (b) has seen substantial progress: Wolke, Kolountzakis, and Ruzsa successively improved the upper bound, with Ruzsa achieving $\ll \omega(N)\log N$ for any $\omega\to\infty$, and a lower bound $\liminf A(x)/\log x\ge e^\gamma$ is known; whether $O(\log N)$ is attainable remains open (Erdős offered $50). Part (c) is the Erdős–Danzer conjecture, which was confirmed by Sárközy and Szemerédi (1994), who proved that for infinite additive complements with $\limsup A(x)B(x)/x\le 1$ one must have $A(x)B(x)-x\to\infty$. Part (a) about removing the $\log\log x$ factor for powers of 2 appears still open.

The Erdős–Turán conjecture on additive bases (1941) is widely regarded as still open. Let $D(a_i, r_i) = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z - a_i| < r_i\}$ for $1 \le i \le n$ be finitely many pairwise disjoint open disks in the complex plane, with centers $a_1, \dots, a_n \in \mathbb{C}$ and radii $r_1, \dots, r_n > 0$. The union $\bigcup_{i=1}^n D(a_i, r_i)$ is the set where the real-valued function
$$\rho(z) = \prod_{i=1}^n \bigl(|z - a_i|^2 - r_i^2\bigr)$$
is negative (assuming $n$ is even) or has the appropriate sign; in any case its polarization is the polynomial
$$Q(z, w) = \prod_{i=1}^n \bigl((z - a_i)(\overline{w} - \overline{a_i}) - r_i^2\bigr),$$
which is Hermitian in the sense that $Q(z,w) = \overline{Q(w,z)}$ and satisfies $Q(z,z) = \rho(z)$.

Give an elementary proof that the $n \times n$ Hermitian matrix
$$M = \bigl(Q(a_i, a_j)\bigr)_{i,j=1}^n$$
is positive semidefinite.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

A search shows that the Bambah–Chowla bound $a_{k+1}-a_k\ll a_k^{1/4}$ remains the standard pointwise upper bound, with refinements only to the implicit constant by Uchiyama, Shiu, and Jameson. Hooley and others obtained results on moments and on short-interval behavior for almost all intervals, and recent work by Dietmann–Elsholtz and Kalmynin–Konyagin has improved lower bounds for the largest gap up to $X$ (now of order $\log X$). No source found establishes the pointwise improvement to $o(a_k^{1/4})$, so the question as posed appears to still be open.

A pair $\{x,y\} \subseteq S$ is called a diameter pair if $\|x-y\|_2 = 1$. Determine, as a function of $n$ and $d$, the maximum possible number of diameter pairs $f_d(n)$ over all such configurations $S$.

For context, the analogous quantities in low dimensions are known: $f_2(n) = n$ (planar case) and $f_3(n) = 2n-2$ (three-dimensional case). The problem asks for the exact value of $f_d(n)$ when $d \geq 4$.

The maximum number of diameters among n points in d-dimensional Euclidean space has been exactly determined for every d ≥ 4 (for n sufficiently large depending on d), with extremal configurations characterized as Lenz constructions. Setup. Consider grammatical inference in the framework of identification in the limit from positive (or labelled) data. Let A be an alphabet, X = A* the set of finite strings over A, and let R(A) be a class of grammars over A; for G ∈ R(A) write L(G) ⊆ X for its language and |G| for an associated size. A presentation of a target grammar G is an infinite enumeration (f_n)_{n≥1} of strings (or labelled strings) consistent with L(G), with f_n denoting the prefix of length n.

A learning algorithm a, on input a finite sample f_n, outputs a grammar a(f_n) ∈ R(A); write L_A(a(f_n)) for its language. Two notions of "size" of a finite sample W ⊂ X are considered:
  (i) the cardinality measure ‖W‖_# := |W| (the number of strings in W);
  (ii) the bit-length measure ‖W‖_bit := Σ_{w ∈ W} (|w| + 1) (the total number of symbols/bits needed to encode W).

Definition (Polynomial characteristic sets under a chosen size measure ‖·‖). An algorithm a admits polynomial characteristic sets (with respect to ‖·‖) if there exists a polynomial p such that for every G ∈ R(A) there exists a finite sample W_G ⊂ X satisfying
    ‖W_G‖ ≤ p(|G|),
and such that for every presentation (f_n) of G, whenever W_G ⊂ f_n one has L_A(a(f_n)) = L(G).

Problem. Investigate the choice of size measure for characteristic sets.
(a) Determine whether using the cardinality measure ‖·‖_# (the number of strings) instead of the bit-length measure ‖·‖_bit is a sound and fair criterion for judging an algorithm's polynomial identifiability.
(b) Exhibit, or prove the nonexistence of, classes R(A) of grammars that are polynomially identifiable in the limit under the bit-length measure but are not polynomially identifiable in the limit under the cardinality measure (i.e., classes that become non-learnable when characteristic-set size is measured by the number of strings rather than by total encoded length).

The plane angle determined by an ordered triple of distinct points (A,B,C) in S is the angle ∠ABC at the vertex B; this angle is called acute if it is strictly less than π/2, and obtuse if it is strictly greater than π/2.

(a) Prove or disprove: every set S ⊂ ℝ^k of 2^k + 1 points contains three points that determine an obtuse angle.

(b) Does there exist a set of six points in ℝ^3 such that every plane angle determined by three of the points is acute? Does there exist such a set of seven points?
representations.original:
Let k ≥ 1 be an integer and let S be a finite set of points in Euclidean space ℝ^k. The plane angle determined by an ordered triple of distinct points (A,B,C) in S is the angle ∠ABC at the vertex B; this angle is called acute if it is strictly less than π/2, and obtuse if it is strictly greater than π/2.

(a) Prove or disprove: every set S ⊂ ℝ^k of 2^k + 1 points contains three points that determine an obtuse angle.

(b) Does there exist a set of six points in ℝ^3 such that every plane angle determined by three of the points is acute? Does there exist such a set of seven points?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

Part (a) is the Danzer–Grünbaum theorem (1962): any set of 2^k+1 points in ℝ^k determines an obtuse angle, with at most 2^k points possible if all angles are required to be at most π/2. The proof is reproduced in Aigner–Ziegler's "Proofs from THE BOOK" ("Every large point set has an obtuse angle"). Part (b) is also resolved affirmatively: explicit constructions of acute sets of 6, 7, and even 8 points in ℝ^3 are known (Grünbaum, Croft, and later authors), and the maximum size of an acute set in ℝ^3 is known to be 8. Thus both questions are solved.

Setup. A ranked alphabet is a pair (Σ, ≤) where Σ is a finite alphabet and ≤ is a partial order on Σ. An interval of (Σ, ≤) is a subset of Σ of the form [a,b] = { c ∈ Σ : a ≤ c ≤ b }. A k-edge deterministic finite-state automaton over (Σ, ≤) is a tuple A = (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F) where Q is a finite set of states, q₀ ∈ Q is the initial state, F ⊆ Q is the set of accepting states, and δ associates to each state q ∈ Q a set of at most k labeled transitions of the form (I, q′), where I is an interval of (Σ, ≤) and q′ ∈ Q, with the requirement that any two distinct intervals appearing on outgoing transitions from the same state are disjoint. A word w = a₁a₂…aₙ ∈ Σ* is accepted by A if there is a sequence of states q₀, q₁, …, qₙ with qₙ ∈ F such that for every i ∈ {1,…,n}, the state qᵢ₋₁ has an outgoing transition (Iᵢ, qᵢ) with aᵢ ∈ Iᵢ.

Sample. A sample is a pair ⟨X⁺, X⁻⟩ of finite disjoint subsets of Σ*. A k-edge DFA A is consistent with ⟨X⁺, X⁻⟩ if every word in X⁺ is accepted by A and no word in X⁻ is accepted by A. The sample ⟨X⁺, X⁻⟩ is k-acceptable if some k-edge DFA over (Σ, ≤) is consistent with it.

Problem. Given a finite ranked alphabet (Σ, ≤), a positive integer k, and a finite sample ⟨X⁺, X⁻⟩ over Σ, is there an algorithm that decides in time polynomial in the total size of the input (k, the description of (Σ, ≤), and the sample) whether ⟨X⁺, X⁻⟩ is k-acceptable?

Let Σ be a ranked alphabet and consider deterministic finite-state automata over Σ. For a DFA A, define its number of edges as the total number of transitions in its transition function; call A a k-edge DFA if this number is at most k. Write L(A) for the language recognized by A and |A| for its size (e.g. number of states plus number of edges).

Let $\{z_k\}_{k\ge 1}$ be a sequence of points on the unit circle $\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|=1\}$, and for each $n\ge 1$ define the monic polynomial
$$f_n(z)=\prod_{k=1}^{n}(z-z_k).$$

(a) Prove or disprove: there exists a choice of $\{z_k\}$ such that the sequence of functions $\{f_n\}_{n\ge 1}$ is uniformly bounded on $|z|=1$; equivalently, there exists a constant $C$ with
$$\sup_{|z|=1}|f_n(z)|\le C\qquad\text{for all }n\ge 1.$$

(b) Does there exist an infinite sequence $\{z_k\}$ on the unit circle with the following local discrepancy property: for every arc $(a,b)\subseteq[0,2\pi)$ on $|z|=1$ there is a constant $c(a,b)$ (depending only on the arc) such that, writing $N_n(a,b)$ for the number of indices $1\le k\le n$ with $z_k=e^{i\theta}$, $\theta\in(a,b)$,
$$\left|N_n(a,b)-\frac{b-a}{2\pi}\,n\right|<c(a,b)\qquad\text{for every }n\ge 1?$$

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Part (a) — Erdős's conjecture that $\max_{|z|=1}|f_n(z)|$ cannot remain bounded — was resolved affirmatively by J. Beck, "The modulus of polynomials with zeros on the unit circle: a problem of Erdős," Annals of Mathematics 134 (1991), 609–651, where in fact a lower bound tending to infinity is established. The companion discrepancy formulation in (b) is closely related and is generally believed to admit no such sequence; available sources point to Beck's work as the source of the resolution but do not give a single explicit citation for the precise arc-discrepancy statement, so its status is reported here as partially solved.

Consider deterministic finite-state automata over a ranked alphabet (an alphabet in which each symbol is assigned a fixed nonnegative integer arity). For a fixed positive integer k, define a k-edge deterministic finite-state automaton (k-edge DFA) to be a DFA in which the total number of transition edges is at most k. Let L_k denote the class of languages recognized by k-edge DFAs.

Every k-edge DFA is a DFA, so each language in L_k is regular; however, there exist regular languages that are not in L_k for any k. Develop the formal-language theory of the classes L_k. In particular:

(a) Establish a pumping lemma characterizing membership (or providing a necessary condition for membership) in L_k: find a structural property P(k) of words in L such that every sufficiently long word w in L admits a decomposition w = xyz (with y nonempty and obeying length constraints depending on k) for which xy^i z ∈ L for all i ≥ 0, in a form that meaningfully exploits the bound k on the number of edges.

(b) Determine the closure properties of L_k (and of the union ⋃_k L_k) under the standard language operations: union, intersection, concatenation, Kleene star, complement, homomorphism, inverse homomorphism, and intersection with regular languages. For each operation, decide whether the class is closed; when not closed, quantify how the parameter k must grow.

Consider polynomials with unimodular coefficients on the unit circle. For each integer n ≥ 2, let
   P(z) = a_1 z + a_2 z^2 + ... + a_n z^n,
where a_k ∈ ℂ and |a_k| = 1 for every k = 1, ..., n. By Parseval's identity one has
   max_{|z|=1} |P(z)| ≥ √n.
Question: Does there exist a universal constant c > 0, independent of n and of the choice of coefficients, such that for every n ≥ 2 and every choice of unimodular coefficients a_1, ..., a_n one has
   max_{|z|=1} |P(z)| ≥ (1 + c) √n ?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The question (originally asked in Erdős's spirit) is resolved in the negative. Kahane (1980) constructed "ultraflat" unimodular polynomials P_n of degree n with max_{|z|=1}|P_n(z)| = (1+o(1))√n, so no such universal constant c > 0 exists. Subsequent refinements (Bombieri–Bourgain, Beck, and others) sharpened the o(1) error term. Thus the Erdős-type conjecture predicting a uniform multiplicative gap above √n is disproved.

Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet. Let $\mathrm{REG}(\Sigma)$ denote the class of regular languages over $\Sigma$ and $\mathrm{CF}(\Sigma)$ the class of context-free languages over $\Sigma$. Fix a context-free language $L_2 \subseteq \Sigma^*$ (the "background knowledge") and a regular language $L_1 \subseteq \Sigma^*$, and put $L = L_1 \cap L_2$.

A presentation of $L$ with respect to $L_2$ is any function $f:\mathbb{N}\to\Sigma^*\times\{0,1\}$ whose image equals $(L\times\{1\})\cup((L_2\setminus L_1)\times\{0\})$; that is, the learner is fed labeled examples drawn entirely from $L_2$, with positive label on strings in $L$ and negative label on strings in $L_2\setminus L_1$.

A learning algorithm $A$ takes as input a finite prefix $f(0),f(1),\ldots,f(n-1)$ of such a presentation and outputs a regular hypothesis $H_n \in \mathrm{REG}(\Sigma)$ (e.g., as a DFA). Say that $A$ learns $\mathrm{REG}(\Sigma)$ from $\mathrm{CF}(\Sigma)$-knowledge in the polynomial learning-with-help sense if there is a two-variable polynomial $p$ such that for every regular $L_1$, every context-free $L_2$, and every presentation $f$ of $L=L_1\cap L_2$ with respect to $L_2$:
1. $A$ runs in time polynomial in the total size of its input;
2. there exists a finite subset $S$ of the presentation (a "characteristic sample") with $|S| \le p(\|L_1\|,\|L_2\|)$, where $\|\cdot\|$ denotes the size of a smallest DFA / CFG representation, such that whenever $S$ is contained in the prefix seen by $A$, the output hypothesis $H$ satisfies $H \cap L_2 = L$ and remains stable on all longer prefixes.

Problem: Does such an algorithm $A$ exist?

Let Σ be a finite alphabet. A stochastic deterministic finite automaton (SDFA) is a tuple A = (Q, Σ, q0, δ, p, f), where Q is a finite set of states, q0 ∈ Q is the initial state, δ : Q × Σ → Q is a (partial) deterministic transition function, p : Q × Σ → [0,1] assigns a probability to each transition, and f : Q → [0,1] assigns a halting (final) probability, with the normalization f(q) + Σ_{a∈Σ} p(q,a) = 1 for every q ∈ Q. Such an automaton induces a probability distribution D_A over Σ* in the natural way: the probability of a string w = a_1 … a_n is f(q_n) · Π_{i=1}^{n} p(q_{i-1}, a_i), where q_i = δ(q_{i-1}, a_i).

Fix a distance d between probability distributions on Σ* (for instance the total variation distance or the L_∞ distance). The problem is the following:

Either exhibit an algorithm, or prove that none exists, that takes as input
 • two finite i.i.d. samples S_A and S_B drawn respectively from D_A and D_B for two unknown SDFAs A and B,
 • parameters ε > 0 and δ ∈ (0,1),
and outputs a decision of whether d(D_A, D_B) < ε, with the following guarantees:
 (i) the answer is correct with probability at least 1 − δ;
 (ii) the required sample sizes |S_A|, |S_B| and the running time are bounded by a polynomial in |A|, |B|, 1/ε, and 1/δ.

Determine whether such an algorithm exists and, if so, construct one; otherwise prove an impossibility result.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The general question (b) was answered affirmatively: for any two countable dense subsets A, B of ℂ there is an entire (in fact transcendental entire) function mapping A onto B. Fix a target regular language $L\subseteq \Sigma^*$ over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$, recognized by an unknown deterministic finite automaton (DFA). Consider an Angluin-style active learning model in which a learner interacts with a teacher through two kinds of queries:

1. $\varepsilon$-correct membership queries: given a string $w\in\Sigma^*$, the teacher returns a bit $b\in\{0,1\}$ such that $\Pr[b = \mathbf{1}_{w\in L}] \ge 1-\varepsilon$, where $0<\varepsilon<1/2$ is a fixed parameter. The teacher's answers must be consistent across repeated queries: if the same string $w$ is queried more than once, the same bit must be returned each time.

2. Equivalence queries: given a hypothesis DFA $A$, the teacher answers "yes" if $L(A)=L$, and otherwise returns a counterexample string $x\in L(A)\,\triangle\, L$.

Question: Does there exist a learning algorithm that, for every regular language $L$ and every $\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)$, using only $\varepsilon$-correct membership queries and equivalence queries of the above forms, identifies a DFA recognizing $L$ exactly, with high probability and in time polynomial in the size of the minimal DFA for $L$, in $|\Sigma|$, in the length of the longest counterexample returned, and in $1/(1-2\varepsilon)$?

Fix a target regular language $L\subseteq \Sigma^*$ over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$, recognized by an unknown deterministic finite automaton (DFA). Consider an Angluin-style active learning model in which a learner interacts with a teacher through two kinds of queries:

1. $\varepsilon$-correct membership queries: given a string $w\in\Sigma^*$, the teacher returns a bit $b\in\{0,1\}$ such that $\Pr[b = \mathbf{1}_{w\in L}] \ge 1-\varepsilon$, where $0<\varepsilon<1/2$ is a fixed parameter. The teacher's answers must be consistent across repeated queries: if the same string $w$ is queried more than once, the same bit must be returned each time.

2. Equivalence queries: given a hypothesis DFA $A$, the teacher answers "yes" if $L(A)=L$, and otherwise returns a counterexample string $x\in L(A)\,\triangle\, L$.

Question: Does there exist a learning algorithm that, for every regular language $L$ and every $\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)$, using only $\varepsilon$-correct membership queries and equivalence queries of the above forms, identifies a DFA recognizing $L$ exactly, with high probability and in time polynomial in the size of the minimal DFA for $L$, in $|\Sigma|$, in the length of the longest counterexample returned, and in $1/(1-2\varepsilon)$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

Recent work (e.g., 2023–2024 analyses of the robustness of Angluin's L* under noise) studies related noise models but does not appear to settle the exact question of polynomial-time exact learnability of DFA from ε-correct membership queries together with equivalence queries with consistency on repeated queries. No definitive positive or negative result for this specific formulation was found.

Let f(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n z^n be a transcendental entire function. For r > 0, define the maximum modulus
\[ M(r) = \max_{\theta \in [0, 2\pi)} |f(re^{i\theta})| \]
and the maximal term of the power series
\[ \mu(r) = \max_{n \geq 0} |a_n| r^n. \]
It is known that, apart from trivial cases (e.g., monomials), one has \mu(r) < M(r) for all sufficiently large r, and that 0 < \mu(r)/M(r) \le 1.

Prove or disprove: if the limit
\[ L = \lim_{r \to \infty} \frac{\mu(r)}{M(r)} \]
exists (as a real number in [0,1]), then necessarily L = 0.

representations.normalized: A partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) is given by a finite set of states Q, a finite input alphabet Σ, an initial state q0 ∈ Q, a probabilistic transition function δ : Q × Σ × Q → [0,1] with Σ_{q'} δ(q,a,q') = 1 for every q ∈ Q and a ∈ Σ, and a probabilistic reward function. The POMDP is called deterministic when for every state q ∈ Q and every action a ∈ Σ there exists a (necessarily unique) state q' ∈ Q with δ(q,a,q') = 1. Develop a learnability theory for the class of deterministic POMDPs: specify a suitable learning criterion (for example, identification in the limit with probability 1, or convergence in a reinforcement-learning sense) and design an algorithm that, given access to interactions or sample trajectories with rewards, provably learns an unknown deterministic POMDP under the chosen criterion; in particular, determine whether such POMDPs are identifiable in the limit with probability 1 from a polynomial amount of data and characterize the appropriate efficiency and convergence guarantees.

Do there exist absolute positive constants c_1 and c_2 such that for every positive integer n there is a polynomial
  f_n(z) = sum_{k=1}^{n} epsilon_{n,k} z^k,
with each coefficient epsilon_{n,k} in {+1, -1}, satisfying
  c_1 sqrt(n) < |f_n(e^{i theta})| < c_2 sqrt(n)
for every real theta? In other words, does there exist a sequence of Littlewood polynomials (coefficients in {-1,+1}) of every degree n whose modulus on the unit circle is uniformly comparable to sqrt(n) from both above and below, with constants independent of n and of theta?

  c_1 sqrt(n) < |f_n(e^{i theta})| < c_2 sqrt(n)

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The problem was resolved affirmatively by Balister, Bollobás, Morris, Sahasrabudhe, and Tiba in their 2019 preprint "Flat Littlewood Polynomials Exist," published in the Annals of Mathematics (Vol. 192, Issue 3, 2020, pp. 977–1004). They proved the existence of absolute constants δ, Δ > 0 such that for every n ≥ 2 there is a {-1,+1}-polynomial of degree n satisfying δ√n ≤ |P(z)| ≤ Δ√n on the unit circle, confirming the conjecture.

A partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) is a tuple $M=(S,A,O,T,Z,R,\iota)$ where $S$ is a finite set of states, $A$ a finite set of actions, $O$ a finite set of observations, $T:S\times A\times S\to[0,1]$ a transition probability function with $\sum_{s'}T(s,a,s')=1$, $Z:S\times A\times O\to[0,1]$ an observation probability function with $\sum_{o}Z(s,a,o)=1$, $R:S\times A\to\mathbb{R}$ a reward function, and $\iota$ an initial distribution over $S$. A learner interacts with $M$ by choosing actions and receiving observations and rewards, without access to the underlying states.

Develop a learnability theory for the class of all (general, probabilistic, non-deterministic) POMDPs in this sense. Concretely:

1. Identify a precise success criterion for learning a POMDP from interaction data — for instance (a) identification in the limit with probability 1 of the underlying model (up to equivalence preserving the distribution over observation/reward sequences under every policy), (b) convergence of the learner's average regret with respect to the optimal policy of $M$ to zero, or (c) convergence in the sense of strategy learning, where the learner's policy converges to an optimal policy of $M$.

2. For the chosen criterion, determine whether the class of all POMDPs (or natural subclasses such as those satisfying explicit identifiability/observability conditions) is learnable, and if so provide a learning algorithm together with sample- or interaction-complexity bounds.

3. Clarify the relationships between the criteria in (1) and between learnability of POMDPs and learnability of related models such as hidden Markov models, probabilistic finite automata, and Markov decision processes.

The deterministic special case (deterministic transitions and observations) should be recovered as a particular instance of the theory.

The general learnability theory for POMDPs in the grammatical-inference identification-in-the-limit sense remains open. While substantial progress exists in the reinforcement-learning literature on regret/sample-complexity bounds for POMDPs under structural assumptions (e.g., hindsight observability, weakly revealing or decodable POMDPs), no unified learnability theory analogous to that for DFAs/PFAs exists for the general probabilistic POMDP model, and the problem continues to be cited as open.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The existence of such an absolute constant is known: this is Turán's second main problem on power sums, and Atkinson proved a lower bound $R_n > 1/6$ (later improved to $1/5$ and beyond), confirming the existence of an absolute constant $c > 0$. The determination of the optimal value of the constant remains an active problem, with bounds refined by Biró and others to roughly $[1/2 + q, 5/6]$ for large $n$.

representations.normalized:
Consider the following two-player negotiation game between adversaries A1 and A2. Each player Ai (i=1,2) holds a regular language Li ⊆ Σ* over a fixed finite alphabet Σ, given by a deterministic finite automaton known only to that player. The common (target) language is L* = L1 ∩ L2, and the goal of each player is to identify L*.

The game proceeds in rounds. On each turn, the active player Ai chooses a string w ∈ Li (a player may query only with strings from its own language) and submits it to the opponent Aj, who answers truthfully "yes" if w ∈ Lj and "no" otherwise. Each player updates an internal hypothesis from the yes/no information accumulated, and at any time a player may propose a string as a "candidate member of L*"; if such a proposal receives the answer "no", the proposing player incurs a penalty (error). A player "wins" by identifying L* (i.e., converging to a description of L1 ∩ L2) with fewer errors than the opponent, or by forcing a configuration favorable under an agreed payoff.

Address the following questions about this game:

1. Devise a good general strategy for each player (a query/hypothesis policy) that controls the number of errors while making progress toward identifying L1 ∩ L2.

2. Determine whether a player can avoid being identified — i.e., whether there exist strategies under which the opponent provably fails to learn L1 ∩ L2 in polynomial time / with polynomially many errors.

3. Determine whether "no-win" situations exist: pairs (L1, L2) and strategy profiles for which neither player can identify L* with bounded error.

4. Analyze the case where L1 and L2 are nearly identical "lock-automata-like" languages (i.e., constructed so that membership queries require exponentially many strings to distinguish key states): does this force prohibitively long membership-query interaction before identification?

5. Analyze the variant in which the two players "agree" on a stalemate: both settle on a common hypothesis language L ⊆ L1 ∩ L2 that is a strict subset of the true target L*. Characterize when such stable stalemates are possible and what the equilibria of the game look like.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

Keränen (1992, "Abelian squares are avoidable on 4 letters") constructed an infinite word over a 4-letter alphabet containing no two adjacent blocks that are permutations of each other. Hence N(4) is infinite, settling Erdős's question.

Setup. Fix a finite alphabet Σ. For a regular language L ⊆ Σ*, let dfa-size(L) denote the number of states of the minimal deterministic finite automaton (DFA) accepting L.

A learner is a (deterministic) algorithm that, given an infinite presentation of examples for a target language T ⊆ Σ*, outputs a (possibly revised) hypothesis after each example and is said to identify T in the limit if its sequence of hypotheses stabilises on a representation of T.

Negotiation game. A game ⟨L1, L2⟩ involves two players A and B, where each player i ∈ {A, B} privately knows a regular language Li and is told the minimal DFA-sizes n1 = dfa-size(L1) and n2 = dfa-size(L2). The players exchange queries: each player may pose strings to the opponent who must classify them truthfully as members or non-members of the opponent's language. A "negative-query error" by a player is each instance in which that player issues a query whose answer (received from the opponent) is "no" (i.e., the queried string does not belong to the opponent's language). Let errors(P) denote the set (or count) of such negative-query errors made by player P throughout the play.

Winning criterion. Player A wins the play of ⟨L1, L2⟩ against player B if:
(i) A identifies L1 ∩ L2 in the limit, and
(ii) either B fails to identify L1 ∩ L2 in the limit, or B also identifies L1 ∩ L2 in the limit and |errors(A)| < |errors(B)|.

Problem. Restricting attention to instances in which n1 = n2 (i.e., the two players' minimal DFAs have the same number of states), exhibit a deterministic learning algorithm that, when used by a player, wins against every deterministic strategy of the opponent under the above winning criterion; or prove that no such algorithm exists.

representations.normalized:
The Standard Model of particle physics is a quantum field theory with gauge group SU(3)_C × SU(2)_L × U(1)_Y, coupled to three generations of chiral fermions (each generation containing a charged lepton, a neutrino, an up-type quark, and a down-type quark) together with a complex scalar Higgs doublet that breaks the electroweak symmetry SU(2)_L × U(1)_Y down to U(1)_EM via a nonzero vacuum expectation value. The Lagrangian of this theory contains a set of free dimensionless parameters that are not fixed by its internal consistency: the three gauge couplings, the Higgs self-coupling and mass parameter, and the Yukawa couplings of the Higgs to the fermions, which after electroweak symmetry breaking determine the masses of the charged leptons, the quarks, and (together with possible Majorana terms) the neutrinos, as well as the CKM (and PMNS) mixing parameters.

Address the following two questions within this framework:

(a) Provide a theoretical principle, derivation, or first-principles mechanism that determines the observed values of the elementary fermion masses (equivalently, the Yukawa couplings) of the Standard Model, rather than treating them as independent free parameters whose numerical values must be measured experimentally.

(b) Explain why the chiral fermion content of nature consists of exactly three generations, each an apparent replica of the first under the gauge group and differing only in mass, and account for the existence and role of the heavier second and third generations given that stable ordinary matter is composed only of first-generation fermions (electron, electron neutrino, up quark, down quark).

The flavor puzzle—why the Standard Model has the specific Yukawa couplings/fermion masses it does and why there are three generations of fermions—remains an unsolved problem in theoretical particle physics. Proposed frameworks such as Froggatt–Nielsen models, family symmetries, anarchy in the neutrino sector, and string-theoretic constructions provide partial ideas but no accepted derivation of the parameters or of the number three. The status is widely recognized as open in review literature and Standard Model overviews.

Consider a quantum system whose state is described by a vector $|\psi\rangle$ in a complex separable Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$, evolving in time according to the linear Schrödinger equation $i\hbar\,\partial_t|\psi\rangle = H|\psi\rangle$ for a self-adjoint Hamiltonian $H$. Because the evolution is linear and unitary, any superposition $|\psi\rangle = \sum_n c_n|\phi_n\rangle$ of eigenstates of an observable $A = \sum_n a_n |\phi_n\rangle\langle\phi_n|$ remains a superposition for all time. The standard measurement postulate, however, asserts that upon measurement of $A$ the state discontinuously "collapses" to a single eigenstate $|\phi_n\rangle$ with probability $|c_n|^2$ (the Born rule), yielding a definite outcome $a_n$.

Couple such a microscopic system to a macroscopic apparatus (and possibly an environment), modeled as a larger quantum system on $\mathcal{H}_{\text{sys}}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{\text{app}}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{\text{env}}$ evolving under a global self-adjoint Hamiltonian and hence linearly and unitarily. The problem is the following:

Provide a mathematically precise dynamical mechanism, derivable from (or consistent with) the linear unitary quantum dynamics of the composite system alone — i.e., without invoking the collapse postulate as an additional axiom — that
(i) explains why and how a single definite outcome $a_n$ is realized in any individual measurement,
(ii) reproduces the Born rule probabilities $|c_n|^2$,
(iii) accounts for the absence of observable macroscopic superpositions of distinguishable pointer states, and
(iv) is compatible with the empirical fact that classical, definite macroscopic configurations emerge from the underlying quantum description.

Equivalently: identify and justify the precise mathematical modification, interpretation, or derivation (e.g., a nonlinear stochastic extension of the Schrödinger equation, a decoherence-plus-branching account, a hidden-variable completion, or another scheme) that resolves the tension between linear unitary evolution and the occurrence of definite measurement outcomes.

Let $t=(t_0,t_1,t_2,\ldots)$ be a fixed real (or complex) sequence such that the formal power series
$$R(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} t_k z^k$$
defines a function analytic on the open unit disk $\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$. Let $\sigma$ denote the left shift acting on sequences, so that $\sigma(t)=(t_1,t_2,t_3,\ldots)$ and $\sigma^l(t)=(t_l,t_{l+1},t_{l+2},\ldots)$ for $l\ge 0$. For $b=(b_0,b_1,b_2,\ldots)\in \ell_1$ and a sequence $s=(s_0,s_1,\ldots)$ for which the sum converges, write
$$b\cdot s=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} b_k s_k.$$
Define
$$H_t=\{\,b\in\ell_1 : \sigma^l(b)\cdot t = 0 \text{ for all } l=0,1,2,\ldots\,\},$$
where $\sigma^l(b)\cdot t=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} b_{k+l} t_k$ (equivalently, $b\cdot\sigma^l(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} b_k t_{k+l}$, according to the convention used to define $H_t$).

Assume that $R(z)\neq 0$ for every $z$ with $|z|<1$. Prove or disprove: $H_t=\{0\}$.

Let $\{\lambda_n\}_{n\geq 1}$ be a nonincreasing sequence of positive real numbers such that
$$L_n = \sum_{k=n+1}^{\infty}\lambda_k < \infty \quad \text{for every } n\geq 0,$$
and define
$$H = \Big\{ x \in \mathbb{R} : x = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\varepsilon_n \lambda_n,\ \varepsilon_n \in \{0,1\} \Big\}.$$
Assume that $H$ contains a nondegenerate interval. Suppose $(a_n)_{n\geq 1} \in \ell_1$ has the property that, for every sequence $(\delta_n)_{n\geq 1}$ with $\delta_n \in \{-1,0,1\}$,
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\delta_n \lambda_n = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\delta_n a_n = 0.$$
Prove or disprove: under these hypotheses, the ratio $a_n/\lambda_n$ must be the same constant for every $n\geq 1$.

Consider the four fundamental interactions currently recognized in physics — gravitation, electromagnetism, the strong nuclear force, and the weak nuclear force — together with the established laws (quantum field theory and general relativity) that govern them. Call a description of nature "constructionist" if the qualitative and quantitative behavior of every physical system, at every scale, can in principle be derived from these fundamental laws alone (without introducing further independent organizing principles). Determine whether the constructionist hypothesis holds. Specifically:

(a) Is it possible, in principle, to derive in detail the behavior of mildly complex many-body systems (e.g., systems exhibiting self-organization, pattern formation, phase coexistence, or collective dynamics) from the four fundamental forces and their underlying dynamical laws alone, or must additional, scale-dependent principles be postulated?

(b) Within such a framework, give a precise account of: (i) the phenomenon of self-organization in non-equilibrium matter; (ii) the origin of life from non-living chemistry, including a rigorous definition of what constitutes a "living" system; and (iii) how subjective conscious experience can arise from the interactions of atoms and molecules in a physical brain.

Provide either a derivation showing reduction to the fundamental laws is sufficient, or identify and formulate the additional emergent principles required at larger scales.

Let $1<q<2$ and set $\theta=1/q$. Fix a parameter $\eta\in[\theta,\ \theta^2/(1-\theta)]$, and let $L=\theta\eta/(1-\theta)$ (so that $q\eta = \eta + \theta L$ when $\eta=\theta L/(1-\theta)\cdot(1-\theta)/\theta$; more concretely, work on the natural invariant interval $I_\eta=[0,L]$ that contains $[0,q\eta)$).

For $x\in[0,q\eta)$, define the level-$\eta$ regular expansion by the iteration
$$x = \varepsilon_1(x)\,\theta + \theta\, x_1,\qquad \varepsilon_n(x)\in\{0,1\},\ x_n\in[0,q\eta),$$
where the digit is determined by
$$\varepsilon_1(x)=\begin{cases}0,& x\in[0,\eta),\\ 1,& x\in[\eta,q\eta),\end{cases}$$
and $x_1=(x-\varepsilon_1(x)\theta)/\theta$; iterate this rule to obtain the digit sequence $(\varepsilon_n(x))_{n\ge 1}\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}$.

Now let $\eta_1<\eta_2$ both lie in $[\theta,\ \theta^2/(1-\theta)]$, and define
$$H(\eta_1,\eta_2)=\bigl\{x:\ \varepsilon_n^{(\eta_1)}(x)=\varepsilon_n^{(\eta_2)}(x)\ \text{for every }n\ge 1\bigr\},$$
i.e. the set of points whose level-$\eta_1$ and level-$\eta_2$ regular expansions coincide as binary sequences.

Prove or disprove: for every such pair $\eta_1<\eta_2$, the Lebesgue measure of $H(\eta_1,\eta_2)$ is zero.

Within the framework of the Standard Model of particle physics together with standard Big Bang cosmology, an initially hot, dense, and approximately symmetric early universe is expected to produce baryons and antibaryons in equal abundance. Observationally, however, the present universe contains a small but nonzero baryon-to-photon ratio η = (n_B − n_{B̄})/n_γ ≈ 6 × 10^{−10}, with no significant primordial antimatter component. Sakharov's conditions (baryon number violation, C and CP violation, and departure from thermal equilibrium) are necessary for any dynamical mechanism that generates such an asymmetry, but the CP violation present in the Cabibbo–Kobayashi–Maskawa quark mixing matrix of the Standard Model is quantitatively far too small to account for the observed value of η.

Problem: Identify and describe a physical mechanism — specifying the underlying microscopic dynamics, the new sources of CP violation (if any), the relevant out-of-equilibrium process, and the baryon-number-violating interactions — that can, starting from a matter–antimatter symmetric initial state in the early universe, dynamically generate the observed baryon asymmetry η ≈ 6 × 10^{−10}, in quantitative agreement with cosmological and laboratory constraints.

Consider nonlinear parabolic evolution equations of the form
  u_t = F(u, Du, D^2 u, ..., D^{2m} u),  x ∈ R^n, t ∈ [0,T),
including higher-order analogues (m ≥ 1) such as semilinear and quasilinear 2m-th order parabolic PDEs, for which a finite-time singularity occurs at t = T < ∞: the solution u or some of its spatial/temporal derivatives diverge as t → T^-. Near such a singularity, the asymptotic behaviour is often described by local self-similar solutions of the form
  u(x,t) = (T-t)^α f((x-x_0)/(T-t)^β),
where (α, β) are determined by the scaling invariance of the equation and f satisfies an associated nonlinear elliptic profile equation. For higher-order (m ≥ 2) models the set of admissible self-similar profiles f may be countably infinite.

Problem: Develop a general rigorous framework, applicable across classes of such nonlinear parabolic PDEs (including the higher-order case where countably many self-similar profiles coexist), that determines, for each local self-similar singularity profile, whether it is stable (i.e., attracts an open set of initial data in a suitable topology under the renormalised flow obtained by self-similar rescaling) or unstable. In particular, give criteria—formulated via the spectrum of the linearised operator around f in appropriate weighted function spaces, or via other intrinsic invariants—that decide stability without resorting to case-by-case analysis for each equation and each profile.

Current literature on higher-order semilinear parabolic blow-up (notably the monograph by Galaktionov–Mitidieri–Pohozaev and related SIAM J. Appl. Math. papers) constructs countable families of self-similar singularity profiles and analyses their stability by case-specific linearisation and Hamilton–Jacobi matching arguments. representations.normalized:
Consider an isolated physical system composed of N atoms whose microscopic time evolution is governed by the Schrödinger equation
  i ℏ ∂_t |ψ(t)⟩ = H |ψ(t)⟩,
with a self-adjoint Hamiltonian H on a Hilbert space ℋ. This microscopic dynamics is unitary and time-reversal symmetric: if t ↦ |ψ(t)⟩ is a solution and T denotes the antiunitary time-reversal operator (assuming [H,T]=0 up to complex conjugation), then t ↦ T|ψ(−t)⟩ is also a solution, so no dissipation or friction is present at the microscopic level.

At the macroscopic level, however, one observes phenomena such as a hockey puck sliding on ice and coming to rest: a kinetic-energy-bearing degree of freedom is irreversibly damped, and the time-reversed process (the puck spontaneously starting to move) is never observed.

Provide a rigorous derivation, starting from the unitary quantum dynamics above (possibly together with a precisely specified prescription such as a partition of degrees of freedom into "macroscopic" and "microscopic / environmental" variables, a coarse-graining map Π: ℋ → ℳ onto a space of macroscopic observables, an initial-state assumption, and a thermodynamic / large-N limit), that yields:

(a) An effective macroscopic equation of motion for a selected macroscopic degree of freedom (e.g. the center-of-mass momentum P(t) of a solid body in contact with another) of the form
  dP/dt = F_ext − γ(P) + ξ(t),
with a strictly positive friction coefficient γ > 0 and noise ξ obeying a fluctuation–dissipation relation; and

(b) A proof that the resulting macroscopic evolution is not invariant under t ↦ −t, i.e. it generates a semigroup rather than a group, thereby establishing a thermodynamic arrow of time as an emergent consequence of the time-reversal-symmetric microscopic Schrödinger dynamics.

The problem is to give such a derivation under physically natural and minimal assumptions, and to characterize precisely which assumptions (e.g. typicality of initial states, locality of H, ergodicity, finite observational time resolution) are necessary for friction and macroscopic irreversibility to emerge.

The reconciliation of reversible microscopic (quantum) dynamics with irreversible macroscopic friction and a thermodynamic arrow of time is widely regarded as a long-standing open foundational problem. Recent works (2025–2026) propose partial mechanisms — e.g. temporal coarse-graining as the origin of friction in quantum spin chains, semigroup-vs-group obstructions, and open-system formulations — but no universally accepted first-principles derivation exists. The problem remains active and open.

Consider a partial differential equation (or system of PDEs) of the form $\partial_t u = F(u, \nabla u, \nabla^2 u, \dots)$ on a spatial domain $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, where $F$ is invariant (or asymptotically invariant) under a one-parameter scaling group $u(x,t) \mapsto \lambda^{\alpha} u(\lambda x, \lambda^{\beta} t)$ for suitable exponents $\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{R}$. A solution $u(x,t)$ is called self-similar if it is exactly invariant under this group, i.e. it has the form $u(x,t) = (T-t)^{-\alpha/\beta} U\bigl(x/(T-t)^{1/\beta}\bigr)$ (for finite-time singular evolutions, with blow-up time $T < \infty$) or $u(x,t) = t^{-\alpha/\beta} U(x/t^{1/\beta})$ (for long-time evolutions). A solution is called quasi-self-similar if it satisfies the governing equations only asymptotically, in the sense that, after passing to similarity variables $\xi = x/(T-t)^{1/\beta}$, $\tau = -\log(T-t)$ (or analogous variables for long-time behaviour), the rescaled profile $U(\xi,\tau)$ converges as $\tau \to \infty$ to a profile $U_\infty(\xi)$ which solves the reduced (scaling-invariant) profile equation, while $U(\xi,\tau)$ itself does not exactly solve the profile equation at finite $\tau$.

Develop a rigorous framework that:
(a) characterizes when quasi-self-similar solutions exist and govern the long-time behaviour or the behaviour close to a finite-time singularity for solutions of such PDEs;
(b) determines their stability under the rescaled flow in similarity variables, by combining:
   (i) similarity (scaling) reductions to a profile equation,
   (ii) dynamical-systems analysis of the rescaled flow (fixed points, invariant manifolds, center manifolds, spectral analysis of the linearization about $U_\infty$),
   (iii) perturbative asymptotic expansions in $1/\tau$ or other small parameters capturing the deviation from exact self-similarity,
   (iv) numerical continuation and time-marching schemes in similarity variables to detect and validate $U_\infty$;
(c) proves, in a class of model PDEs of physical interest (for example semilinear heat equations, nonlinear Schrödinger equations, geometric flows, or compressible Euler/Navier–Stokes equations), that the ultimate evolution is described by a quasi-self-similar profile when no exact self-similar solution with the required regularity and stability exists.

Formulate and prove such characterization, stability, and selection results, or exhibit counterexamples.

This explanation, however, requires that the entropy of the universe was extraordinarily low at early times (the "past hypothesis"). Provide a fundamental physical explanation for the arrow of time, and in particular give a principled account of why the early universe was in such an exceptionally low-entropy, highly ordered macrostate. As part of the analysis, address the question of whether time, as it currently appears in physical theories (classical mechanics, quantum mechanics, general relativity, quantum field theory, and candidate theories of quantum gravity), is a fundamental feature of reality or instead an emergent, effective, or illusory notion arising from more basic timeless structure.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The origin of the arrow of time and the low-entropy initial state of the universe (the "past hypothesis") remains a widely acknowledged open problem in physics and cosmology, with active proposals (Penrose's Weyl Curvature Hypothesis, Carroll–Chen eternal inflation models, Barbour's timeless approaches, etc.) but no consensus solution. The question of whether time is fundamental or emergent is likewise still open, with ongoing work in quantum gravity (Wheeler–DeWitt, loop quantum gravity, causal set theory).

The question is a programmatic research direction rather than a single precise conjecture. Available references (Barenblatt's monograph on scaling and intermediate asymptotics, Olver's and Bluman's work on symmetry methods, and surveys of nonclassical/potential symmetries) develop partial machinery — Lie-group reductions, nonclassical symmetries, and renormalization-group approaches — that yields first-kind and, in some cases, second-kind similarity solutions, but no systematic, fully general algorithm guaranteeing identification of all intermediate-asymptotic candidates for broad PDE classes has been established. The status is therefore best regarded as open with substantial partial progress.

Consider the planar system of rational difference equations
\[ x_{n+1} = \frac{\alpha_1 + \beta_1 x_n + \gamma_1 y_n}{A_1 + B_1 x_n + C_1 y_n}, \qquad y_{n+1} = \frac{\alpha_2 + \beta_2 x_n + \gamma_2 y_n}{A_2 + B_2 x_n + C_2 y_n}, \qquad n = 0,1,2,\ldots, \]
where all twelve parameters \(\alpha_i, \beta_i, \gamma_i, A_i, B_i, C_i\) (\(i=1,2\)) are nonnegative real numbers, and the initial condition \((x_0, y_0)\) is nonnegative and chosen so that the denominators remain positive for all \(n \ge 0\).

By normalizing one nonzero parameter in each equation to 1 and by considering all possible patterns of zero/nonzero parameters, one obtains finitely many special cases of this family. Among these, identify the subfamily consisting of those special cases for which, after a suitable change of variables, the system reduces to a (possibly variable-coefficient) Riccati difference equation
\[ z_{n+1} = \frac{a_n + b_n z_n}{c_n + d_n z_n}. \]
There are exactly 595 such Riccati-reducible special cases. For each of these 595 special cases, determine:

(a) the boundedness character of all solutions with admissible nonnegative initial conditions (i.e., for which parameter values are all solutions bounded, and for which do unbounded solutions exist);

(b) the periodic nature of solutions (existence, periods, and structure of periodic solutions);

(c) the global asymptotic stability behavior of equilibria (local stability, global attractivity, and global asymptotic stability on the admissible set of initial conditions).

The problem is posed as an open problem concerning the comprehensive classification of dynamical behavior (boundedness, periodicity, global stability) of 595 Riccati-reducible planar rational systems.
