Consider the second-order rational difference equation
  x_{n+1} = (a + b x_n + g x_{n-1}) / (A + B x_n + C x_{n-1}),  n = 0, 1, 2, ...,
where the parameters a, b, g, A, B, C are nonnegative real numbers and the initial conditions x_{-1}, x_0 are positive numbers chosen so that the denominator A + B x_n + C x_{n-1} is positive for every n ≥ 0. Equivalently, view this as a planar first-order system
  x_{n+1} = (a + b x_n + g y_n) / (A + B x_n + C y_n),
  y_{n+1} = x_n,
with (x_0, y_0) in the positive quadrant such that all iterates are well-defined.

An equilibrium is a point x̄ > 0 satisfying x̄ = (a + b x̄ + g x̄)/(A + B x̄ + C x̄). Such an equilibrium is locally asymptotically stable if the linearization at the corresponding fixed point (x̄, x̄) of the planar map has both eigenvalues of modulus less than 1. The equilibrium is a global attractor if every positive solution (with well-defined iterates) converges to x̄.

Prove or disprove: for every choice of nonnegative parameters (a, b, g, A, B, C) (with the system non-degenerate so that solutions exist), local asymptotic stability of an equilibrium of this equation implies that the equilibrium is a global attractor of all positive solutions.

This is a long-standing conjecture of Kulenović and Ladas (often phrased "when does local asymptotic stability imply global attractivity in rational equations?", Camouzis–Ladas 2006). It has been resolved affirmatively for many special parametric subcases of the second-order rational equation, and several recent papers claim complete proofs for particular families of conjectures of this form, but a fully general resolution covering all admissible nonnegative-parameter choices does not appear to be established. The status is best described as partially solved with many cases settled.

Consider the planar rational system of difference equations
  x_{n+1} = (α₁ + β₁ x_n + γ₁ y_n) / (A₁ + B₁ x_n + C₁ y_n),
  y_{n+1} = (α₂ + β₂ x_n + γ₂ y_n) / (A₂ + B₂ x_n + C₂ y_n),
where all parameters α_i, β_i, γ_i, A_i, B_i, C_i (i = 1, 2) are nonnegative real numbers, the initial conditions (x₀, y₀) are nonnegative, and the parameters are chosen so that both denominators remain strictly positive for every n ≥ 0.

By a "special case" of this system we mean a choice of which of the twelve parameters are zero and which are positive (with the convention that any positive parameter may be normalized, e.g. to 1, by rescaling), yielding finitely many distinct parameter patterns that give rise to genuinely different rational systems.

An equilibrium of the system is a point (x̄, ȳ) ∈ [0, ∞)² satisfying x̄ = (α₁ + β₁ x̄ + γ₁ ȳ)/(A₁ + B₁ x̄ + C₁ ȳ) and ȳ = (α₂ + β₂ x̄ + γ₂ ȳ)/(A₂ + B₂ x̄ + C₂ ȳ). The equilibrium is called locally asymptotically stable if it is Lyapunov stable and attracting on some neighborhood, and a global attractor (relative to the set of admissible initial conditions) if every admissible solution converges to it.

Problem: Determine exactly the set of special cases of the above system for which the following implication holds at every equilibrium:
  local asymptotic stability of the equilibrium  ⟹  global attractivity of the equilibrium
on the full set of nonnegative initial conditions yielding positive denominators for all n.

The question of characterizing all special cases of planar rational systems with nonnegative parameters for which local asymptotic stability implies global attractivity is a standing open problem in the theory of rational difference equations, going back to work of Camouzis and Ladas. Consider the planar rational system of difference equations
  x_{n+1} = (a_1 + b_1 x_n + g_1 y_n)/(A_1 + B_1 x_n + C_1 y_n),
  y_{n+1} = (a_2 + b_2 x_n + g_2 y_n)/(A_2 + B_2 x_n + C_2 y_n),
for n = 0, 1, 2, …, where all parameters a_i, b_i, g_i, A_i, B_i, C_i (i = 1, 2) are nonnegative real numbers, the initial conditions (x_0, y_0) are nonnegative, and the denominators are assumed to be positive for all n ≥ 0 along every admissible orbit. An equilibrium (x̄, ȳ) of the system is a fixed point of the map defining the recurrence. Local asymptotic stability of (x̄, ȳ) is defined in the usual sense (Lyapunov stable together with local attractivity), while global asymptotic stability means that (x̄, ȳ) is Lyapunov stable and attracts every admissible orbit in the nonnegative quadrant.

Assume that a particular special case of the above system (i.e., a specification of the parameters within the allowed nonnegative range) has the following two properties:
 (i) the system has a unique equilibrium point in the nonnegative quadrant;
 (ii) every admissible solution of the system is bounded.

Question: Under these assumptions, does local asymptotic stability of the unique equilibrium imply its global asymptotic stability?

Consider the scalar third-order-type rational difference equation
  x_{n+1} = (a + b x_n + g x_{n-1}) / (A + B x_n + C x_{n-1}),  n = 0, 1, 2, …,
with nonnegative parameters a, b, g, A, B, C and nonnegative initial conditions x_{-1}, x_0 chosen so that the denominator is positive for all n. For this equation the following trichotomy is known:
 (i) If C > 0, then every solution is bounded.
 (ii) If C = 0 and B > 0, then every solution is bounded if and only if g ≤ b + A; moreover,
   – when g = b + A every solution converges to a (not necessarily prime) period-two solution, and
   – when g < b + A every solution has a finite limit.

Now consider a planar system of rational difference equations of the form
  x_{n+1} = (α_1 + β_1 x_n + γ_1 y_n) / (A_1 + B_1 x_n + C_1 y_n),
  y_{n+1} = (α_2 + β_2 x_n + γ_2 y_n) / (A_2 + B_2 x_n + C_2 y_n),
with nonnegative coefficients and nonnegative initial data such that both denominators remain positive for every n ≥ 0 (and more generally any planar rational system that arises as a natural two-dimensional analogue of the scalar equation above).

Formulate and prove the planar-system analogue of the trichotomy: identify the precise hypotheses on the coefficients of the planar system under which every solution is bounded, the precise sharp conditions separating the bounded from the unbounded regime, and the corresponding global dynamical alternatives (convergence to an equilibrium versus convergence to a period-two solution) that replace cases (i) and (ii).

Research on rational systems in the plane (Camouzis, Ladas, Garić-Demirović, Palladino, and others) has settled the global behavior for several specific families of planar rational systems, but no source found gives a complete planar-system trichotomy fully generalizing the scalar (a+bx+gx_{n-1})/(A+Bx_n+Cx_{n-1}) result with sharp boundedness/convergence alternatives. Consider the planar system of difference equations
  x_{n+1} = b_1 x_n / (A_1 + y_n),
  y_{n+1} = (b_2 x_n + g_2 y_n) / (x_n + y_n),
with positive parameters b_1, b_2, g_2, A_1 satisfying b_2 ≠ g_2 and
  A_1 + b_2 < b_1 < A_1 + g_2,
and with positive initial conditions x_0, y_0 > 0 (so that the iteration remains well-defined and the solution stays in the open positive quadrant).

Under these hypotheses the system has the boundary equilibrium E_0 = (0, g_2), which is locally asymptotically stable, and the interior (positive) equilibrium
  E_+ = ( (b_1 - A_1)(b_1 - A_1 - g_2) / (b_2 - (b_1 - A_1)),  b_1 - A_1 ).

Determine explicitly:
(a) the basin of attraction B(E_0) ⊂ (0, ∞)^2 of the equilibrium E_0 = (0, g_2), that is, the set of all (x_0, y_0) ∈ (0, ∞)^2 for which the forward orbit converges to (0, g_2);
(b) the set of all positive initial conditions (x_0, y_0) ∈ (0, ∞)^2 whose forward orbit converges instead to the positive equilibrium E_+.

Consider the two-dimensional system of rational difference equations
  x_{n+1} = β₁ x_n / (A₁ + y_n),
  y_{n+1} = (β₂ x_n + γ₂ y_n) / (x_n + y_n),
for n = 0, 1, 2, …, where the parameters β₁, β₂, γ₂, A₁ are positive real numbers with β₂ ≠ γ₂, the initial conditions satisfy x₀ > 0 and y₀ > 0, and the parameters obey
  A₁ + γ₂ < β₁ < A₁ + β₂.

Under these hypotheses the system has a unique positive equilibrium (x̄, ȳ) ∈ (0, ∞)². Prove or disprove that this positive equilibrium is globally asymptotically stable; that is, it is locally asymptotically stable, and for every choice of positive initial conditions (x₀, y₀) the solution (x_n, y_n) converges to (x̄, ȳ) as n → ∞.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

A 2014 paper by L.-X. Hu and X.-M. Jia in Abstract and Applied Analysis ("Global Asymptotic Stability of a Rational System") studies precisely this system and proves that, in the case γ₂ < β₂ (which is equivalent to the hypothesis A₁ + γ₂ < β₁ < A₁ + β₂ since this forces γ₂ < β₁ − A₁ < β₂), the unique positive equilibrium is globally asymptotically stable. This resolves the conjecture in the affirmative.

Consider planar rational difference systems of the form
\[
 x_{n+1} = \frac{\alpha_1 + \beta_1 x_n + \gamma_1 y_n}{A_1 + B_1 x_n + C_1 y_n}, \qquad y_{n+1} = \frac{\alpha_2 + \beta_2 x_n + \gamma_2 y_n}{A_2 + B_2 x_n + C_2 y_n},
\]
where all parameters are nonnegative reals (with denominators positive on the relevant invariant region of $[0,\infty)^2$), and where each of the two equations is chosen from the finite list of normalized rational forms obtained by taking subsets of the terms $\{1,x,y\}$ in numerator and denominator (yielding a finite catalogue of system types indexed by pairs $(k,l)$ of equation labels).

Call a map $T:(x,y)\mapsto(f(x,y),g(x,y))$ on a rectangular region of $[0,\infty)^2$ \emph{competitive} if $f$ is nondecreasing in $x$ and nonincreasing in $y$, and $g$ is nonincreasing in $x$ and nondecreasing in $y$; call it \emph{cooperative} if $f,g$ are both nondecreasing in each variable. Consider the following two monotonicity criteria for a competitive map $T$ and its iterates $(x_n,y_n)=T^n(x_0,y_0)$:

(H1) For every orbit, whenever both $x_{n+1}\le x_n$ and $y_{n+1}\le y_n$ (resp.\ $\ge$) occur at some step, the same simultaneous inequalities held at the previous step. Under (H1) both sequences $\{x_n\}$ and $\{y_n\}$ are eventually monotonic.

(H2) The analogous two-step condition: whenever simultaneous weak inequalities of the two components occur at step $n+1$, they held at step $n-1$. Under (H2) the four subsequences $\{x_{2n}\},\{x_{2n+1}\},\{y_{2n}\},\{y_{2n+1}\}$ are eventually monotonic.

Now restrict to the following 47 system types (labelled by index pairs $(k,l)$ from the catalogue) which are known to be competitive on some nonempty parameter region and which are nowhere cooperative:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(14,l),\ (15,l),\ (29,l)\ \text{for } l\in\{30,35,36,43,45,47,48,49\};\\
&(30,l)\ \text{for } l\in\{30,35,36,38,43,45,47,48,49\};\\
&(35,38),\ (35,43),\ (36,38),\ (36,43);\\
&(38,l),\ (43,l)\ \text{for } l\in\{43,45,47,48,49\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

For each such system, and for each parameter subregion on which the system is competitive on a forward-invariant rectangle:

(a) Determine whether hypothesis (H1) holds (so that every orbit has eventually monotone components), or whether (H2) holds (so that the even- and odd-indexed subsequences are eventually monotone).

(b) Using such monotonicity, together with boundedness/invariance analysis, classify the global asymptotic behavior of every solution with initial condition in the invariant region: identify all fixed points and period-two points, their local stability, the basins of attraction, and the limiting behavior (convergence to an equilibrium, to a period-two cycle, or escape) of every orbit.

Let $\beta_1,\beta_2,\gamma_1,\gamma_2$ be positive real parameters satisfying the degeneracy conditions
\[ \beta_1 = \beta_2 + 1, \qquad \gamma_2 = \gamma_1 + 1. \]
Consider the planar rational system
\[ x_{n+1} = \frac{\beta_1 x_n + \gamma_1 y_n}{1 + y_n}, \qquad y_{n+1} = \frac{\beta_2 x_n + \gamma_2 y_n}{1 + x_n}, \qquad n = 0,1,2,\dots, \]
with initial conditions $(x_0,y_0) \in [0,\infty)^2 \setminus \{(0,0)\}$, chosen so that the iteration is well defined (denominators remain nonzero) for all $n \ge 0$.

Under these parameter conditions, every point on the curve
\[ \mathcal{E} = \Bigl\{ (x,y) : y = \frac{(\beta_2 - 1)x}{x - \gamma_1},\ x > \gamma_1 \Bigr\} \]
is an equilibrium of the system, and the system has no other equilibria (other than possibly the origin if admissible).

Problem. For every admissible initial condition $(x_0,y_0)$, determine explicitly the limits
\[ \lim_{n \to \infty} x_n \quad \text{and} \quad \lim_{n \to \infty} y_n \]
as functions of $(x_0,y_0)$ (and of the parameters), showing in particular that these limits exist and identifying the equilibrium point on $\mathcal{E}$ to which each solution converges.

representations.normalized:
Consider a preemptive uniprocessor real-time system modeled as a finite sporadic task system τ = {τ₁, …, τₙ}. Each task τᵢ is described by three positive parameters: a worst-case execution time Cᵢ, a relative deadline Dᵢ, and a period Tᵢ. Task τᵢ may generate an infinite sequence of jobs, subject to the constraint that consecutive jobs of τᵢ are released at least Tᵢ time units apart; each released job requires at most Cᵢ units of processor execution and must complete within Dᵢ time units after its release. A scheduling algorithm A is said to schedule τ successfully if, for every legal sequence of job releases that τ may generate, A meets every job's deadline. Fixed-priority (FP) scheduling is the algorithm that, given a total priority order on the tasks, at each instant executes some incomplete job belonging to the highest-priority task that currently has an unfinished released job.

Restrict attention to implicit-deadline task systems, i.e., systems in which Dᵢ = Tᵢ for every i. The decision problem FP-SCHED(implicit) is: given as input an implicit-deadline sporadic task system τ together with a specified total priority ordering on its tasks (with all parameters encoded in binary), decide whether τ is FP-schedulable under the given priority ordering.

Determine the exact computational complexity of FP-SCHED(implicit). In particular, is it decidable in polynomial time, is it NP-hard or coNP-hard, or does it lie at some intermediate level of complexity?

The exact computational complexity of fixed-priority schedulability for implicit-deadline sporadic task systems remains a recognized open problem, but partial results exist. Consider a preemptive uniprocessor real-time system specified by a constrained-deadline sporadic task system τ = {τ_1, …, τ_n}. Each task τ_i = (C_i, D_i, T_i) consists of a worst-case execution requirement C_i ∈ ℤ_{>0}, a relative deadline D_i ∈ ℤ_{>0}, and a minimum inter-arrival separation (period) T_i ∈ ℤ_{>0}, subject to C_i ≤ D_i ≤ T_i. A task τ_i releases an (a priori unbounded) sequence of jobs: each released job has execution requirement at most C_i, and two consecutive jobs of τ_i are released at least T_i time units apart; a job released at time r has absolute deadline r + D_i. The Earliest Deadline First (EDF) scheduler is the on-line preemptive scheduler that, at each instant, executes the pending job with the smallest absolute deadline (ties broken arbitrarily). The system τ is EDF-schedulable if, for every legal sequence of job arrivals consistent with the parameters above, EDF completes every job by its absolute deadline.

Question: Does there exist an algorithm that, given as input a constrained-deadline sporadic task system τ (with all parameters encoded in binary), decides whether τ is EDF-schedulable and runs in time bounded by a polynomial in n and in the largest numerical parameter max_i max{C_i, D_i, T_i} (i.e., a pseudo-polynomial-time algorithm)? Equivalently, exhibit such an algorithm or prove that none exists (e.g., by establishing strong coNP-hardness).

representations.normalized:
A sporadic task system is a finite collection τ = {τ_1, …, τ_n} of tasks, where each task τ_i = (C_i, D_i, T_i) is specified by a worst-case execution requirement C_i ∈ ℚ_{>0}, a (relative) deadline D_i ∈ ℚ_{>0}, and a minimum inter-arrival separation T_i ∈ ℚ_{>0}. No restriction is imposed between D_i and T_i (the "arbitrary-deadline" model). A legal job-arrival sequence generated by τ consists of, for each task τ_i, an arbitrary (possibly infinite) sequence of jobs whose successive release times differ by at least T_i; the job released at time r by τ_i has execution requirement C_i and absolute deadline r + D_i.

Given an integer m > 1, a platform of m identical preemptive processors is governed by the global scheduling paradigm: at every instant, any subset of at most m jobs may be executed in parallel (each on a distinct processor), and a preempted job may later resume execution on any processor (migration is allowed at no cost). A job is assumed to never execute on more than one processor simultaneously.

The task system τ is said to be feasible on m processors under global scheduling if, for every legal job-arrival sequence generated by τ, there exists a schedule on the m processors in which every job receives C_i units of execution between its release time and its absolute deadline.

Problem. Determine the computational complexity of deciding, given as input a sporadic task system τ with arbitrary deadlines and an integer m > 1, whether τ is feasible on m preemptive processors under global scheduling.

Subsequent work after the problem was posed produced exact decision procedures for the arbitrary-deadline global feasibility problem (notably state-space / antichain algorithms by Baker–Cirinei and by Bonifaci–Marchetti-Spaccamela), and PSPACE-hardness has been established for related multiprocessor sporadic feasibility problems. An implicit-deadline sporadic task system is a finite collection τ = {τ_1, …, τ_n} of tasks. Each task τ_i is described by a pair (C_i, T_i) of positive rationals with C_i ≤ T_i, where T_i is both the minimum inter-arrival separation and the relative deadline (so D_i = T_i), and C_i is the worst-case execution requirement. The utilization of τ is U(τ) = Σ_i C_i / T_i.

Fix an integer m > 1 and consider a platform of m identical preemptive processors. Global Earliest Deadline First (EDF) scheduling works as follows: at every instant, among all jobs that have been released and are not yet complete, schedule (on the m processors) up to m jobs with the smallest absolute deadlines, breaking ties arbitrarily but consistently; preemption and migration of jobs across processors are allowed at no cost. A job sequence is legal if it respects the sporadic inter-arrival and execution-bound constraints of τ. The system τ is said to be globally EDF-schedulable on m processors if, for every legal sequence of job releases, the global EDF schedule meets every absolute deadline.

Problem. Given as input an implicit-deadline sporadic task system τ and an integer m > 1, determine the exact computational complexity of deciding whether τ is globally EDF-schedulable on m preemptive processors, and in particular exhibit an exact decision procedure for this problem.

Problem. Given as input an implicit-deadline sporadic task system τ, an integer m > 1, and a total priority assignment on τ:

(a) Is the question "Is τ FP-schedulable on m processors under the given priority assignment?" decidable by an exact algorithm?

(b) If decidable, determine its computational complexity.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Subsequent work has established decidability of exact global fixed-priority schedulability for implicit-deadline sporadic tasks on identical multiprocessors by exhibiting a bounded "decidability interval" and a pre-order/simulation-based exact test, but the resulting algorithms are of very high complexity and only handle small systems (a handful of tasks/processors). The precise computational complexity (e.g., tight hardness classification) remains unresolved, so the problem is at best partially solved.

representations.normalized:
Consider a sporadic task system τ = {τ_1, …, τ_n} to be scheduled on a platform of m identical processors. Each task τ_i is specified by a triple (C_i, D_i, T_i) of positive integers, where C_i is the worst-case execution requirement, D_i is the relative deadline, and T_i is the minimum inter-arrival separation. Each task τ_i generates a (possibly infinite) sequence of jobs; successive jobs of τ_i are released at least T_i time units apart, each job requires up to C_i units of execution, and each job released at time t must complete by time t + D_i. A legal sequence of job arrivals is any sequence consistent with these constraints.

Under continuous preemptive scheduling on m processors, time is treated as a continuum: at any instant, each processor may execute at most one job, each job may execute on at most one processor, and preemption and migration are permitted at arbitrary real-valued time instants. The system τ is said to be (multiprocessor) feasible if for every legal sequence of job arrivals there exists a continuous preemptive schedule on m processors that meets every deadline.

A discrete schedule partitions the non-negative time line into unit-length, indivisible slots [k, k+1), k ∈ ℤ_{≥0}, and assigns to each slot, for each processor, at most one job of τ; the constraints that no job runs on two processors in the same slot and that a job receives at most C_i slots of execution within each window [r, r+D_i) (where r is its release time) must be respected, and every job must complete by its deadline.

Question (Integer Boundary Constraint for multiprocessors): Is it true that, for every sporadic task system τ with integer parameters and every integer m ≥ 1, τ is multiprocessor feasible under continuous preemptive scheduling on m processors if and only if, for every legal sequence of job arrivals (with integer release times), there exists a discrete schedule on m processors that meets all deadlines?

Let $\mathbb{D}$ denote the open unit disk in $\mathbb{C}$ with normalized area measure $dA$. For $1<p<\infty$, the Bergman space $A^p=A^p(\mathbb{D})$ is the closed subspace of $L^p(\mathbb{D},dA)$ consisting of holomorphic functions on $\mathbb{D}$. Let $P:L^2(\mathbb{D},dA)\to A^2$ be the orthogonal Bergman projection; for a suitable symbol $f$, the Toeplitz operator $T_f$ is defined (densely) by $T_f g = P(fg)$. The Berezin transform of an operator $S$ on $A^2$ is
$$\widetilde{S}(z)=\langle S k_z,k_z\rangle,\qquad z\in\mathbb{D},$$
where $k_z(w)=(1-|z|^2)/(1-\bar z w)^2$ is the normalized reproducing kernel of $A^2$. For a symbol $f$, write $\widetilde{f}=\widetilde{T_f}$.

For a function $g$ on $\mathbb{D}$ and $r\in(0,1)$, let
$$MO_r(g)(z)=\left(\frac{1}{|D(z,r)|}\int_{D(z,r)}|g-g_{D(z,r)}|^2\,dA\right)^{1/2},$$
where $D(z,r)$ is the hyperbolic disk of radius $r$ centered at $z$ and $g_{D(z,r)}$ is its average. Say $g\in BMO^p_\partial$ (with $p>2$) if $MO_r(g)\in L^p$ near the boundary in the appropriate hyperbolic sense, i.e. condition
$$\int_{\mathbb{D}} MO_r(g)(z)^p\,d\lambda(z)<\infty \quad (\text{where }d\lambda \text{ is the Möbius-invariant measure}). \tag{$*$}$$

Zorboska's compactness theorem states: if $f\in BMO^2_\partial$ satisfies $(*)$ with $p=2$, then $T_f:A^2\to A^2$ is compact if and only if $\widetilde{f}(z)\to 0$ as $|z|\to 1^-$.

Problem. Generalize this result to the Bergman spaces $A^p(\mathbb{D})$ for $1<p<\infty$, $p\ne 2$. Precisely, identify a natural symbol class (in the spirit of $BMO_\partial$ with the condition $(*)$ for appropriate exponents) such that for $f$ in that class, $T_f:A^p\to A^p$ is compact if and only if the Berezin transform $\widetilde{f}$ vanishes on the boundary of $\mathbb{D}$.

Let $\mathbb{D}$ denote the open unit disk in $\mathbb{C}$ and, for $1<p<\infty$, let $A^p=A^p(\mathbb{D})$ be the Bergman space of analytic functions $f:\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{C}$ with $\|f\|_{A^p}^p=\int_{\mathbb{D}}|f(z)|^p\,dA(z)<\infty$, where $dA$ is normalized area measure. Let $P$ denote the Bergman projection from $L^p(\mathbb{D},dA)$ onto $A^p$. For a bounded measurable symbol $a:\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{C}$, the Toeplitz operator $T_a:A^p\to A^p$ is defined by $T_af=P(af)$. A symbol $a\in L^\infty(\mathbb{D})$ is called piecewise continuous if it is continuous on $\overline{\mathbb{D}}$ outside a finite set of boundary points $\{\zeta_1,\dots,\zeta_N\}\subset\partial\mathbb{D}$, at each of which $a$ admits finite one-sided non-tangential limits along the two arcs of $\partial\mathbb{D}$ meeting at $\zeta_j$ (and along curves inside $\mathbb{D}$ ending at $\zeta_j$).

(a) Develop a Fredholm theory for Toeplitz operators $T_a$ on $A^p(\mathbb{D})$ with piecewise continuous symbols $a$: namely, give a complete description of the essential spectrum of $T_a$ and a formula for the Fredholm index of $T_a$ when it is Fredholm, valid for all $1<p<\infty$.

Classical Fredholm theory for Toeplitz operators with piecewise continuous symbols on $A^2(\mathbb{D})$ is known (Vasilevski and collaborators), and various partial extensions to $A^p$ and weighted Bergman spaces, as well as block/matrix-valued symbol settings, have appeared in subsequent literature (e.g., Taskinen–Virtanen, and the Douglas-type index formula for block Toeplitz operators on Bergman spaces of the ball). Let $G$ be a finitely generated group, $N \trianglelefteq G$ a normal subgroup with abelian quotient $Q = G/N$, and write $Q_{\mathbb{R}} = Q \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{R}$. The Bieri–Neumann–Strebel–Renz invariant $\Sigma(N;Q) \subseteq S(Q) = (Q_{\mathbb{R}} \setminus \{0\})/\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ is defined as the set of equivalence classes $[\chi]$ of nonzero homomorphisms $\chi: Q \to \mathbb{R}$ such that the monoid $N \rtimes Q_\chi$ (where $Q_\chi = \{q \in Q : \chi(q) \geq 0\}$) is finitely generated over $G$ in a suitable sense; equivalently, viewed as a conical subset of $Q_{\mathbb{R}} \setminus \{0\}$. Let $\Sigma^c(N;Q) = (Q_{\mathbb{R}} \setminus \{0\}) \setminus \Sigma(N;Q)$ denote its complement, regarded as a conical (i.e., $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$-invariant) subset of $Q_{\mathbb{R}}$.

A conical subset $U \subseteq Q_{\mathbb{R}}$ is called $m$-tame if $0 \notin U + U + \cdots + U$ (with $m$ summands), i.e., one cannot write $0$ as the sum of $m$ elements of $U$.

Recall that a group $G$ is of type $\mathrm{FP}_m$ if the trivial $\mathbb{Z}G$-module $\mathbb{Z}$ admits a projective resolution that is finitely generated in degrees $\leq m$.

Prove or disprove: for every integer $m \geq 2$, the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $G$ is of type $\mathrm{FP}_m$;
\item the complement $\Sigma^c(N;Q)$ is $m$-tame.
\end{enumerate>

where $N$ and $Q$ are abelian, $N$ is torsion-free, and $Q$ is finitely generated abelian (so $G$ is a split finitely generated abelian-by-abelian group of "metabelian" type). Let $M_1 = N$, viewed as a $\mathbb{Z}Q$-module via the conjugation action.

Recall the Bieri–Strebel geometric invariant: write $S(Q) = (Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb R\setminus\{0\})/\mathbb R_{>0}$ for the character sphere of $Q$. For a finitely generated $\mathbb{Z}Q$-module $M$, define
$$\Sigma_M = \{[\chi]\in S(Q) : M \text{ is finitely generated over the monoid ring }\mathbb{Z}Q_\chi\},$$
where $Q_\chi = \{q\in Q : \chi(q)\ge 0\}$, and let $\Sigma_M^c = S(Q)\setminus\Sigma_M$ be its complement. For an integer $m\ge 1$, a subset $A\subseteq S(Q)$ is called $m$-tame if no $m$ points of $A$ have characters that sum to $0$ (equivalently, for every $\chi_1,\dots,\chi_m\in A$ one has $\chi_1+\cdots+\chi_m\ne 0$ in $\mathrm{Hom}(Q,\mathbb R)$).

Recall that a group $G$ is of type $\mathrm{FP}_m$ if the trivial $\mathbb{Z}G$-module $\mathbb{Z}$ admits a projective resolution that is finitely generated in degrees $0,1,\dots,m$.

Prove or disprove: for every integer $m\ge 2$, the following two conditions are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $G$ is of type $\mathrm{FP}_m$.
\item The complement $\Sigma_{M_1}^c \subseteq S(Q)$ is $m$-tame, and the integral homology groups $H_i(N;\mathbb Z)$ are finitely generated as $\mathbb{Z}Q$-modules for all $i\in\{1,2,\dots,m\}$.
\end{enumerate}

The FP_m-conjecture for metabelian groups, due to Bieri–Strebel and refined using the m-tameness of the BNSR/Sigma invariant, is widely described in current literature as still open in general. Partial results are known (e.g. the implication from FP_m to m-tameness of $\Sigma^c$ is established by Bieri–Groves, and the converse is known in low ranks or for special module classes), but no full proof of the equivalence has been published as of 2026.

Fix a real number $r$ with $1<r<2$. Consider trigonometric polynomials on $\mathbb{R}$ of the form $P(t)=\sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k e^{i\lambda_k t}$ with $a_k\in\mathbb{C}$ and $\lambda_k\in\mathbb{R}$, and define the seminorm
$$\|P\|_r=\Big(\sum_{k=1}^{n}|a_k|^{r}\Big)^{1/r}.$$
Let $\mathrm{AP}_r(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C})$ denote the completion of the space of such trigonometric polynomials with respect to $\|\cdot\|_r$. Each element $x\in\mathrm{AP}_r(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C})$ has an associated Fourier series $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} a_k e^{i\lambda_k t}$ (with distinct real exponents $\lambda_k$), and one has $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}|a_k|^{r}<\infty$, i.e. $(a_k)\in\ell^r$.

Question: Is the converse true? That is, given any sequence of distinct real numbers $(\lambda_k)_{k\ge 1}$ and any sequence $(a_k)_{k\ge 1}\in\ell^r$, does the formal trigonometric series $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} a_k e^{i\lambda_k t}$ determine (as the limit of its partial sums in $\|\cdot\|_r$) an element of $\mathrm{AP}_r(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C})$?

Background and notation. For 1 ≤ r ≤ ∞, define the space AP_r(ℝ, ℂ) of almost periodic functions as follows. Let T denote the linear space of complex trigonometric polynomials on ℝ, i.e. finite sums of the form P(t) = Σ_{k=1}^N a_k e^{iλ_k t} with a_k ∈ ℂ and λ_k ∈ ℝ. For 1 ≤ r < ∞, equip T with the Minkowski (Marcinkiewicz) seminorm

  ‖P‖_r = ( limsup_{T→∞} (1/(2T)) ∫_{-T}^{T} |P(t)|^r dt )^{1/r},

and define AP_r(ℝ, ℂ) to be the completion of T with respect to ‖·‖_r. The spaces AP_r form a decreasing scale: AP_∞ ⊂ … ⊂ AP_2 ⊂ AP_r ⊂ AP_1 for r ≤ 2, and AP_2 coincides with the Besicovitch space B^2 (the largest scale element for which Parseval's identity holds).

For f ∈ AP_r(ℝ, ℂ) with Bohr–Fourier expansion f ∼ Σ_k a_k(f) e^{iλ_k(f) t}, a formal derivative is defined by f' ∼ Σ_k iλ_k(f) a_k(f) e^{iλ_k(f) t} (when this expression represents an element of some AP_s), and a formal antiderivative ("integral") F is any series F ∼ c + Σ_{λ_k ≠ 0} (a_k(f)/(iλ_k(f))) e^{iλ_k(f) t} (when it represents an element of some AP_s).

Problem. Fix 1 < r < 2. Determine, for a generic element f ∈ AP_r(ℝ, ℂ):

(a) under what conditions f is differentiable in the AP_s scale (i.e. when does the formal derivative belong to AP_s for some s, and for which s), and which properties of f are preserved or newly created by differentiation;

(b) under what conditions f admits an antiderivative in the AP_s scale, for which s ∈ [1, ∞] this antiderivative lies, and which properties of f are preserved or newly created by integration.

In particular, characterize the precise mapping properties of the differentiation and integration operators between the spaces AP_r for 1 < r < 2.

The AP_r scale (a completion of trigonometric polynomials in Marcinkiewicz/Minkowski seminorms, interpolating between absolutely convergent exponential series and Besicovitch's B^2) was introduced in a 2011 paper "A scale of almost periodic functions spaces". The behavior of differentiation and integration on this scale for 1 < r < 2 is posed as an open problem, and no subsequent literature located through search resolves the mapping properties of derivatives/antiderivatives between AP_r spaces for this range. Status appears open.

Let $G(z)$ be a strictly proper rational discrete-time single-input single-output transfer function with nonnegative impulse response, written in lowest terms as $G(z)=p(z)/q(z)$, and let $n=\deg q$ be the McMillan degree of $G$. A positive realization of $G$ is a triple $(A,b,c)$ with $A\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{N\times N}$, $b\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{N\times 1}$, $c\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{1\times N}$ (entries nonnegative) such that $G(z)=c(zI-A)^{-1}b$. The minimal positive realization dimension $N^{*}(G)$ is the smallest $N$ for which such a positive realization exists; in general $N^{*}(G)\ge n$, and the spectrum of $A$ in a minimal positive realization may contain eigenvalues that are not poles of $G(z)$ (so-called "hidden modes," i.e., eigenvalues $\lambda\in\operatorname{spec}(A)\setminus\{\text{poles of }G\}$).

Provide a complete characterization of the set of possible hidden modes that can or must arise in a minimal positive realization of a given $G(z)$. Specifically:
(a) For each strictly proper $G(z)$ with nonnegative impulse response, describe the set of multisets $S\subset\mathbb{C}$ of complex numbers (with multiplicities) such that there exists a minimal positive realization $(A,b,c)$ in which $\operatorname{spec}(A)$ equals the poles of $G$ (with their multiplicities) together with $S$.
(b) Express $N^{*}(G)$ as $n+|S^{*}|$, where $S^{*}$ is a minimum-cardinality such multiset, and characterize $|S^{*}|$ in terms of structural data of $G$ (poles, residues, dominant pole, etc.).

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The general characterization of "hidden modes" and of the minimal positive realization dimension for an arbitrary strictly proper SISO transfer function with nonnegative impulse response is still open. Complete answers are known only in special cases (e.g., transfer functions with positive real poles, nonnegative multiple poles, or two-different-pole systems), but no general necessary-and-sufficient characterization is available. Recent surveys reiterate that minimality of positive realizations and the structure of required extra modes remain unresolved in full generality.

Consider a discrete-time linear time-invariant system with p inputs and q outputs whose transfer function matrix H(z) is a q×p matrix of strictly proper rational functions with nonnegative impulse-response coefficients (i.e., the Markov parameters H_k satisfying H(z) = Σ_{k≥1} H_k z^{-k} all have nonnegative entries). A positive realization of H(z) is a triple (A, B, C) with A ∈ ℝ^{n×n}, B ∈ ℝ^{n×p}, C ∈ ℝ^{q×n}, all entries nonnegative, such that H(z) = C(zI − A)^{-1} B. Its order is n. The minimal positive realization order N_+(H) is the smallest such n.

Problem: Provide a complete characterization of the minimal positive realization order N_+(H) for an arbitrary nonnegative q×p transfer matrix H(z). In particular:

(a) Give necessary and sufficient conditions on H(z) (in terms of its poles, residues, Hankel matrix structure, or associated polyhedral cones) for N_+(H) to equal a prescribed integer n.

(b) Describe how, and in what essential ways, such a characterization differs from the single-input single-output case (p = q = 1), where partial results based on invariant polyhedral cones containing the reachable/observable sets are available.

(c) Determine whether the gap N_+(H) − deg H(z) between the minimal positive order and the McMillan degree can be bounded by a function of (p, q, deg H), and if so, give sharp such bounds.

Let $H(z) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} h_k z^{-k}$ be a strictly proper rational transfer function of a discrete-time linear time-invariant SISO system, with partial-fraction expansion
$$H(z) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{r_i}{z-\lambda_i},$$
so that its impulse response is $h_k = \sum_{i=1}^{n} r_i \lambda_i^{k-1}$ for $k \geq 1$ (the $\lambda_i \in \mathbb{C}$ are the eigenvalues/poles and the $r_i \in \mathbb{C}$ are the residues, complex pairs occurring conjugately). A positive realization of $H$ is a triple $(A,b,c)$ with $A \in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{N \times N}$, $b \in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{N}$, $c \in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{1 \times N}$ such that $h_k = cA^{k-1}b$ for all $k \geq 1$; the minimal positive realization dimension $N^+(H)$ is the smallest $N$ for which such a triple exists.

The system is externally nonnegative if $h_k \geq 0$ for all $k \geq 1$. Define
$$K^\ast(H) := \min\bigl\{ K \in \mathbb{N} : \text{for every } H'\text{ with the same residue/eigenvalue structure as } H,\ (h'_1,\dots,h'_K \geq 0) \Rightarrow (h'_k \geq 0\ \forall k \geq 1)\bigr\},$$
i.e., the smallest integer such that checking nonnegativity of the first $K^\ast(H)$ impulse-response samples suffices to certify nonnegativity of the entire impulse response, with the bound expressible purely in terms of the residues $r_i$ and eigenvalues $\lambda_i$.

Problems:
(a) Give an explicit formula or sharp bound for $K^\ast(H)$ in terms of $\{(r_i,\lambda_i)\}_{i=1}^{n}$.
(b) Determine the precise relationship between $K^\ast(H)$ and the minimal positive realization dimension $N^+(H)$.

Let $H(z) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} h_k z^{-k}$ be a strictly proper rational transfer function of a discrete-time linear time-invariant SISO system, with partial-fraction expansion
$$H(z) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{r_i}{z-\lambda_i},$$
so that its impulse response is $h_k = \sum_{i=1}^{n} r_i \lambda_i^{k-1}$ for $k \geq 1$ (the $\lambda_i \in \mathbb{C}$ are the eigenvalues/poles and the $r_i \in \mathbb{C}$ are the residues, complex pairs occurring conjugately). A positive realization of $H$ is a triple $(A,b,c)$ with $A \in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{N \times N}$, $b \in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{N}$, $c \in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{1 \times N}$ such that $h_k = cA^{k-1}b$ for all $k \geq 1$; the minimal positive realization dimension $N^+(H)$ is the smallest $N$ for which such a triple exists.

The system is externally nonnegative if $h_k \geq 0$ for all $k \geq 1$. Define
$$K^\ast(H) := \min\bigl\{ K \in \mathbb{N} : \text{for every } H'\text{ with the same residue/eigenvalue structure as } H,\ (h'_1,\dots,h'_K \geq 0) \Rightarrow (h'_k \geq 0\ \forall k \geq 1)\bigr\},$$
i.e., the smallest integer such that checking nonnegativity of the first $K^\ast(H)$ impulse-response samples suffices to certify nonnegativity of the entire impulse response, with the bound expressible purely in terms of the residues $r_i$ and eigenvalues $\lambda_i$.

Problems:
(a) Give an explicit formula or sharp bound for $K^\ast(H)$ in terms of $\{(r_i,\lambda_i)\}_{i=1}^{n}$.
(b) Determine the precise relationship between $K^\ast(H)$ and the minimal positive realization dimension $N^+(H)$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Recent surveys and papers on positive realizations indicate that determining the minimal dimension of a positive realization is still open in general; only lower and upper bounds are available. Explicit finite-sample nonnegativity tests are known only in special cases (e.g., third-order systems with distinct real poles), and no general formula tying such a finite-sample bound to minimality is established. The question therefore appears to remain open.

Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^N$ ($N \ge 1$) be a bounded domain with smooth boundary, let $f \in L^\infty(\Omega)$ with $f \ge 0$, $f \not\equiv 0$, let $\lambda > 0$ be a real parameter, and fix an exponent $\alpha \in (0,1)$. Consider the singular semilinear Dirichlet problem
$$-\Delta u + \frac{1}{u^\alpha} = \lambda\, f(x) \quad \text{in } \Omega, \qquad u \ge 0 \text{ in } \Omega, \qquad u = 0 \text{ on } \partial\Omega,$$
where the singular term $1/u^\alpha$ is interpreted as $0$ on the set $\{u = 0\}$ (so that nonnegative solutions with compact support / free boundary inside $\Omega$ are admissible). It is known that for $\lambda$ sufficiently large there exists a maximal positive solution $u_\lambda$ of this problem, while for $\lambda > 0$ small enough there are no solutions.

Question: For $\lambda$ in the existence regime (large enough), do there exist solutions other than the maximal positive solution? More precisely, determine whether there must exist either (i) an additional strictly positive solution different from the maximal one, or (ii) a nonnegative solution with compact support in $\Omega$ (a free-boundary solution), and if so, describe the structure of such additional branches as a function of $\lambda$.

Fix p > 1 and consider the one-dimensional p-Laplacian Dirichlet problem
   -(|u'(x)|^{p-2} u'(x))' = f(u(x)),  x ∈ (-1, 1),    u(-1) = u(1) = 0,
with the nonlinearity
   f(u) = λ u^β - u^α,    u > 0,
where the exponents satisfy -1 < α < β < p - 1 and λ > 0 is a parameter chosen large enough that positive solutions exist (more precisely, in the parameter regime where the time-map associated with the ODE admits positive solutions and where, for fixed β, varying α through the interval (-1, -1/(p+1)) — sometimes written (-1, -1/p+1) — yields a transition in the number of positive solutions).

For fixed p, β, and λ in this regime, regard the number N(α) of positive classical solutions u ∈ C^1([-1,1]) of the above problem as a function of α ∈ (-1, -1/(p+1)).

Question: Does there exist a unique critical value α* ∈ (-1, -1/(p+1)) such that
   N(α) = 1   for every α ∈ (-1, α*],   and   N(α) = 2   for every α ∈ (α*, -1/(p+1))?

It is known that this is the case under the additional relation β = 1 + 2α. Prove or disprove the existence of such a unique threshold α* in general (within the stated parameter regime).

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^N$ ($N\ge 1$) be a bounded smooth domain containing the origin, and let $k\ge 0$ and $\alpha\in(0,1)$ be real parameters. Consider the singular semilinear elliptic problem with absorption

$$
\text{(III)}\qquad
\begin{cases}
-\Delta u + |x|^{k}\, u^{-\alpha}\,\chi_{\{u>0\}} \;=\; \lambda\, u & \text{in } \Omega,\\[2pt]
u\ge 0 & \text{in } \Omega,\\[2pt]
u = 0 & \text{on } \partial\Omega,
\end{cases}
$$

where $\lambda>0$ is a parameter and $\chi_{\{u>0\}}$ is the characteristic function of the set on which $u$ is positive (so that the absorption term $|x|^{k}u^{-\alpha}$ is defined only where $u>0$ and is set to $0$ where $u=0$). By a solution one means a nonnegative function $u\in H_0^1(\Omega)\cap L^\infty(\Omega)$ satisfying the equation in the sense of distributions on $\Omega$.

A solution $u$ is said to have *compact support* if the set $\{x\in\Omega:u(x)>0\}$ is compactly contained in $\Omega$; equivalently, $u$ vanishes identically on a neighborhood of $\partial\Omega$, producing a free boundary $\partial\{u>0\}\subset\Omega$.

Question: In the parameter regime $k-\alpha<1$, do there exist compact‑support solutions of problem (III)? If so, describe the structure of the set of such compact‑support solutions (e.g., multiplicity, monotonicity in $\lambda$, dependence on $\Omega$).

Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, and let $V$ be a vector space over $k$. A linear automorphism $R\colon V\otimes V \to V\otimes V$ is called a (braided) solution of the Yang-Baxter equation if it satisfies the braid relation
$$(R\otimes \mathrm{id}_V)\circ(\mathrm{id}_V\otimes R)\circ(R\otimes \mathrm{id}_V) \;=\; (\mathrm{id}_V\otimes R)\circ(R\otimes \mathrm{id}_V)\circ(\mathrm{id}_V\otimes R)$$
as automorphisms of $V\otimes V\otimes V$.

Problem. Classify, up to a suitable notion of equivalence (e.g. conjugation by $A\otimes A$ for $A\in \mathrm{GL}(V)$), all such linear automorphisms $R$ of $V\otimes V$. Equivalently, give a complete description of all braided solutions of the Yang-Baxter equation on an arbitrary finite-dimensional vector space $V$ over $k$.

Let $k$ be a field and let $V$ be a $k$-vector space. A Yang–Baxter operator on $V$ is a $k$-linear isomorphism $R: V\otimes V \to V\otimes V$ satisfying the braid relation
$$ (R\otimes \mathrm{id}_V)(\mathrm{id}_V\otimes R)(R\otimes \mathrm{id}_V) = (\mathrm{id}_V\otimes R)(R\otimes \mathrm{id}_V)(\mathrm{id}_V\otimes R) $$
on $V\otimes V\otimes V$.

Given a unital associative $k$-algebra $A$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in k$ (not all zero, satisfying the standard non-degeneracy condition that ensures invertibility), the operator
$$ R^A_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}(a\otimes b) = \alpha\, ab\otimes 1 + \beta\, 1\otimes ab - \gamma\, a\otimes b $$
on $A\otimes A$ is a Yang–Baxter operator; the family of such operators (as $A$ and the parameters vary) is referred to as the family of Yang–Baxter operators from algebra structures.

A quasi-triangular bialgebra is a pair $(H,\mathcal{R})$ where $H$ is a $k$-bialgebra and $\mathcal{R}\in H\otimes H$ is an invertible element (called a universal $R$-matrix) satisfying
$$ \Delta^{\mathrm{op}}(h) = \mathcal{R}\,\Delta(h)\,\mathcal{R}^{-1}\quad (h\in H), $$
$$ (\Delta\otimes \mathrm{id})(\mathcal{R}) = \mathcal{R}_{13}\mathcal{R}_{23},\qquad (\mathrm{id}\otimes \Delta)(\mathcal{R}) = \mathcal{R}_{13}\mathcal{R}_{12}. $$
Every representation $\rho: H \to \mathrm{End}(V)$ of a quasi-triangular bialgebra gives rise to a Yang–Baxter operator $R = \tau\circ (\rho\otimes\rho)(\mathcal{R})$ on $V\otimes V$, where $\tau$ is the flip.

Question: Can every Yang–Baxter operator from an algebra structure (i.e., every operator of the form $R^A_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}$ as above) be realized as arising from a universal $R$-matrix of some quasi-triangular bialgebra, via a suitable representation?
representations.original:
Let $k$ be a field and let $V$ be a $k$-vector space. A Yang–Baxter operator on $V$ is a $k$-linear isomorphism $R: V\otimes V \to V\otimes V$ satisfying the braid relation
$$ (R\otimes \mathrm{id}_V)(\mathrm{id}_V\otimes R)(R\otimes \mathrm{id}_V) = (\mathrm{id}_V\otimes R)(R\otimes \mathrm{id}_V)(\mathrm{id}_V\otimes R) $$
on $V\otimes V\otimes V$. 

Given a unital associative $k$-algebra $A$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in k$ (not all zero, satisfying the standard non-degeneracy condition that ensures invertibility), the operator
$$ R^A_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}(a\otimes b) = \alpha\, ab\otimes 1 + \beta\, 1\otimes ab - \gamma\, a\otimes b $$
on $A\otimes A$ is a Yang–Baxter operator; the family of such operators (as $A$ and the parameters vary) is referred to as the family of Yang–Baxter operators from algebra structures.

A quasi-triangular bialgebra is a pair $(H,\mathcal{R})$ where $H$ is a $k$-bialgebra and $\mathcal{R}\in H\otimes H$ is an invertible element (called a universal $R$-matrix) satisfying
$$ \Delta^{\mathrm{op}}(h) = \mathcal{R}\,\Delta(h)\,\mathcal{R}^{-1}\quad (h\in H), $$
$$ (\Delta\otimes \mathrm{id})(\mathcal{R}) = \mathcal{R}_{13}\mathcal{R}_{23},\qquad (\mathrm{id}\otimes \Delta)(\mathcal{R}) = \mathcal{R}_{13}\mathcal{R}_{12}. $$
Every representation $\rho: H \to \mathrm{End}(V)$ of a quasi-triangular bialgebra gives rise to a Yang–Baxter operator $R = \tau\circ (\rho\otimes\rho)(\mathcal{R})$ on $V\otimes V$, where $\tau$ is the flip.

Question: Can every Yang–Baxter operator from an algebra structure (i.e., every operator of the form $R^A_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}$ as above) be realized as arising from a universal $R$-matrix of some quasi-triangular bialgebra, via a suitable representation?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The conjecture that Yang–Baxter operators from algebra structures arise from some universal R-matrix (related to quasi-triangular bialgebras) is stated as an open problem in the literature on the Yang–Baxter equation and continues to be referenced as an active conjecture in subsequent surveys and papers by Nichita and collaborators. No resolution was found.

representations.normalized:
Consider a 3D bipedal walking robot modeled as a hybrid dynamical system

  Σ:  ẋ = f(x) + g(x)u   when x ∈ 𝒳 ∖ 𝒮,
        x⁺ = Δ(x⁻)        when x⁻ ∈ 𝒮,

where 𝒳 ⊂ ℝⁿ is the state manifold of joint positions and velocities, 𝒮 ⊂ 𝒳 is a switching surface representing foot impacts with the ground, Δ: 𝒮 → 𝒳 is a (possibly discontinuous) reset map encoding the impact dynamics and leg swap, and u ∈ ℝᵐ is the control input applied through joint actuators.

Most of the existing analysis and feedback-control framework for such systems (including hybrid zero dynamics and Poincaré-map-based stability analysis) assumes the closed-loop walking gait is a periodic orbit of Σ. The task is the following:

1. Define a precise and useful notion of stability for non-periodic (aperiodic) walking trajectories of Σ, applicable in particular to:
   (a) walking over terrain whose ground-height profile is not periodic and is not known in advance, and
   (b) maneuvering tasks where the biped must change heading and step placement to avoid obstacles, so that successive steps cannot be assumed identical.

2. Develop modeling, analysis procedures, and constructive feedback control designs that certify this stability notion for the hybrid system Σ in three spatial dimensions, without reducing the problem to tracking or stabilizing a predetermined periodic orbit.

Provide:
  - a formal definition of aperiodic-gait stability for Σ (e.g., in terms of forward invariance of a step-to-step set-valued map, input-to-state stability with respect to terrain/obstacle disturbances, or contraction of a non-autonomous Poincaré-like map);
  - analysis tools sufficient to certify this stability property;
  - a control synthesis methodology producing feedback laws u = k(x, ξ), with ξ encoding terrain/obstacle information, that achieve the stability property on a non-trivial class of 3D bipedal models.

This is a long-standing open research direction in legged locomotion control. While there has been substantial progress since 2014 on aperiodic and rough-terrain walking (e.g., step-to-step dynamics, control Lyapunov function and MPC-based approaches, capture-point/ALIP methods, and contraction-based analyses), no universally accepted stability notion or general control-design framework for aperiodic 3D bipedal gaits has emerged. The problem is generally regarded as still open.

Consider a 3D bipedal robot modeled as a hybrid dynamical system: during each single-support phase the robot evolves according to Lagrangian dynamics with the stance foot acting as a pivot subject to unilateral ground-contact constraints (non-negative normal reaction force, friction-cone constraints, and no roll/slip of the stance foot), and at foot touchdown the state undergoes an impact reset map. A periodic walking gait is a hybrid limit cycle of this system that respects the unilateral contact constraints throughout, and is called dynamically stable if the associated Poincaré return map has a locally exponentially stable fixed point.

Develop a feedback control design methodology for executing maneuvers — in particular, turning or steering to change the robot's heading direction — that satisfies all of the following:

(i) Throughout the maneuver, the closed-loop trajectory satisfies the unilateral ground-contact constraints (positive normal force, friction-cone, and no foot rotation/slip) at every instant.

(ii) The maneuver is realized by transitioning between, or continuously deforming, families of parametrized periodic gaits (e.g., gaits parametrized by turning radius or heading rate), and the transitions admit a rigorous proof of stability — for instance, via a common Lyapunov function, a multiple Lyapunov function with dwell-time conditions, or contraction-based arguments applied to the hybrid Poincaré map.

(iii) The method yields verifiable certificates (analytical or computational) that the robot can change direction by a prescribed amount while maintaining dynamic stability and contact feasibility.

Provide either such a construction together with a proof, or establish obstructions showing why such guarantees cannot be obtained under stated assumptions on the model.

Consider a 3D bipedal robot modeled as a rigid multibody system whose feet (or ankles) are passive, i.e., the ankle joints supply no active torque and the foot–ground interaction is only a unilateral contact (the foot rolls or pivots freely about its support region subject to non-penetration and friction constraints). Let the joint configuration be q ∈ Q with actuated coordinates q_a (legs, hips, torso, arms) and unactuated coordinates q_u (the rigid-body pose modulo the contact and the passive ankle degrees of freedom), governed by the constrained Euler–Lagrange dynamics

    M(q) q̈ + C(q,q̇) q̇ + G(q) = B u + J(q)^T λ,

with contact wrench λ constrained to a friction cone and supported on the foot contact region, and B selecting only the actuated joints.

Design a feedback control law u = k(q, q̇) (possibly with internal state and hybrid switching among contact modes such as flat-foot, toe-roll, heel-roll, or stepping) such that:

(i) (Quiet stance) The closed-loop system admits an asymptotically stable equilibrium corresponding to a desired upright standing posture q* with q̇* = 0, while keeping the contact wrench inside the friction cone and the center of pressure within the support polygon.

(ii) (Push recovery) There exists a non-empty, characterizable set D of admissible external impulsive disturbances applied to the robot's body such that, for every disturbance in D, the closed-loop trajectory returns asymptotically to the quiescent standing posture q*, possibly after a finite number of automatic stepping or contact transitions, while maintaining all unilateral contact and friction constraints throughout.

Either exhibit such a controller together with a proof and an explicit characterization of the disturbance set D, or show that no such controller exists under the passive-ankle constraint.

The problem of stable quiet standing and push recovery for bipeds with passive feet/ankles remains an active research topic. Recent work proposes partial solutions (e.g., whole-body locomotion control for passive-ankle robots, footstep-adjustment push recovery, series-elastic ankle reflex control), but no general controller with provable recovery guarantees for arbitrary admissible pushes on fully passive-ankle 3D bipeds has been established. The problem is therefore considered open in general, with partial results in restricted settings.

Consider a planar or three-dimensional bipedal walking robot modeled as a hybrid dynamical system: continuous-time rigid-body Lagrangian dynamics during the single- (and possibly double-) support phase, together with a discrete reset map modeling the instantaneous impact of the swing leg with the ground. Let the closed-loop system, under a chosen feedback controller, admit an exponentially stable periodic orbit O (a hybrid limit cycle) corresponding to a desired walking gait, with associated Poincaré return map P having a fixed point x* whose linearization is Schur stable.

(1) Develop a constructive method to compute or rigorously inner-approximate the domain of attraction D(O) := { x in the hybrid state space : the trajectory starting at x is defined for all forward time and converges to O } of such a hybrid periodic orbit, going beyond local linearization at x*.

(2) Extend the method to the robust setting: given a family of admissible perturbations to the continuous and discrete dynamics (e.g., bounded parametric model errors in inertia, mass, link lengths, contact location, and impact map), characterize or inner-approximate the robust domain of attraction—the set of initial conditions guaranteed to converge to a neighborhood of the nominal gait for every admissible perturbation—so that the estimate yields practical guarantees when transferring a controller designed in simulation to the physical robot.

Provide either an algorithmic procedure (with convergence/soundness guarantees) or analytic characterizations producing certified inner approximations of D(O), together with quantitative bounds in terms of the size of the modeling errors.

Background. A hybrid dynamical system is a tuple H = (Γ, D, U, S, Δ, F) consisting of a directed graph Γ with vertices V and edges E, a domain D_v ⊂ R^{n_v} and admissible control set U_v for each v ∈ V, a guard (switching surface) S_e ⊂ D_{source(e)} and a reset map Δ_e : S_e → D_{target(e)} for each e ∈ E, and a family of controlled vector fields F_v on D_v. An execution (solution) of H is a piecewise-smooth trajectory that flows under F_v inside each domain and jumps across edges via Δ_e whenever it reaches a guard. A periodic walking gait of a bipedal robot or a human is a periodic execution of such a hybrid system.

Two different bipedal walkers (e.g., a robot model with given mechanical parameters and feedback controller, or a human modeled from motion-capture data) are typically described by hybrid systems H_1 and H_2 whose graphs, domain dimensions, guards, and reset maps need not coincide.

Problem. Construct a metric d that assigns to any pair (x_1, x_2) of executions of (possibly distinct) hybrid systems H_1 and H_2 a nonnegative real number d(x_1, x_2) such that:

(i) d is a metric (nonnegativity, identity of indiscernibles up to a natural equivalence, symmetry, and triangle inequality) on a space containing executions of arbitrary hybrid systems of the above form, including the case H_1 ≠ H_2 with differing graphs, domain dimensions, guards, and reset maps;

(ii) d restricts to a meaningful distance on periodic gaits, so that, given a fixed hybrid robot model H with various feedback controllers producing periodic solutions x^*_1, …, x^*_k, the value d(x^*_i, x^*_human) ranks the controllers by closeness to a reference human gait x^*_human (which is itself an execution of a different hybrid system H_human);

(iii) d is computable from finite measured trajectory data and is well-defined when applied to recorded robotic walking data and recorded human walking data.

Provide an explicit construction of such a metric, prove that it satisfies the metric axioms, and demonstrate that it can distinguish "more human-like" from "less human-like" gaits in a principled way.

An execution (solution) of H is a piecewise-smooth trajectory that flows under F_v inside each domain and jumps across edges via Δ_e whenever it reaches a guard. A periodic walking gait of a bipedal robot or a human is a periodic execution of such a hybrid system.

Two different bipedal walkers (e.g., a robot model with given mechanical parameters and feedback controller, or a human modeled from motion-capture data) are typically described by hybrid systems H_1 and H_2 whose graphs, domain dimensions, guards, and reset maps need not coincide.

Problem. Construct a metric d that assigns to any pair (x_1, x_2) of executions of (possibly distinct) hybrid systems H_1 and H_2 a nonnegative real number d(x_1, x_2) such that:

(i) d is a metric (nonnegativity, identity of indiscernibles up to a natural equivalence, symmetry, and triangle inequality) on a space containing executions of arbitrary hybrid systems of the above form, including the case H_1 ≠ H_2 with differing graphs, domain dimensions, guards, and reset maps;

(ii) d restricts to a meaningful distance on periodic gaits, so that, given a fixed hybrid robot model H with various feedback controllers producing periodic solutions x^*_1, …, x^*_k, the value d(x^*_i, x^*_human) ranks the controllers by closeness to a reference human gait x^*_human (which is itself an execution of a different hybrid system H_human);

(iii) d is computable from finite measured trajectory data and is well-defined when applied to recorded robotic walking data and recorded human walking data.

Provide an explicit construction of such a metric, prove that it satisfies the metric axioms, and demonstrate that it can distinguish "more human-like" from "less human-like" gaits in a principled way.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

No general metric on solutions of hybrid systems with differing underlying models has been established in the literature. Existing approaches (e.g., RMSE on spatiotemporal/kinematic features, the Combined Gait Asymmetry Metric CGAM, and various task-specific gait similarity scores) compare gaits via fixed scalar parameter sets rather than as solutions of hybrid dynamical systems with possibly different graphs, dimensions, guards, and resets. The general problem appears to remain open.

Consider a 3D bipedal robot modeled as a hybrid dynamical system with continuous single-support phases governed by Lagrangian dynamics and discrete impact maps at foot contact. Suppose the feet are not flat point-contacts but instead have a nontrivial geometry — in particular, spherical feet that roll on the ground during the single-support phase, producing additional unactuated rotational degrees of freedom (rolling in both sagittal and frontal planes) and thereby higher-degree underactuation than the planar case.

(a) Develop a hybrid dynamic model and a feedback-control design (for instance, in the spirit of virtual constraints and hybrid zero dynamics) for such a 3D biped with spherical feet, and prove the existence of an exponentially stable periodic walking gait. Specifically, exhibit a controller under which the restricted Poincaré return map of the hybrid zero dynamics has all eigenvalues strictly inside the unit disk.

(b) Extend the framework to a biped (or human-robot hybrid) in which one or both lower limbs are replaced by a prosthetic component — passive (purely mechanical, no actuation) or active (with one or more actuators) — whose foot interacts with the ground through a rolling contact mimicking the human ankle-foot complex. Provide conditions on the prosthesis design, the controller of the intact limb (and of the active prosthesis when applicable), and the gait parameters under which an exponentially stable periodic 3D walking gait exists.

Let $J$ denote the James space, that is, the Banach space of all sequences $(x_n)_{n\geq 1}$ of real numbers with $x_n \to 0$ and finite squared variation norm
$$\|x\|_J = \sup\Big\{\Big(\sum_{k=1}^{m-1}(x_{p_{k+1}}-x_{p_k})^2 + (x_{p_1}-x_{p_m})^2\Big)^{1/2} : 1\le p_1<p_2<\cdots<p_m\Big\}^{1/2}\cdot 2^{-1/2},$$
(equivalently, the standard James-space norm under which $J$ is quasi-reflexive of order one). Say that a Banach space $X$ has the 2-Daugavet property if every finite-rank operator $T: X \to X$ satisfies
$$\|\mathrm{Id} + T\|^2 \geq 1 + \|T\|^2.$$
Question: Does there exist an equivalent norm $\|\cdot\|$ on $J$ under which $J$ has the 2-Daugavet property?

Let $1\le p<\infty$ with $p\ne 2$, and let $L^p=L^p[0,1]$ be the standard Lebesgue space on $[0,1]$ with Borel $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{B}$ and Lebesgue measure $\mu$. A bounded linear operator $T\in\mathcal{L}(L^p)$ is called \emph{narrow} if for every $A\in\mathcal{B}$ and every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $x\in L^p$ such that
\[ x^2=\mathbf{1}_A,\qquad \int_{[0,1]} x\,d\mu = 0,\qquad \|Tx\|_{L^p}<\varepsilon. \]
For each $T\in\mathcal{L}(L^p)$ define the lower and upper Maurey derivatives $f_T,F_T:[0,1]\to[0,\infty]$ by
\[ f_T(t)=\liminf_{\substack{A\ni t\\ \mu(A)\to 0}}\;\inf\Bigl\{\frac{\|Tx\|}{\mu(A)^{1/p}}: x\in L^p,\;x^2=\mathbf{1}_A,\;\int x\,d\mu=0\Bigr\}, \]
\[ F_T(t)=\limsup_{\substack{A\ni t\\ \mu(A)\to 0}}\;\sup\Bigl\{\frac{\|Tx\|}{\mu(A)^{1/p}}: x\in L^p,\;x^2=\mathbf{1}_A,\;\int x\,d\mu=0\Bigr\}, \]
and set the Maurey seminorm $\|T\|_M=\max(\|f_T\|_\infty,\|F_T\|_\infty)$. Call $T$ a \emph{Maurey operator} if $\|T\|_M=0$.

Question: Does there exist a Maurey operator $T\in\mathcal{L}(L^p)$ that is not narrow?

Let $\mathcal{P}$ denote the Banach operator ideal of absolutely summing operators between Banach spaces, equipped with its usual ideal norm $\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal{P}}$ (an operator $T:X\to Y$ is absolutely summing if there is a constant $C$ such that for every finite family $(x_i)\subset X$, $\sum_i \|Tx_i\| \le C \sup_{\|x^*\|\le 1}\sum_i |x^*(x_i)|$, and $\|T\|_{\mathcal{P}}$ is the least such $C$). For a Banach space $X$, let $\mathcal{F}(X,X)$ denote the space of finite-rank operators on $X$.

Say that a Banach space $X$ has the metric approximation property (MAP) with respect to $\mathcal{P}$ if for every Banach space $Y$ and every absolutely summing operator $T \in \mathcal{P}(X,Y)$ there exists a net $(S_\alpha)\subset \mathcal{F}(X,X)$ such that:
(i) $S_\alpha \to \mathrm{id}_X$ uniformly on compact subsets of $X$, and
(ii) $\limsup_\alpha \|T S_\alpha\|_{\mathcal{P}} \le \|T\|_{\mathcal{P}}$.

Problem: Give an intrinsic characterization of those Banach spaces $X$ which possess the MAP with respect to $\mathcal{P}$.

- $\mathcal{P}_p$, the ideal of absolutely $p$-summing operators (so that $\mathcal{P}_1 = \mathcal{P}$ is the classical absolutely summing-operator ideal).

For a Banach operator ideal $(\mathcal{A}, \|\cdot\|_{\mathcal{A}})$, say that a Banach space $X$ has the metric approximation property for $\mathcal{A}$ (MAP for $\mathcal{A}$) if there exists a net $(S_\alpha)$ of finite-rank operators on $X$ with $\|S_\alpha\| \le 1$ for all $\alpha$ such that $S_\alpha 	o \mathrm{id}_X$ uniformly on compact subsets of $X$, and such that for every Banach space $Y$ and every operator $T \in \mathcal{A}(X, Y)$ one has
$$\lim_\alpha \|T \circ S_\alpha - T\|_{\mathcal{A}} = 0 \quad 	ext{(or, equivalently, } \limsup_\alpha \|T \circ S_\alpha\|_{\mathcal{A}} \le \|T\|_{\mathcal{A}}	ext{)}.$$

Let $X$ be a Banach space, and let $B(X)$ denote the space of bounded linear operators on $X$ and $F(X)\subset B(X)$ the subspace of finite-rank operators. Recall:

(i) $X$ has the approximation property (AP) if for every compact set $K\subset X$ and every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $T\in F(X)$ with $\|Tx-x\|<\varepsilon$ for all $x\in K$.

(ii) $X$ has the metric approximation property (MAP) if the operators $T$ in (i) can be chosen with $\|T\|\le 1$.

(iii) $X$ has the weak metric approximation property (weak MAP) if for every Banach space $Y$, every weakly compact operator $S\in B(X,Y)$, every compact set $K\subset X$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists $T\in F(X)$ with $\|ST\|\le \|S\|$ and $\|Tx-x\|<\varepsilon$ for all $x\in K$.

It is known that MAP implies weak MAP, which implies AP. Answer the following:

(a) Does there exist a Banach space that has the weak metric approximation property but does not have the metric approximation property? Equivalently, is the weak MAP strictly weaker than the MAP?

(b) If a dual Banach space $X^*$ has the approximation property, must $X^*$ also have the metric approximation property?

Let $X$ be a Banach space. For a closed subspace $E \subseteq X$, the density character $\operatorname{dens} E$ is the least cardinality of a dense subset of $E$. Say that $X$ has the separable complementation property (SCP) if every separable closed subspace $E$ of $X$ is contained in a separable closed subspace $F$ of $X$ that is complemented in $X$ (i.e., $F$ is the range of a bounded linear projection $X \to X$). For an infinite cardinal $\mathfrak{m}$, say that $X$ has the $\mathfrak{m}$-complementation property ($\mathfrak{m}$-CP) if every closed subspace $E$ of $X$ with $\operatorname{dens} E = \mathfrak{m}$ is contained in a complemented closed subspace $F$ of $X$ with $\operatorname{dens} F = \mathfrak{m}$.

Question: Does the SCP imply the $\mathfrak{m}$-CP for every infinite cardinal $\mathfrak{m}$? That is, if a Banach space $X$ has the separable complementation property, must $X$ have the $\mathfrak{m}$-complementation property for every infinite cardinal $\mathfrak{m}$?

representations.normalized:
Definitions. A Köthe Banach space on [0,1] is a Banach space E with E ⊆ L^1[0,1] such that the constant function 1_{[0,1]} belongs to E and such that, for every measurable x and every y ∈ E with |x| ≤ |y| almost everywhere, one has x ∈ E and ‖x‖_E ≤ ‖y‖_E.

Let E be a Köthe Banach space on [0,1] and let X be a Banach space. A bounded linear operator T : E → X is called narrow if for every measurable set A ⊆ [0,1] and every ε > 0 there exists a function x ∈ E with x = -x on A (i.e. x takes only two opposite values on A and vanishes off A; equivalently, a "sign" of mean zero supported on A: x = 1_{A_1} − 1_{A_2} with A_1, A_2 disjoint and A_1 ∪ A_2 = A) such that ‖T(x)‖ < ε.

A bounded linear operator T : E → X is called ℓ_2-strictly singular if there is no closed infinite-dimensional subspace Y ⊆ E which is isomorphic to ℓ_2 and on which T acts as an into-isomorphism (i.e. there is no Y ⊆ E with Y ≃ ℓ_2 such that T|_Y is bounded below).

Question. Is it true that for every Köthe Banach space E on [0,1], every Banach space X, and every bounded linear operator T : E → X, if T is ℓ_2-strictly singular then T is narrow?

The general question (going back to Plichko–Popov, 1990) appears to still be open in full generality for arbitrary Köthe Banach spaces on [0,1]. Significant partial progress is known: Mykhaylyuk, Popov, Randrianantoanina, and Schechtman (Israel J. No source found that resolves the question for all Köthe Banach spaces.

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

In the Banach space setting, a theorem of León-Saavedra and Müller implies that every nonzero scalar multiple of a hypercyclic operator is hypercyclic, so such operators exist on any separable infinite-dimensional Banach space. For non-normable separable Fréchet spaces the corresponding rotation/scalar invariance is more delicate, and no published resolution of the existence question in this exact form was located in the search; the question appears to remain open.

Let $X$ be a separable infinite-dimensional Fréchet space (i.e., a complete metrizable locally convex topological vector space) over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. A continuous linear operator $T:X\to X$ is said to be:

(i) hypercyclic if there exists a vector $x\in X$ whose orbit $\{T^n x : n\in\mathbb{N}\}$ is dense in $X$;

(ii) chaotic (in the sense of Devaney) if it is hypercyclic and its set of periodic points $\mathrm{Per}(T) := \{x\in X : T^n x = x \text{ for some integer } n\geq 1\}$ is dense in $X$.

Characterize, in terms of intrinsic topological/linear structural properties, those separable infinite-dimensional Fréchet spaces $X$ on which there exists at least one chaotic continuous linear operator $T:X\to X$.

(ii) chaotic (in the sense of Devaney) if it is hypercyclic and its set of periodic points $\mathrm{Per}(T) := \{x\in X : T^n x = x \text{ for some integer } n\geq 1\}$ is dense in $X$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The general characterization remains open. Positive results are known: every separable infinite-dimensional Banach (and many Fréchet) spaces support hypercyclic operators (Ansari, Bernal-González, Bonet–Peris), and spaces with an unconditional Schauder decomposition support chaotic (and frequently hypercyclic) operators (Bonet–Martínez-Giménez–Peris, De la Rosa–Frerick–Grivaux–Peris). On the negative side, Bonet–Martínez-Giménez–Peris (2001) exhibited a separable Banach space admitting no chaotic operator. No intrinsic characterization of Fréchet spaces admitting a chaotic operator is known.

For a real Banach space $X$, define the modulus of convexity
$$\delta_X(\varepsilon) = \inf\bigl\{\, 1 - \tfrac{1}{2}\|x+y\| \;:\; \|x\|\le 1,\ \|y\|\le 1,\ \|x-y\|\ge \varepsilon \,\bigr\}, \qquad \varepsilon\in[0,2],$$
and the characteristic of convexity
$$\varepsilon_0(X) = \sup\{\varepsilon\in[0,2] : \delta_X(\varepsilon) = 0\}.$$
Fix $a \in [0,2)$ and let $\mathcal{E}_a$ denote the class of all two-dimensional real Banach spaces $E$ with $\varepsilon_0(E) = a$. For each $\varepsilon \in [a,2)$, determine
$$\Delta_a(\varepsilon) \;=\; \sup_{E \in \mathcal{E}_a} \delta_E(\varepsilon),$$
and (if attained) identify the two-dimensional Banach spaces $E \in \mathcal{E}_a$ achieving this supremum.

Let $X$ be a complex Banach space and $T \in L(X)$ a bounded linear operator. Define:
- the point spectrum $\pi(T) = \{\lambda \in \mathbb{C} : \lambda - T \text{ is not injective}\}$;
- the surjective spectrum $\pi'(T) = \{\lambda \in \mathbb{C} : \lambda - T \text{ is not surjective}\}$.

For each $\lambda \in \mathbb{C}$, let $(\lambda - T)^{-\infty}(0) = \bigcup_{n \ge 1} \ker((\lambda - T)^n)$ denote the generalized kernel at $\lambda$. Define the algebraic subspace
$$Y = E_X(T) := \bigcup_{\substack{p \in \mathbb{C}[z] \\ p \ne 0}} \ker p(T) = \sum_{\lambda \in \mathbb{C}} (\lambda - T)^{-\infty}(0),$$
which is a (not necessarily closed) $T$-invariant linear subspace of $X$. Let $T_Y : Y \to Y$ denote the restriction of $T$ to $Y$, viewed as a linear operator on the vector space $Y$.

Question: Is it true that
$$\pi(T) = \pi(T_Y) = \pi'(T_Y)?$$

Fix a positive integer m. A bounded linear operator T on a complex Hilbert space H is called an m-isometry if
  sum_{k=0}^{m} (-1)^{m-k} C(m,k) (T*)^k T^k = 0,
where T* denotes the Hilbert-space adjoint of T and C(m,k) is the binomial coefficient. Given two bounded operators A on a Hilbert space K and B on a Hilbert space H, B is said to be unitarily equivalent to the restriction A|_M (for some closed A-invariant subspace M ⊆ K) if there exists a unitary operator U : H → M such that A U = U B.

Question: Does there exist a Hilbert space K and a bounded linear operator A on K such that A is an m-isometry and, for every separable complex Hilbert space H and every m-isometry T on H, there is a closed A-invariant subspace M ⊆ K with T unitarily equivalent to A|_M? (Such an A would be called a universal m-isometry.)

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The question was resolved in the negative: there exist injective bounded linear operators on $\ell^\infty(\mathbb{N})$ with dense, non-closed (hence proper) range, constructed via injective Tauberian operators on $L_1$. This appears in work of W. B. Johnson and collaborators (arXiv:1408.1443), showing that dense range does not imply surjectivity on $\ell^\infty$.

Let $X$ be a separated locally convex topological vector space. For a subset $S\subseteq X$, let $\operatorname{cone}(S)=\{\lambda s : \lambda\ge 0,\ s\in S\}$ denote the conic hull of $S$, and let $\overline{\operatorname{cone}}(S)$ denote its closure in $X$. For a nonempty convex set $E\subseteq X$, define the quasi-relative interior of $E$ by
$$\operatorname{qri}(E) := \{x\in E : \overline{\operatorname{cone}}(E-x) \text{ is a linear subspace of } X\}.$$
Let $C,D\subseteq X$ be nonempty convex subsets such that $\operatorname{qri}(C)\cap\operatorname{qri}(D)\neq\emptyset$. Determine whether the inclusion
$$\operatorname{qri}(C\cap D) \subseteq \operatorname{qri}(C)\cap\operatorname{qri}(D)$$
holds in general, or provide a counterexample.

representations.normalized:
Let $M^{m\times n}$ denote the space of real $m\times n$ matrices. A Borel-measurable, locally bounded function $f\colon M^{m\times n}\to\mathbb{R}$ is called **quasiconvex** (in the sense of Morrey) if for every $A\in M^{m\times n}$, every bounded open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n$, and every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^m)$,
$$\int_\Omega f(A+D\varphi(x))\,dx \;\ge\; |\Omega|\,f(A).$$
The function $f$ is called **polyconvex** if there exists a convex function $g\colon\mathbb{R}^{\tau(m,n)}\to\mathbb{R}$ such that
$$f(A) \;=\; g(T(A)) \qquad\text{for all } A\in M^{m\times n},$$
where $T(A)$ is the vector of all minors (subdeterminants of all orders) of $A$ and $\tau(m,n)$ is their total number.

It is classical that polyconvexity implies quasiconvexity, and that the converse fails in general (for instance, in dimensions $m=n=2$ there exist quasiconvex functions that are not polyconvex).

**Problem.** Develop a systematic theory, or provide an effective criterion, that decides for an arbitrary given quasiconvex function $f\colon M^{m\times n}\to\mathbb{R}$ whether or not $f$ is polyconvex.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

No systematic theory or decidable criterion is known for determining when a quasiconvex function on matrices is polyconvex. While the strict implications among the convexity hierarchy (convex ⇒ polyconvex ⇒ quasiconvex ⇒ rank-one convex) are well established and explicit examples of quasiconvex non-polyconvex functions exist (e.g. Šverák's 2D example), characterizing polyconvexity inside the quasiconvex class remains an outstanding problem in the vectorial calculus of variations, closely tied to the still-open planar Morrey conjecture.

Let $m,n$ be positive integers and let $\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ denote the space of real $m\times n$ matrices. A function $f:\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\to\mathbb{R}$ is called:

(a) quasiconvex if for every bounded domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n$, every matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$, and every smooth, compactly supported vector field $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^m)$, one has
$$\frac{1}{|\Omega|}\int_\Omega f\bigl(A+D\varphi(x)\bigr)\,dx \;\geq\; f(A);$$

(b) rank-one convex if for every $A_0\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ and every rank-one matrix $B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$, the function $s\mapsto f(A_0+sB)$ is convex on $\mathbb{R}$.

It is known that every quasiconvex function is rank-one convex, and that for $m\geq 3$ and $n\geq 2$ there exist rank-one convex functions that are not quasiconvex.

Question: For $m=2$ and every $n\geq 2$, is every rank-one convex function $f:\mathbb{R}^{2\times n}\to\mathbb{R}$ necessarily quasiconvex?

Let $n\ge 2$ and $p\ge n$. For a smooth, compactly supported map $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n$, let $Df(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ denote its Jacobian matrix at $x$, let $|Df(x)|$ denote the Hilbert–Schmidt (Frobenius) norm of $Df(x)$, and let $J(x,f)=\det Df(x)$. The pointwise Hadamard inequality $n^{n/2}|J(x,f)|\le |Df(x)|^n$ implies, after multiplying by $|Df(x)|^{p-n}$ and integrating, that
$$\left|\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} |Df(x)|^{p-n}\, J(x,f)\, dx\right| \le \lambda \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} |Df(x)|^p\, dx$$
for some constant $\lambda$. Determine the best (smallest) constant $\lambda_p(n)$ for which this inequality holds for every smooth compactly supported $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n$.

$$\left|\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} |Df(x)|^{p-n}\, J(x,f)\, dx\right| \le \lambda \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} |Df(x)|^p\, dx$$

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The sharp value of the constant in this integral Hadamard inequality for Jacobians is a long-standing open question associated with work of T. Iwaniec and collaborators. Recent literature on "Hadamard's inequality in the mean" (e.g., 2023–2024 work) studies closely related sharpness questions and indicates that the cancellation phenomenon producing the gap with the pointwise Hadamard bound is still not fully understood; no general formula for $\lambda_p(n)$ appears in the literature.

Let $S$ denote the Ahlfors–Beurling transform on the complex plane, that is, the singular integral operator on $L^p(\mathbb{C})$ ($1 < p < \infty$) defined (for sufficiently nice functions $\omega$) by the principal-value integral
$$ (S\omega)(z) \;=\; -\frac{1}{\pi}\,\mathrm{p.v.}\!\int_{\mathbb{C}} \frac{\omega(\zeta)}{(z-\zeta)^2}\, dA(\zeta), $$
where $dA$ is two-dimensional Lebesgue measure. Equivalently, for every smooth, compactly supported complex-valued function $f:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}$ one has $S(\bar{\partial} f) = \partial f$, where $\partial = \tfrac{1}{2}(\partial_x - i\partial_y)$ and $\bar{\partial} = \tfrac{1}{2}(\partial_x + i\partial_y)$.

For $1 < p < \infty$, define
$$ A_p \;=\; \|S\|_{L^p(\mathbb{C}) \to L^p(\mathbb{C})} \;=\; \sup\bigl\{\|S\omega\|_p : \omega \in L^p(\mathbb{C}),\ \|\omega\|_p \le 1\bigr\}. $$

Determine the exact value of $A_p$ for every $p \in (1,\infty)$. In particular, prove or disprove the conjectured identity
$$ A_p \;=\; p^{*} - 1, \qquad \text{where } p^{*} = \max\{p,\, p/(p-1)\}. $$

The exact $L^p$ operator norm of the Beurling–Ahlfors transform (Iwaniec's conjecture $A_p = p^*-1$) remains a well-known open problem. Substantial partial results provide upper bounds, e.g. Bañuelos–Wang $\le 4(p^*-1)$, Nazarov–Volberg $\le 2(p^*-1)$, with subsequent refinements (e.g. $\le 1.575(p^*-1)$), but the sharp constant has not been established for general $p \ne 2$.
