The endpoint characterizations (division depth 0 = P, depth 1 = P^{#P}, polynomial depth = PSPACE) are established in the membrane-computing literature, but no published characterization of the intermediate constant-depth classes or of logarithmic division depth appears to exist; the question of whether constant division depth yields a proper hierarchy with matching upper bounds is listed as an open problem in surveys on P systems with active membranes.

Consider P systems with active membranes, a model of distributed parallel computation in which objects (multisets of symbols) reside inside a hierarchically nested structure of membranes and evolve in parallel by means of local rewriting and communication rules (object evolution, send-in, send-out, dissolution, and membrane division). The depth of a P system is the maximum nesting depth of its membrane structure; a system is called shallow when this depth equals 1 (a skin membrane containing only elementary membranes), and deep otherwise. A P system is confluent if every nondeterministic computation on a given input yields the same accept/reject answer, and non-confluent otherwise. A recognizer P system family decides a language in polynomial time if there is a uniform polynomial-time construction of systems whose computations halt in polynomial time and correctly decide membership.

It is known that:
(i) polynomial-time uniform families of shallow non-confluent recognizer P systems with active membranes can decide exactly the languages in PSPACE;
(ii) deep membrane structures provide hierarchical combination of results, while shallow systems with exponentially many parallel sub-computations can only collect their outcomes in the outermost membrane.

Determine the precise relationship between the computational power gained from allowing non-confluence and the computational power gained from increasing membrane depth in polynomial-time uniform families of recognizer P systems with active membranes. In particular, characterize the class of languages decided by deep confluent P systems with active membranes in polynomial time, and compare it to PSPACE and to the classes obtained by combining or separating these two features (depth versus non-confluence).

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question is the Eilenberg–Ganea conjecture (1957), which remains an open problem. It is known that any group of cohomological dimension 2 admits a 3-dimensional $K(G,1)$. Bestvina and Brady (1997) constructed groups providing potential counterexamples, showing that at least one of the Eilenberg–Ganea conjecture and the Whitehead asphericity conjecture must fail, but neither has been resolved.

Let $G$ be a discrete group and let $\mathbb{Q}G$ denote its rational group ring. For an idempotent matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(\mathbb{Q}G)$, define two traces of $A$:

1. The Kaplansky trace $\kappa(A)\in\mathbb{Q}$ is the sum $\sum_{i=1}^{n} c_e(a_{ii})$, where for $x=\sum_{g\in G} x_g\, g\in\mathbb{Q}G$ the coefficient $c_e(x)=x_e$ is the value at the identity element $e\in G$.

2. The augmentation trace $\varepsilon(A)\in\mathbb{Q}$ is $\sum_{i=1}^{n}\varepsilon(a_{ii})$, where $\varepsilon\colon\mathbb{Q}G\to\mathbb{Q}$ is the augmentation homomorphism sending $\sum_g x_g g$ to $\sum_g x_g$.

Both traces are invariant under conjugation by invertible matrices and additive under direct sums, so they descend to maps $K_0(\mathbb{Q}G)\to\mathbb{Q}$, denoted again by $\kappa$ and $\varepsilon$. Equivalently, for a finitely generated projective $\mathbb{Q}G$-module $P$ represented by an idempotent matrix $A$, one defines $\kappa(P):=\kappa(A)$ and $\varepsilon(P):=\varepsilon(A)$.

Weak Bass trace conjecture for $\mathbb{Q}G$: prove or disprove that for every finitely generated projective $\mathbb{Q}G$-module $P$,
$$\kappa(P)=\varepsilon(P).$$

Does this equality hold for every (discrete) group $G$?

A group $G$ is called perfect if it equals its own commutator subgroup, i.e., $G = [G,G]$. An element $g \in G$ is called a normal generator of $G$ if the smallest normal subgroup of $G$ containing $g$ is all of $G$; equivalently, $G$ is the normal closure $\langle\!\langle g \rangle\!\rangle^G$. The normal rank of $G$ is the minimum cardinality of a subset $S \subseteq G$ whose normal closure equals $G$.

Question (Wiegold): Does every finitely generated perfect group admit a single normal generator? In other words, is it true that for every finitely generated group $G$ with $G = [G,G]$, there exists an element $g \in G$ such that $G$ is the normal closure of $\{g\}$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

A 2025 preprint by Chen and Heuer ("The Wiegold problem and free products of left-orderable groups", arXiv:2510.26073) announces a negative solution to Wiegold's problem: they prove that any free product of nontrivial left-orderable groups has normal rank greater than one, and combining this with the existence of finitely generated perfect left-orderable groups yields finitely generated perfect groups that are not normally generated by a single element. Prior to this, the problem (posed by Wiegold in 1976) had been considered open.

Recall the following invariants of a finitely presentable group $G$:
- The weight $w(G)$ is the minimum number of elements of $G$ whose normal closure equals $G$.

Consider the class $\mathcal{C}$ of all groups $G$ that arise as the link group of some $w$-component $n$-link with $n \geq 2$ and that satisfy $w(G) = \mathrm{def}(G) = w$.

Question: Does every $G \in \mathcal{C}$ satisfy $\mathrm{cd}(G) \leq 2$?

Let $\pi$ be a finitely presentable group. Recall that the deficiency of $\pi$ is the maximum, over all finite presentations of $\pi$, of the number of generators minus the number of relators. Recall also that $\pi$ is said to have one end if for some (equivalently any) finite, connected $K(\pi,1)$-like complex, the number of ends of its universal cover is one; equivalently, $\pi$ is infinite, finitely generated, and the reduced $0$-th $L^2$-cohomology of $\pi$ does not vanish in the relevant sense — more concretely, for finitely generated $\pi$, having one end means $H^1(\pi; \mathbb{Z}\pi) = 0$ with $\pi$ infinite and not virtually $\mathbb{Z}$. Let $\beta_1^{(2)}(\pi)$ denote the first $L^2$-Betti number of $\pi$ (the von Neumann dimension of the reduced first $\ell^2$-cohomology of $\pi$).

It is known that if $\pi$ is finitely presentable, has deficiency exactly $1$, and has abelianization $\pi/[\pi,\pi] \cong \mathbb{Z}$, then $\beta_1^{(2)}(\pi) = 0$.

Question: Suppose $\pi$ is a finitely presentable group such that $\pi/[\pi,\pi] \cong \mathbb{Z}$ and $\pi$ has exactly one end, but without any assumption on the deficiency of $\pi$. Does it follow that $\beta_1^{(2)}(\pi) = 0$?

Let R be a Prüfer domain (an integral domain in which every nonzero finitely generated ideal is invertible), and let P be a nonzero prime ideal of R. Let R_P denote the localization of R at P. Recall that an overring of R is a ring T with R ⊆ T ⊆ K, where K is the field of fractions of R, and that a nonzero fractional ideal I of a domain T is called divisorial if I equals the intersection of all principal fractional ideals of T containing it (equivalently, I = (T : (T : I))).

(a) Does there exist a Prüfer domain R, a nonzero prime ideal P of R, and a countably infinite strictly ascending chain of overrings
   R = R_0 ⊂ R_1 ⊂ R_2 ⊂ ··· ⊆ R_P
such that for every integer n ≥ 0, the extended ideal P R_{2n} is a divisorial ideal of R_{2n}, while P R_{2n+1} is not a divisorial ideal of R_{2n+1}?

(b) If such a chain exists, determine whether the extended ideal P S is divisorial or not divisorial as an ideal of the union S = ⋃_{m ≥ 0} R_m (which is itself an overring of R contained in R_P).

Let $J =  ig(\partial r_i/\partial x_j ig)\in M_{m	imes n}(\mathbb{Z}G)$ be the Fox–Jacobian matrix of the presentation, where $\partial/\partial x_j$ denotes the Fox free derivative followed by the projection $\mathbb{Z}F	o\mathbb{Z}G$.

A connected CW 2-complex $X$ is called aspherical if $\pi_n(X)=0$ for all $n\ge 2$ (equivalently, its universal cover is contractible). Call $X$ subaspherical if it is homotopy equivalent to (or embeds as) a subcomplex of some aspherical 2-complex. A covering space $\widetilde X \to X$ is called acyclic if the reduced integral homology $\widetilde H_*(\widetilde X;\mathbb Z)$ vanishes, and is called regular if the action of $\pi_1(X)$ permutes its sheets transitively (i.e., the covering corresponds to a normal subgroup of $\pi_1(X)$).

Question: Does there exist a nonaspherical subaspherical 2-complex $X$ that admits a regular acyclic covering space $\widetilde X \to X$ whose fundamental group $\pi_1(\widetilde X)$ is finitely generated?

Setup. Let $S$ be a finitely dominated connected 2-dimensional CW complex with fundamental group $G=\pi_1(S)$. Let $p\colon S_N\to S$ be a regular covering corresponding to a normal subgroup $N\trianglelefteq G$, and assume that $S_N$ is acyclic (i.e., $H_i(S_N;\mathbb{Z})=0$ for all $i\geq 1$). A 2-complex is aspherical if $\pi_n=0$ for all $n\geq 2$.

A known asphericity criterion in this setting asserts: if $G$ contains a nontrivial amenable normal subgroup $E$ such that $E\not\subseteq N$, then $S$ is aspherical.

Question. Can the hypothesis "$E\not\subseteq N$" be omitted from this criterion? More precisely: if $S$ is a finitely dominated 2-complex with fundamental group $G$, $N\trianglelefteq G$ is a normal subgroup such that the regular cover $S_N$ is acyclic, and $G$ contains a nontrivial amenable (in particular, elementary amenable) normal subgroup $E$ with $E\subseteq N$, must $S$ still be aspherical? Equivalently, does the asphericity conclusion hold without any restriction on the relative position of $E$ and $N$, at least in the case where $N$ itself is elementary amenable?

More precisely: if $S$ is a finitely dominated 2-complex with fundamental group $G$, $N\trianglelefteq G$ is a normal subgroup such that the regular cover $S_N$ is acyclic, and $G$ contains a nontrivial amenable (in particular, elementary amenable) normal subgroup $E$ with $E\subseteq N$, must $S$ still be aspherical? Equivalently, does the asphericity conclusion hold without any restriction on the relative position of $E$ and $N$, at least in the case where $N$ itself is elementary amenable?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The Whitehead asphericity question, of which this is a refinement involving acyclic covers and amenable normal subgroups, remains open. Related work by Howie, Hillman, and others establishes asphericity criteria under conditions like $E\not\subseteq N$, but the specific question of whether this condition can be dropped (e.g., when $N$ is elementary amenable) is recorded as an open problem in the surveying literature. No published resolution was located.

A connected 2-dimensional CW complex $K$ is called aspherical if its second homotopy group $\pi_2(K)$ vanishes (equivalently, its universal cover is contractible). The Whitehead Conjecture asserts that every connected subcomplex of an aspherical 2-complex is aspherical. The finite Whitehead Conjecture is the restriction of this assertion to finite 2-complexes: every subcomplex of a finite aspherical 2-complex is aspherical.

A finitely presentable group $G$ has weight 1 if it can be normally generated by a single element, and has deficiency 1 if it admits a finite presentation with one more generator than relator. The rational cohomological dimension $\mathrm{cd}_{\mathbb{Q}}(G)$ is the projective dimension of $\mathbb{Q}$ over the rational group ring $\mathbb{Q} G$. The "knot-like" case of the Whitehead Conjecture is known to be equivalent to the statement:
$$\text{Every finitely presentable group } G \text{ of weight } 1 \text{ and deficiency } 1 \text{ satisfies } \mathrm{cd}_{\mathbb{Q}}(G) \le 2.$$

Question: Is the knot-like case of the Whitehead Conjecture (as formulated above) equivalent to the finite Whitehead Conjecture, or is the knot-like case strictly weaker than the finite Whitehead Conjecture?

representations.normalized:
A sequence $(a_n)_{n\ge 0}$ of distinct integers is called self-ordered if, for every prime $p$, the sequence itself is a $p$-ordering of the set $S=\{a_n : n\ge 0\}$ in the sense of Bhargava. That is, for every prime $p$ and every $n\ge 1$,
$$v_p\!\left(\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}(a_n-a_k)\right)=\min_{a\in S}\, v_p\!\left(\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}(a-a_k)\right),$$
where $v_p$ denotes the $p$-adic valuation.

Two classes of examples are known:

(1) Dynamical examples: sequences obtained by iterating a nonconstant polynomial $f(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$, i.e. $a_n=f^{\circ n}(a_0)$.

(2) Affine images of the three classical examples
$\;a_n=n,\quad a_n=q^n\text{ (for a fixed integer }q\ge 2),\quad a_n=\binom{2n}{n}\cdot\frac{1}{n+1}\text{ (or another specified classical sequence)},$
i.e. sequences of the form $\alpha a_n+\beta$ with $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{Z}$, $\alpha\ne 0$, where $(a_n)$ is one of the three known basic self-ordered sequences.

Question: Does there exist a "natural" self-ordered sequence of integers that neither arises from a dynamical construction as in (1) nor is an affine image of one of the three classical examples as in (2)?

representations.normalized:
Consider a two-dimensional quantum lattice system on $\mathbb{Z}^2$ (or finite portions thereof of arbitrary size), with a finite-dimensional Hilbert space attached to each site. Let $H = \sum_{x} h_x$ be a local Hamiltonian, meaning each $h_x$ acts non-trivially on a uniformly bounded number of sites contained in a region of uniformly bounded diameter, and the operator norms $\|h_x\|$ are uniformly bounded. Assume that $H$ is gapped: there exists a constant $\gamma > 0$, independent of system size, such that the spectral gap between the ground-state energy and the rest of the spectrum is at least $\gamma$.

A Projected Entangled Pair State (PEPS) with bond dimension $D$ on a 2D lattice is a tensor network state obtained by placing at each site a tensor with one physical index (of dimension equal to the local Hilbert space dimension) and one virtual index of dimension $D$ for each lattice edge incident to that site, and contracting all virtual indices along edges.

Say that a family of states $\{|\psi_N\rangle\}$ on regions of size $N$ admits a global PEPS approximation if there exist PEPS $\{|\phi_N\rangle\}$ with bond dimension $D(N, \varepsilon)$ growing at most quasi-polynomially in $N$ and $1/\varepsilon$ such that $\big\| |\psi_N\rangle - |\phi_N\rangle \big\| \le \varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$.

Question: Does every ground state of every two-dimensional local gapped Hamiltonian (in the above sense) admit a global PEPS approximation, using only the spectral gap hypothesis and without any additional assumption controlling the density or concentration of low-energy eigenvalues near the ground-state energy?

Let $a, b, u_0, u_1 \in \mathbb{Z}$ and define the second-order linear recursive integer sequence $(u_n)_{n\ge 0}$ by
$$u_{n+1} = a\, u_n + b\, u_{n-1}, \qquad n \ge 1,$$
with initial values $u_0$ and $u_1$. Let
$$E = \{u_n : n \ge 0\} \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$$
denote the set of values taken by this sequence, and consider the $\mathbb{Z}$-module of integer-valued polynomials on $E$,
$$\operatorname{Int}(E; \mathbb{Z}) = \{ f(X) \in \mathbb{Q}[X] : f(E) \subseteq \mathbb{Z} \}.$$
A sequence of polynomials $(f_n)_{n \ge 0}$ in $\operatorname{Int}(E; \mathbb{Z})$ is called a regular basis of this $\mathbb{Z}$-module if it is a $\mathbb{Z}$-basis and $\deg f_n = n$ for every $n \ge 0$.

Construct an explicit regular basis of the $\mathbb{Z}$-module $\operatorname{Int}(E; \mathbb{Z})$ in terms of the parameters $a, b, u_0, u_1$.

Let $E$ be a recursive (i.e., computable) subset of $\mathbb{Z}$. Define
$$\mathrm{Int}(E;\mathbb{Z}) \;=\; \{\, f \in \mathbb{Q}[X] : f(a) \in \mathbb{Z} \text{ for every } a \in E \,\},$$
the ring of integer-valued polynomials on $E$. For each integer $n \ge 0$, let $\mathcal{I}_n(E)$ denote the fractional ideal of $\mathbb{Z}$ consisting of $0$ together with the leading coefficients of those elements of $\mathrm{Int}(E;\mathbb{Z})$ that have degree at most $n$.

Fix a prime $p$ and write $v_p$ for the $p$-adic valuation, extended to nonzero fractional ideals of $\mathbb{Z}$ in the natural way (so $v_p(\mathcal{I}_n(E))$ is the unique integer $k$ with $\mathcal{I}_n(E) \otimes \mathbb{Z}_{(p)} = p^{k}\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$). The characteristic sequence of $\mathrm{Int}(E;\mathbb{Z})$ at $p$ is the sequence
$$\alpha_p(n) \;=\; -\,v_p\!\bigl(\mathcal{I}_n(E)\bigr), \qquad n = 0, 1, 2, \dots .$$

Problem. Give an effective procedure (e.g., a recursive description, closed form, or algorithm) that, given the recursive set $E$ and the prime $p$, computes the characteristic sequence $\bigl(\alpha_p(n)\bigr)_{n \ge 0}$.

Fix a prime number p and an integer d ≥ 2. Let E denote the subset of nonnegative integers consisting of all d-th powers,
   E = { k^d : k ∈ ℤ_{≥0} } ⊂ ℤ.
For each integer n ≥ 0, consider the fractional ideal
   I_n(E) = { leading coefficient of f : f ∈ ℚ[X], deg f ≤ n, and f(E) ⊆ ℤ } ∪ {0} ⊂ ℚ,
i.e. the ideal of leading coefficients of integer-valued polynomials on E of degree at most n. Define the p-adic characteristic sequence of E by
   α(n) = α_{p,d}(n) := − v_p( I_n(E) ),
where v_p is the p-adic valuation (and v_p of a fractional ideal is the minimum of v_p over its nonzero elements). The sequence (α(n))_{n ≥ 0} is known to be superadditive (α(m+n) ≥ α(m) + α(n)) and bounded by a linear function of n, so by Fekete's subadditive lemma the limit
   L(p,d) := lim_{n → ∞} α(n)/n
exists in [0, ∞).

Determine, as a function of the prime p and the exponent d, the value of L(p,d). In particular, give a closed-form expression (or explicit formula) for lim_{n → ∞} α(n)/n.

Let $S = [0,\ell] \times [0,\ell]$ be a closed square of side length $\ell > 0$ in the Euclidean plane. A subset $B \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ is called an opaque barrier (or opaque set) for $S$ if every straight line in the plane that meets $S$ also meets $B$. Restrict attention to opaque barriers $B$ that are rectifiable and consist of exactly two connected components.

Among all such two-component opaque barriers for $S$, consider the following candidate $B_0$:
- Three vertices of $S$ are joined by their (interior) Steiner tree: the unique tree inside $S$ with one Steiner point at which three segments meet pairwise at $120^\circ$ angles, connecting those three vertices.
- The remaining (fourth) vertex of $S$ is joined to the center of $S$ by a straight segment (a "half-diagonal"), forming the second connected component.

The total length of $B_0$ equals
$$\mathcal{H}^1(B_0) \;=\; \frac{2+\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{2}}\,\ell \;\approx\; 2.6389\,\ell.$$

Question: Is $B_0$ the shortest possible opaque barrier for $S$ among all opaque barriers with exactly two connected components? Equivalently, prove or disprove that for every two-component opaque barrier $B$ of $S$ one has $\mathcal{H}^1(B) \geq \frac{2+\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{2}}\,\ell$.

Every strongly $n$-absorbing ideal is clearly $n$-absorbing. Determine whether the converse holds: must every $n$-absorbing ideal of an arbitrary commutative ring $R$ be strongly $n$-absorbing?

A proper ideal $I$ of $R$ is called strongly $n$-absorbing if whenever $I_1, I_2, \ldots, I_{n+1}$ are ideals of $R$ with $I_1 I_2 \cdots I_{n+1} \subseteq I$, then there exist $n$ of these ideals whose product is contained in $I$.

Every strongly $n$-absorbing ideal is clearly $n$-absorbing. Determine whether the converse holds: must every $n$-absorbing ideal of an arbitrary commutative ring $R$ be strongly $n$-absorbing?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The equivalence was known in special cases (e.g., Prüfer domains, and for n=2 by Anderson–Badawi). A 2023 arXiv preprint by Spencer Secord (arXiv:2305.03878) claims a proof that every n-absorbing ideal of a commutative ring is strongly n-absorbing, resolving the first of the Anderson–Badawi conjectures. As this result is a recent preprint and its peer-reviewed status is unclear, the problem is best classified as partially solved pending verification.

Let f : R^n → R be a twice continuously differentiable (possibly nonconvex) function bounded below, and consider the unconstrained minimization problem min_{x ∈ R^n} f(x). The Polak–Ribière–Polyak (PRP) nonlinear conjugate gradient method generates a sequence {x_k} by

  x_{k+1} = x_k + α_k d_k,

where g_k = ∇f(x_k), the search directions are

  d_1 = -g_1,   d_{k+1} = -g_{k+1} + β_k^{PRP} d_k,   β_k^{PRP} = (g_{k+1}^T (g_{k+1} - g_k)) / ‖g_k‖^2,

and the step length α_k > 0 is chosen by the weak Wolfe–Powell (WWP) line search: given constants 0 < δ < σ < 1,

  f(x_k + α_k d_k) ≤ f(x_k) + δ α_k g_k^T d_k,
  g(x_k + α_k d_k)^T d_k ≥ σ g_k^T d_k.

It is known (Powell, Dai) that the standard PRP method with exact line search may fail to converge globally on nonconvex functions, which in turn prevents convergence under the WWP rule.

Question. Does there exist a PRP-type conjugate gradient algorithm (possibly modifying the update rule of x_{k+1} or the line search using auxiliary mechanisms such as projections) that, when applied with the weak Wolfe–Powell line search to a general twice continuously differentiable nonconvex function f bounded below with Lipschitz continuous gradient, achieves global convergence in the sense liminf_{k → ∞} ‖g_k‖ = 0?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The question is the Anderson–Badawi conjecture on polynomial extensions of n-absorbing ideals. It has been verified in several special cases (e.g., when R is a Prüfer domain, when R is a Gaussian ring with torsion-free additive group, and when R has torsion-free additive group with I a radical ideal), but no proof or counterexample for arbitrary commutative rings appears in the literature, so the general case remains open.

Consider an iterative algorithm for the unconstrained optimization problem

   minimize f(x),  x ∈ ℝⁿ,

where f : ℝⁿ → ℝ is continuously differentiable (and, where needed, twice continuously differentiable). A projection-based variant of such an algorithm (for example, a Polak–Ribière–Polyak conjugate-gradient method or a BFGS quasi-Newton method under a weak Wolfe–Powell line search) generates a sequence of iterates {xₖ} together with search directions {dₖ} and step lengths {αₖ}, and classifies each iterate xₖ as an "in-point" or an "out-point" according to a chosen scalar boundary condition B(xₖ, dₖ, ∇f(xₖ), …) ⋛ 0. In-points are kept as ordinary iterates, while out-points are replaced by a projection step designed to restore descent and to guarantee global convergence (including in nonconvex settings, where standard examples show that circle-type cycling can occur).

A particular boundary condition has been used in such a projection scheme to separate the in-points from the out-points and to ensure global convergence under the weak Wolfe–Powell line search. The problem is the following:

Determine whether there exist boundary conditions, essentially different from the one just described, that

  (i) partition the iterates into in-points and out-points in such a way that the resulting projection-based modification of the algorithm is well-defined,
  (ii) preserve sufficient descent and the standard step-length and direction properties of the underlying method, and
  (iii) yield global convergence of the algorithm for general (possibly nonconvex) continuously differentiable objective functions f under the weak Wolfe–Powell line search.

Exhibit such an alternative boundary condition explicitly and prove the corresponding convergence theorem, or otherwise characterize the class of admissible boundary conditions that can effectively separate the in-points from the out-points in this projection framework.

Let $R$ be an integral domain. Call $R$ stable if every nonzero ideal $I$ of $R$ is invertible in its endomorphism ring $E(I) := (I : I) = \{x \in \mathrm{Frac}(R) : xI \subseteq I\}$. Call $R$ Archimedean if $\bigcap_{n \geq 1} a^n R = 0$ for every nonunit $a \in R$.

Is it true that every stable Archimedean integral domain has Krull dimension equal to $1$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

Subsequent work on finitely stable and stable domains (notably by Gabelli–Roitman) exhibits an example of an Archimedean stable Prüfer domain that is not one-dimensional, answering the question in the negative. Positive results hold in special cases (e.g., the semilocal case, and Archimedean Prüfer domains of finite character with finitely many height-one primes), but the general question has a negative answer.

Let $D$ be an integral domain with quotient field $K$. For a nonzero fractional ideal $I$ of $D$, write $I^{-1} = (D:I) = \{x \in K : xI \subseteq D\}$ and $I_v = (I^{-1})^{-1}$; the ideal $I$ is called divisorial if $I = I_v$. A nonzero ideal $I$ is said to be $2$-$v$-generated if there exist $x, y \in I$ such that $I_v = (x,y)_v$. The domain $D$ is called a Mori domain if it satisfies the ascending chain condition on divisorial (integral) ideals.

For a nonzero fractional ideal $I$, let $E(I) = (I:I) = \{x \in K : xI \subseteq I\}$. A nonzero ideal $I$ of $D$ is called $v$-invertible if $(I\,I^{-1})_v = D$, and $v$-stable if $I_v$ is $v$-invertible as an ideal of the overring $E(I_v)$. The domain $D$ is called $v$-stable if every nonzero ideal of $D$ is $v$-stable.

Question: Let $D$ be a Mori domain in which every divisorial ideal is $2$-$v$-generated. Must $D$ be $v$-stable?

Let $D$ be an integral domain with quotient field $K$, and let $S$ be a multiplicatively closed subset of $D$. Let $D_S$ denote the localization of $D$ at $S$, and let $X$ be an indeterminate over $K$. Consider the subring
$$R \;=\; D + X\,D_S[X]$$
of $D_S[X]$, consisting of polynomials in $D_S[X]$ whose constant term lies in $D$.

Recall the $v$-operation on a domain $A$ with quotient field $K$: for a nonzero fractional ideal $I$ of $A$, $I^{-1} = (A:I) = \{x\in K : xI\subseteq A\}$ and $I_v = (I^{-1})^{-1}$. A nonzero fractional ideal $I$ is called $v$-invertible if $(II^{-1})_v = A$, and $A$ is called a $v$-domain if every nonzero finitely generated (fractional) ideal of $A$ is $v$-invertible.

(a) Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on $D$ and $S$ for $R = D + X\,D_S[X]$ to be a $v$-domain.

(b) Prove or disprove the following conjecture: $R$ is a $v$-domain if and only if $D$ is a $v$-domain and the ideal $(d, X)$ of $R$ is $v$-invertible for every nonzero $d \in D$.

Let $(L,\le)$ be a complete lattice, i.e., a partially ordered set in which every subset has a supremum and an infimum. A subset $D\subseteq L$ is directed if it is nonempty and every pair of elements of $D$ has an upper bound in $D$. A subset $U\subseteq L$ is Scott open if (i) $U$ is an upper set ($x\in U$ and $x\le y$ imply $y\in U$), and (ii) for every directed set $D\subseteq L$ with $\sup D\in U$, one has $D\cap U\neq\emptyset$. The collection $\sigma(L)$ of Scott open sets is a topology on $L$, and the resulting space $\Sigma L=(L,\sigma(L))$ is called the Scott space of $L$.

A topological space $X$ is sober if every nonempty irreducible closed subset of $X$ (a closed set $A$ that is not the union of two proper closed subsets) is the closure $\overline{\{x\}}$ of a unique point $x\in X$. Otherwise $X$ is non-sober.

Question: Does there exist a countable complete lattice $L$ such that the Scott space $\Sigma L=(L,\sigma(L))$ is non-sober?

For a commutative ring R with finite Krull dimension, let dim(R) denote its Krull dimension and let R[X] denote the polynomial ring in one indeterminate over R. Recall:
- An integral domain D is a Krull domain if there is a family {V_i}_{i∈I} of discrete valuation rings of the field of fractions of D such that D = ∩_i V_i, and every nonzero element of D is a non-unit in only finitely many V_i.
- An integral domain D is a factorial domain (unique factorization domain) if every nonzero non-unit factors uniquely (up to units and order) into irreducible elements.

It is known that for any integral domain D of finite Krull dimension, 1 + dim(D) ≤ dim(D[X]) ≤ 1 + 2·dim(D).

Question: Does there exist a Krull domain D — or, more particularly, a factorial domain D — of finite Krull dimension such that
    1 + dim(D) < dim(D[X])?

Background and definitions.

(1) Jaffard domain. An integral domain $R$ of finite Krull dimension $n$ is called a Jaffard domain if its valuative dimension $\dim_v(R)$ equals $\dim(R)=n$, where $\dim_v(R)$ is the supremum of the Krull dimensions of all valuation overrings of $R$ contained in the quotient field of $R$.

(2) Locally Jaffard domain. $R$ is said to be locally Jaffard if for every prime ideal $P$ of $R$ the localization $R_P$ is a Jaffard domain (equivalently, $R[X_1,\dots,X_n]$ is a Jaffard domain for every $n\ge 0$).

(3) David's example. There exists an example, due to a construction of J.~David, of a $3$-dimensional factorial (UFD) integral domain $J$ obtained as the ascending union $J=\bigcup_{n\ge 1} J_n$ of a chain $J_1\subseteq J_2\subseteq \cdots$ of $3$-dimensional Noetherian (in fact regular) factorial domains, with the property that $J$ itself is non-Noetherian and serves as a counterexample to several finiteness questions in the theory of factorial domains.

Problem. For this $3$-dimensional factorial ascending-union domain $J=\bigcup_{n\ge 1} J_n$, determine whether $J$ is a locally Jaffard domain.

Let $X$ be a $T_0$ topological space. A subset $A\subseteq X$ is called saturated if it equals the intersection of its open neighborhoods (equivalently, $A$ is an upper set with respect to the specialization order). A nonempty closed set $C\subseteq X$ is called irreducible if $C=C_1\cup C_2$ with $C_1,C_2$ closed implies $C=C_1$ or $C=C_2$.

A family $\mathcal{K}$ of nonempty compact saturated subsets of $X$ is called filtered if for any $K_1,K_2\in\mathcal{K}$ there exists $K_3\in\mathcal{K}$ with $K_3\subseteq K_1\cap K_2$. A closed set $A\subseteq X$ is said to have the Rudin property if there exists a filtered family $\mathcal{K}$ of nonempty compact saturated subsets of $X$ such that $A$ is a minimal closed set meeting every member of $\mathcal{K}$ (i.e., $A\cap K\neq\emptyset$ for every $K\in\mathcal{K}$, and no proper closed subset of $A$ has this property).

The space $X$ is called a Rudin space if every irreducible closed subset of $X$ has the Rudin property.

Recall that $X$ is called core compact if its open-set lattice $\mathcal{O}(X)$ is a continuous lattice; equivalently, for every open set $U$ and every $x\in U$ there exists an open set $V$ with $x\in V$ and $V\ll U$, where $V\ll U$ means that every open cover of $U$ has a finite subfamily covering $V$.

Let $R$ be a commutative Noetherian ring and let $I \subseteq R$ be an ideal. An element $x \in R$ is called integral over $I$ if it satisfies an equation of the form
$$x^n + a_1 x^{n-1} + a_2 x^{n-2} + \cdots + a_n = 0$$
with $a_i \in I^i$ for each $i = 1, \dots, n$. The set of all such elements forms an ideal $\overline{I}$, the integral closure of $I$. Equivalently, $\overline{I}$ can be recovered from the integral closure of the Rees algebra $R[It] = \bigoplus_{n \ge 0} I^n t^n$ inside $R[t]$, since this integral closure is $\bigoplus_{n \ge 0} \overline{I^n}\, t^n$.

The standard algorithmic approach to computing $\overline{I}$ proceeds by first computing the integral closure (normalization) of the entire Rees algebra $R[It]$ and then extracting the degree-one piece.

Problem. Does there exist an algorithm that computes the integral closure $\overline{I}$ of a general ideal $I$ in a more direct fashion than by first computing the integral closure of the whole Rees algebra $R[It]$?

For a $T_0$ space $X$ and a nonempty subset $A\subseteq X$, $A$ is said to be well-filtered determined (or $\mathbf{Top}_w$-determined) if for every well-filtered space $Y$ and every continuous map $f\colon X\to Y$, there exists a (necessarily unique) point $y_A\in Y$ such that $\overline{f(A)} = \overline{\{y_A\}}$.

Let $\{X_i\}_{i\in I}$ be a family of $T_0$ spaces and form the product space $X=\prod_{i\in I} X_i$ with the product topology. Suppose that for each $i\in I$, a subset $A_i\subseteq X_i$ is well-filtered determined in $X_i$.

Question: Must the product subset $\prod_{i\in I} A_i \subseteq X$ be well-filtered determined in $X$?

Consider the Segre variety $\mathbb{P}^3 \times \mathbb{P}^3 \times \mathbb{P}^3 \hookrightarrow \mathbb{P}(\mathbb{C}^4 \otimes \mathbb{C}^4 \otimes \mathbb{C}^4) = \mathbb{P}^{63}$, embedded by sending $([u],[v],[w])$ to $[u\otimes v\otimes w]$. Let $\sigma_4 = \sigma_4(\mathbb{P}^3 \times \mathbb{P}^3 \times \mathbb{P}^3)$ denote its fourth secant variety, i.e. the Zariski closure of the set of tensors in $\mathbb{C}^4\otimes\mathbb{C}^4\otimes\mathbb{C}^4$ of tensor rank at most $4$. Statistically, $\sigma_4$ is the model of joint distributions $(p_{ijk})_{i,j,k=1}^{4}$ of three observed four-state random variables $X_1,X_2,X_3$ that are conditionally independent given a hidden four-state random variable $Y$ (the naive Bayes model $[X_1 \perp\!\!\!\perp X_2 \perp\!\!\!\perp X_3 \mid Y]$).

Two families of $\mathrm{GL}_4 \times \mathrm{GL}_4 \times \mathrm{GL}_4$-invariant polynomials are known to vanish on $\sigma_4$: certain degree-$5$ invariants coming from Strassen-type commutation conditions, and certain degree-$9$ invariants coming from symmetrization (Strassen/Landsberg–Manivel-type) conditions.

Questions:
(a) Do the degree-$5$ and degree-$9$ invariants together cut out $\sigma_4$ set-theoretically as a subvariety of $\mathbb{P}^{63}$?
(b) Do they generate the homogeneous prime ideal of $\sigma_4$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The set-theoretic version (the "Salmon Conjecture") was established by Friedland and Gross, who proved that $\sigma_4(\mathbb{P}^3\times\mathbb{P}^3\times\mathbb{P}^3)$ is cut out set-theoretically by polynomial equations of degrees $5$, $6$, and $9$ (with the degree-$6$ Landsberg–Manivel polynomials needed in addition to the degree $5$ and $9$ invariants originally proposed). Thus the degree-$5$ and degree-$9$ invariants alone are not known to suffice set-theoretically. The ideal-theoretic version (the original "Salmon Prize" problem of E. Allman) remains open.

Let $X$ be a $T_0$ topological space, and let $\mathcal{O}(X)$ denote the lattice of open subsets of $X$. Recall that a family $\mathcal{H}\subseteq \mathcal{O}(X)$ is Scott-open if (i) it is an upper set (i.e., $U\in\mathcal{H}$ and $U\subseteq V\in\mathcal{O}(X)$ imply $V\in\mathcal{H}$) and (ii) whenever a directed family of open sets has union in $\mathcal{H}$, some member already lies in $\mathcal{H}$. For a compact saturated subset $K\subseteq X$ (saturated meaning $K$ equals the intersection of its open neighborhoods), define $\Phi(K)=\{U\in\mathcal{O}(X): K\subseteq U\}$. The space $X$ is called consonant if every Scott-open family $\mathcal{H}\subseteq \mathcal{O}(X)$ is a union of sets of the form $\Phi(K)$ for compact saturated $K\subseteq X$.

The Smyth power space $P_S(X)$ has underlying set the collection of all nonempty compact saturated subsets of $X$, equipped with the topology generated by the basic open sets $\square U=\{K\in P_S(X): K\subseteq U\}$ for $U\in\mathcal{O}(X)$.

Question: If $X$ is a consonant $T_0$ space, must the Smyth power space $P_S(X)$ also be consonant?

Let $\mathbf{Top}_0$ denote the category of $T_0$ topological spaces with continuous maps. A full subcategory $\mathbf{K}$ of $\mathbf{Top}_0$ is called a reflective subcategory if the inclusion functor has a left adjoint, called the $\mathbf{K}$-reflection; for each $T_0$ space $X$, this yields a space $X^{\mathbf{K}} \in \mathbf{K}$ and a continuous map $\eta_X : X \to X^{\mathbf{K}}$ universal among continuous maps from $X$ to objects of $\mathbf{K}$.

For a $T_0$ space $X$, let $\mathcal{H}(X)$ denote the irreducible-closed-subsets approach: equip the set of nonempty closed subsets of $X$ with the lower Vietoris-type topology generated by $\{A \subseteq X : A \cap U \neq \emptyset\}$ for $U$ open in $X$, and let $P_H(X)$ denote the resulting space (the Smyth/Hoare-type hyperspace as used for K-reflections). Call $\mathbf{K}$ adequate if $\mathbf{K}$ is a full subcategory of $\mathbf{Top}_0$ closed under homeomorphisms such that for every $T_0$ space $X$, the canonical subspace $P_H(\mathbf{K}(X))$ associated with the $\mathbf{K}$-reflection construction is itself an object of $\mathbf{K}$ (so that the standard construction produces a reflection). Examples of adequate categories include the categories of sober spaces, $d$-spaces, well-filtered spaces, and the Keimel–Lawson category.

Question: Suppose $\mathbf{K}$ is an adequate full subcategory of $\mathbf{Top}_0$ that is closed under homeomorphisms. Does the $\mathbf{K}$-reflection functor preserve arbitrary products of $T_0$ spaces? Equivalently, for every family $\{X_i\}_{i \in I}$ of $T_0$ spaces, is the canonical continuous map
$$\Big(\prod_{i \in I} X_i\Big)^{\mathbf{K}} \longrightarrow \prod_{i \in I} X_i^{\mathbf{K}}$$
a homeomorphism?

Let $\Sigma = (\sigma_{ij})$ be a $5 \times 5$ real symmetric positive definite matrix, regarded as the covariance matrix of a centered multivariate Gaussian random vector $(X_1, \ldots, X_5)$. For disjoint $K \subset \{1,2,3,4,5\}$ and $i, j \in \{1,2,3,4,5\} \setminus K$ with $i \ne j$, the almost-principal minor $[i \perp\!\!\!\perp j \mid K]$ is defined as the determinant of the submatrix of $\Sigma$ with row index set $\{i\} \cup K$ and column index set $\{j\} \cup K$. It is known that $[i \perp\!\!\!\perp j \mid K] = 0$ if and only if $X_i$ and $X_j$ are conditionally independent given the random vector $(X_k)_{k \in K}$.

Determine, combinatorially, all subsets $\mathcal{S}$ of the set of triples $\{(i,j \mid K) : i \ne j,\ K \subseteq \{1,\ldots,5\} \setminus \{i,j\}\}$ for which there exists a positive definite symmetric $5 \times 5$ matrix $\Sigma$ such that $[i \perp\!\!\!\perp j \mid K] = 0$ if and only if $(i,j \mid K) \in \mathcal{S}$. In other words, classify all realizable conditional independence patterns (zero sets of almost-principal minors) for $5 \times 5$ Gaussian covariance matrices.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The problem of classifying zero patterns of almost-principal minors of 5×5 positive definite covariance matrices is closely related to the realizability problem for gaussoids on 5 elements. Boege, D'Alì, Kahle and Sturmfels (FoCM 2019, "The Geometry of Gaussoids") gave a census of gaussoids for n=5 via SAT computations and classified small realizable and non-realizable gaussoids, but gaussoids are only a combinatorial axiomatization (they coincide with realizable patterns for n ≤ 4 but not in general), and a complete intrinsic characterization of realizable patterns for n=5 has not been established. The problem remains partially solved.

Background and definitions. A topological space $X$ is called $T_0$ if for any two distinct points there is an open set containing exactly one of them. For a $T_0$ space $X$, write $\mathcal{O}(X)$ for its topology and let $\mathrm{Irr}_c(X)$ denote the set of irreducible closed subsets. A subset $K\subseteq X$ is called compact saturated if it is compact and equal to the intersection of all open sets containing it. A $T_0$ space $X$ is called well-filtered (WF) if, for every filtered family $\{K_i\}_{i\in I}$ of compact saturated subsets of $X$ and every open set $U$ with $\bigcap_{i\in I} K_i \subseteq U$, there exists $i_0\in I$ with $K_{i_0}\subseteq U$.

Let $\mathbf{Top}_0$ denote the category of $T_0$ spaces with continuous maps, and let $\mathbf{Top}_w$ denote its full subcategory consisting of well-filtered spaces. The subcategory $\mathbf{Top}_w$ is reflective in $\mathbf{Top}_0$: for each $T_0$ space $X$ there exist a well-filtered space $X^w$ and a continuous map $\eta_X\colon X\to X^w$ such that every continuous map from $X$ to a well-filtered space factors uniquely through $\eta_X$. The assignment $X\mapsto X^w$ extends to a functor (the well-filtered reflection functor) from $\mathbf{Top}_0$ to $\mathbf{Top}_w$, left adjoint to the inclusion.

Question. Does the well-filtered reflection functor preserve arbitrary products? Equivalently, for every family $\{X_i\}_{i\in I}$ of $T_0$ spaces, is the canonical continuous map
$$\Big(\prod_{i\in I} X_i\Big)^{w} \longrightarrow \prod_{i\in I} X_i^{w}$$
induced by the universal property a homeomorphism?

Let $(M^n, g)$ be a complete noncompact Riemannian manifold. A function $u:M\to\mathbb{R}$ is harmonic if $\Delta_g u = 0$, where $\Delta_g$ is the Laplace–Beltrami operator. For a fixed basepoint $p\in M$ and $d\geq 0$, let $\mathcal{H}_d(M)$ denote the space of harmonic functions $u$ on $M$ satisfying $|u(x)|\leq C(1+\operatorname{dist}(x,p))^d$ for some constant $C=C(u)$.

Address the following two questions:

(A) Bounded harmonic functions / Dirichlet problem at infinity. Suppose $M$ is simply connected with sectional curvature bounded between two negative constants, $-b^2 \leq \mathrm{Sec}_M \leq -a^2 < 0$. The geometric boundary at infinity $\partial_\infty M$ is defined as equivalence classes of geodesic rays under the relation of being asymptotic, equipped with the cone topology so that $\overline{M} = M \cup \partial_\infty M$ becomes a compact topological space homeomorphic to a closed ball. The Dirichlet problem at infinity asks: for every continuous function $f:\partial_\infty M\to\mathbb{R}$, does there exist a unique harmonic function $u\in C^\infty(M)\cap C^0(\overline{M})$ with $u|_{\partial_\infty M}=f$? Characterize, in geometric terms, the classes of complete noncompact negatively curved manifolds for which this Dirichlet problem at infinity is solvable, and describe the structure of the space of bounded harmonic functions on such manifolds.

(B) Harmonic functions of polynomial growth. Suppose $M$ has nonnegative Ricci curvature (or, more generally, satisfies appropriate volume-doubling and Poincaré-type hypotheses). Determine the dimension and structure of $\mathcal{H}_d(M)$: in particular, establish whether $\dim \mathcal{H}_d(M) < \infty$ for every $d\geq 0$, give sharp dimension bounds in terms of $n$ and $d$, and describe the asymptotic structure of elements of $\mathcal{H}_d(M)$ (for instance via separation-of-variables-type expansions on asymptotic cones).

Let M be a complete Riemannian manifold. Recall that for a locally symmetric space of noncompact type, the rank is the maximal dimension of a flat totally geodesic subspace of its universal cover, and that for a nonpositively curved manifold the rank of a geodesic c in the universal cover is defined as the dimension of the space of parallel Jacobi fields along c, with the rank of the manifold being the minimum of these ranks over all geodesics. A manifold is said to have higher rank if its rank is at least 2, and rank one otherwise.

(a) Formulate a notion of rank for general Riemannian manifolds (not assumed to be of nonpositive curvature or locally symmetric) that specializes to the classical rank for symmetric spaces of noncompact type, and prove rigidity theorems analogous to Mostow strong rigidity: namely, that closed manifolds of higher rank are, up to suitable equivalence, locally symmetric.

(b) Provide a complete classification, up to isometry, of closed irreducible Riemannian manifolds of nonpositive sectional curvature having higher rank, beyond the known case where such manifolds are locally symmetric spaces of noncompact type.

(c) Give a structural characterization of closed rank-one Riemannian manifolds of nonpositive sectional curvature, describing their geometric, dynamical, and topological properties in a way that parallels what is known for manifolds of strictly negative curvature.

Let $X$ be a compact complex Kähler manifold, and let $L \to X$ be an ample line bundle (a polarization). Recall the following notions:

(a) A Kähler metric $\omega$ on $X$ is called Kähler–Einstein if $\mathrm{Ric}(\omega) = \lambda\,\omega$ for some real constant $\lambda$; more generally, a Kähler metric $\omega \in c_1(L)$ is said to have constant scalar curvature (cscK) if its scalar curvature is constant.

(b) A holomorphic vector bundle $E \to X$ is slope-stable (with respect to $L$) if for every coherent subsheaf $\mathcal{F} \subset E$ with $0 < \mathrm{rank}(\mathcal{F}) < \mathrm{rank}(E)$ one has $\mu_L(\mathcal{F}) < \mu_L(E)$, where $\mu_L(\cdot) = \deg_L(\cdot)/\mathrm{rank}(\cdot)$.

(c) The polarized manifold $(X,L)$ is K-stable if for every nontrivial test configuration $(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{L})$ for $(X,L)$ the Donaldson–Futaki invariant satisfies $\mathrm{DF}(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{L}) > 0$ (with appropriate normalizations such as uniform or reduced K-stability when automorphisms are present).

Problem. Determine the precise relationship between the existence of canonical Kähler metrics and algebro-geometric stability:

(1) Prove that if $X$ admits a Kähler–Einstein metric, then its holomorphic tangent bundle $T_X$ is slope-polystable with respect to the relevant polarization, and identify the sharpest hypotheses under which this implication and its variants hold.

(2) For an arbitrary polarized Kähler manifold $(X,L)$, establish the equivalence
$$(X,L)\ \text{admits a cscK metric in } c_1(L) \iff (X,L)\ \text{is K-stable (in a suitable uniform/reduced sense)},$$
specializing to: $X$ Fano admits a Kähler–Einstein metric iff $(X,-K_X)$ is K-stable.

Provide a complete characterization, including necessary and sufficient conditions linking existence of Kähler–Einstein / cscK metrics to stability of $(X,L)$ and of $T_X$.

Let X be a T0 topological space. A nonempty subset A of X is called irreducible if whenever A is contained in the union of two closed sets, it is contained in one of them. A subset is saturated if it equals the intersection of its open neighborhoods (equivalently, it is an upper set in the specialization order). Denote by K(X) the collection of all nonempty compact saturated subsets of X. For x in X, write ↑x for the saturation {y in X : x ≤ y in the specialization order}.

Call a nonempty compact saturated subset K of X k-irreducible if, whenever K = K1 ∪ K2 with K1, K2 nonempty compact saturated, then K = K1 or K = K2. The space X is called co-sober if every k-irreducible member of K(X) is of the form ↑x for a unique x in X.

The Smyth power space PS(X) is the set K(X) equipped with the upper Vietoris topology, generated by the sets ☐U := {K in K(X) : K ⊆ U} as U ranges over open subsets of X.

Question: If X is a co-sober T0 space, must its Smyth power space PS(X) again be co-sober?

representations.normalized:
Let $X$ be a Calabi–Yau $n$-fold, i.e. a compact Kähler manifold of complex dimension $n$ with trivial canonical bundle and a Ricci-flat Kähler metric. Mirror symmetry predicts the existence of a "mirror" Calabi–Yau $n$-fold $X^\vee$ such that the complex geometry of $X$ is exchanged with the symplectic geometry of $X^\vee$ (in particular, the Hodge numbers satisfy $h^{p,q}(X) = h^{n-p,q}(X^\vee)$, and the A-model on $X$ is equivalent to the B-model on $X^\vee$).

The Strominger–Yau–Zaslow (SYZ) proposal asserts that, near a large complex structure limit point in the moduli space, $X$ admits a special Lagrangian torus fibration $\pi : X \to B$ over a real $n$-dimensional base $B$ (with singular fibers over a discriminant locus), and that the mirror $X^\vee$ can be constructed as the fiberwise dual fibration $\pi^\vee : X^\vee \to B$, obtained by replacing each smooth special Lagrangian torus fiber $T \subset X$ with its dual torus $\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_1(T), U(1))$, with suitable instanton corrections accounting for the singular fibers.

Problem. Carry out the SYZ program rigorously and explicitly for the relevant classes of Calabi–Yau manifolds. Specifically:

(a) Prove that a Calabi–Yau $n$-fold $X$ near a large complex structure limit admits a special Lagrangian torus fibration $\pi: X \to B$, and describe the structure of its discriminant locus and singular fibers.

(b) Give an explicit construction of the mirror manifold $X^\vee$ as a (suitably corrected) dual special Lagrangian torus fibration over the same base $B$, and prove that the result is a Calabi–Yau manifold mirror to $X$ in the sense of mirror symmetry (e.g., matching Hodge numbers, Yukawa couplings, or yielding a derived equivalence of categories).

(c) Use the construction to clarify the geometric mechanism underlying mirror symmetry.

Background and definitions. Let $X$ be a topological space. A nonempty closed subset $A\subseteq X$ is called irreducible if whenever $A=B\cup C$ with $B,C$ closed, then $A=B$ or $A=C$. The space $X$ is sober if it is $T_0$ and every irreducible closed subset is the closure $\overline{\{x\}}$ of a unique point $x\in X$.

A subset $K\subseteq X$ is saturated if $K$ equals the intersection of all open sets containing it (equivalently, $K$ is an upper set in the specialization order $\leq$ defined by $x\leq y\iff x\in\overline{\{y\}}$). A nonempty compact saturated subset $K\subseteq X$ is called $k$-irreducible (or supercompact / irreducible compact saturated) if whenever $K\subseteq U\cup V$ with $U,V$ open, then $K\subseteq U$ or $K\subseteq V$. The space $X$ is called co-sober if it is $T_0$ and every $k$-irreducible compact saturated subset of $X$ is of the form ${\uparrow}x=\{y\in X: x\leq y\}$ for some (necessarily unique) $x\in X$.

A subspace $Y\subseteq X$ is called a retract of $X$ if there exists a continuous map $r:X\to Y$, called a retraction, such that $r(y)=y$ for every $y\in Y$ (equivalently, $r\circ i=\mathrm{id}_Y$ where $i:Y\hookrightarrow X$ is the inclusion).

Problem. Suppose $X$ is a co-sober $T_0$ topological space and $Y\subseteq X$ is a retract of $X$ (in particular, $Y$ is then a $T_0$ space in the subspace topology). Must $Y$ also be co-sober?

A nonempty compact saturated subset $K\subseteq X$ is called $k$-irreducible (or supercompact / irreducible compact saturated) if whenever $K\subseteq U\cup V$ with $U,V$ open, then $K\subseteq U$ or $K\subseteq V$. The space $X$ is called co-sober if it is $T_0$ and every $k$-irreducible compact saturated subset of $X$ is of the form ${\uparrow}x=\{y\in X: x\leq y\}$ for some (necessarily unique) $x\in X$.

A subspace $Y\subseteq X$ is called a retract of $X$ if there exists a continuous map $r:X\to Y$, called a retraction, such that $r(y)=y$ for every $y\in Y$ (equivalently, $r\circ i=\mathrm{id}_Y$ where $i:Y\hookrightarrow X$ is the inclusion).

Problem. Suppose $X$ is a co-sober $T_0$ topological space and $Y\subseteq X$ is a retract of $X$ (in particular, $Y$ is then a $T_0$ space in the subspace topology). Must $Y$ also be co-sober?

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

Web searches did not reveal a published resolution to the question of whether retracts of co-sober $T_0$ spaces are co-sober. Related results in the literature (e.g., closed and saturated subspaces of co-sober spaces are co-sober; not every sober space is co-sober) are known, but the specific retract problem appears to remain unresolved as of the searches performed.

Consider the problem of automatically generating mapping rules between two knowledge bases (KBs), each modeled as a set of concepts, properties, and instance data, together with a schema (metadata) layer naming the concepts and properties. A standard schema-level correspondence between a source KB S and a target KB T relates a source schema element (concept, property, or path) to a target schema element, and induces data-to-data mapping rules.

A metadata-data (MAD) correspondence, by contrast, asserts one of the following relationships:
(i) a source data value v occurring as an instance value in S must appear as a target metadata symbol in T (for example, as the name of a property or a class in T), or
(ii) a target data value must be produced from a source metadata symbol (for example, the name of a property in S must appear as data in T).

Develop a formal framework and algorithm for knowledge-base mapping generation that, given a set of correspondences between S and T including MAD correspondences, produces executable mapping rules whose execution on instances of S yields instances of T consistent with all correspondences. In particular:

1. Provide a precise semantics for MAD correspondences within a chosen KB data model (e.g., RDF/RDFS or OWL).
2. Define when a set of generated mapping rules is sound and complete with respect to a set of correspondences that may mix schema-level and MAD correspondences.
3. Give a generation procedure that handles MAD correspondences in both directions (data→metadata and metadata→data) and analyze its correctness and complexity.

Consider two knowledge bases, a source KB S and a target KB T, each described under an open-world assumption (i.e., absence of a fact is not interpreted as its negation). A schema/instance correspondence is a declarative specification of how data in S relates to data in T. Simple correspondences map a source attribute (or class) directly to a target attribute (or class). A complex correspondence is one that takes any of the following forms:

(a) Functional transformation: there is a function f such that one or more source values v1, …, vk are transformed into one or more target values f(v1, …, vk) (e.g., concatenation, splitting, type conversion, unit conversion).
(b) Filtered transfer: only those source values satisfying a predicate φ are transferred to the target.
(c) Constrained value invention: when a target individual or value must be invented (e.g., a fresh IRI), additional constraints (uniqueness, typing, functional dependencies) must be imposed on the invented term.
(d) Aggregation: a target value is obtained by an aggregate operation (sum, count, average, max, min, group-concatenation, …) over a multiset of source values, taking into account the open-world semantics of S.

Design a general framework for automatic (or semi-automatic) knowledge-base mapping generation tools that:

1. Provides a formal language able to express complex correspondences of types (a)–(d), including a precise semantics under the open-world assumption of both S and T (in particular, give an unambiguous semantics for aggregation in (d) when the source is potentially incomplete).
2. Specifies an algorithm that, given S, T, and a set of complex correspondences in this language, produces an executable mapping (e.g., in a rule language such as R2RML, SPARQL CONSTRUCT, or a Datalog-like formalism) implementing the correspondences.
3. Guarantees correctness properties such as: soundness with respect to the declared correspondences, preservation of target schema constraints introduced in (c), and a well-defined behavior of aggregates in (d) (for instance, by formally distinguishing certain answers from possible answers).

Provide such a framework, or prove that no framework simultaneously achieving (1)–(3) for all four kinds of complex correspondences (a)–(d) exists.

Let a knowledge base (KB) be a pair $K = (S, I)$ where $S$ is a schema (a finite set of classes, properties, and constraints, e.g.\ an RDF/OWL vocabulary) and $I$ is an instance: a (possibly very large, "web-scale") set of assertions over $S$ (e.g.\ RDF triples). Given two knowledge bases $K_1 = (S_1, I_1)$ and $K_2 = (S_2, I_2)$, a KB mapping is a finite set $M$ of logical rules (e.g.\ source-to-target tuple-generating dependencies, or executable transformation rules such as R2RML/SPARQL CONSTRUCT) that, when applied to $I_1$, produce data conforming to $S_2$.

Traditional schema-level mapping generation tools produce $M$ using only the schema-level correspondences $C \subseteq S_1 \times S_2$ (e.g.\ element-to-element alignments). In contrast, data-driven (example-based) mapping generation methods construct $M$ from a finite set of input/output data examples $E = \{(d_i, d_i')\}_{i=1}^n$ with $d_i$ a fragment of $I_1$ and $d_i'$ the intended fragment of $I_2$.

Problem. Design and formally characterize a mapping generation procedure $\mathcal{A}$ which, given $(S_1, S_2, C, E)$ where $E$ is drawn from web-scale instances $I_1, I_2$, outputs a KB mapping $M$ satisfying:
(i) Soundness with respect to examples: for every $(d_i, d_i') \in E$, applying $M$ to $d_i$ yields $d_i'$ (up to a specified semantic equivalence).
(ii) Generalization: $M$ correctly transforms instance fragments outside $E$ that follow the same regularities, in a precisely defined sense (e.g.\ minimality, certain-answer preservation, or PAC-style generalization over a distribution on $I_1$).
(iii) Scalability: $\mathcal{A}$ runs in time and memory sublinear (or otherwise tractable) in $|I_1| + |I_2|$, exploiting the web-scale availability of data examples rather than enumerating instances.

Provide an algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ together with formal guarantees of soundness, generalization, and tractability under explicit assumptions on $S_1, S_2, C$ and on the example sampling process, or prove impossibility results delimiting the trade-offs between (i)–(iii).

Let K_1 and K_2 be two knowledge bases, each consisting of a schema (a set of classes, properties, and logical axioms expressed in some description-logic or first-order fragment) together with an instance set (a collection of ground assertions over that schema). A correspondence is a logical relationship (e.g., subclass, equivalence, sameAs, or more general first-order implication) between symbols or compound expressions of K_1 and K_2. A mapping rule is a (possibly existential, possibly probabilistic) implication of the form φ(x) → ψ(x), where φ is a formula over the vocabulary of K_1 and ψ is a formula over the vocabulary of K_2 (or vice versa). A data example is a pair (a, b) of instances such that a ∈ K_1 and b ∈ K_2 are intended to correspond under some mapping rule.

Design and prove the existence of a Knowledge-Graph Mapping Tool (KGMT), specified as an algorithm M taking (K_1, K_2) as input and outputting a triple (C, E, R) where C is a set of correspondences, E is a set of data examples, and R is a set of mapping rules, satisfying all of the following requirements:

1. (Joint learning) The components C, E, and R are learned collectively: each is used as evidence in inferring the others, and the algorithm performs a single optimization (rather than a strict pipeline) over a joint objective combining logical entailment constraints and a statistical likelihood (e.g., via a Markov logic network, probabilistic soft logic, or analogous formalism).

2. (Logical + statistical reasoning) The objective combines hard logical constraints derived from the axioms of K_1 and K_2 with soft statistical scores derived from instance-level co-occurrence and embedding-based similarities, and admits a precise semantics (e.g., maximum a posteriori inference in a probabilistic logic).

3. (Beyond simple axioms) The output R must be expressive enough to capture deep structural and semantic heterogeneity that cannot be expressed solely by sameAs, isA (subclass), or equivalentClass axioms — for instance, n-ary relational restructurings, attribute-to-relation conversions, conditional mappings, and existential value-creating rules.

4. (Correctness guarantee) Provide a soundness and (approximate) completeness theorem with respect to a declared semantics of correct mappings between K_1 and K_2, together with complexity bounds.

The problem asks whether such an algorithm M exists, and if so, to exhibit one and prove the corresponding correctness and complexity results.

Let K_1 and K_2 be two knowledge bases, each consisting of a schema (a finite set of relation/class/property symbols together with integrity constraints) and an instance (a finite set of ground facts over the schema). A mapping rule is an expression of the form phi(x) -> psi(x), where phi is a conjunctive query over the schema of K_1 and psi is a conjunctive query over the schema of K_2, expressing how data from K_1 should be translated into data conforming to K_2. A set M of such rules is said to enable data exchange between K_1 and K_2 if, applied to the instance of K_1, it produces an instance of K_2 that satisfies the constraints of K_2 and preserves the intended semantic correspondences between the two schemas.

Suppose a candidate set M of mapping rules has been generated automatically. Design and analyze a procedure that interacts with one or more domain experts in the following way:

1. (Example selection.) Given M, the procedure must choose a finite set E of example instances (pairs of source facts and induced target facts) such that E is a sufficient illustration of M, in the sense that: (a) every rule in M is exemplified by at least one element of E (coverage), and (b) any alternative consistent rule set M' that agrees with M on E is, under a stated equivalence relation on mapping rule sets, equivalent to M (distinguishability).

2. (Presentation.) The examples in E are presented to one or more domain experts, who return feedback consisting of labels (accept/reject/correct) on individual examples or rules. The feedback may be noisy, mutually contradictory across experts, or simply incorrect.

3. (Incorporation.) Using the (possibly inconsistent) expert feedback, the procedure must update M to a refined set M* of mapping rules that (i) is consistent with as much of the trusted feedback as possible under a precise aggregation/repair semantics for conflicting inputs, (ii) still enables data exchange between K_1 and K_2 as defined above, and (iii) converges, as the interaction proceeds, to a target mapping in a precise sense (e.g., probabilistic identification in the limit, PAC-style guarantees, or minimization of an explicit loss).

The problem is to give formal definitions of "sufficient illustration", of the feedback model with contradictions and errors, and of the convergence criterion, and to exhibit an algorithm meeting all three requirements, together with provable guarantees on the quality of the refined mapping M* (e.g., bounds on the number of examples queried, robustness to a specified fraction of erroneous expert answers, and correctness of the resulting data exchange).

Let a source knowledge base S and a target knowledge base T each be specified as a set of typed entities together with a finite set of binary properties; a property path in T is a finite composition p_1 ∘ p_2 ∘ ... ∘ p_k of such properties. A source-to-target mapping is a function that assigns, to each source attribute or relation, a property path in T whose evaluation produces values of the intended type. A mapping is called ambiguous when several distinct property paths in T are type-compatible candidates for the same source attribute.

Consider the following classes of integrity constraints that may either be declared in T or be inferred automatically from instance data in T by profiling/mining procedures:
  (i) cardinality constraints on properties,
  (ii) functional-property constraints (a property is single-valued on its domain),
  (iii) inverse-functional-property constraints (the inverse is single-valued),
  (iv) disjointness constraints between classes or properties,
  (v) join-path constraints (e.g., approximate or exact inclusion dependencies between compositions of properties),
  (vi) more general mined dependencies (such as conditional functional dependencies or denial constraints).

Develop a formal framework in which such constraints are used to filter or rank candidate property paths in T for each source attribute, and prove that there exists a constraint-driven disambiguation procedure that, given any source-to-target mapping instance with at least one ambiguous property-path choice, produces a unique or strictly smaller set of candidate property paths whose induced mapping has provably higher quality (under a precisely defined quality measure, e.g., preservation of source dependencies, consistency with target constraints, and faithfulness to instance data) than mappings produced without using the constraints.

Equivalently: determine whether automatically inferred constraints of types (i)–(vi) are sufficient, in general, to resolve ambiguous property-path choices in source-to-target mappings and thereby improve mapping quality, and characterize the conditions on S, T, and the constraint set under which such improvement can be guaranteed.

Let S and T be two ontologies, each given as a set of logical axioms over a signature of classes, properties, and individuals, and let a mapping between S and T be a finite set M of rules of the form φ(x) → ψ(x), where φ is a conjunctive query over S and ψ a conjunctive query over T. Suppose one is given a finite collection of positive examples E⁺ ⊆ S × T (pairs of entities that should be linked by the mapping) and negative examples E⁻ ⊆ S × T (pairs that should not). A rule-mining algorithm A takes as input an ontology O together with a set of instance data and outputs a finite set of Horn rules (constraints) C(O) such that O ∪ C(O) remains consistent and each rule in C(O) has support and confidence above prescribed thresholds with respect to the instance data.

Question: Does there exist a rule-mining procedure A and a mapping-induction procedure F such that, for a suitable class of ontology pairs (S, T) and examples (E⁺, E⁻), the mapping
   F(S ∪ C(S), T ∪ C(T), E⁺, E⁻)
is provably superior — with respect to a fixed evaluation measure such as F-score on a held-out test set of correct correspondences — to the mapping F(S, T, E⁺, E⁻) obtained without enriching the ontologies by induced constraints? Equivalently, characterize conditions on (S, T, E⁺, E⁻) under which enrichment by mined rules strictly improves the quality of induced mapping rules, and identify a class where such improvement is impossible.

representations.normalized:
Let a knowledge base (KB) be a pair K = (I, Σ), where I is an instance (a finite set of ground facts over a relational/ontological signature) and Σ is a set of logical sentences (constraints and inference rules, e.g., tuple-generating dependencies, equality-generating dependencies, or description-logic axioms) under which the certain answers (or chase-closure) of K are defined. A source KB K_S = (I_S, Σ_S) and a target KB K_T = (I_T, Σ_T) are given, together with a schema mapping M = (Σ_ST) consisting of source-to-target dependencies. A knowledge exchange solution is a target instance J extending I_T such that (J, Σ_T) together with (I_S, Σ_ST) satisfies all dependencies, while preserving the certain-answer semantics with respect to a chosen query language.

Classical knowledge exchange assumes that the target instance I_T is empty and that Σ_T is restricted (e.g., to dependencies admitting a terminating chase). The problem is to develop a theory and algorithms for knowledge exchange in the general setting where:

(a) the target KB is already populated, i.e., I_T ≠ ∅, and may contain facts that overlap with or conflict with material induced from I_S via M;
(b) Σ_T expresses richer inference (for instance, full first-order constraints, expressive description logics such as members of the DL-Lite, EL, or SHIQ families, or existential rules beyond known decidable fragments);
(c) the construction of J must incorporate deduplication and record linkage, producing same-as (owl:sameAs-style) links that identify co-referent constants/individuals between I_S and I_T; and
(d) value-level conflicts between facts in I_T and facts derived from I_S must be resolved by an explicit conflict-resolution policy.

Formalize the notion of a "merging solution" J in this setting (existence, universality, and certain-answer preservation under M and Σ_T), characterize the complexity of computing such a solution and of answering queries over it, and provide algorithms that simultaneously perform chase-based materialization, entity resolution (production of same-as links), and value-conflict resolution while remaining sound and complete with respect to the chosen semantics.

representations.normalized:
Let a knowledge base (KB) be a pair $K = (S, A)$ where $S$ is a schema (a finite set of classes and properties with subclass/subproperty relations and domain/range constraints) and $A$ is a finite set of assertions over $S$. A mapping between two knowledge bases $K_1 = (S_1, A_1)$ and $K_2 = (S_2, A_2)$ is a finite set $M$ of mapping rules, each of the form $\varphi(\bar x) \rightsquigarrow \psi(\bar x)$, where $\varphi$ is a conjunctive query over $S_1$ and $\psi$ is a conjunctive query over $S_2$. A knowledge-base mapping generation tool (KMGT) is an algorithm that, given $K_1$ and $K_2$, outputs such a set $M$.

Consider the following scalability problem. Suppose $|S_1|, |S_2|, |A_1|, |A_2|$ are too large to be processed in memory by a direct KMGT. A simple slicing approach partitions each KB into disjoint chunks of bounded size and applies the KMGT independently to each pair of chunks; this can miss mapping rules that span chunks and can produce redundant or inconsistent rules.

Problem. Design a KMGT framework that scales to arbitrarily large source and target knowledge bases by using either
(i) modularization, in which each KB is decomposed into a family of modules $\{M_i\}$ such that for every signature $\Sigma$ of interest there exists a module $M_i$ that is a conservative extension of the relevant fragment of the KB with respect to $\Sigma$; or
(ii) partitioning, in which each KB is split into possibly overlapping parts according to a structural or semantic criterion (e.g., graph cuts on the schema graph, clustering of assertions, or locality-based partitions).

Specifically, give an algorithm together with a formal correctness and efficiency analysis establishing:
(a) Soundness: every rule produced is logically entailed by the full KBs.
(b) Completeness (relative to a specified mapping language): every rule that a non-scalable reference KMGT would produce on the entire KBs is recovered, up to logical equivalence.
(c) Scalability: the total running time and memory are sub-linear in a meaningful parameter (e.g., polynomial in the largest module/partition size and near-linear in the total KB size), strictly improving upon simple slicing.

Either exhibit such an algorithm with proofs of (a)–(c), or prove an impossibility result identifying intrinsic obstacles (e.g., that no modularization/partitioning scheme of bounded module size can preserve completeness for a given mapping language).

Consider a class of neural sequence models, referred to as Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), which are trained on large text corpora and additionally optimized to produce intermediate step-by-step "reasoning traces" (e.g., chain-of-thought or scratchpad outputs) before emitting a final answer. Let a problem family be specified by a parameter (such as instance size, recursion depth, or compositional structure) that controls its intrinsic complexity, and let an LRM's performance on the family be measured by its accuracy as a function of this complexity parameter, evaluated on instances drawn from distributions that may differ from the training distribution.

Determine whether such LRMs exhibit genuinely generalizable reasoning — meaning that they implement procedures whose accuracy remains robust as problem complexity grows and as instances move out of the training distribution — or whether their apparent reasoning improvements over standard language models are explained instead by sophisticated pattern matching, in which performance degrades systematically with increased complexity or distribution shift. Provide either: (a) a precise definition of generalizable reasoning together with theoretical or empirical demonstrations that current LRMs satisfy it across problem families of unbounded complexity; or (b) a demonstration that for every current LRM there exist problem families on which accuracy collapses as complexity increases, in a manner consistent with pattern matching rather than algorithmic reasoning.

Let a knowledge base be a set of RDF triples over an infinite set of IRIs and literals, and let a mapping rule between two such knowledge bases be a function that, given a source pattern (a conjunctive query over the source RDF graph), produces a target pattern (a set of RDF triples possibly containing variables bound by the source pattern). Consider a declarative mapping language L (for instance, one in the style of R2R) whose expressions denote finite sets of such mapping rules, equipped with a formal semantics that, given a source RDF graph, yields a target RDF graph.

Formulate and answer the following:

(1) Define a declarative mapping language L expressive enough to capture a useful class of knowledge-base-to-knowledge-base mapping rules, and give it a precise denotational semantics in terms of RDF graphs.

(2) Define a notion of equivalence between expressions of L (two expressions are equivalent if they yield identical target graphs for every source graph) and a notion of optimization (a rewriting relation preserving this equivalence, intended to reduce some cost measure such as the size of intermediate results or query evaluation time).

(3) Provide a compilation function C from L into SPARQL (or another standard execution language) such that for every expression e of L and every source RDF graph G, evaluating C(e) on G returns the same target graph as the semantics of e on G.

(4) Prove the correctness of the compilation and demonstrate that nontrivial optimizations at the level of L can be performed before compilation in a way that yields more efficient SPARQL queries than naive compilation followed by SPARQL-level optimization.

Determine whether such a language, semantics, optimization framework, and compilation can be realized, and characterize the class of mapping rules for which this is possible.

Consider a class of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs): autoregressive language models that, prior to producing a final answer, generate an extended internal "thinking" trace (chain-of-thought, self-reflection, or search-like steps). Fix a family of controllable reasoning tasks parametrized by a complexity parameter N (for example, the number of disks in Tower of Hanoi, the number of blocks in a Blocks-World plan, the number of segments in a River-Crossing puzzle, or the depth of a compositional logical derivation), so that larger N forces longer sequential reasoning chains and greater compositional depth, while keeping the rule set of the task fixed.

For each task family, let Acc(N) denote the final-answer accuracy of a given LRM on instances of complexity N (averaged over a representative distribution of instances), and let T(N) denote the average number of thinking tokens the model expends on such instances before producing its final answer.

Characterize, both empirically and theoretically, the joint scaling behavior of Acc(N) and T(N) as N increases. In particular:

(a) Determine whether there exists, for each task family and model, a critical complexity N* beyond which Acc(N) collapses to near zero, and describe how N* depends on model size, training compute, and the availability of an explicit "thinking" mode versus a matched non-thinking baseline.

(b) Describe the behavior of the reasoning-effort curve T(N): does T(N) grow monotonically with N up to the model's context limit, or does it exhibit a counter-intuitive decrease near N*, indicating that the model reduces its reasoning effort precisely when the task becomes hardest?

(c) Identify and formalize the three regimes suggested by such experiments: (i) a low-complexity regime in which non-thinking models match or outperform thinking models, (ii) a medium-complexity regime in which extended thinking provides a clear advantage, and (iii) a high-complexity regime in which both thinking and non-thinking variants collapse to zero accuracy.

(d) Provide a quantitative model (e.g., a scaling law of the form Acc(N) ≈ f(N/N*) with explicit dependence on model and task parameters) that predicts the location of these transitions and the collapse of reasoning effort, and prove or disprove the conjecture that current LRMs fail to develop generalizable algorithmic reasoning, in the sense that no finite increase in inference-time compute suffices to push N* to infinity for the above task families.

Consider SPARQL, the standard query language for RDF graphs. A basic graph pattern (BGP) is a finite set of triple patterns of the form (s, p, o) in which each component is either an IRI/literal or a variable. The OPTIONAL operator combines two patterns P1 and P2 into a pattern (P1 OPT P2) whose evaluation over an RDF graph G is the left outer join of the evaluations of P1 and P2: every solution of P1 is preserved, extended by a compatible solution of P2 when one exists. SPARQL queries with arbitrarily nested OPTIONAL patterns are known to have PSPACE-complete evaluation in general, and queries built from BGPs and OPT only (well-designed or not) are typically executed by query engines using a left-outer-join physical plan.

In knowledge-base integration and ontology-based data-access scenarios, automatically generated transformation queries that materialize mappings from heterogeneous sources into a target schema routinely produce SPARQL queries that contain many deeply nested OPTIONAL clauses, since attributes in the source may or may not exist for each entity (open-world assumption). The cost of evaluating such queries via left outer joins grows rapidly with the depth and number of OPT operators, because left outer joins admit only restricted reordering and force the engine to retain unmatched tuples padded with nulls.

Problem. Develop a query-evaluation algorithm (with proofs of correctness with respect to the standard SPARQL set/bag semantics) for SPARQL queries of the form

   Q ::= BGP | (Q OPT Q) | (Q AND Q) | (Q FILTER F)

such that, for queries with n triple patterns and k nested OPTIONAL operators, the worst-case evaluation cost on an RDF graph with m triples is asymptotically strictly better than the cost obtained by treating every OPT as a generic left outer join in a relational engine. Specifically: identify a syntactic or semantic subclass of SPARQL OPTIONAL queries that captures the patterns arising from automatic knowledge-base mapping generation, give a sound and complete evaluation procedure for this subclass whose complexity is polynomial in m and n (and ideally independent of k beyond a low-degree polynomial), and prove matching lower bounds showing that no further asymptotic improvement is possible within the subclass.
