Let $n$ be a positive integer and let $A \in \mathbb{C}^{n \times n}$. Define the numerical range (field of values) of $A$ by
$$W(A) = \{\langle Ax, x\rangle : x \in \mathbb{C}^n, \ \|x\| = 1\},$$
where $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ is the standard Hermitian inner product on $\mathbb{C}^n$ and $\|\cdot\|$ is the associated Euclidean norm. For a polynomial $p \in \mathbb{C}[z]$, let $\|p(A)\|$ denote the operator (spectral) norm of $p(A)$ acting on $(\mathbb{C}^n, \|\cdot\|)$, and let
$$\|p\|_{W(A)} = \sup\{|p(z)| : z \in W(A)\}.$$
Decide whether the inequality
$$\|p(A)\| \le 2\,\|p\|_{W(A)}$$
holds for every positive integer $n$, every matrix $A \in \mathbb{C}^{n \times n}$, and every polynomial $p \in \mathbb{C}[z]$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Crouzeix's conjecture (the constant 2 bound) remains open as of 2026. It is known to hold in many special cases (normal matrices, 2×2 and 3×3 matrices, near-Jordan blocks, certain tridiagonal and Toeplitz classes), and the best known universal constant is $1+\sqrt{2}$ due to Crouzeix and Palencia (2017). Ongoing workshops and publications continue to treat it as an unresolved problem.

Consider a finite arrangement of great circles on the unit sphere $S^2$ in general position, meaning that no three circles pass through a common point (so every intersection of circles is a transversal crossing of exactly two great circles). Define the associated arrangement graph $G$ as follows: the vertices of $G$ are the intersection points of the great circles, and two vertices are joined by an edge whenever the corresponding intersection points are connected by an arc on some great circle that contains no other intersection point in its interior. Under the general-position hypothesis, $G$ is a 4-regular planar graph embedded on $S^2$.

Question: Is it true that for every such arrangement, the graph $G$ admits a proper vertex 3-coloring (i.e., an assignment of one of three colors to each vertex such that adjacent vertices receive distinct colors)?

Equivalently: is every zonohedron, viewed as a planar map of its faces, 3-face-colorable?

Aichholzer (2002) confirmed 3-colorability for all arrangements of up to 11 great circles, and partial theoretical results have been obtained (e.g., a 2004 preprint by S. Felsner et al.), but no general proof or counterexample is known.

Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ and let $H^2(\mathbb{D})$ denote the Hardy space on $\mathbb{D}$. For a finite Blaschke product $\Theta$ of degree $n$, define the associated model space
$$K_\Theta = H^2(\mathbb{D})\ominus \Theta H^2(\mathbb{D}),$$
an $n$-dimensional subspace of $H^2(\mathbb{D})$. Let $P_\Theta$ be the orthogonal projection of $H^2(\mathbb{D})$ onto $K_\Theta$, and let $M_z$ be multiplication by the independent variable on $H^2(\mathbb{D})$. Define the compressed shift
$$S_\Theta = P_\Theta M_z\big|_{K_\Theta},$$
a bounded linear operator on $K_\Theta$ with numerical range
$$W(S_\Theta) = \{\langle S_\Theta f, f\rangle : f\in K_\Theta,\ \|f\|=1\}.$$

Question: For every finite Blaschke product $\Theta$ and every finite Blaschke product $B$ with $\deg(B) < \deg(\Theta)$, must
$$\max\{|B(z)| : z\in \overline{W(S_\Theta)}\} \ \geq\ \tfrac{1}{2}\,?$$

A set S of points in the Euclidean plane is called universal for n-vertex planar graphs if, for every simple planar graph G on n vertices, there exists an injective mapping of the vertices of G to points of S such that drawing each edge of G as the straight line segment between the images of its endpoints yields a planar (crossing-free) embedding of G.

Let f(n) denote the minimum cardinality of a universal point set for n-vertex planar graphs. Determine the asymptotic behavior of f(n). In particular, decide whether f(n) = O(n).

The general case of arbitrary matrices with elliptical numerical range does not appear to have been resolved.

A 3D orthogonal point-drawing of a simple graph G is an embedding that maps each vertex of G to a distinct point of the integer cubic lattice Z^3, and maps each edge to a lattice path (a sequence of axis-parallel unit segments) between its endpoints, such that two such paths intersect only at common endpoints. A bend of an edge-path is an interior lattice point at which two consecutive segments of the path meet in different axis directions; equivalently, a path with k bends consists of k+1 maximal collinear segments (links). Since each vertex has only six available axis directions, only graphs with maximum degree at most 6 can admit such a drawing.

Question: Does every simple graph with maximum vertex degree Δ ≤ 6 admit a 3D orthogonal point-drawing in which every edge-path has at most two bends (equivalently, consists of at most three orthogonal line segments)?

Let $\Theta$ be a finite Blaschke product with $n$ distinct zeros, namely
$$\Theta(z) \;=\; \prod_{j=1}^{n} \frac{z-\lambda_j}{1-\overline{\lambda_j}z}, \qquad \lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n \in \mathbb{D} \text{ distinct},$$
and let $K_\Theta = H^2 \ominus \Theta H^2$ denote the associated model space inside the Hardy space $H^2$ of the open unit disk $\mathbb{D}$. Let $S \colon H^2 \to H^2$ be the unilateral shift $(Sf)(z)=zf(z)$, and let
$$S_\Theta \;=\; P_{K_\Theta} S\big|_{K_\Theta}$$
be the compression of $S$ to $K_\Theta$, where $P_{K_\Theta}$ is the orthogonal projection onto $K_\Theta$. The operator $S_\Theta$ acts on the $n$-dimensional space $K_\Theta$ and its spectrum is $\{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n\}$; in particular it is diagonalizable, so for any matrix representation $A$ of $S_\Theta$ in an orthonormal basis of $K_\Theta$ there exists an invertible $X \in \mathbb{C}^{n\times n}$ and a diagonal $D \in \mathbb{C}^{n\times n}$ with $A = X D X^{-1}$.

Determine, as a function of the zeros $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n$, the minimal possible value of the condition number
$$\kappa(X) \;=\; \|X\|\,\|X^{-1}\|$$
(with respect to the spectral / operator $2$-norm) over all such eigenvector matrices $X$ diagonalizing $S_\Theta$.

Question: Does every pair of simple polygons of equal area admit a hinged dissection from one to the other?

$$\overline{D}(\zeta, \sigma_\infty(p)) = \{ z \in \mathbb{C} : |z - \zeta| \leq \sigma_\infty(p)\}$$
contains at least one critical point of $p$ (i.e., a zero of the derivative $p'$).

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Schmeisser's conjecture is a strengthening of the Sendov conjecture, replacing the requirement that $\zeta$ be a zero of $p$ with $\zeta$ being any point in the convex hull of the zeros. While Sendov's conjecture itself has been proven only in special cases and remains open in general for arbitrary degree, the Schmeisser strengthening is correspondingly open. Recent work (e.g., on intersections of convex hulls of polynomial shifts and partial bounds of the form $|z-\zeta|\le\sqrt{1-|\zeta|^2}$ for $\zeta$ in the convex hull of critical points) addresses related and weaker forms but does not settle Schmeisser's conjecture.

Determine the computational complexity of this problem. In particular, decide whether the Planar Euclidean Maximum TSP is solvable in polynomial time or is NP-hard.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The complexity of the Planar Euclidean Maximum TSP appears to remain open. Maximum TSP is known to be polynomial-time solvable for polyhedral norms in fixed dimension (e.g., rectilinear in the plane) and NP-hard for the Euclidean metric in dimensions $d \geq 3$, but the two-dimensional Euclidean case has neither a polynomial-time algorithm nor a hardness proof. The TOPP problem page (Problem 49) and related literature continue to list it as open, while a PTAS is known.

A triangulation T of P is a maximal planar straight-line graph with vertex set P, so that the bounded faces are triangles and the union of all faces is the convex hull of P. Given a triangulation T of P, a vertex v of T is called pointed if at least one of the faces of T incident to v has an interior angle greater than π at v (equivalently, all edges of T incident to v lie in some open halfplane through v). Question: Is it true that for every finite point set P in the plane in general position, every triangulation T of P contains a pointed spanning tree as a subgraph?

Question: Does there exist an absolute constant $C$ such that every planar graph $G$ satisfies $\operatorname{qn}(G)\le C$?

Let $\mathbb{C}_+ = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : \operatorname{Re} z > 0\}$ denote the right half-plane, and let $H^2(\mathbb{C}_+)$ be the Hardy space on $\mathbb{C}_+$, consisting of analytic functions $f : \mathbb{C}_+ \to \mathbb{C}$ with
$$\|f\|^2 := \sup_{x>0} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |f(x+iy)|^2\, dy < \infty.$$
For an analytic self-map $\varphi : \mathbb{C}_+ \to \mathbb{C}_+$ for which the composition operator $C_\varphi f := f \circ \varphi$ is bounded on $H^2(\mathbb{C}_+)$, write $C_\varphi^*$ for its Hilbert space adjoint.

A bounded operator $U$ on a separable infinite-dimensional Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ is called universal if, for every bounded linear operator $T$ on $\mathcal{H}$, there exist a nonzero scalar $\mu \in \mathbb{C}$ and a closed $U$-invariant subspace $\mathcal{M} \subset \mathcal{H}$ such that $\mu T$ is similar to the restriction $U|_{\mathcal{M}}$.

An affine self-map of $\mathbb{C}_+$ is a map of the form $\varphi(z) = az + b$ with $a > 0$ and $\operatorname{Re} b \ge 0$. Such a $\varphi$ is called elliptic when it has a fixed point in $\mathbb{C}_+$, and it is an automorphism of $\mathbb{C}_+$ precisely when $b \in i\mathbb{R}$ (so $\varphi$ is a translation when $a=1$).

Problem: Prove or disprove that, for every affine self-map $\varphi$ of $\mathbb{C}_+$ such that $C_\varphi$ is bounded on $H^2(\mathbb{C}_+)$, the operator $C_\varphi^* - \lambda I$ is universal on $H^2(\mathbb{C}_+)$ for some $\lambda \in \mathbb{C}$ if and only if $\varphi$ is elliptic and not an automorphism of $\mathbb{C}_+$.

Consider the plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ equipped with a finite collection $\mathcal{M} = \{S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_n\}$ of line segments, called mirrors. Each $S_i$ is taken to be an open segment (its two endpoints are excluded), and the corresponding closed segments $\overline{S_i}$ are required to be pairwise disjoint. Each mirror is two-sided and perfectly reflecting: a light ray hitting the relative interior of any $S_i$ obeys the law of reflection (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection) on whichever side it arrives from. A light ray emanating from a point source $p \in \mathbb{R}^2$ (with $p \notin \bigcup_i \overline{S_i}$) is the polygonal trajectory obtained by emitting a ray from $p$ in some direction and reflecting it off mirrors whenever it strikes their open part; if the trajectory ever reaches an endpoint of a mirror, the trajectory is considered to terminate or be undefined for that direction (such directions may be ignored). The ray is said to be trapped if every point of its trajectory lies in the convex hull $\mathrm{conv}\!\left(\bigcup_i \overline{S_i}\right)$ of the mirrors — i.e., no point of the trajectory lies strictly outside this convex hull.

Question: Does there exist a point $p \in \mathbb{R}^2$ and a finite collection $\mathcal{M}$ of mirrors as above, with $p$ disjoint from the mirrors, such that every light ray emitted from $p$ (in every direction for which the trajectory is defined for all time) is trapped?

A planar grid graph is a graph whose vertex set is a finite set of points of the integer lattice Z^2, and whose edges connect exactly those pairs of vertices that are at Euclidean distance 1. A cycle cover of such a graph is a collection of (not necessarily simple) closed walks along edges of the graph such that every vertex is visited by at least one of the walks. For a cycle cover, count the number of 90-degree turns made along the walks, where a 180-degree U-turn (i.e., traversing an edge and immediately returning along the same edge) is counted as two 90-degree turns. The cost of a cycle cover is the total number of such 90-degree turns.

Determine the computational complexity of the following decision/optimization problem: given a planar grid graph G and an integer k, decide whether G admits a cycle cover with at most k 90-degree turns (equivalently, compute a cycle cover of G minimizing the total number of 90-degree turns). Is this problem solvable in polynomial time, or is it NP-hard?

A planar grid graph is a graph whose vertex set is a finite subset of the integer lattice Z^2 and whose edges connect exactly those pairs of vertices at Euclidean distance 1. A planar grid graph G is said to be solid if its complement in Z^2 (i.e., the set of lattice points not belonging to V(G)) induces a connected subgraph of the infinite lattice graph — equivalently, G has no "holes." For two vertices u, v of G, define their distance d_G(u,v) to be the length (number of edges) of a shortest path between them in G; equivalently, this is the Manhattan distance realized along edges of G. A tour of G is a closed walk that visits every vertex of G at least once, and its length is the sum of the distances (in G) traversed along consecutive vertices of the walk.

Problem: Determine the computational complexity of the following decision/optimization problem. Given a solid planar grid graph G and an integer k, decide whether G admits a tour of length at most k (equivalently, compute a tour of minimum length). Is this problem solvable in polynomial time, or is it NP-hard?

Determine the computational complexity of the following decision problem (the Pallet Loading Problem):

Input: five positive integers $A, B, a, b, n$ (encoded in binary).

Question: Can $n$ axis-aligned rectangles of dimensions $a \times b$ (each placed in either of the two axis-parallel orientations, $a \times b$ or $b \times a$, with sides parallel to the sides of the big rectangle, with disjoint interiors, and contained inside the big rectangle) be packed into a single $A \times B$ rectangle?

Specifically: is this problem in NP? Is it NP-complete? Is it decidable in polynomial time? Note that since the input consists of only five binary-encoded integers, a packing itself (a list of coordinates and orientations for all $n$ rectangles) may be exponentially large in the input size, so it is not immediate that the problem lies in NP.

Specifically: is this problem in NP? Is it NP-complete? Is it decidable in polynomial time? Note that since the input consists of only five binary-encoded integers, a packing itself (a list of coordinates and orientations for all $n$ rectangles) may be exponentially large in the input size, so it is not immediate that the problem lies in NP.

The complexity of the Pallet Loading Problem with this compact 5-integer input remains open. It is not known whether the problem lies in NP (since a packing certificate may have size exponential in the input length), nor is a polynomial-time algorithm known. Recent literature continues to describe the theoretical complexity status as unresolved.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

This is the Hadwiger–Nelson problem. The classical bounds $4 \le \chi(\mathbb{R}^2) \le 7$ stood from 1950 until 2018, when Aubrey de Grey constructed a unit-distance graph proving $\chi(\mathbb{R}^2) \ge 5$. The current bounds are $5 \le \chi(\mathbb{R}^2) \le 7$, and the exact value remains unknown.

Note that circularity is at least 1, with values close to 1 corresponding to nearly circular shapes.

A convex partition of the unit square S is a finite collection {P_1, ..., P_n} of convex polygons with pairwise disjoint interiors whose union is S. Define the circularity of such a partition to be max_{1 ≤ i ≤ n} R(P_i)/r(P_i).

Determine the infimum, over all finite convex partitions of the unit square, of the partition's circularity, and exhibit a partition (or sequence of partitions) attaining this infimum.

An analytic multifunction on $\mathbb{C}$ is an upper semicontinuous set-valued map $K$ that assigns to each $z\in\mathbb{C}$ a non-empty compact subset $K(z)\subset\mathbb{C}$, such that for every open set $U\subset\mathbb{C}$ the set $\{z:K(z)\subset U\}$ is open and such that $-\log\mathrm{dist}(\cdot,K(\cdot))$ (or, equivalently, the appropriate plurisubharmonic test) makes $K$ behave analytically; concretely, $K$ is analytic if for every open $V\subset\mathbb{C}$ and every subharmonic function $u$ on a neighborhood of the graph of $K$ over $V$, the function $z\mapsto \sup\{u(z,w):w\in K(z)\}$ is subharmonic on $V$. For a compact set $L\subset\mathbb{C}$, let $\widehat{L}$ denote its polynomial hull, namely the set of all $w\in\mathbb{C}$ for which $|p(w)|\le\sup_{\zeta\in L}|p(\zeta)|$ for every polynomial $p$ (equivalently, $\widehat{L}$ is $L$ together with the bounded components of $\mathbb{C}\setminus L$). For an analytic multifunction $K$ on $\mathbb{C}$, define $\widehat{K}(z):=\widehat{K(z)}$ and
$$\widehat{K}(\mathbb{C}):=\bigcup_{z\in\mathbb{C}}\widehat{K}(z)\subset\mathbb{C}.$$
Assume $K$ is non-constant.

How large can the exceptional set $\mathbb{C}\setminus\widehat{K}(\mathbb{C})$ be? In particular, does there exist a non-constant analytic multifunction $K$ on $\mathbb{C}$ for which $\mathbb{C}\setminus\widehat{K}(\mathbb{C})$ is uncountable?

A Boolean function in $n$ variables is a map $f:\mathbb{F}_2^n \to \mathbb{F}_2$. Its Walsh-Hadamard transform is $W_f(a) = \sum_{x\in\mathbb{F}_2^n}(-1)^{f(x)+a\cdot x}$ for $a\in\mathbb{F}_2^n$. The function $f$ is called bent if $|W_f(a)| = 2^{n/2}$ for every $a\in\mathbb{F}_2^n$ (which requires $n$ to be even). The algebraic degree of $f$ is the degree of its (unique) algebraic normal form as a multilinear polynomial over $\mathbb{F}_2$. A Boolean function $f$ in $n$ variables (with $n$ even) is called normal if there exists an $(n/2)$-dimensional affine subspace $V \subseteq \mathbb{F}_2^n$ on which $f$ is constant; otherwise $f$ is called non-normal.

Question: Does there exist a non-normal Boolean bent function in $8$ variables whose algebraic degree equals $4$?

Let C be a convex region in the plane with unit area, whose boundary is either a smooth curve or a convex polygon. A perimeter-halving folding of C is defined as follows: choose two points x and y on the boundary of C that divide the boundary into two arcs of equal length (each equal to half the perimeter of C), and identify the two boundary arcs by gluing the arc from x to y (going one way around) to the arc from y to x (going the other way), matching points at equal arc-length distances from x and y. It is known that such an identification always yields a unique convex surface in three-dimensional space (a convex polyhedron when C is a convex polygon), enclosing a well-defined volume.

Determine the unit-area convex shape C, together with the choice of perimeter-halving pair (x, y), that maximizes the enclosed three-dimensional volume produced by a perimeter-halving folding.

A polycube is an orthogonal polyhedron obtained by gluing finitely many axis-aligned unit cubes face-to-face (the three-dimensional analogue of a polyomino). Its surface is naturally subdivided into unit squares, and the edges of this subdivision (the unit segments where two adjacent unit squares meet on the surface) are called the surface edges of the polycube. An edge-unfolding of such a polyhedron is a choice of a subset of the surface edges to cut along so that, after the cuts, the surface can be developed into the plane as a single non-overlapping simply connected planar polygon (faces may not be further subdivided beyond the unit-square grid, and only cuts along surface edges are allowed).

Question: Does there exist a polycube of genus zero (i.e., whose surface is topologically a sphere) that admits no edge-unfolding in the above sense?

Let P be a finite set of points in the (real) projective or Euclidean plane, with |P| ≥ 3 and not all points equal. Assign to each point p ∈ P a positive real weight w(p) > 0. A line determined by P is a line passing through at least two points of P. Call (P, w) a magic configuration if there exists a constant c such that for every line ℓ determined by P, the sum of the weights of points of P lying on ℓ equals c.

Prove or disprove the following classification: up to projective equivalence and positive rescaling of the weights, the only magic configurations are:

1. Points in general position (no three collinear), with every point assigned the same weight (e.g. weight 1).
2. All points collinear, with arbitrary positive weights.
3. For n ≥ 3: n − 1 points collinear, each of weight 1, together with one additional point off that line of weight n − 2.
4. A particular 7-point configuration (and its projective equivalents): take a triangle together with its three edge midpoints and its centroid; assign weight 2 to each of the three edge midpoints and weight 1 to each of the other four points. Then all nine determined lines have weighted sum 4.

Show that no other magic configurations exist.

Determine $\rho(n)$ exactly as a function of $n$. In particular, decide whether $\rho(n) = \lfloor n/4 \rfloor$.

Let $K \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a tree (a compact, connected, simply connected $1$-dimensional polyhedron) embedded in the Euclidean plane, and let $\varepsilon > 0$.

(i) Call $K$ genuinely $\varepsilon$-disjoinable if there exists a continuous (equivalently, piecewise-linear) map $f \colon K \to \mathbb{R}^2$ such that $f(K) \cap K = \emptyset$ and $|x - f(x)| < \varepsilon$ for every $x \in K$.

(ii) Consider two closed round disks $D_1, D_2 \subset \mathbb{R}^2$, each of diameter $\varepsilon$, whose centers $c_1(t), c_2(t)$ move continuously along $K$ as functions of $t \in [0,1]$, and which are required to remain disjoint at every time $t$ (that is, $D_1(t) \cap D_2(t) = \emptyset$ for all $t$). The trace of $D_i$ on $K$ at time $t$ is the set $D_i(t) \cap K$. Call $K$ $\varepsilon$-spanned if there is no such admissible motion of the two disks that results in their two traces on $K$ coinciding at the end (i.e.\ one cannot move the disks so that, at some time, $D_1(t) \cap K = D_2(t) \cap K$ as subsets of $K$). Call $K$ symmetrically $\varepsilon$-spanned if no such admissible motion exchanges the disks (i.e.\ achieves $(c_1(1), c_2(1)) = (c_2(0), c_1(0))$).

Answer the following:

(a) Does genuine $\varepsilon$-disjoinability of $K$ imply that $K$ is $\varepsilon$-spanned?

(b) Does symmetric $\varepsilon$-spannedness of $K$ imply that $K$ is $\varepsilon$-spanned?

A fair partitioning of a polygon P ⊂ ℝ² is a partition of P into finitely many pieces such that all pieces have the same area and the same perimeter. If, in addition, every piece is convex, the partition is called a fair convex partitioning.

(a) For every positive integer n and every convex polygon P ⊂ ℝ², does there exist a fair convex partitioning of P into exactly n pieces?

(b) If the answer to (a) is negative in general, give an effective criterion that, taking as input a convex polygon P and a positive integer n, decides whether P admits a fair convex partitioning into n pieces.

(c) Whenever such a partition exists for given P and n, describe a procedure for finding one that minimizes either (i) the total length of the cut segments used to define the partition, or (ii) the sum of the perimeters of the n pieces.

(d) Formulate and study the analogous problem in dimension d ≥ 3: given a convex polytope P ⊂ ℝ^d and a positive integer n, can P be partitioned into n convex pieces having equal d-dimensional volume and equal (d−1)-dimensional surface area, and what are the corresponding optimization questions?

Work in the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$. A plane tree is a topological tree (a compact, connected, locally connected, 1-dimensional space with no simple closed curves) embedded in $\mathbb{R}^2$. Fix $\varepsilon > 0$ and let $K \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a plane tree.

Define the following three notions.

(1) An $\varepsilon$-triod in $K$ is a subset $T \subset K$ that is the union of three arcs $A_1, A_2, A_3$ meeting only at one common endpoint $v$, such that each $A_i$ contains a point whose distance from $A_j \cup A_k$ (where $\{i,j,k\} = \{1,2,3\}$) is greater than $\varepsilon$.

(2) $K$ is $\varepsilon$-narrow if there exists an arc $I \subset K$ such that every point of $K$ lies within Euclidean distance $\varepsilon$ of $I$.

(3) $K$ is $\varepsilon$-spanned if there do not exist two continuous motions of closed disks $D_1(t), D_2(t)$ of diameter $\varepsilon$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$, whose centers are constrained to lie on $K$, such that $D_1(t) \cap D_2(t) = \emptyset$ for all $t$ and such that $\{D_1(t) \cap K : t\} = \{D_2(t) \cap K : t\}$ as families of subsets of $K$ (i.e., the disks cannot be moved along $K$, while remaining disjoint, in such a way that they trace out the same set on $K$).

Prove or disprove the following two assertions:

(a) Every plane tree $K$ that contains no $\varepsilon$-triod is $10\varepsilon$-narrow.

(b) Every $\varepsilon$-spanned plane tree $K$ is $10\varepsilon$-narrow.

Let R be an axis-aligned rectangular board of m×n unit lattice squares with one corner at the origin. Suppose every unit square s of R is assigned a label ℓ(s) ∈ {1,2,3,4,5,6}.

A "rolling tour" of R is a sequence of rolls starting from some initial position and orientation of the cube on R such that:
(i) the cube visits each unit square of R exactly once, and
(ii) whenever the cube occupies a square s, the label on its top face equals ℓ(s).

Determine the computational complexity of the following decision problem: given a rectangular board R together with a complete labeling ℓ: R → {1,2,3,4,5,6}, decide whether there exists a rolling tour of R.

Say that $K$ is $\varepsilon$-spanned if there do not exist two continuous motions of two disjoint round closed disks of diameter $\varepsilon$, whose centers move along $K$, such that the two centers trace out the same subset of $K$ during the motion.

Decide whether the following is true: every $\varepsilon$-spanned plane tree $K\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ of diameter $1$ is necessarily $10\varepsilon$-chainable.

Let G be a planar graph together with a fixed planar embedding such that every interior face is a triangle (i.e., G is interior triangulated). A straight-line drawing of G is an assignment of distinct points in the plane to the vertices of G together with the realization of each edge as the straight segment between its endpoints. Call such a drawing isosceles if every (interior) triangular face of G is drawn as an isosceles triangle, that is, a triangle having at least two sides of equal Euclidean length.

(a) Does every interior-triangulated planar graph admit a planar (crossing-free) isosceles straight-line drawing?

(b) Does every interior-triangulated planar graph admit an isosceles straight-line drawing if crossings are allowed?

(c) Whenever such drawings exist, determine the smallest grid size on which they can be realized, and decide whether they can always be realized using integer coordinates.

(d) If such drawings do not always exist, determine the computational complexity of deciding whether a given interior-triangulated planar graph admits an isosceles straight-line drawing (in particular, is the decision problem NP-hard?).

Let $P$ be a finite set of points in the Euclidean plane and let $k \geq 2$ be an integer. The Yao graph $Y_k(P)$ is defined as follows: at each point $u \in P$, partition the plane around $u$ into $k$ closed cones of angle $2\pi/k$ with apex $u$ (using a fixed orientation, with ties broken consistently). In each cone, $u$ adds a directed edge to the point $v \in P$ in that cone (other than $u$) that minimizes the Euclidean distance $|uv|$, if such a point exists.

The Yao-Yao graph $YY_k(P)$ is obtained from $Y_k(P)$ by a second pruning step: at each point $u$ and within each cone of $u$, among all incoming directed edges of $Y_k(P)$ falling into that cone at $u$, keep only the shortest one and discard the others. The resulting edges are then regarded as undirected.

For a real number $t \geq 1$, a geometric graph $G$ on $P$ is called a $t$-spanner if for every pair of points $p, q \in P$, the length of a shortest path from $p$ to $q$ in $G$ (with edge weights equal to Euclidean lengths) is at most $t \cdot |pq|$.

Question: Does there exist an integer $k_0$ and a constant $t \geq 1$ (both independent of $P$) such that for every $k \geq k_0$, the Yao-Yao graph $YY_k(P)$ is a $t$-spanner for every finite point set $P$ in the plane? More generally, for which values of $k$ is $YY_k$ a $t$-spanner for some constant $t$?

The problem is partially resolved. It is known that $YY_4$ and $YY_5$ are not spanners, and that odd Yao-Yao graphs $YY_{2k+1}$ for small $k$ fail to be spanners. The general question of characterizing exactly which $k$ yield a spanner remains open.

A finite graph is regarded as a one-dimensional topological space (a finite CW complex). Given finite graphs $K$, $X$, and $Y$, an embedding $f:K\hookrightarrow X\times Y$ is called basic if every continuous function $\varphi:K\to\mathbb{R}$ can be represented in the form
$$\varphi(p) = \alpha(\pi_X(f(p))) + \beta(\pi_Y(f(p))) \quad \text{for all } p\in K,$$
for some continuous functions $\alpha:X\to\mathbb{R}$ and $\beta:Y\to\mathbb{R}$, where $\pi_X$ and $\pi_Y$ denote the projections from $X\times Y$ onto its factors. The graph $K$ is said to be basically embeddable in $X\times Y$ if such an embedding exists.

Question: Is there an algorithm that, given any triple $(K,X,Y)$ of finite graphs as input, decides whether $K$ is basically embeddable in $X\times Y$?

Let S be a finite set of points in the Euclidean plane in convex position, meaning every point of S lies on the boundary of the convex hull of S. The Delaunay triangulation DT(S) is the planar straight-line graph on vertex set S in which three points form a triangle if and only if the open disk through them contains no other point of S; edges of DT(S) are weighted by Euclidean length. For a real number t ≥ 1, a geometric graph G on S is called a t-spanner if for every pair u, v ∈ S the length of a shortest path from u to v in G is at most t · |uv|, where |uv| denotes the Euclidean distance; the infimum of such t is the stretch factor (or dilation) of G.

Question: Is it true that for every finite point set S in convex position, the Delaunay triangulation DT(S) is a (π/2)-spanner? That is, does the stretch factor of DT(S) satisfy the bound π/2 whenever S is in convex position?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The π/2 bound has been disproven: explicit constructions of point sets in convex position give Delaunay triangulations with stretch factor strictly greater than π/2 (lower bounds exceeding 1.5810 are known, while π/2 ≈ 1.5708). Subsequent work has further improved both lower and upper bounds (current upper bound around 1.77 in the convex case), so the original π/2-spanner conjecture for points in convex position is settled in the negative.

Let X and Y be finite (topological) graphs, regarded as one-dimensional compact metric spaces. A finite graph K (viewed as a compact metric space) is said to be basically embeddable in the product X × Y if there exists an embedding e: K → X × Y such that for every continuous function f: K → ℝ there exist continuous functions g: X → ℝ and h: Y → ℝ with f(p) = g(π_X(e(p))) + h(π_Y(e(p))) for all p ∈ K, where π_X and π_Y are the coordinate projections.

A finite graph H is called a prohibited (obstruction) subgraph for basic embeddability in X × Y if H is not basically embeddable in X × Y but every proper subgraph of H is basically embeddable in X × Y (equivalently, the class of finite graphs basically embeddable in X × Y is characterized by the absence of subgraphs from some family, and H is a minimal forbidden member of this family).

Prove or disprove the following statement: for every fixed pair of finite graphs X and Y, there exist only finitely many prohibited subgraphs (up to isomorphism) characterizing the finite graphs K that are basically embeddable in X × Y.

Two polygons in the plane are said to be congruent if one can be mapped onto the other by an isometry (translation, rotation, or reflection). Given a polygon P in the plane and a positive integer n, a congruent partition of P into n pieces is a collection of n pairwise congruent polygonal pieces contained in P with pairwise disjoint interiors. The uncovered area of such a partition is the area of P minus the total area of the n pieces. A congruent partition that minimizes this uncovered area (over all choices of n pairwise congruent polygonal pieces fitting in P with disjoint interiors) is called an optimal congruent partition of P into n pieces; if the uncovered area is zero, the partition is called a perfect congruent partition.

Problem: Develop a general method to determine, for an arbitrary input polygon P and an arbitrary positive integer n, an optimal congruent partition of P into n pieces. In particular, characterize for which pairs (P, n) a perfect congruent partition exists, and for those pairs where it does not, determine the minimum possible uncovered area and a partition achieving it.

Two polygons in the plane are said to be congruent if one can be mapped onto the other by an isometry (translation, rotation, or reflection). Given a polygon P in the plane and a positive integer n, a congruent partition of P into n pieces is a collection of n pairwise congruent polygonal pieces contained in P with pairwise disjoint interiors. The uncovered area of such a partition is the area of P minus the total area of the n pieces. A congruent partition that minimizes this uncovered area (over all choices of n pairwise congruent polygonal pieces fitting in P with disjoint interiors) is called an optimal congruent partition of P into n pieces; if the uncovered area is zero, the partition is called a perfect congruent partition.

Problem: Develop a general method to determine, for an arbitrary input polygon P and an arbitrary positive integer n, an optimal congruent partition of P into n pieces. In particular, characterize for which pairs (P, n) a perfect congruent partition exists, and for those pairs where it does not, determine the minimum possible uncovered area and a partition achieving it.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The general problem of congruent partitions of polygons remains open. It is listed in The Open Problems Project in computational geometry. A short survey (arXiv:1002.0122) and work on partitioning a polygon into two mirror-congruent pieces address only restricted cases; no general solution is reported.

Let $n \geq 2$ and let $P$ be a set of $n$ points in the plane in general position (no three collinear). Form the complete geometric graph $K_n(P)$ by drawing the straight-line segment between every pair of points of $P$; by the general position assumption, any two segments either share a common endpoint, are disjoint, or cross in a single interior point (a proper crossing). A coloring of the edges of $K_n(P)$ is called crossing-free if no two edges that properly cross are assigned the same color (edges that share an endpoint may receive the same color). Let $\chi_\times(K_n(P))$ denote the minimum number of colors in such a coloring, and define
$$f(n) \;=\; \max_{P}\, \chi_\times(K_n(P)),$$
where the maximum is taken over all $n$-point sets $P$ in general position in the plane.

Determine $f(n)$, or equivalently determine the minimum number of colors that always suffice (and is sometimes necessary) to color the edges of every straight-line drawing of $K_n$ on $n$ points in general position so that no two crossing edges have the same color.

A colored graph (also called a gem or crystallization in the sense of graph-encoded manifolds) is a pair (G, γ), where G is a finite multigraph that is regular of degree n+1, and γ : E(G) → {0, 1, …, n} is an edge coloring such that the edges meeting at every vertex receive pairwise distinct colors. Associated to (G, γ) is a pseudocomplex K(G, γ), constructed by taking, for each vertex of G, an abstract n-simplex with vertices labeled 0, 1, …, n, and identifying the (n−1)-face opposite to the vertex labeled i in two simplices whenever the corresponding two vertices of G are joined by an edge of color i (the identification preserving vertex labels). The polyhedron |K(G, γ)| is the geometric realization of this pseudocomplex.

Problem. For each integer n ≥ 3, give an algebraic characterization (in terms of the combinatorial/algebraic invariants of the coloring, such as the structure of the subgraphs induced by subsets of colors, their connected components, and associated chain or group-theoretic data) of those colored graphs (G, γ) of degree n+1 for which |K(G, γ)| is PL homeomorphic to the standard n-sphere S^n.

The problem of classifying or constructing all k-equiprojective polyhedra (first posed by Shephard in 1968) remains open. Background. A closed PL 3-manifold M can be represented by a 4-colored graph (also called a crystallization, in the irreducible case), i.e. a finite multigraph G whose edges are properly colored by the set {0,1,2,3} such that every vertex has exactly one edge of each color, with the property that the regular 4-dimensional pseudo-complex K(G) associated to G has |K(G)| ≅ M. By a classical theorem of Lickorish and Wallace, every closed orientable 3-manifold can be obtained from the oriented 3-sphere S^3 by Dehn surgery along an oriented framed link L ⊂ S^3, that is, by an oriented link together with a choice of surgery coefficient (a rational number, or ∞) on each component.

Problem. Construct an explicit, simple algorithm with the following specification:
- Input: an oriented link L in S^3 (given, for instance, by a planar diagram) together with a surgery coefficient assigned to each component of L.
- Output: a 4-colored graph G that represents the closed 3-manifold M obtained from S^3 by performing the prescribed Dehn surgery on L.

The algorithm should be combinatorial and effective, taking only the link diagram and the surgery coefficients as data and producing the edge-colored graph directly, without first passing through an arbitrary triangulation or handle decomposition of M.

Let P be a convex polyhedron in three-dimensional Euclidean space, viewed as a closed surface (the boundary of a convex body). A zipper unfolding of P is obtained by choosing a simple path γ on the surface of P that passes through every vertex of P (i.e., γ is a Hamiltonian path on the vertex set, with segments that are geodesic on the surface but not required to lie along edges of P), cutting the surface open along γ, and then developing the resulting simply connected surface isometrically into the Euclidean plane. The unfolding is called valid (non-overlapping) if the developed image is a simple planar polygon (no two points of the surface map to the same point of the plane, except along the cut).

Question: Does every convex polyhedron P admit a zipper unfolding in this sense, i.e., a Hamiltonian cut-path on the surface of P whose unfolding produces a non-overlapping planar polygon?

An (n+1)-edge-colored graph is a pair (G, γ) where G is a finite multigraph (without loops) that is regular of degree n+1, and γ : E(G) → {0, 1, …, n} is an edge-coloring such that any two edges sharing a vertex receive distinct colors. To such a colored graph one associates an n-dimensional pseudocomplex K(G) as follows: take one n-simplex σ(v) for each vertex v of G, label the vertices of each σ(v) by the colors 0, 1, …, n, and glue σ(v) to σ(w) along their (n−1)-faces opposite the vertex labeled c whenever v and w are joined in G by an edge of color c. The colored graph (G, γ) is said to represent a closed PL n-manifold M if K(G) is piecewise-linearly homeomorphic to M; equivalently, for every choice of n colors, each connected component of the subgraph spanned by the edges of those n colors represents the standard PL (n−1)-sphere.

Problem. Develop, for every integer i ≥ 2, a purely combinatorial description (a procedure depending only on the colored graph data (G, γ)) of the i-th homotopy group π_i(M) of the closed PL n-manifold M represented by (G, γ). That is, give a combinatorial algorithm or formula that takes (G, γ) as input and outputs a presentation of π_i(M) for each i ≥ 2.

An (n+1)-colored graph is a pair (G, γ) where G is a finite multigraph (loops not allowed but multiple edges permitted) which is regular of degree n+1, and γ : E(G) → {0, 1, …, n} is an edge-coloring such that edges incident to the same vertex receive pairwise distinct colors. For each subset B ⊆ {0,…,n}, let G_B denote the subgraph of G obtained by keeping only the edges whose color lies in B; its connected components are called B-residues.

To each (n+1)-colored graph one associates an n-dimensional simplicial cell complex K(G) as follows: take an n-simplex σ_v for each vertex v of G, label the (n−1)-faces of σ_v by the colors {0,…,n}, and for each edge of G with color c joining v and w glue the c-labeled (n−1)-faces of σ_v and σ_w via the simplicial map preserving the color labels of their (n−2)-faces. The colored graph (G, γ) is said to represent a closed connected PL n-manifold M if |K(G)| is PL-homeomorphic to M; this happens iff for every color c ∈ {0,…,n}, every ({0,…,n}∖{c})-residue of G represents the standard PL (n−1)-sphere. Such (G, γ) (with K(G) having exactly n+1 vertices in the contracted case) is called a crystallization of M.

Problem. Determine purely combinatorial conditions on a colored graph (G, γ) representing a closed PL n-manifold M that imply the vanishing of specified homotopy groups π_k(M). In particular, find such combinatorial criteria on (G, γ) that force π_1(M) = 0, and, separately, criteria that force π_2(M) = 0.

Let $E$ be an elliptic curve defined over $\mathbb{Q}$. The Mordell–Weil theorem asserts that the abelian group $E(\mathbb{Q})$ of rational points of $E$ is finitely generated, so
$$E(\mathbb{Q}) \;\cong\; \mathbb{Z}^{r} \oplus E(\mathbb{Q})_{\mathrm{tors}}$$
for some non-negative integer $r$, called the (algebraic) rank of $E$. For each prime $p$ of good reduction, let $a_p = p + 1 - \#E(\mathbb{F}_p)$, and define the Hasse–Weil $L$-function $L(E,s)$ by the Euler product
$$L(E,s) \;=\; \prod_{p \mid N} \bigl(1 - a_p p^{-s}\bigr)^{-1} \prod_{p \nmid N} \bigl(1 - a_p p^{-s} + p^{1-2s}\bigr)^{-1},$$
where $N$ is the conductor of $E$. By the modularity theorem, $L(E,s)$ admits an analytic continuation to the whole complex plane. Define the analytic rank of $E$ to be the order of vanishing of $L(E,s)$ at $s=1$.

Prove or disprove: for every elliptic curve $E/\mathbb{Q}$, the analytic rank of $E$ equals its algebraic rank $r$; that is,
$$\operatorname{ord}_{s=1} L(E,s) \;=\; \operatorname{rank}\, E(\mathbb{Q}).$$

The Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture is one of the seven Clay Millennium Prize Problems and remains open in general. Partial results are known: Coates–Wiles, Gross–Zagier, and Kolyvagin established the conjecture for analytic rank 0 and 1 for elliptic curves over Q (subject to modularity, now a theorem). No proof is known for analytic rank ≥ 2.

representations.normalized:
Background and definitions. A colored graph of dimension n+1 is a pair (G, γ) where G = (V(G), E(G)) is a finite multigraph (loops forbidden) which is regular of degree n+1, and γ : E(G) → {0,1,…,n} is an edge-coloring such that distinct edges sharing a vertex have distinct colors. Such a graph has an associated n-dimensional pseudocomplex K(G): take an n-simplex σ_v for each vertex v ∈ V(G), labeled at its vertices by {0,1,…,n}, and glue σ_v to σ_w along the (n−1)-face opposite to the vertex labeled c whenever v and w are joined by an edge colored c. The colored graph (G, γ) is said to represent the closed PL n-manifold M if |K(G)| is PL-homeomorphic to M; every closed PL n-manifold admits such a representing colored graph.

For each integer k with 0 ≤ k ≤ n, let C_{n−k}(G) be the free abelian group generated by the (n−k)-dimensional simplices of K(G) (equivalently, the (k+1)-residues of (G, γ) of an appropriate type), and let rk C_{n−k}(G) denote its rank. Define the k-complexity of a closed PL n-manifold M by
    c_k(M) = min { rk C_{n−k}(G) : (G, γ) is a colored graph representing M }.
Let S^n denote the n-sphere, and define the reduced k-complexity by
    c̃_k(M) = c_k(M) − c_k(S^n).

Connected sum of two closed orientable PL n-manifolds M and M' is denoted M # M'.

Problem. Let M and M' be closed orientable PL 4-manifolds. Determine whether the reduced 4-complexity is additive under connected sum, that is, whether
    c̃_4(M # M') = c̃_4(M) + c̃_4(M')
holds for every such pair (M, M').

Web searches surface related results on additivity of regular genus and on gem-complexity / k-complexity invariants of 4-manifolds via crystallizations (notably work of Casali–Cristofori), where additivity is established only under restrictive hypotheses such as the existence of (weak) semi-simple crystallizations. Background and definitions.

(1) An (n+1)-colored graph is a pair (G, γ) where G = (V(G), E(G)) is a finite multigraph (loops are forbidden, multiple edges are allowed) that is regular of degree n+1, together with an edge-coloring γ : E(G) → Δn = {0, 1, …, n} such that any two edges sharing a vertex receive different colors. For each subset S ⊆ Δn, let G_S denote the subgraph of G whose edges are those colored by elements of S, and let g_S denote the number of connected components of G_S.

(2) From an (n+1)-colored graph (G, γ) one constructs an n-dimensional simplicial cell complex K(G) as follows: take an n-simplex σ_v for each vertex v of G, label the vertices of σ_v injectively by Δn, and for every edge of color c joining v and w glue the (n−1)-faces of σ_v and σ_w opposite to the c-labeled vertices via the unique color-preserving simplicial map. The graph G is said to represent the closed PL n-manifold M when |K(G)| is PL-homeomorphic to M.

(3) Define, for an (n+1)-colored graph G representing a closed PL n-manifold, the invariant
   β_n(G) = (#V(G))/2 − 1
(equivalently, half the number of vertices minus 1). The n-complexity (gem-complexity) of a closed PL n-manifold M is
   c_n(M) = min { β_n(G) : G is an (n+1)-colored graph representing M }.
A colored graph G representing M is called minimal if β_n(G) = c_n(M).

Problem. Investigate the graph-theoretic structure of minimal (n+1)-colored graphs representing closed PL n-manifolds, and provide intrinsic combinatorial characterizations of minimality. More precisely, identify necessary and/or sufficient combinatorial conditions on an (n+1)-colored graph (G, γ) — for example, conditions on the numbers g_S of components of its color-induced subgraphs, on its bipartite structure, on the regular genus, or on the existence/absence of certain local configurations (dipoles, ρ-pairs, blobs, etc.) — that ensure G realizes the minimum β_n among all colored graphs representing |K(G)|.

Background. A 4-colored graph is a finite multigraph $\Gamma=(V(\Gamma),E(\Gamma))$ together with an edge-coloring $\gamma:E(\Gamma)\to\{0,1,2,3\}$ such that any two edges meeting at a common vertex have distinct colors (in particular, $\Gamma$ is 4-regular). Such a graph determines a 3-dimensional pseudocomplex $K(\Gamma)$ by associating to each vertex a tetrahedron, identifying $i$-faces of two tetrahedra whenever the corresponding vertices are joined by an edge of color $i$, and the topological space $|K(\Gamma)|$ is called the geometric realization. A 4-colored graph $\Gamma$ is said to represent a closed 3-manifold $M^3$ if $|K(\Gamma)|\cong M^3$.

It is known that every closed orientable 3-manifold of Heegaard genus at most two can be represented by a 4-colored graph constructed from a 6-tuple of positive integers
$$(n_1,h_1;\,n_2,h_2;\,n_3,h_3),$$
according to the following standard construction: for each $i\in\{1,2,3\}$ one builds an elementary "block" depending on the parameters $(n_i,h_i)$, and the three blocks are assembled using the colors $\{0,1,2,3\}$ to obtain a 4-colored graph $\Gamma(n_1,h_1;n_2,h_2;n_3,h_3)$ whose associated pseudocomplex is a closed 3-manifold of Heegaard genus $\le 2$.

Problem.
(a) Determine an explicit set of moves/relations on 6-tuples $(n_1,h_1;n_2,h_2;n_3,h_3)$ of positive integers such that two such 6-tuples give rise to 4-colored graphs representing the same closed 3-manifold (up to homeomorphism) if and only if they are related by a finite sequence of these moves.

(b) Using (a), give a complete classification of the homeomorphism types of closed orientable 3-manifolds of Heegaard genus at most two in terms of equivalence classes of 6-tuples under these relations.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Partial progress exists: a G-equivalence relation on 6-tuples is known to preserve the represented genus-two 3-manifold, and catalogues of prime genus-two 3-manifolds of small complexity (e.g. 78 prime 3-manifolds of complexity ≤ 21) have been compiled. However, a complete set of moves giving a sufficient and necessary equivalence, together with a full homeomorphism classification in terms of 6-tuples, does not appear to have been established. The problem appears to remain open in its full generality.

Background and construction. A 4-colored graph is a finite multigraph $G=(V,E)$ together with an edge-coloring $\gamma:E	o\{0,1,2,3\}$ such that at every vertex the four edges incident to it carry the four distinct colors. From such a graph one builds a 3-dimensional pseudocomplex $K(G)$ by taking one tetrahedron $\sigma_v$ for each vertex $v\in V$, labeling the four 2-faces of $\sigma_v$ by the colors $0,1,2,3$, and gluing the $c$-labeled faces of $\sigma_v$ and $\sigma_w$ whenever $v$ and $w$ are joined by a $c$-colored edge. If $|K(G)|$ is a closed 3-manifold, $G$ is called a crystallization (or gem) of that manifold.

It is known that every closed orientable 3-manifold of Heegaard genus at most two admits a 4-colored graph representation that is determined by a 6-tuple of integers
$$ (n_1,h_1;\; n_2,h_2;\; n_3,h_3) $$
subject to the conditions $n_i\ge 1$ and $0\le h_i\le n_i-1$ for $i=1,2,3$, via the following standard construction. Take three disjoint cycles of lengths $2n_1,2n_2,2n_3$ formed alternately by edges of colors $0$ and $1$, and attach edges of colors $2$ and $3$ according to cyclic permutations determined by the shifts $h_1,h_2,h_3$, yielding a regular 4-colored graph $G(n_1,h_1;n_2,h_2;n_3,h_3)$ of order $2(n_1+n_2+n_3)$ which (when it represents a manifold) is a crystallization of a closed orientable 3-manifold $M(n_1,h_1;n_2,h_2;n_3,h_3)$ of Heegaard genus at most two.

Problem. Determine necessary and sufficient arithmetic conditions on the integers $(n_1,h_1;n_2,h_2;n_3,h_3)$ (with $n_i\ge 1$ and $0\le h_i<n_i$) so that the resulting 3-manifold $M(n_1,h_1;n_2,h_2;n_3,h_3)$ is an integral homology 3-sphere, i.e. $H_1(M;\mathbb{Z})=0$.

The question asks for explicit arithmetic conditions on the 6-tuple parameters characterizing homology 3-spheres among genus-two crystallizations. The available literature describes algorithms and enumerations producing homology spheres from 6-tuples, but no closed-form arithmetic characterization of exactly which 6-tuples yield homology 3-spheres was located. The problem appears to remain open.

representations.normalized:
Background. A crystallisation of a closed connected 3-manifold $M$ is a 4-edge-coloured graph $(\Gamma,\gamma)$ with $\gamma:E(\Gamma)\to\{0,1,2,3\}$ such that edges of each colour form a perfect matching, $\Gamma$ is regular of degree 4, and the dual ball complex of $(\Gamma,\gamma)$ is a pseudo-triangulation of $M$ with exactly one vertex of each colour. Casali and Grasselli showed that every closed orientable 3-manifold of Heegaard genus at most two can be encoded by a 6-tuple of nonnegative integers
$$(n_1,h_1;\,n_2,h_2;\,n_3,h_3)$$
that determines a crystallisation $\Gamma(n_1,h_1;n_2,h_2;n_3,h_3)$ of the manifold together with a genus-two Heegaard splitting; the integers $n_i$ control the lengths of the three "arc systems" of the crystallisation and the integers $h_i$ are shift parameters.

Problem. Produce an explicit finite presentation
$$\pi_1\bigl(M(n_1,h_1;n_2,h_2;n_3,h_3)\bigr)=\langle\,x,y\mid R_1(n_1,h_1;n_2,h_2;n_3,h_3),\,R_2(n_1,h_1;n_2,h_2;n_3,h_3)\,\rangle$$
of the fundamental group of the closed 3-manifold $M(n_1,h_1;n_2,h_2;n_3,h_3)$ associated to such an admissible 6-tuple, in which the generators and the relators are written as explicit words determined directly by the six integers $n_1,h_1,n_2,h_2,n_3,h_3$ (without invoking an algorithm applied to the crystallisation in each individual case).

Searches reveal that genus-two 3-manifolds encoded by admissible 6-tuples have been catalogued and their fundamental group presentations computed case-by-case via Gagliardi's algorithm applied to the crystallisation, but no closed-form 2-generator 2-relator presentation expressed uniformly in terms of the six parameters appears to be available. The problem's status as of the latest accessible literature is not clearly resolved.

representations.normalized:
A triangular norm is a binary operation T:[0,1]×[0,1]→[0,1] that is commutative, associative, monotone non-decreasing in each argument, and satisfies T(a,1)=a for every a∈[0,1]. A distribution function is a non-decreasing, left-continuous map F:[0,∞)→[0,1] with F(0)=0 and sup F=1. A generalized Menger space is a triple (X,F,T), where X is a non-empty set, T is a triangular norm, and F assigns to every ordered pair (x,y)∈X×X a distribution function F_{x,y} such that:
 (i) F_{x,y}(t)=1 for all t>0 iff x=y,
 (ii) F_{x,y}=F_{y,x},
 (iii) F_{x,z}(t+s) ≥ T(F_{x,y}(t), F_{y,z}(s)) for all x,y,z∈X and t,s≥0.
Equip X with the (ε,λ)-uniformity; (X,F,T) is called complete if every Cauchy sequence in this uniformity converges.

Let α:[0,∞)→[0,∞) and β:[0,1]→[0,1] be non-decreasing functions such that α(t)≤t for all t≥0 and the iterates α^n(t) tend to 0 for every t>0, β(u)≥u for all u∈[0,1], and the function γ(s):=max(α(s), 1−β(1−s)) is continuous. Assume further that for every s<1 the series ∑_{n≥0} γ^n(s) is finite (where γ^n denotes the n-fold iterate of γ as a control function).

Let A:X→X be a self-map satisfying
 F_{Ax,Ay}(α(t)) ≥ β(F_{x,y}(t)) for all x,y∈X and t≥0,
and assume there exists x_0∈X and u_0>0 with F_{x_0,Ax_0}(u_0)>0.

Problem. Characterize the class of triangular norms T such that, for every complete generalized Menger space (X,F,T) and every map A and every pair (α,β) satisfying the hypotheses above, the map A necessarily has a fixed point in X.

The characterization is known: V. Radu showed that the continuous t-norms guaranteeing the fixed-point property in this probabilistic contraction setting are precisely those of Hadžić type (H-type), and answers to the listed open problems of Radu, including the one about admissible t-norms for the generalized contraction principle, are provided in subsequent work by Hadžić, Pap, and Radu.

representations.normalized:
Let $(S,\mathcal{F},T)$ be a Menger probabilistic metric space, where $S$ is a nonempty set, $\mathcal{F}:S\times S\to\Delta^+$ assigns to each pair $(x,y)$ a distribution function $F_{x,y}\in\Delta^+$ (with $\Delta^+$ the set of left-continuous nondecreasing functions $F:[0,\infty)\to[0,1]$ satisfying $F(0)=0$ and $\sup_{t\ge 0}F(t)=1$), and $T:[0,1]\times[0,1]\to[0,1]$ is a triangular norm, in such a way that the usual Menger axioms hold:
(i) $F_{x,y}=H_0$ if and only if $x=y$, where $H_0(t)=0$ for $t\le 0$ and $H_0(t)=1$ for $t>0$;
(ii) $F_{x,y}=F_{y,x}$;
(iii) $F_{x,z}(s+t)\ge T(F_{x,y}(s),F_{y,z}(t))$ for all $x,y,z\in S$ and $s,t\ge 0$.

Recall that a triangular norm $T$ is called Archimedean if it is continuous and satisfies $T(a,a)<a$ for every $a\in(0,1)$.

Let $\alpha,\beta:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be control functions, and define
$$\gamma(s)=\max\bigl(\alpha(s),\,1-\beta(1-s)\bigr).$$
A mapping $f:S\to S$ is called a generalized probabilistic $(\alpha,\beta)$-contraction if for all $x,y\in S$ and all $t>0$,
$$F_{f(x),f(y)}(\alpha(t))\ge \beta\bigl(F_{x,y}(t)\bigr).$$

Problem. Assume $T$ is an arbitrary Archimedean triangular norm. Determine appropriate conditions on the control functions $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $\gamma$ that guarantee that every generalized probabilistic $(\alpha,\beta)$-contraction $f:S\to S$ on a complete Menger space $(S,\mathcal{F},T)$ admits a (unique) fixed point.

Web search reveals a substantial literature extending probabilistic contraction principles in Menger spaces under various t-norm classes (Archimedean, H-type, Dombi, Aczél–Alsina, Sugeno–Weber families) with control functions, including works by Hadžić, Pap, Mihet, and Radu. However, no source was found that explicitly settles the precise question of identifying optimal conditions on the triple $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ ensuring a fixed point for an arbitrary Archimedean t-norm; the question appears to remain a topic of ongoing research, so its status is unclear.

representations.normalized:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a bounded domain (the parametric/logical domain) with coordinates $u = (u^1, u^2)$, and let $D \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a bounded target domain with coordinates $x = (x^1, x^2)$. Consider the Dirichlet energy
$$E[x] = \frac{1}{2} \int_\Omega \operatorname{tr}\!\big((\nabla_u x)^T \nabla_u x\big)\, du$$
for maps $x : \Omega \to D$ subject to a prescribed homeomorphism boundary condition $x|_{\partial \Omega} : \partial \Omega \to \partial D$. A minimizer $x(u)$ of $E$ is a harmonic map; assume it is a diffeomorphism onto $D$, so that the inverse map $u(x) : D \to \Omega$ is well defined. After interchanging dependent and independent variables, the energy of the inverse map can be written as
$$F[u] = \frac{1}{2} \int_{D} \frac{\operatorname{tr}\!\big((\nabla_x u)^T \nabla_x u\big)}{\det (\nabla_x u)}\, dx,$$
to be considered over orientation-preserving maps $u : D \to \Omega$ with $\det(\nabla_x u) > 0$ a.e.\ and matching boundary correspondence $u|_{\partial D} = (x|_{\partial \Omega})^{-1}$.

Questions:
1. Establish an existence theorem for minimizers (or, more generally, extremals) of the functional $F$ within a suitable class of orientation-preserving Sobolev mappings with the prescribed boundary correspondence.
2. Identify precise conditions (on the domains, the boundary correspondence, and the admissible class) under which every extremal of $F$ is exactly the inverse of the harmonic map $x(u)$ minimizing $E$.

Let $\Omega, \Omega^* \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ ($d=2$ or $3$) be bounded Lipschitz domains, and let $y:\Omega \to \Omega^*$ be a mapping in a suitable Sobolev space $W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^d)$ subject to prescribed boundary data $y|_{\partial\Omega} = y_0$. Consider a quasi-isometric variational principle in which one minimizes a polyconvex stored-energy functional
$$ I[y] = \int_\Omega F(\nabla y, \det \nabla y)\, dx $$
over the admissible class
$$ \mathcal{A}_t = \{\, y \in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^d) : y|_{\partial\Omega} = y_0,\ \det \nabla y(x) > t\,\Phi(\det \nabla y(x), \nabla y(x)) \text{ a.e. in } \Omega \,\}, $$
where $t > 0$ is a fixed parameter and $\Phi:\mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}^{d\times d} \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ is a continuous function chosen so that the constraint guarantees a uniform bilipschitz (quasi-isometry) bound on $y$ with a constant depending only on $t$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The problem of approximating homeomorphisms (and quasi-isometric / Sobolev locally invertible maps) by piecewise-affine homeomorphisms is classical and has been resolved in the planar case (results of Iwaniec–Kovalev–Onninen, Hencl–Pratelli and others), but in dimensions n ≥ 3 the analogous approximation question remains largely open. Recent work (e.g. on diffeomorphic approximation of piecewise affine homeomorphisms, 2025) explicitly states that the higher-dimensional approximation of Sobolev homeomorphisms by piecewise-affine homeomorphisms or diffeomorphisms is open in dimensions 3 and 4, with only partial progress.

Recent work on "lowest distortion mappings" and "practical lowest distortion mapping" (Garanzha et al., 2022) reports algorithmic, variational constructions of piecewise-affine quasi-isometric mappings whose distortion can be controlled and which converge to a target quasi-isometric map. Let $S \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ be a (possibly non-smooth) surface admitting parameterizations $\mathbf{r}: \Omega 	o S$, where $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ is a parameter domain. A surface-grid generation method assigns to such a parameterization a discrete grid on $S$ obtained as the minimizer of some discrete functional $F_h(\mathbf{x}_1,\dots,\mathbf{x}_N; \mathbf{r})$ defined on the nodal positions of a triangulation (or quadrangulation) of $\Omega$ pulled back to $S$.

Formulate a discrete variational principle for surface grid generation with the following two properties:

(a) Parameterization invariance. For any two parameterizations $\mathbf{r}_1: \Omega_1 	o S$ and $\mathbf{r}_2: \Omega_2 	o S$ of the same surface $S$, related by a (possibly non-smooth, e.g. only Lipschitz or piecewise smooth) change of coordinates $\varphi: \Omega_1 	o \Omega_2$ with $\mathbf{r}_1 = \mathbf{r}_2 \circ \varphi$, the set of optimal grids on $S$ produced by minimizing $F_h$ is the same; equivalently, $F_h$ depends only on the intrinsic geometric data on $S$ and not on the choice of $\mathbf{r}$.

(b) Discrete patch test. State and justify a discrete analogue of the finite-element patch test, suitable for grids viewed as discrete spatial mappings $\mathbf{x}_h: \Omega 	o S$, which replaces the standard finite-element patch-test condition (exact reproduction of affine functions on a patch of elements) by an appropriate condition for the discrete grid mapping. The condition should guarantee consistency of the discrete variational principle with its continuous counterpart in the limit of mesh refinement, in a manner compatible with property (a).

Provide an explicit construction of such a functional $F_h$, prove that it satisfies (a) under the stated class of parameterization changes, and formulate and verify the corresponding discrete patch-test condition in (b).

Let $M$ and $N$ be two-dimensional manifolds, each equipped with a polyhedral metric (i.e., a metric arising from a triangulation by Euclidean triangles glued isometrically along edges, with cone-type singularities at vertices). For a Lipschitz mapping $f:M\to N$, define the quasi-isometric variational functional
$$ I(f) \;=\; \int_M \Big( \tfrac{1}{2}\,\big(\lambda_1(f)^2+\lambda_2(f)^2\big) \;+\; \Phi\!\big(\lambda_1(f)\lambda_2(f)\big) \Big)\,d\mu_M, $$
where $\lambda_1(f),\lambda_2(f)$ are the singular values of the differential $df$ (defined almost everywhere with respect to the polyhedral area measure $\mu_M$) and $\Phi:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ is a convex barrier with $\Phi(t)\to+\infty$ as $t\to 0^+$ that penalises non-injectivity. Restrict admissible mappings to the class of bounded-curvature mappings, namely those whose pull-back metric $f^*g_N$ is a metric of bounded integral curvature in the sense of Alexandrov.

Address the following:

(1) Show that $I(\cdot)$ is well-defined on this class, that minimisers (or critical points) exist among bounded-curvature mappings with prescribed boundary correspondence, and formulate the corresponding Euler–Lagrange system in a weak sense intrinsic to the polyhedral setting.

(2) Suppose $(M_n,g_n)$ and $(N_n,h_n)$ are sequences of polyhedral metrics that converge proportionally (i.e., with uniformly bounded bi-Lipschitz distortion and vanishing distortion as $n\to\infty$) to metrics $(M,g)$ and $(N,h)$ that satisfy a tangent-cone condition: at every point the metric admits a unique metric tangent cone which is a Euclidean cone. Prove that if $f_n:M_n\to N_n$ are bounded-curvature minimisers (or weak Euler–Lagrange solutions) of the associated functionals $I_n$, then
$$ I_n(f_n)\longrightarrow I(f_\infty), \qquad df_n \rightharpoonup df_\infty \;\text{weakly}, $$
where $f_\infty$ is a bounded-curvature minimiser (or weak Euler–Lagrange solution) of $I$ on $(M,g)\to(N,h)$.

Setting. In variational grid generation one seeks a mapping (a grid) from a parameter domain into a target region by minimizing a functional whose integrand depends on the Jacobian of the mapping and on a prescribed Riemannian or polyhedral "control" metric g that encodes the desired local size, shape, and orientation of grid cells. Suppose that the control metric g produced (or required) by such a variational principle is a polyhedral metric on a manifold M, i.e. a metric obtained by gluing finitely many Euclidean simplices along isometries of their faces, so that (M, g) is a flat manifold with conical singularities concentrated on a codimension-2 set.

By a classical theorem of Alexandrov, every polyhedral metric of nonnegative curvature on the 2-sphere can be realized as the induced intrinsic metric on the boundary of a convex polytope in Euclidean 3-space; analogous realization questions exist in higher dimensions and for metrics of mixed curvature signs.

Problem. Decide whether, for the purposes of carrying out numerical simulation and minimization of variational grid-generation functionals with a polyhedral control metric g, it is mathematically or computationally necessary to first construct an isometric realization of (M, g) as an actual polyhedron (e.g. embedded or immersed in some Euclidean space) before performing the optimization, or whether one can equivalently and rigorously formulate and solve the variational problem intrinsically on the abstract manifold-with-polyhedral-metric (M, g) without ever producing such a realization. Provide either:
(a) a proof that an intrinsic formulation on (M, g) is sufficient — including a precise definition of the discrete variational functional on (M, g), an existence/convergence theory for its minimizers, and algorithms that operate solely on the combinatorial-metric data of (M, g); or
(b) a proof that some essential analytic or computational obstruction forces one to realize (M, g) as a polyhedron, identifying the obstruction explicitly.

Let $M$ be a smooth compact two-dimensional manifold (possibly with boundary) embedded in $\mathbb{R}^3$, equipped with the induced Riemannian metric. A "cut system" on $M$ is a finite collection $\mathcal{C}$ of disjoint simple arcs and loops on $M$ such that the complement $M\setminus\mathcal{C}$, after a cut-and-paste operation, becomes a (possibly disconnected) surface that admits a parameterization $\varphi:M\setminus\mathcal{C}\to\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ into a planar domain $\Omega$. The parameterization $\varphi$ is called quasi-isometric with constant $K\ge 1$ if for every tangent vector $v$ one has
$$K^{-1}\|v\|\le\|d\varphi(v)\|\le K\|v\|.$$
For a point $p\in M$, define its "pocket depth" with respect to a cut system $\mathcal{C}$ as the intrinsic distance from $p$ to the nearest cut or boundary component, taken along paths that remain in the connected component of $M\setminus\mathcal{C}$ containing $p$.

Problem: Develop a constructive procedure that, given $M$ and a target distortion bound $K$, selects a finite cut system $\mathcal{C}$ which is optimal in the following sense:
(a) The complement $M\setminus\mathcal{C}$ admits a $K$-quasi-isometric flattening into the plane, either as a single global unfolding or as a union of planar polygons cut from $M$; and
(b) Among all cut systems satisfying (a), $\mathcal{C}$ minimizes a suitable functional measuring the total length (or number) of cuts and the maximum pocket depth.

Formulate precise existence, uniqueness, and characterization theorems for such optimal cut systems, and describe an algorithm to compute them.

Let $S \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ be a piecewise smooth surface, and let $T$ be a triangulation (surface tessellation) whose vertices lie on $S$ and whose Hausdorff (chordal) distance to $S$ is at most a prescribed tolerance $\varepsilon > 0$. Equip $T$ with its induced polyhedral metric $g_T$ (the metric obtained by isometrically gluing the planar triangles). Assume $T$ is geometrically ill-conditioned in the sense that its triangles may have arbitrarily small minimum angles and that the aspect-ratio quality $Q(T) := \min_{t \in T} ho(t)/h(t)$ (in-radius over longest edge) may be arbitrarily close to $0$.

A quasi-isometric flattening of $(T, g_T)$ is a homeomorphism $\varphi : T 	o \Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$, piecewise affine on each triangle of $T$, whose quasi-isometric distortion
$$K(\varphi) := \operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{x \in T} \max\Big(\|D\varphi(x)\|_2,\; \|D\varphi(x)^{-1}\|_2\Big)$$
is bounded by a constant $K^\star$ depending only on the intrinsic geometry of $S$ (and not on the quality $Q(T)$).

Problem. Devise an algorithm that, given any such tessellation $T$ approximating $S$ to within chordal error $\varepsilon$, produces a quasi-isometric flattening $\varphi$ with $K(\varphi) \le K^\star$, in such a way that the image $\Omega = \varphi(T)$ can subsequently be remeshed into a triangulation $T'$ all of whose triangles are $\delta$-close to equilateral (i.e.\ all angles in $[\pi/3 - \delta, \pi/3 + \delta]$ for a prescribed $\delta > 0$), and such that the resulting remeshed surface $\varphi^{-1}(T')$ satisfies a finite-element patch test guaranteeing convergence of standard piecewise-linear approximations on it.

Prove existence of such an algorithm and provide explicit bounds on $K^\star$ in terms of the curvature and feature size of $S$, or show that no such algorithm exists under these hypotheses.

Let $X$ be a nonempty set and let $A:X\to X$ be an operator. Define $A^0=\mathrm{id}_X$ and $A^{n+1}=A\circ A^n$ for $n\ge 0$, and let $F_A=\{x\in X : A(x)=x\}$ denote the fixed point set of $A$. Assume there exists $x^*\in X$ such that
\[ F_A = F_{A^n} = \{x^*\} \qquad \text{for every } n\in\mathbb{N},\ n\ge 1. \]

Let $K$ be an ordered Banach space with positive cone, and call a map $d:X\times X\to K$ a $K$-metric on $X$ if for all $x,y,z\in X$:
(i) $d(x,y)\ge 0$ and $d(x,y)=0$ iff $x=y$;
(ii) $d(x,y)=d(y,x)$;
(iii) $d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$.

The operator $A$ is called a $K$-metric contraction on $(X,d)$ if there exists a positive linear operator $Q:K\to K$ with $\lVert Q\rVert<1$ such that
\[ d(A(x),A(y))\le Q\bigl(d(x,y)\bigr) \qquad \text{for all } x,y\in X. \]

Problem: Construct an ordered Banach space $K$ and a $K$-metric $d$ on $X$ such that $A:(X,d)\to (X,d)$ is a $K$-metric contraction in the sense above.

Let $\Gamma$ and $\Delta$ be residually finite groups (so the canonical maps from each group to its profinite completion are injective). For a group $G$, let $\widehat{G}$ denote the profinite completion of $G$, i.e. the inverse limit of the finite quotients $G/N$ over all normal subgroups $N$ of finite index in $G$.

Suppose $\psi:\Gamma\to\Delta$ is a group homomorphism such that the induced continuous homomorphism $\widehat{\psi}:\widehat{\Gamma}\to\widehat{\Delta}$ is an isomorphism of profinite groups.

(a) Quantify how far $\psi$ itself can fail to be an isomorphism. In particular, exhibit or rule out examples (beyond known constructions in the finitely generated and finitely presented settings) in which $\psi$ is not an isomorphism.

(b) Identify natural structural or finiteness hypotheses on $\Gamma$ and $\Delta$ (for instance, restrictions on subgroup growth, geometric, cohomological, or representation-theoretic finiteness properties) that are sufficient to force $\psi$ to be an isomorphism whenever $\widehat{\psi}$ is.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Grothendieck's original question (must $\psi$ be an isomorphism when $\widehat{\psi}$ is?) has been answered negatively: Platonov–Tavgen (1986) gave finitely generated counterexamples, and Bridson–Grunewald (Annals 2004) produced finitely presented, residually finite counterexamples, with further constructions giving continuously many such pairs and examples involving hyperbolic groups (e.g., recent work on relatively hyperbolic Grothendieck pairs, 2025). However, the broader question of classifying how far $\psi$ can fail to be an isomorphism and identifying sharp sufficient conditions on $\Gamma,\Delta$ forcing $\psi$ to be an isomorphism remains an active area with only partial sufficient conditions known.

Define the true prosoluble completion of a residually soluble discrete group Γ as the inverse limit
  PS(Γ) = lim_{←} Γ/N,
taken over the directed system of all normal subgroups N of Γ such that Γ/N is a soluble group, endowed with the natural profinite-style topology making it a complete Hausdorff topological group in which every nonidentity element is separated from 1 by an open normal subgroup with soluble quotient.

Call a complete Hausdorff topological group G "prosoluble-Hausdorff" if for every g ∈ G with g ≠ 1 there exists an open normal subgroup N ◁ G with g ∉ N and such that G/N is a (discrete) soluble group.

Problem. Find useful intrinsic characterizations of those prosoluble-Hausdorff topological groups G that arise as true prosoluble completions of residually soluble discrete groups. Specifically:

(a) Give a criterion, formulated intrinsically in terms of G, deciding whether there exists a finitely generated residually soluble group Γ such that G ≅ PS(Γ) as topological groups.

(b) Give a criterion, formulated intrinsically in terms of G, deciding whether there exists a finitely presented residually soluble group Γ such that G ≅ PS(Γ) as topological groups.

Let $\Gamma$ be an abstract (discrete) group. Define the ordinary derived series of $\Gamma$ by $D_0(\Gamma) = \Gamma$ and $D_{n+1}(\Gamma) = [D_n(\Gamma), D_n(\Gamma)]$ for $n \geq 0$. The group $\Gamma$ is called residually soluble if $\bigcap_{n \geq 0} D_n(\Gamma) = \{1\}$. The true prosoluble completion $PS(\Gamma)$ is the inverse limit of the system of all finite-index-or-not soluble quotients of $\Gamma$ (equivalently, the inverse limit of $\Gamma/D_n(\Gamma)$ over $n \geq 0$ together with further soluble refinements), and the kernel of the natural map $\Gamma \to PS(\Gamma)$ — called the true prosoluble kernel of $\Gamma$ — coincides with
$$K(\Gamma) := \bigcap_{n=0}^{\infty} D_n(\Gamma).$$

Investigate the structure of $K(\Gamma)$ for groups $\Gamma$ that are not residually soluble. In particular:

$$K(\Gamma) := \bigcap_{n=0}^{\infty} D_n(\Gamma).$$

Investigate the structure of $K(\Gamma)$ for groups $\Gamma$ that are not residually soluble. In particular:

(i) Determine $K(\Gamma)$ for non-residually-soluble one-relator groups.

(ii) Determine $K(\Gamma)$ for wreath products $A \wr B$ of suitable groups $A, B$ that fail to be residually soluble.

(iii) Determine $K(\Gamma)$ for free products with amalgamation $N_1 *_H N_2$ where $N_1, N_2$ are nilpotent groups.

(iv) Determine $K(\Gamma)$ for parafree groups $\Gamma$ (i.e., residually nilpotent groups having the same nilpotent quotients as some free group) which are not residually soluble.

(v) Determine $K(\Gamma)$ for meta-residually-soluble groups, i.e., groups $\Gamma$ admitting a normal subgroup $N \trianglelefteq \Gamma$ such that both $N$ and $\Gamma/N$ are residually soluble; in particular for free-by-free groups that are not residually soluble.

Subsequent work of Jaikin-Zapirain on the finite and solvable genus of finitely generated free and surface groups establishes a Grothendieck-rigidity result for free groups in the soluble setting: if F is a finitely generated free group, G is a finitely generated residually (finite) soluble group, and u: F → G induces an isomorphism on pro-(finite soluble) completions, then u is itself an isomorphism, so G is free. Since the hypothesis F/D_j(F) ≅ Γ/D_j(Γ) for all j (equivalently, PS(ψ) is an isomorphism) implies the pro-(finite soluble) completion is an isomorphism, this rules out any non-free Γ as in the question. The answer is therefore negative.

Work over the complex numbers. Let $\mathcal{M}_2$ denote the coarse moduli space of smooth projective curves of genus $2$. For an integer $n\ge 2$, define the locus
$$L_n \;=\; \{\,[C]\in \mathcal{M}_2 \;:\; \text{the Jacobian } J_C \text{ is } (n,n)\text{-isogenous to a product } E_1\times E_2 \text{ of two elliptic curves}\,\},$$
where an $(n,n)$-isogeny means an isogeny $J_C \to E_1\times E_2$ whose kernel is isomorphic to $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^2$ and is isotropic with respect to the Weil pairing induced by the principal polarization on $J_C$. Equivalently, $[C]\in L_n$ if and only if there exists a degree-$n$ maximal cover $\psi_1:C\to E_1$ to an elliptic curve $E_1$ (so that $\psi_1$ does not factor through a nontrivial isogeny of elliptic curves), in which case a complementary degree-$n$ elliptic subcover $\psi_2:C\to E_2$ is determined up to isogeny.

Take $n=7$.

(a) Determine $L_7$ explicitly as an algebraic subvariety of $\mathcal{M}_2$, e.g.\ by giving defining equations for $L_7$ in terms of the Igusa invariants $(J_2,J_4,J_6,J_{10})$ of genus-$2$ curves.

(b) For each point $[C]\in L_7$, determine the relation between the two degree-$7$ elliptic subcovers $E_1$ and $E_2$, e.g.\ a parametrization of the pair $(j(E_1),j(E_2))$ and the modular relation satisfied by their $j$-invariants.

Explicit algebraic descriptions of the locus $L_n$ in $\mathcal{M}_2$ of genus-$2$ curves with $(n,n)$-split Jacobian are known classically for $n=2$ and by Shaska–Völklein/Shaska for $n=3,5$. Consider the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations on $\mathbb{R}^3$:
$$\partial_t u_i + \sum_{j=1}^{3} u_j \,\partial_{x_j} u_i = \nu \,\Delta u_i - \partial_{x_i} p, \qquad \sum_{j=1}^{3} \partial_{x_j} u_j = 0,$$
for the velocity field $u(x,t) = (u_1, u_2, u_3)(x,t)$ and pressure $p(x,t)$, with viscosity $\nu > 0$. Let the initial data $u(x,0) = u_0(x)$ be a divergence-free vector field on $\mathbb{R}^3$ that is smooth ($C^\infty$) and sufficiently decaying at infinity (for instance, Schwartz class).

Decide one of the following:
(a) Prove that there exists a unique solution $u(x,t)$, smooth on $\mathbb{R}^3 \times (0,\infty)$, with $u(\cdot,t)$ remaining well-behaved at infinity, and a corresponding smooth pressure $p$, satisfying the system above for all $t > 0$ for every such initial data $u_0$.
(b) Exhibit smooth, divergence-free, decaying initial data $u_0$ for which no such globally smooth solution exists (i.e., demonstrate finite-time blow-up or non-uniqueness in the smooth category).

The global existence, uniqueness, and smoothness of solutions to the 3D incompressible Navier–Stokes equations with smooth initial data is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems and remains open as of 2026. Partial results exist (Leray–Hopf weak solutions, local-in-time smooth solutions, conditional regularity criteria, and recent non-uniqueness results for weak solutions by Buckmaster–Vicol and Albritton–Brué–Colombo for forced equations), but the central question for smooth Cauchy data is unresolved.
