Let $g \geq 2$ be an integer, let $G$ be a finite group, and let $\sigma = (g_0; m_1, \dots, m_r)$ be a signature, where $g_0 \geq 0$ and $m_1, \dots, m_r \geq 2$ are integers. Recall that $G$ is said to act on a compact Riemann surface (equivalently, a smooth projective complex algebraic curve) $X$ of genus $g$ with signature $\sigma$ if the quotient $X/G$ has genus $g_0$ and the quotient map $X \to X/G$ is branched over $r$ points with ramification indices $m_1, \dots, m_r$; equivalently, there is a surface-kernel epimorphism from the Fuchsian group with signature $\sigma$ onto $G$ whose kernel is a torsion-free surface group of genus $g$, and the Riemann–Hurwitz relation
$$2g - 2 = |G|\left(2g_0 - 2 + \sum_{i=1}^{r}\left(1 - \frac{1}{m_i}\right)\right)$$
is satisfied.

Assume that the pair $(G, \sigma)$ is admissible in the sense that there exists at least one smooth projective curve of genus $g$ admitting a faithful $G$-action with signature $\sigma$. The problem is to produce, for every such admissible pair $(G, \sigma)$, explicit defining polynomial equations for a curve (or for a family parametrizing the locus of all such curves) of genus $g$ whose automorphism group contains $G$ acting with the prescribed signature $\sigma$.

Let $X$ be a smooth projective algebraic curve over $\mathbb{C}$ of genus $g$ with $2 \le g \le 48$, and let $G = \operatorname{Aut}(X)$ be its full automorphism group. For each subgroup $H \le G$, let $X/H$ denote the quotient curve and $\operatorname{Jac}(X/H)$ its Jacobian. By the Kani–Rosen theorem, idempotent relations in the rational group algebra $\mathbb{Q}[G]$ yield isogeny decompositions of $\operatorname{Jac}(X)$ as products of abelian subvarieties, which in favorable cases are Jacobians of quotient curves $X/H$.

Problem: For every genus $g$ in the range $2 \le g \le 48$ and every group $G$ that occurs as the full automorphism group of some curve $X$ of genus $g$, determine, using the subgroup structure of $G$ and the corresponding quotient curves $X/H$, all possible isogeny decompositions
$$\operatorname{Jac}(X) \sim A_1^{n_1} \times \cdots \times A_k^{n_k},$$
giving in particular all decompositions in which each factor $A_i$ is isogenous to the Jacobian of a quotient curve of $X$ by some subgroup of $G$.

The problem is classical and only partially understood. A smooth projective curve $C$ of genus $3$ over an algebraically closed field $k$ is called hyperelliptic if it admits a degree-$2$ morphism to $\mathbb{P}^1$; equivalently (in characteristic $\neq 2$), it can be written as $y^2 = f(x)$ for a separable polynomial $f \in k[x]$ of degree $7$ or $8$. Two such curves are isomorphic if and only if the corresponding binary octic forms (obtained by homogenizing $f$) are equivalent under the natural action of $\mathrm{GL}_2(k)$.

Determine an explicit finite system of invariants $I_1, \ldots, I_n$ (polynomial/rational functions in the coefficients of the defining binary form, invariant under the $\mathrm{GL}_2$-action) such that the tuple $(I_1(C), \ldots, I_n(C))$ classifies the isomorphism class of a genus-$3$ hyperelliptic curve $C$; equivalently, exhibit a set of invariants that separates the points of the coarse moduli space of genus-$3$ hyperelliptic curves.

The Shioda invariants $J_2, J_3, \ldots, J_{10}$ of binary octic forms classify isomorphism classes of genus-$3$ hyperelliptic curves in characteristic $0$ or $p > 7$. Explicit algorithms (Lercier–Ritzenthaler and others) compute these invariants and reconstruct curves from them. In small positive characteristics ($p = 3, 5, 7$), additional invariants have been described to complete the classification. Thus the problem is solved.

A minimal generating set is classically known: nine invariants of degrees 2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9,10, found by von Gall (1880) and confirmed by Shioda (1967), with the ideal of relations generated in degrees 16–20. However, Shioda's explicit syzygies were later found to contain errors. Subsequent work (e.g., Lercier–Ritzenthaler and follow-ups on hyperelliptic genus-3 moduli) has redefined the invariants and corrected/computed the algebraic relations among them, so the problem is essentially resolved in the literature, though the original formulation of "fully correct generators and relations" was open at the time of posing and has been progressively settled.

representations.normalized:
Background. Let $M_g$ denote the coarse moduli space of smooth projective algebraic curves of genus $g \ge 2$ over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. A smooth curve $X$ of genus $g$ is called cyclic if it admits a cyclic cover $X \to \mathbb{P}^1$, i.e. a non-trivial cyclic subgroup $C_n \le \mathrm{Aut}(X)$ such that $X/C_n \cong \mathbb{P}^1$. For a fixed signature (genus $g$, order $n$, and ramification data), the cyclic curves with that signature form a locally closed sublocus $\mathcal{L} \subset M_g$, which may have positive dimension.

For the special case of hyperelliptic curves of genus $g$ that admit an extra (non-hyperelliptic) involution, one can put the curve in a normal form whose coefficients are acted on by a dihedral group $D_g$, and the invariants of this action — the so-called dihedral invariants $u_1,\dots,u_{2g-1}$ — give a birational parametrization of the corresponding sublocus of $M_g$ and can be used to determine the field of moduli of points in that sublocus.

Problem. For every cyclic family of curves whose corresponding sublocus $\mathcal{L} \subset M_g$ has positive dimension, construct an explicit set of invariants (analogous to the dihedral invariants in the hyperelliptic case with extra involution) that:
(i) are polynomial (or rational) invariants of the natural group action on the coefficients of a chosen normal form for the family;
(ii) provide a birational parametrization of $\mathcal{L}$;
(iii) allow one to read off the field of moduli of any point of $\mathcal{L}$ from the values of the invariants.

Use these invariants to give an explicit description of the cyclic moduli sublocus $\mathcal{L}$ in $M_g$.

The general program — defining dihedral-type invariants for cyclic covers of the line giving positive-dimensional loci in M_g — has been advanced in numerous works by Shaska and collaborators. A smooth structure on a topological manifold $M$ is a maximal atlas of charts whose transition maps are $C^\infty$. Two smooth manifolds are said to be diffeomorphic if there exists a bijection between them that is $C^\infty$ in both directions with respect to their smooth structures. Let $S^4 = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^5 : \|x\| = 1\}$ denote the standard 4-sphere with its standard smooth structure inherited from $\mathbb{R}^5$. An exotic smooth structure on $S^4$ is a smooth structure on the topological manifold $S^4$ that is not diffeomorphic to the standard one. Equivalently, an exotic $S^4$ is a smooth 4-manifold that is homeomorphic but not diffeomorphic to the standard $S^4$.

Question: Does there exist a smooth 4-manifold that is homeomorphic to $S^4$ but not diffeomorphic to the standard smooth $S^4$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The smooth Poincaré conjecture in dimension 4 — equivalently, the question of whether $S^4$ admits an exotic smooth structure — is widely regarded as one of the major open problems in geometric topology. As of 2026, no exotic smooth structure on $S^4$ has been confirmed, and no proof of its nonexistence is known; several candidate exotic 4-spheres have been proposed and subsequently shown to be standard or remain undetermined.

Setting: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. For an integer $g \ge 2$, let $\mathcal{H}_g$ denote the moduli space of hyperelliptic curves of genus $g$. Inside $\mathcal{H}_g$, consider the sublocus $\mathcal{L}_g$ consisting of isomorphism classes of hyperelliptic curves admitting an extra involution (i.e., an involution in the reduced automorphism group other than the identity). A curve in this locus has an affine model of the form
$$y^2 = x^{2g+2} + a_g x^{2g} + a_{g-1} x^{2g-2} + \cdots + a_1 x^2 + 1,$$
on which the dihedral group $D_{2(g+1)}$ acts via $x \mapsto \zeta x$ (for a primitive $(g+1)$-th root of unity $\zeta$) together with $x \mapsto 1/x$. The ring of invariants $k[a_1,\dots,a_g]^{D_{2(g+1)}}$ is generated by certain explicit symmetric polynomials $u_1,\dots,u_m$ in $a_1,\dots,a_g$, called the dihedral invariants; the tuple $(u_1,\dots,u_m)$ generically classifies isomorphism classes of curves in $\mathcal{L}_g$.

More generally, a cyclic curve is a smooth projective curve $C$ admitting a cyclic subgroup $\langle \tau \rangle$ in its automorphism group such that $C / \langle \tau \rangle$ has genus $0$. The cyclic moduli is the locus inside $\mathcal{M}_g$ parametrizing such curves, stratified by signature data of the cyclic cover. On each stratum, one may analogously define dihedral-type invariants associated with the normalizer of $\langle \tau \rangle$ in $\mathrm{Aut}(C)$.

Problem: For every sublocus of the cyclic moduli of algebraic curves, determine explicitly the ideal of algebraic relations satisfied by the corresponding dihedral invariants. That is, for each such stratum, give generators of the relation ideal $I \subset k[U_1,\dots,U_N]$ such that $k[U_1,\dots,U_N]/I$ is the coordinate ring of the image of the stratum under the map given by the dihedral invariants.

Dihedral invariants of hyperelliptic curves with extra involutions were introduced by Gutierrez and Shaska, who determined the algebraic relations explicitly in low genus (g=2,3,4). Subsequent work on superelliptic and cyclic curves has extended the framework, but a complete determination of the relations among dihedral invariants on every sublocus of the cyclic moduli is not available in the literature; the general problem appears to remain open, with only partial results in special families.

Let $g \geq 3$ be an integer and let $\mathcal{M}_g$ denote the coarse moduli space of smooth projective curves of genus $g$ over $\mathbb{C}$. For a smooth projective complex curve $X$ of genus $g$ and a finite group $G$ acting faithfully on $X$, the signature of the action is the tuple $\sigma = (g_0; m_1, \ldots, m_r)$, where $g_0$ is the genus of the quotient $X/G$ and $m_1, \ldots, m_r$ are the orders of the (non-trivial) stabilizers at the branch points of the quotient map $X \to X/G$. Define
$$\mathcal{M}_g(G,\sigma) = \{[X] \in \mathcal{M}_g : G \hookrightarrow \operatorname{Aut}(X) \text{ with signature } \sigma\}.$$

Recall that for a principally polarized abelian variety $(A,\Theta)$ of dimension $g$ with a chosen symplectic basis, the theta nulls are the values $\theta\!\left[{a \atop b}\right](0,\tau)$ at the origin of the Riemann theta functions with half-integer characteristics $a,b \in \tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}^g/\mathbb{Z}^g$, evaluated at the period matrix $\tau$ in the Siegel upper half-space $\mathfrak{H}_g$. Via the Torelli map $\mathcal{M}_g \to \mathcal{A}_g$, these provide coordinates (modulo the action of $\operatorname{Sp}(2g,\mathbb{Z})$) on the image of $\mathcal{M}_g$.

Problem. For every triple $(g, G, \sigma)$ with $g \geq 3$, give an explicit description of the locus $\mathcal{M}_g(G,\sigma)$ in terms of equations, vanishing conditions, and algebraic relations among the theta nulls of the corresponding Jacobians.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Hilbert's tenth problem over $\mathbb{Q}$ is widely regarded as a major open problem. While Matiyasevich (building on Davis, Putnam, Robinson) settled the negative answer over $\mathbb{Z}$ in 1970, decidability of Diophantine equations over $\mathbb{Q}$ remains unresolved. Recent work (e.g., Koenigsmann's universal definition of $\mathbb{Z}$ in $\mathbb{Q}$, results over rings of integers in number fields by Garcia-Fritz–Pasten, and 2024 progress extending undecidability to more rings of integers) has advanced the area, but the rational case is still open as of 2026.

Let $k$ be a field and let $\varphi : k^n \dashrightarrow k^m$ be a rational map whose coordinate functions are $f_i(x) = p_i(x)/q_i(x)$, where $p_i, q_i \in k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ are polynomials of degrees $d_i$ for $i=1,\dots,m$. The degree of $\varphi$ is defined as the cardinality of a generic fibre $\varphi^{-1}(y)$ (equivalently, the degree of the extension of function fields $[k(x_1,\dots,x_n) : k(f_1,\dots,f_m)]$ when $\varphi$ is dominant and generically finite, and $0$ otherwise).

One standard but computationally expensive way to compute $\deg(\varphi)$ is to solve the generic polynomial system
$$p_i(x) - y_i\, q_i(x) = 0, \qquad i = 1,\dots,m,$$
in the variables $x_1,\dots,x_n$ (with $y_1,\dots,y_m$ kept as parameters) by means of a Gröbner-basis computation and to count the number of solutions in a generic fibre.

Design an efficient algorithm, combining symbolic computation and numerical methods (such as homotopy continuation or other techniques of numerical algebraic geometry), that determines $\deg(\varphi)$ from the data $(p_i, q_i)_{i=1}^m$ without relying solely on a Gröbner-basis solution of the above generic system. Establish the correctness of the algorithm and analyze its complexity.

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

There has been substantial progress on computing degrees of rational maps via symbolic techniques (e.g., projective-degree algorithms in the Macaulay2 Cremona package; specialization and syzygy-based methods in works such as arXiv:1901.06599 and arXiv:2007.13017) and via numerical algebraic geometry (homotopy continuation as in Bertini and HomotopyContinuation.jl, which can numerically count fibre points). However, no single hybrid symbolic-numerical algorithm is universally recognized as the definitive efficient solution to the problem as posed, so the open-ended algorithmic design problem appears to remain partially addressed rather than fully resolved.

Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero and let $X \subset \mathbb{A}^n_k$ (or $\mathbb{P}^n_k$) be an irreducible algebraic surface that is parametrizable, i.e., there exists a dominant rational map $\varphi: \mathbb{A}^2_k \dashrightarrow X$ given by rational functions in two parameters whose image is Zariski-dense in $X$. Equivalently, the function field $k(X)$ is a purely transcendental extension of $k$ of transcendence degree two.

Design an efficient algorithm which, given as input the defining ideal (or implicit equations) of such a surface $X$, decides parametrizability and, when $X$ is parametrizable, outputs an explicit rational parametrization $\varphi(s,t) = (\varphi_1(s,t), \ldots, \varphi_n(s,t)) \in k(s,t)^n$ of $X$. The algorithm should work for arbitrary parametrizable algebraic surfaces (not only special classes such as quadrics, cubics, or surfaces of fixed degree), and its complexity should be analyzed.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Algorithms for parametrizing rational algebraic surfaces have been developed, notably by Schicho (1998) who gave a general algorithm for rational surfaces, and by Sendra and collaborators who treated properness, inversion, and radical parametrizations. However, designing a uniformly efficient algorithm for arbitrary parametrizable surfaces remains an active topic, and follow-up work on radical parametrizations and reparametrization continues. The problem is thus partially solved: existence of algorithms is known, but efficiency and full generality are still being investigated.

Consider planar polynomial differential systems of degree 2, that is, vector fields of the form
  dx/dt = P(x,y),   dy/dt = Q(x,y),
where P, Q ∈ ℝ[x,y] are polynomials with max(deg P, deg Q) = 2. A limit cycle of such a system is an isolated periodic orbit in the phase plane ℝ². Let H(2) denote the supremum, over all such quadratic vector fields, of the number of limit cycles a single system can possess. It is known that H(2) ≥ 4 (explicit quadratic systems with four limit cycles have been constructed).

Question: Does there exist a quadratic polynomial vector field on the plane having five or more limit cycles? Equivalently, is H(2) > 4?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question of whether a planar quadratic polynomial vector field can have more than four limit cycles remains open. The best known lower bound is 4 (Shi Songling, Chen-Wang, 1979–80), disproving an earlier claim by Petrovskii and Landis of an upper bound of 3. No upper bound is known, and the problem is part of Hilbert's 16th problem for n = 2.

A Moore graph is a regular graph that achieves the Moore bound: for a graph of maximum degree $k$ and diameter $d$, the number of vertices is at most
$$1 + k\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}(k-1)^i.$$
Equivalently, a Moore graph of degree $k$ and diameter $2$ is a $k$-regular graph on $k^2+1$ vertices with girth $5$ (every two non-adjacent vertices have exactly one common neighbor, and every two adjacent vertices have no common neighbor).

It is known that a Moore graph of diameter $2$ can exist only for degree $k \in \{2, 3, 7, 57\}$. Examples are known for $k=2$ (the $5$-cycle), $k=3$ (the Petersen graph), and $k=7$ (the Hoffman–Singleton graph).

Question: Does there exist a Moore graph of degree $57$ and diameter $2$, i.e., a $57$-regular graph on $3250$ vertices with girth $5$?

Let $E$ be an elliptic curve defined over the rational numbers $\mathbb{Q}$, i.e., a smooth projective curve of genus one with a specified $\mathbb{Q}$-rational point, given (after a change of variables) by a Weierstrass equation $y^2 = x^3 + ax + b$ with $a, b \in \mathbb{Q}$ and nonzero discriminant. By the Mordell-Weil theorem, the abelian group $E(\mathbb{Q})$ of $\mathbb{Q}$-rational points is finitely generated, so $E(\mathbb{Q}) \cong \mathbb{Z}^{r(E)} \oplus T$ for some finite torsion group $T$ and a nonnegative integer $r(E)$, called the rank of $E$.

Question: Does there exist an absolute constant $R$ such that $r(E) \le R$ for every elliptic curve $E$ defined over $\mathbb{Q}$? Equivalently, is the set $\{r(E) : E\text{ elliptic curve over }\mathbb{Q}\}$ bounded?

Let $n \geq 3$ be an integer. Call an $n \times n$ real matrix $A = (a_{ij})$ doubly stochastic if $a_{ij} \geq 0$ for all $i,j$ and $\sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij} = \sum_{i=1}^n a_{ij} = 1$ for every $i$ and every $j$. The permanent of $A$ is defined by
$$\operatorname{per}(A) = \sum_{\sigma \in S_n} \prod_{i=1}^n a_{i\sigma(i)},$$
where $S_n$ is the symmetric group on $\{1,\dots,n\}$. Let $\Omega_n^0$ denote the set of all $n\times n$ doubly stochastic matrices $A$ with $a_{ii} = 0$ for all $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$. Define $M_n \in \Omega_n^0$ to be the matrix whose diagonal entries equal $0$ and whose off-diagonal entries all equal $\tfrac{1}{n-1}$.

Prove or disprove: $\operatorname{per}(A) \geq \operatorname{per}(M_n)$ for every $A \in \Omega_n^0$, with equality if and only if $A = M_n$.

Olga Taussky observed that a number of theorems valid for Hermitian positive semidefinite matrices (Hermitian matrices $A$ satisfying $x^{*}Ax \ge 0$ for every vector $x$) have close analogues that hold for matrices whose entries (or whose minors of all orders) are nonnegative, but that the known proofs in the two settings are typically different. Examples of this parallel include the nonnegativity of eigenvalues, monotonicity properties of eigenvalues under principal submatrix extraction, the positivity of principal minors, and various permanent inequalities (such as inequalities of Schur, Marcus, and Lieb type), all of which are known for both positive semidefinite Hermitian matrices and for entrywise/totally nonnegative matrices.

Problem. Provide a single unified mathematical framework that explains, in a rigorous way, the parallel between the following two notions of "positivity" for a square matrix $A$ with complex entries:
(i) operator positivity: $A$ is Hermitian and $x^{*}Ax \ge 0$ for all vectors $x$;
(ii) entrywise positivity / total nonnegativity: every entry of $A$ (respectively every minor of $A$) is nonnegative.

More precisely, identify a common structural principle (for instance a common axiomatic class of matrices, a common cone-theoretic or representation-theoretic mechanism, or a common proof technique) from which the shared theorems — in particular the parallel permanent inequalities and the shared spectral and minor-positivity properties — can be deduced simultaneously for both classes.

No known obstructions rule it out in dimensions ≥ 5 (unlike dimension 4, where Hitchin–Thorpe and LeBrun-type obstructions exist), and no general existence theorem is known.

Let $A=(a_{ij})$ be an $n\times n$ positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix. Fix an ordering of the symmetric group $S_n$ and define the Schur power matrix $\pi(A)$ of $A$ to be the $n!\times n!$ matrix indexed by pairs $(\sigma,\tau)\in S_n\times S_n$ with entries
$$\pi(A)_{\sigma,\tau}=\prod_{i=1}^{n}a_{\sigma(i),\tau(i)}.$$
The matrix $\pi(A)$ is positive semidefinite, and one of its eigenvalues equals the permanent
$$\operatorname{per}(A)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^{n}a_{i,\sigma(i)}.$$
Determine whether $\operatorname{per}(A)$ is always the largest eigenvalue of $\pi(A)$; that is, decide whether for every $n$ and every $n\times n$ positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix $A$, $\operatorname{per}(A)$ equals the spectral radius of $\pi(A)$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The permanent-on-top (Soules) conjecture has been disproved. Counterexamples have been constructed, including a simple complex 5×5 positive semidefinite matrix of rank 2 for which per(A) is not the largest eigenvalue of the Schur power matrix π(A). Earlier computer-assisted counterexamples were also found, settling the conjecture negatively.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem (known as the prime power conjecture for projective planes) is open. Order 6 was ruled out by Tarry (1901), order 10 by Lam, Thiel and Swiercz (1989) via computer search, and the Bruck–Ryser–Chowla theorem excludes many orders. The smallest open non-prime-power case is order 12, and no projective plane of non-prime-power order is known.

Let $n$ be a positive integer and let $A=(a_{ij})$ be an $n\times n$ complex positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix. Recall that the permanent of $A$ is
$$\operatorname{per}(A)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^{n}a_{i,\sigma(i)},$$
where $S_n$ denotes the symmetric group on $\{1,\dots,n\}$. Let $G\leq S_n$ be a subgroup and let $\chi:G\to\mathbb{C}$ be a (complex) character of $G$. Define the generalized matrix function (immanant-type function) associated to $(G,\chi)$ by
$$d^{G}_{\chi}(A)=\sum_{\sigma\in G}\chi(\sigma)\prod_{i=1}^{n}a_{i,\sigma(i)}.$$
Prove or disprove: for every $n$, every positive semidefinite Hermitian $n\times n$ matrix $A$, every subgroup $G\leq S_n$, and every character $\chi$ of $G$,
$$\chi(\mathrm{id})\,\operatorname{per}(A)\;\geq\;d^{G}_{\chi}(A).$$
(Equivalently, with the normalization $\chi(\mathrm{id})=1$ as a linear character or in the form stated above, the permanent dominates the corresponding generalized matrix function.)

The permanental dominance conjecture (often attributed to Lieb, 1966) remains open in general. Recent surveys and papers (e.g., a 2022 arXiv survey by Shchesnovich and a 2024 paper in Advances in Applied Mathematics) describe it as a long-standing unresolved problem, with only partial results known for specific groups, characters, and small dimensions.

This problem was resolved affirmatively in 2016 by Croot–Lev–Pach (in the related group $(\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z})^n$) and Ellenberg–Gijswijt, who proved using the polynomial method that the maximum cap set in $(\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z})^r$ has size $O(c^r)$ for an explicit constant $c \approx 2.756 < 3$, giving such a $\delta > 0$.

Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix, and fix an integer $k$ with $1\le k\le n-1$. Let $G_{k,n}$ denote the set of strictly increasing functions from $\{1,\dots,k\}$ to $\{1,\dots,n\}$ (equivalently, the set of $k$-element subsets of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ listed in increasing order). For $\alpha,\beta\in G_{k,n}$, let $A[\alpha,\beta]$ denote the $k\times k$ submatrix of $A$ obtained by selecting the rows indexed by $\alpha$ and the columns indexed by $\beta$, and let $A(\alpha,\beta)$ denote the complementary $(n-k)\times(n-k)$ submatrix obtained by deleting the rows indexed by $\alpha$ and the columns indexed by $\beta$. Let $\operatorname{per}$ denote the permanent. Define the matrix $C_k(A)$, indexed by $G_{k,n}\times G_{k,n}$, by
$$\bigl(C_k(A)\bigr)_{\alpha,\beta} \;=\; \operatorname{per}\bigl(A(\alpha,\beta)\bigr)\,\operatorname{per}\bigl(A[\alpha,\beta]\bigr).$$
Prove or disprove: for every such $A$ and every $k\in\{1,\dots,n-1\}$, $\operatorname{per}(A)$ is the largest eigenvalue of $C_k(A)$.

For an $n\times n$ complex (or real) positive semidefinite matrix $A=(a_{ij})$ and a real parameter $q$, define the $q$-permanent of $A$ by
$$\operatorname{per}_q(A)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n} q^{\operatorname{inv}(\sigma)} \prod_{i=1}^{n} a_{i,\sigma(i)},$$
where $S_n$ is the symmetric group on $\{1,\dots,n\}$ and $\operatorname{inv}(\sigma)=\#\{(i,j):1\le i<j\le n,\ \sigma(i)>\sigma(j)\}$ is the number of inversions of $\sigma$. Note that $\operatorname{per}_{-1}(A)=\det(A)$, $\operatorname{per}_{1}(A)=\operatorname{per}(A)$, and $\operatorname{per}_{0}(A)=\prod_{i=1}^{n} a_{ii}$.

Prove or disprove: for every $n\ge 1$ and every $n\times n$ positive semidefinite matrix $A$, the function $q\mapsto \operatorname{per}_q(A)$ is monotonically nondecreasing on the interval $[-1,1]$.

Let q ≥ 2 be a prime power and let V be a 7-dimensional vector space over the finite field F_q. For a non-negative integer k, let [V choose k]_q denote the set of all k-dimensional subspaces of V. A q-analog of the Fano plane (equivalently, a 2-(7,3,1)_q design) is a collection B ⊆ [V choose 3]_q of 3-dimensional subspaces of V such that every 2-dimensional subspace of V is contained in exactly one member of B. Geometrically (viewing PG(6,q) as the projective space associated with V), this is a set of planes in PG(6,q) that covers each line of PG(6,q) exactly once.

Question: For which prime powers q ≥ 2 does a q-analog of the Fano plane exist? In particular, does such a design exist for any prime power q ≥ 2?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The existence of a q-analog of the Fano plane remains open for every prime power q ≥ 2. The problem dates back to 1972, and recent work has only made partial progress: bounds on automorphism groups (the automorphism group of a putative binary q-Fano plane has order at most 2), the existence of non-α-points and blocking-set structure of non-α-points, and constructions of residual q-Fano planes. No construction or nonexistence proof of an actual q-analog of the Fano plane is known.

Let $A=(a_{ij})$ be an $n\times n$ positive semidefinite (Hermitian) matrix and let $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$. Define the $\alpha$-determinant of $A$ by
$$\det{}_{\alpha}(A)\;=\;\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\alpha^{\,n-\nu(\sigma)}\prod_{i=1}^{n}a_{i,\sigma(i)},$$
where $S_n$ is the symmetric group on $n$ letters and $\nu(\sigma)$ denotes the number of cycles of $\sigma$ (including fixed points). Note that $\det_{-1}(A)=\det(A)$ and $\det_{1}(A)=\operatorname{per}(A)$.

Prove or disprove: for every integer $n\ge 1$, every $n\times n$ positive semidefinite matrix $A$, and every real number $\alpha$ with $0\le\alpha\le 2$,
$$\det{}_{\alpha}(A)\;\ge\;0.$$

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The positivity problem for the alpha-determinant was raised by Shirai and Takahashi and studied by Vere-Jones and others. Positivity is known for special values such as α = 1 (the permanent of a PSD matrix, Schur) and α a nonnegative integer multiple of 1/2 via Wishart-type identities, and for α in a neighborhood of 0 (Shirai). The full claim that det_α(A) ≥ 0 for all PSD A whenever 0 ≤ α ≤ 2 remains a conjecture in general; it is established only in restricted parameter ranges or low dimensions, while α > 2 is known to fail.

Let $n\ge 2$ and fix positive vectors $c, b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_{n-1} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ (i.e. vectors with strictly positive entries). For an $n\times n$ matrix $M$, let $\operatorname{per}(M)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^n M_{i,\sigma(i)}$ denote the permanent of $M$. Given column vectors $v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\mathbb{R}^n$, write $\operatorname{per}[v_1,\ldots,v_n]$ for the permanent of the matrix whose $j$-th column is $v_j$.

For an integer $r$ with $1\le r\le n$ and a positive vector $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$, define
$$S_{r,n}(x) \;=\; \frac{\operatorname{per}[\,\underbrace{x,\ldots,x}_{r\text{ times}},\,b_1,\ldots,b_{n-r}\,]}{\operatorname{per}[\,\underbrace{x,\ldots,x}_{r-1\text{ times}},\,b_1,\ldots,b_{n-r},\,c\,]}.$$

Determine whether, for every choice of positive vectors $x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n$ and every $r$ with $1\le r\le n$, the superadditivity inequality
$$S_{r,n}(x+y) \;\ge\; S_{r,n}(x) + S_{r,n}(y)$$
holds.

Let $q$ be a prime power, $A=\mathbb{F}_q[t]$, $K=\mathbb{F}_q(t)$, and let $K_\infty=\mathbb{F}_q((1/t))$ denote the completion at the place at infinity. For a positive integer $s$ and a non-negative integer $d$, set
$$ S_d(s) \;=\; \sum_{\substack{n\in A\text{ monic} \\ \deg n = d}} \frac{1}{n^s} \;\in\; K. $$
For positive integers $s_1,\dots,s_k$ define the function-field multizeta value
$$ \zeta_A(s_1,\dots,s_k) \;=\; \sum_{d_1 > d_2 > \cdots > d_k \ge 0} S_{d_1}(s_1)\,S_{d_2}(s_2)\cdots S_{d_k}(s_k) \;=\; \sum \frac{1}{n_1^{s_1}\cdots n_k^{s_k}} \;\in\; K_\infty, $$
the second sum running over $k$-tuples of monic polynomials $n_i\in A$ with $\deg n_1 > \deg n_2 > \cdots > \deg n_k \ge 0$. The integer $k$ is called the depth and $s_1+\cdots+s_k$ the weight.

Problem. Determine all $\mathbb{F}_p$-linear (equivalently, all polynomial) algebraic relations among the values $\zeta_A(s_1,\dots,s_k)$, $k\ge 1$, $s_i\ge 1$. Specifically:

(a) Identify a complete family of "shuffle-type" identities that, in positive characteristic, replace the classical sum-shuffle and integral-shuffle product formulas; that is, for any positive integers $r_1,\dots,r_a$ and $u_1,\dots,u_b$, express
$$ \zeta_A(r_1,\dots,r_a)\cdot \zeta_A(u_1,\dots,u_b) $$
as an explicit $\mathbb{F}_p$-linear combination of multizeta values of the same weight $r_1+\cdots+r_a+u_1+\cdots+u_b$, and prove that the resulting set of identities generates the full ideal of relations.

(b) Formulate and prove the additional "digit-phenomena" identities (relations forced by carries/digit interactions in base $q$ arising from the power sums $S_d(s)$) that are not consequences of the shuffle-type identities in (a).

(c) Show that the relations in (a) and (b) together generate all $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebraic relations among the $\zeta_A(s_1,\dots,s_k)$, and deduce the dimension of the $\mathbb{F}_p$-vector space spanned by multizeta values of each fixed weight $w$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Major progress has been made: Thakur established shuffle-type product relations for multizeta values over $\mathbb{F}_q[t]$ with $\mathbb{F}_p$-coefficients, making their span an algebra, and Chen and others gave a $t$-motivic interpretation. Conjectural dimensions (Todd's conjecture) and many explicit relations including digit-phenomena identities have been proved. However, a complete description of all algebraic relations (and a full proof that shuffle plus digit-phenomena identities generate the entire ideal of relations, with proved dimension formulas in every weight) is still considered an open program.

Let $\mathbb{F}_q$ be a finite field with $q$ elements, set $A = \mathbb{F}_q[t]$, let $K = \mathbb{F}_q(t)$, let $K_\infty = \mathbb{F}_q((1/t))$ be the completion at the infinite place, and let $\mathbb{C}_\infty$ be the completion of an algebraic closure of $K_\infty$. For a positive integer $s$, define the Goss zeta value
$$\zeta_A(s) \;=\; \sum_{\substack{a \in A \\ a \text{ monic}}} \frac{1}{a^s} \;\in\; K_\infty.$$
Goss extended this construction to a continuous interpolation $\zeta_A : S_\infty \to \mathbb{C}_\infty$, where $S_\infty = \mathbb{C}_\infty^\times \times \mathbb{Z}_p$ is the Goss "complex plane", whose domain contains both the positive integers and the negative integers (so that the special values $\zeta_A(-n)$ for $n \geq 0$ are defined, and in fact lie in $A$). For each integer $n \geq 0$ one also has function-field gamma factors $\Gamma(n+1)$ constructed in the theory of $\mathbb{F}_q$-linear (arithmetic and geometric) gamma functions on $A$.

Problem. Formulate and establish a functional equation, in the style of Tate's thesis, that relates the family of special values $\{\zeta_A(s)\}_{s \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}}$ to the family of special values $\{\zeta_A(-n)\}_{n \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}}$ of the Goss zeta function for $A = \mathbb{F}_q[t]$. The functional equation should incorporate the function-field gamma functions as the local factor at the infinite place of $K$, in analogy with the role played by $\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)$ in the classical functional equation of the Riemann zeta function.

No functional equation in the style of Tate's thesis is known relating the Goss zeta values at positive integers to those at negative integers for $A=\mathbb{F}_q[t]$, nor is there an established role for the function-field gamma functions as the factor at infinity. Recent work focuses on zeros and the Riemann-hypothesis analogue (Sheats 1998 and successors), but the desired functional equation remains unestablished.

representations.normalized:
Consider elliptic curves $E$ defined over the field of rational numbers $\mathbb{Q}$. By the Mordell–Weil theorem, the abelian group $E(\mathbb{Q})$ of rational points is finitely generated, and hence isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}^r \oplus T$ for some non-negative integer $r$ (the arithmetic rank) and finite torsion subgroup $T$. The analytic rank of $E$ is defined to be the order of vanishing at $s = 1$ of the Hasse–Weil $L$-function $L(E,s)$.

Question: As $E$ varies over all elliptic curves defined over $\mathbb{Q}$, is there an absolute constant $C$ such that the arithmetic rank of $E(\mathbb{Q})$ is at most $C$? Equivalently, does $\sup_E \mathrm{rank}\, E(\mathbb{Q}) < \infty$? The analogous question is asked for the analytic rank of $E$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The boundedness of ranks of elliptic curves over $\mathbb{Q}$ is a well-known open problem. Recent heuristics (Park, Poonen, Voight, Wood, 2019) suggest ranks should be bounded, with only finitely many curves of rank greater than 21, but this is not proved. Explicit examples are known with rank at least 29 (Elkies–Klagsbrun, 2024). The analytic rank version is similarly unresolved.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The nonnegative inverse eigenvalue problem (NIEP) is classically solved for n ≤ 4 but remains open for all n ≥ 5. The symmetric variant (SNIEP) is likewise solved only for n ≤ 4, with partial progress for n = 5 (e.g., the trace-zero case by Laffey–Meehan, 1999). No general necessary-and-sufficient characterization is known for n ≥ 5.

Fix $\omega>0$. Let $g:(0,+\infty)	o(0,+\infty)$ be a continuous function satisfying $\lim_{x	o 0^+} g(x)=+\infty$ and $\lim_{x	o +\infty} g(x)=0$. For an $\omega$-periodic, Lebesgue integrable function $h:\mathbb{R}	o\mathbb{R}$, consider the second-order scalar equation
$$u''(t)+g(u(t))=h(t)\quad	ext{for a.e. }t\in\mathbb{R},$$
and call a Carathéodory solution $u$ a positive $\omega$-periodic solution if $u\in AC^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R})$, $u(t)>0$ for all $t$, $u(t+\omega)=u(t)$, and the equation holds almost everywhere. Denote the mean value $ ar h= rac{1}{\omega}\int_0^\omega h(s)\,ds$.

It is known that when $h$ is additionally essentially bounded, a positive $\omega$-periodic solution exists if and only if $ ar h>0$.

Question: Does the equivalence ``a positive $\omega$-periodic solution exists $\iff  ar h>0$'' continue to hold for every $\omega$-periodic Lebesgue integrable $h$ (with no essential-boundedness assumption)?

The question is resolved in the negative: when the essential-boundedness hypothesis on $h$ is dropped, the Lazer–Solimini equivalence no longer holds. Counterexamples have been constructed showing that for merely integrable $\omega$-periodic forcings $h$ with $\bar h>0$, no positive $\omega$-periodic solution need exist.

Let $A$ be a paraparticle algebra (for instance, the parabosonic algebra $P_B$, the parafermionic algebra $P_F$, or one of the relative paraparticle algebras $P_{BF}$, $P_{FB}$), realized as a $\mathbb{Z}_2$-graded (or more generally $G$-graded) associative algebra whose generators satisfy trilinear relations of Green's type. Recall Green's ansatz: for each positive integer $p$, the $p$-Fock-like representation of $A$ is obtained by realizing the generators of $A$ as suitable sums of $p$ commuting/anticommuting copies of ordinary (anti)commutation generators acting on a $p$-fold tensor product of bosonic/fermionic Fock spaces, and then restricting to the cyclic submodule generated by the vacuum. In the braided setting, one replaces the ordinary tensor product by a braided tensor product determined by a graded braiding $\psi$ compatible with the grading group $G$, and the resulting construction (the braided Green ansatz) produces, for each $p\ge 1$, a graded $A$-module $V_p$ on a braided tensor power of a single-mode Fock representation.

Question: For the modules $V_p$ produced by the braided Green ansatz, decompose $V_p$ into irreducible $A$-submodules. Does this decomposition contain any irreducible direct summand or irreducible submodule that is not isomorphic to one of the known $p$-Fock-like irreducible representations of $A$? Equivalently, determine whether the family of $p$-Fock-like modules exhausts the irreducible constituents of every braided Green-ansatz tensor representation, or exhibit an irreducible constituent outside this family.

For integers n ≥ 3 and 1 ≤ q ≤ n−1, let CS(n, q) denote the complete split graph consisting of a clique on q vertices and an independent set on the remaining n − q vertices, with every vertex of the clique adjacent to every vertex of the independent set. Let q = ⌊2n/3⌋, so that n − q = ⌈n/3⌉.

Prove or disprove: for every connected graph G on n ≥ 3 vertices,
  s(G) ≤ √(4qn − 3q² − 2q + 1),
with equality if and only if G ≅ CS(n, q). Equivalently, show that the maximum of s(G) over all connected graphs on n vertices is attained exactly by the complete split graph CS(n, ⌊2n/3⌋).

For a finite simple graph H, let ex(n, H) denote the Turán number of H, i.e., the maximum number of edges in an n-vertex simple graph that contains no copy of H as a subgraph. A real number r is called a Turán exponent if there exists a graph H such that ex(n, H) = Θ(n^r), meaning there exist positive constants c_1, c_2 and an integer n_0 such that c_1 n^r ≤ ex(n, H) ≤ c_2 n^r for all n ≥ n_0.

Prove or disprove: for every rational number p/q with 1 < p/q < 2, there exists a bipartite graph G such that ex(n, G) = Θ(n^{p/q}).

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The conjecture remains open in its original single-graph form. Bukh and Conlon (2018) proved a family version: for every rational r ∈ [1,2) there is a finite family of bipartite graphs with Turán number Θ(n^r). For individual bipartite graphs, only special families of rationals are known to be realized (e.g., 1+1/k, 2-1/k, 2-2/(2k+1), and rationals 1+p/q with q > p^2 by Jiang–Qiu, plus further classes obtained via subdivisions and related constructions). No full resolution has been announced.

\]
where all parameters \(\alpha_i,\beta_i,\gamma_i,\delta_i,A_i,B_i,C_i,D_i\) (\(i=1,2,3\)) are nonnegative real numbers, and the initial conditions \((x_0,y_0,z_0)\) are nonnegative. Consider the second-order rational difference equation
  z_{n+1} = (α + β z_n + γ z_{n-1}) / (A + B z_n + C z_{n-1}),   n = 0, 1, 2, ...,
where the parameters α, β, γ, A, B, C are nonnegative real numbers with C > 0, and where initial conditions z_{-1}, z_0 are chosen so that the denominator A + B z_n + C z_{n-1} is positive for all n ≥ 0 (in particular, all positive initial conditions are admissible whenever the equation is well-defined).

An equilibrium of the equation is a point z̄ ≥ 0 satisfying
  z̄ = (α + (β+γ) z̄) / (A + (B+C) z̄).
Such an equilibrium z̄ is called locally asymptotically stable if it is Lyapunov stable and there exists δ > 0 such that every solution {z_n} with |z_{-1} − z̄| + |z_0 − z̄| < δ satisfies z_n → z̄ as n → ∞. The equilibrium z̄ is called a global attractor of all positive solutions if every solution {z_n} with z_{-1}, z_0 > 0 (for which the recurrence is well-defined for all n) satisfies z_n → z̄.

Question: Is it true that, for every choice of nonnegative parameters α, β, γ, A, B, C with C > 0, whenever an equilibrium of the recurrence is locally asymptotically stable, it is a global attractor of all positive solutions?

A polycyclic group $G$ is a group admitting a subnormal series $G = G_1 \triangleright G_2 \triangleright \cdots \triangleright G_{n+1} = 1$ with each quotient $G_i/G_{i+1}$ cyclic; fixing generators $g_i \in G_i$ with $g_iG_{i+1}$ generating $G_i/G_{i+1}$ yields a polycyclic generating sequence, and every element of $G$ has a unique normal form $g_1^{e_1}g_2^{e_2}\cdots g_n^{e_n}$ with $e_i \in \mathbb{Z}$ (and $0 \le e_i < r_i$ when $G_i/G_{i+1}$ is finite of order $r_i$). The "collection" problem is, given an arbitrary word in the generators and their inverses, to compute this normal form.

The Malcev correspondence is the equivalence between the category of finitely generated torsion-free nilpotent groups (viewed inside their rational Mal'cev completions, i.e. $\mathbb{Q}$-powered radicable nilpotent groups of finite rank) and the category of finite-dimensional nilpotent Lie algebras over $\mathbb{Q}$, given by the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula.

Consider the following methodology for collection in a polycyclic group $G$: first determine a large nilpotent normal subgroup $N \trianglelefteq G$ (for example, the Fitting subgroup or a finite-index subgroup of it that is torsion-free), then perform the bulk of the collection inside $N$ by transferring elements across the Malcev correspondence to the associated nilpotent Lie algebra, doing the computations there using the BCH formula, and translating the result back to $N$; finally combine with collection in $G/N$.

Problem: Determine the precise worst-case computational complexity of this Malcev-correspondence-based collection algorithm as a function of natural input parameters (the Hirsch length of $G$, the nilpotency class of $N$, and the bit-length of the input word and of the exponents in the resulting normal form).

The conjugacy search problem in $G$ is: given elements $u, v \in G$ that are known to be conjugate (i.e., there exists $g \in G$ with $g^{-1} u g = v$), produce such an element $g$.

The problem is the following: for infinite polycyclic groups $G$ of arbitrarily large Hirsch length, given by a polycyclic presentation, does there exist an algorithm that solves the conjugacy search problem and runs in time bounded by a stated complexity function (e.g., polynomial in the input size and the Hirsch length)? A faithful linear representation of $G$ over a field $k$ is an injective group homomorphism $\rho : G \hookrightarrow \mathrm{GL}_d(k)$; the smallest such $d$ (over a specified family of fields, e.g. $\mathbb{C}$ or finite fields) is called the minimal faithful linear dimension of $G$, denoted $\mu(G)$.

Linear decomposition and linear centralizer attacks against group-based cryptosystems with platform group $G$ run in time polynomial in $\mu(G)$ (and in the size of the field of definition), provided one can effectively compute a faithful representation $\rho : G \hookrightarrow \mathrm{GL}_{\mu(G)}(k)$.

Problem. For the class of polycyclic groups (and, more generally, for the subclass of metabelian groups), do the following:

1. Determine explicit upper and lower bounds for $\mu(G)$ in terms of standard invariants of $G$ such as the Hirsch length $h(G)$, the number of generators, the derived length, and the orders of the finite cyclic factors $G_i/G_{i+1}$.

2. Provide a constructive procedure that, given a polycyclic presentation of $G$, either produces a faithful linear representation $\rho : G \hookrightarrow \mathrm{GL}_d(k)$ with $d$ matching the bound in (1), or certifies that no such representation of dimension $\le d$ exists.

3. Characterize those polycyclic groups $G$ for which $\mu(G)$ is small enough (e.g. polynomially bounded in the chosen security parameter) that linear decomposition attacks and linear centralizer attacks against cryptosystems with platform group $G$ become tractable, and conversely identify infinite families of polycyclic groups for which $\mu(G)$ grows superpolynomially, so that such linear attacks are provably infeasible.

A polycyclic group is a group $G$ that admits a subnormal series
$$G = G_0 \triangleright G_1 \triangleright \cdots \triangleright G_n = \{1\}$$
such that each quotient $G_i/G_{i+1}$ is cyclic. A faithful linear representation of $G$ over a field $k$ is an injective group homomorphism $\rho : G \hookrightarrow \mathrm{GL}_d(k)$; the smallest such $d$ (over a specified family of fields, e.g. $\mathbb{C}$ or finite fields) is called the minimal faithful linear dimension of $G$, denoted $\mu(G)$.

Linear decomposition and linear centralizer attacks against group-based cryptosystems with platform group $G$ run in time polynomial in $\mu(G)$ (and in the size of the field of definition), provided one can effectively compute a faithful representation $\rho : G \hookrightarrow \mathrm{GL}_{\mu(G)}(k)$.

Problem. For the class of polycyclic groups (and, more generally, for the subclass of metabelian groups), do the following:

1. Determine explicit upper and lower bounds for $\mu(G)$ in terms of standard invariants of $G$ such as the Hirsch length $h(G)$, the number of generators, the derived length, and the orders of the finite cyclic factors $G_i/G_{i+1}$.

2. Provide a constructive procedure that, given a polycyclic presentation of $G$, either produces a faithful linear representation $\rho : G \hookrightarrow \mathrm{GL}_d(k)$ with $d$ matching the bound in (1), or certifies that no such representation of dimension $\le d$ exists.

3. Characterize those polycyclic groups $G$ for which $\mu(G)$ is small enough (e.g. polynomially bounded in the chosen security parameter) that linear decomposition attacks and linear centralizer attacks against cryptosystems with platform group $G$ become tractable, and conversely identify infinite families of polycyclic groups for which $\mu(G)$ grows superpolynomially, so that such linear attacks are provably infeasible.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

No general bounds on the minimal dimension of faithful linear representations of polycyclic groups (or metabelian groups) appear to be known. Constructive algorithms exist for faithful representations of finitely generated torsion-free nilpotent groups, but the general polycyclic case, together with the cryptanalytic tractability question for linear decomposition / linear centralizer attacks, is still listed as an open direction in subsequent surveys and is not addressed by current results on representation dimension of finite groups.

Let G be a finite simple undirected graph with adjacency matrix A(G), and let λ_1, λ_2, …, λ_n denote the eigenvalues of A(G). The energy of G is defined by
   E(G) = Σ_{i=1}^{n} |λ_i|.
Two graphs of the same order are called equienergetic if their energies are equal, and they are cospectral if their adjacency matrices have the same multiset of eigenvalues.

Provide a systematic general construction (not depending on isolated examples, exhaustive computer search, or case-by-case ad hoc methods) that produces, for infinitely many values of n, pairs (T_1, T_2) of trees on n vertices such that:
  (i) T_1 and T_2 each have exactly n vertices;
  (ii) E(T_1) = E(T_2);
  (iii) T_1 and T_2 are not cospectral (i.e., their adjacency spectra differ).

The construction should be described as an explicit procedure or family of operations on trees, applicable in a uniform way, and it should be proved that the resulting trees satisfy (i)–(iii).

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem of systematically constructing pairs of equienergetic non-cospectral trees appears to remain open. While numerous examples are known and systematic constructions for equienergetic non-cospectral graphs (using iterated line graphs of regular graphs, products of complete graphs, etc.) exist, these constructions do not yield trees. Partial progress includes constructions of infinite families of equienergetic trees of diameter 4, but a general systematic construction method is still lacking.

The clients wish to collaboratively train a model by exchanging messages only along edges of $G_t$. A "learning task specification" consists of: (i) the model class (architecture, parameter space), (ii) the training algorithm (e.g., decentralized SGD, gossip averaging, etc.), (iii) the hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size, communication schedule, stopping criterion), and (iv) the assignment of responsibility for monitoring, debugging, and correcting failures during training. Design a formal governance / trust mechanism — i.e., a distributed protocol $\Pi$ executed on $G_t$, together with a decision rule $\mathcal{R}$ — such that the clients can collectively agree upon and update the learning task specification in a way that satisfies the following desiderata: (a) correctness: the agreed-upon specification is well-defined and consistent across all honest clients; (b) incentive compatibility: no client (or coalition of size below a specified threshold) can unilaterally impose a specification that benefits itself at the expense of others; (c) robustness: the mechanism tolerates a bounded fraction of Byzantine or unresponsive clients and adapts to changes in $G_t$; (d) accountability: every decision can be traced to an identifiable subset of clients who can be held responsible for debugging. Either exhibit such a mechanism $(\Pi, \mathcal{R})$ together with a proof of properties (a)–(d), or prove that no protocol satisfying (a)–(d) simultaneously can exist under stated assumptions on the communication and adversary models.

Consider a fully decentralized learning setting in which a set of clients communicates over a peer-to-peer network (no central server). Each client $i$ holds a local data distribution $\mathcal{D}_i$ and the goal is to collaboratively train a (possibly non-convex) deep neural network model with parameters $\theta\in\mathbb{R}^d$ that approximately minimizes $F(\theta)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_i}[\ell(\theta;x)]$, by means of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) updates combined with gossip-style exchanges of parameters or gradients with neighbors in a (possibly time-varying) communication graph $G_t=(V_t,E_t)$.

Assume realistic network conditions in which:
(a) clients may temporarily disappear and later rejoin the network,
(b) new clients may join at arbitrary times,
(c) clients may permanently drop out, and
(d) messages between neighbors may be lost or delayed.

Design a decentralized SGD scheme for training deep models in this setting, and prove that it is robust to the above failure modes while still converging (in expectation, or almost surely) to a stationary point — or, more strongly, to a consensus minimizer — of $F$ under verifiable assumptions on the graph dynamics, message-loss process, step sizes, and stochastic gradient noise. Equivalently, determine whether such a robust, provably convergent decentralized SGD scheme for deep learning exists in fully decentralized peer-to-peer networks subject to client churn and message loss.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Recent works (2023–2025) propose partial solutions—e.g., DeceFL with O(1/T) convergence under time-invariant connected topologies, gradient-tracking schemes with local updates, dropout-resilient aggregation methods, and asynchronous decentralized FL frameworks like DRACO—but each requires restrictive assumptions (connected/time-invariant graphs, specific dropout models, convexity, or limited heterogeneity). Consider a fully decentralized optimization problem of the form

  minimize  F(x) = (1/n) Σ_{i=1}^n F_i(x),    F_i(x) = E_{ξ∼D_i}[ f(x; ξ) ],

where n clients (nodes) are arranged on a connected communication graph G=(V,E) and the local data distributions D_1,…,D_n are heterogeneous (non-IID), so that the local gradients ∇F_i may differ substantially from the global gradient ∇F. Communication is restricted to neighbors in G and is encoded by a sequence of symmetric doubly-stochastic mixing matrices {W_t} ⊂ R^{n×n} supported on G.

Each client i maintains a local model x_i^{(t)} ∈ R^d. In each communication round, every client performs H ≥ 1 local stochastic gradient steps,

  y_i^{(t,0)} = x_i^{(t)},
  y_i^{(t,h+1)} = y_i^{(t,h)} − η ∇f(y_i^{(t,h)}; ξ_i^{(t,h)}),  h = 0,…,H−1,

and then performs a gossip averaging step using the mixing matrix W_t:

  x_i^{(t+1)} = Σ_{j=1}^n (W_t)_{ij} · y_j^{(t,H)}.

Under standard assumptions on f (L-smoothness, possibly (non)convexity, bounded stochastic gradient variance σ^2, and a bounded heterogeneity measure such as (1/n)Σ_i ‖∇F_i(x) − ∇F(x)‖^2 ≤ ζ^2), address the following:

(a) Derive convergence guarantees (rates as functions of n, H, η, σ^2, ζ^2, and the spectral properties of the mixing matrices, such as the second-largest singular value ρ = ‖W − (1/n)11^T‖) that quantify how non-IID data and the number H of local steps affect the convergence of the iterates {x_i^{(t)}} toward a stationary point or minimizer of F.

(b) Determine model-averaging policies — i.e., choices of the (possibly time-varying) mixing matrices W_t supported on G, the local step count H, and the step size η — that achieve the fastest possible convergence rate in this setting, and identify lower bounds matching these rates so as to characterize the optimal averaging policy for decentralized learning with multiple local updates under client data heterogeneity.

Significant progress has been made on understanding decentralized SGD convergence under non-IID data with local steps. Koloskova et al. (ICML 2020) gave a unified convergence theory for decentralized SGD with changing topology and local updates, and subsequent works (e.g., gradient-tracking variants, Huang et al. 2022, momentum-based unified frameworks 2024) have improved dependence on heterogeneity. Consider a fully decentralized federated learning setting consisting of a finite set of agents $\{1,\dots,N\}$, each holding a local dataset $D_i$ drawn from an agent-specific distribution $\mathcal{P}_i$ on $\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}$. There is no trusted central server: agents communicate only along edges of a (possibly time-varying) graph $G=(V,E)$, and each agent $i$ wishes to learn a personalized model $\theta_i\in\Theta$ that approximately minimizes its local population risk $R_i(\theta_i)=\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{P}_i}[\ell(\theta_i;x,y)]$ while benefiting from collaboration with other agents.

Assume the following adversarial conditions hold simultaneously:
(a) Byzantine agents: an unknown subset $B\subset V$ with $|B|\le \beta N$ may send arbitrary, adaptively chosen messages.
(b) Label noise: for each honest agent $i\notin B$, observed labels are corrupted versions of true labels with unknown agent-dependent noise rate.
(c) Data noise: feature vectors of honest agents may be corrupted by unknown, possibly adversarial perturbations bounded in some norm.
(d) No trusted coordinator: there is no entity that can verify identities, audit data, or aggregate gradients honestly.

Design and analyze:
1. A personalized-model protocol that produces, for every honest agent $i$, a model $\hat\theta_i$ satisfying a provable excess-risk guarantee $R_i(\hat\theta_i)-\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}R_i(\theta)\le \varepsilon(N,|D_i|,\beta,\text{noise})$ that degrades gracefully in the fraction $\beta$ of Byzantine agents and in the label/feature noise levels, under conditions (a)–(d).
2. An incentive or mechanism-design scheme (e.g., a payment/contribution rule or game-theoretic protocol) executed peer-to-peer without a trusted third party, such that truthful participation with honest data and labels is a (dominant-strategy or approximate Bayes–Nash) equilibrium for every honest agent, and such that Byzantine deviations cannot improve their utility by more than a vanishing amount while honest agents retain the personalization guarantee from item 1.

Either construct such a protocol and mechanism with explicit conditions and rigorous guarantees, or prove an impossibility result identifying the precise tradeoffs between $\beta$, the noise levels, the connectivity of $G$, and achievable personalized excess risk.

The question is a high-level open research direction in federated learning. Consider a fully decentralized learning setting in which $n$ agents (nodes) are arranged on a connected undirected communication graph $G=(V,E)$, with $|V|=n$. Each agent $i\in V$ holds a local data distribution $\mathcal{D}_i$ and a local loss $F_i(	heta)=\mathbb{E}_{z\sim \mathcal{D}_i}[\ell(	heta;z)]$ for parameter $	heta\in\mathbb{R}^d$, and the agents collectively wish to minimize $F(	heta)= rac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n F_i(	heta)$. Communication is restricted to neighbors in $G$; there is no central server.

Consider a cross-silo federated learning setting with a fixed set of N organizations (silos) indexed by i = 1, ..., N. Each silo i holds a private dataset D_i drawn from a local distribution and, by participating, contributes computational effort and data to train a shared global model f_theta with parameters theta in R^d. Let U_i(theta, a_i, a_{-i}) denote the utility silo i derives from the resulting model when it takes action a_i in A_i (an action space encoding choices such as how much data to contribute, the truthfulness of reported gradients, and whether to inject adversarial or poisoned data) and the other silos take actions a_{-i}. Some silos may also be product-market competitors, so U_i may depend negatively on the quality of the model received by other silos.

Design an incentive mechanism M consisting of:
(1) a participation/reward rule r: (a_1, ..., a_N) -> (r_1, ..., r_N) in R^N that allocates the value V(theta) created by the jointly trained model among the silos,
(2) a contribution-elicitation rule that determines what each silo must submit,
(3) a defense/auditing rule connecting payments r_i to detection of adversarial behavior by silo i,

such that the mechanism simultaneously satisfies the following formal requirements:

(a) Honest participation is a (dominant-strategy or Bayes–Nash) equilibrium: for every silo i and every alternative action a_i' in A_i, E[U_i(theta, a_i^*, a_{-i}^*) + r_i] >= E[U_i(theta', a_i', a_{-i}^*) + r_i'], where a_i^* denotes honest participation.

(b) The value-division rule r is budget-balanced (sum_i r_i = V(theta)) and satisfies a fairness axiom such as the Shapley value characterization with respect to the marginal contributions of each silo's data to model performance.

(c) Participation is individually rational and the equilibrium maximizes the total number of silos that choose to participate, subject to (a) and (b).

(d) The mechanism is robust to adversarial data owners: there exists a detection/penalty function so that any silo deviating to an adversarial action a_i' (e.g., data poisoning, backdoor injection, or model-degradation attack designed to harm competitors) receives expected utility strictly less than under honest participation, while honest silos suffer at most epsilon loss in model quality.

Provide such a mechanism, or prove impossibility, in a model that explicitly captures competition between silos (i.e., where each U_i can depend negatively on U_j for j != i through downstream market effects of the shared model).

Incentive design for cross-silo federated learning with competing organizations remains an active research area. While numerous partial proposals exist (Shapley-value-based reward schemes, contract-theoretic and game-theoretic mechanisms, and various robust aggregation defenses), no mechanism is known that jointly satisfies honest participation, fair value division, optimal participation, and integrated defense against adversarial silos in the competitor setting. The problem is generally regarded as open.

Consider the split learning setting for collaborative training of a neural network: a network with parameters partitioned into a "client side" (early layers) and a "server side" (later layers) is trained across N clients, each holding a private local dataset. During training, each client computes the forward pass of the early layers on its inputs and transmits only the resulting intermediate activations to the server; the server completes the forward pass, computes the loss, and backpropagates, returning gradients with respect to the activations to the client, who then updates its early-layer parameters.

(a) Design a training protocol that parallelizes split learning across resource-constrained edge clients (so that multiple clients can train concurrently rather than sequentially passing the "smashed data" through a single shared model state), specifying how client-side weights are synchronized or aggregated and how server-side updates incorporate the parallel contributions, while preserving correctness of gradient-based optimization.

(b) Provide a formal privacy analysis of the information revealed to the server (and to any eavesdropper) by the communicated intermediate activations and returned gradients across the entire training trajectory. Specifically: define a precise privacy notion (e.g., (ε, δ)-differential privacy with respect to a client's input record, or an indistinguishability/leakage bound against feature-inversion and membership-inference adversaries), and give a mechanism — together with a proof — that achieves this notion with explicit bounds on ε, δ, or the corresponding leakage as a function of the number of training rounds, batch size, the split layer, and any added noise.

Prove correctness and the privacy bounds, and analyze the resulting utility (final model accuracy) versus privacy and parallelism trade-offs.

Consider a federated learning setting in which K clients, indexed by k = 1, …, K, each hold a local data distribution P_k(x, y) over an input space X and label space Y. Cross-client heterogeneity can be decomposed by writing P_k(x, y) = P_k(y | x) P_k(x) = P_k(x | y) P_k(y) and includes the following phenomena:

1. Feature-distribution skew (covariate shift): P_k(x) varies across k while P_k(y | x) is shared.
2. Label-distribution skew (prior probability shift): P_k(y) varies across k while P_k(x | y) is shared.
3. Concept drift (same label, different features): P_k(x | y) varies across k while P_k(y) is shared.
4. Concept shift (same features, different labels): P_k(y | x) varies across k while P_k(x) is shared.
5. Quantity skew: the number of samples n_k varies substantially across clients.
6. Violations of independence: within a client, samples need not be i.i.d., and across clients the availability or selection of clients may be correlated with their distributions (e.g., temporal, geographic, or device-type correlations).
7. General dataset shift: arbitrary combinations of the above.

Problem. Provide a rigorous, quantitative framework for characterizing real-world cross-client differences in federated datasets that simultaneously captures all seven phenomena above. The framework should:

(a) Define formal, measurable divergence quantities D_i({P_k}) for i = 1, …, 7 that isolate each form of skew (for example, by decomposing a joint heterogeneity measure such as Σ_k (n_k / Σ_j n_j) · KL(P_k ‖ P̄), where P̄ = Σ_k (n_k / Σ_j n_j) P_k, into components attributable to marginals, conditionals, sample sizes, and dependence structure);

(b) Yield procedures for estimating these quantities from finite client samples with provable consistency guarantees;

(c) Induce benchmark-generation protocols whereby, given target values of (D_1, …, D_7), one can synthesize federated partitions of standard centralized datasets that realize those values up to controlled error;

(d) Predict, via theorems relating (D_1, …, D_7) to optimization and generalization behavior, the performance degradation and convergence slowdown of canonical federated algorithms (such as FedAvg) relative to a centralized baseline, and identify which mitigation strategies (personalization, clustered FL, multi-task FL, robust aggregation, data augmentation) are provably effective for each individual skew type.

Construct such a framework, or prove obstructions showing that no single framework can simultaneously satisfy (a)–(d).

Consider a federated learning system consisting of a central coordinator (server) and a population of $N$ clients indexed by $i \in \{1,\dots,N\}$, where each client $i$ holds a local data distribution $\mathcal{D}_i$ over an input space $\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}$. For a parameter vector $w \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and a loss function $\ell:\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}$, define the local objective $F_i(w) := \mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}_i}[\ell(w;x,y)]$ and the global federated objective
$$F(w) := \sum_{i=1}^N p_i F_i(w), \qquad \sum_{i=1}^N p_i = 1,\; p_i \ge 0.$$
A federated optimization algorithm is an iterative procedure in which, at each round $t=1,2,\dots,T$, the server selects a (possibly random) subset $S_t \subseteq \{1,\dots,N\}$ of clients, broadcasts state to those clients, each selected client $i \in S_t$ performs local computation on its data and returns a message $m_{i,t}$ to the server, and the server aggregates the messages to update $w_t$.

The algorithm must operate under the following federated constraints simultaneously:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(C1)] \emph{Non-IID and unbalanced data}: the distributions $\mathcal{D}_i$ may differ arbitrarily across clients, and the effective sample sizes may vary widely.
\item[(C2)] \emph{Limited communication bandwidth}: there is a fixed upper bound $B$ on the number of bits exchanged per client per round.
\item[(C3)] \emph{Unreliable availability and client sampling}: at each round only a small random subset of clients is available, governed by an availability process possibly correlated with $i$ and $t$.
\item[(C4)] \emph{Stateless cross-device clients}: each client may participate at most once (or very few times) and cannot maintain persistent state between rounds; the algorithm cannot rely on client-side memory across rounds.
\item[(C5)] \emph{Compatibility with secure aggregation and privacy}: server-side updates must be computable from sums (or otherwise privacy-preserving aggregates) of client messages, so that the server learns only the aggregate and not individual $m_{i,t}$, and the procedure must support a differential-privacy guarantee with parameters $(\varepsilon,\delta)$.
\end{enumerate}

Question: Design a federated optimization algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ satisfying all of (C1)–(C5) that, for the class of (possibly nonconvex) smooth objectives, provably converges to an $\epsilon$-stationary point of $F$ (i.e., $\mathbb{E}\|\nabla F(\hat w)\|^2 \le \epsilon$) with communication, sampling, and privacy complexities that improve over (or at least match) the best known bounds for centralized stochastic optimization adapted naively to the federated setting. Equivalently: characterize the achievable trade-offs between convergence rate, per-round communication cost, client participation rate, statelessness, and privacy parameters under constraints (C1)–(C5), and exhibit an algorithm that attains these trade-offs.

Federated optimization under the combined constraints of non-IID data, communication efficiency, partial participation, statelessness, and privacy/secure-aggregation compatibility remains an active and broadly open research direction. While many partial results exist (e.g., FedAvg, FedProx, SCAFFOLD, FedOpt, and various compressed/DP variants address subsets of the constraints), no single algorithm with matching lower-bound-tight guarantees under all of (C1)–(C5) simultaneously has been established as of 2026.

Consider the distributed stochastic optimization problem
  min_{x ∈ ℝ^d}  F(x) = (1/M) Σ_{i=1}^{M} F_i(x),  with  F_i(x) = E_{ξ∼D_i}[ f(x; ξ) ],
where M clients each hold a local data distribution D_i and can compute unbiased stochastic gradients g_i(x) with E[g_i(x)] = ∇F_i(x) and bounded variance E‖g_i(x) − ∇F_i(x)‖^2 ≤ σ^2. Each F_i is L-smooth, and one may additionally consider the (strongly) convex or nonconvex regimes. Heterogeneity may be quantified by sup_x (1/M) Σ_i ‖∇F_i(x) − ∇F(x)‖^2 ≤ ζ^2.

Federated averaging (FedAvg) / local-update SGD proceeds in rounds: in each round a subset S_t of clients is sampled; each selected client initializes from the server model x_t and performs K local stochastic gradient steps with stepsize η, producing x_{t,i}^{(K)}; the server then aggregates x_{t+1} = (1/|S_t|) Σ_{i∈S_t} x_{t,i}^{(K)}. Mini-batch SGD with batch size MK is the natural baseline (one synchronous step per round using MK stochastic gradients).

Address the following three questions for this family of algorithms:

(a) Provide matching upper and lower bounds on the worst-case convergence rate of local-update SGD/FedAvg as a function of M, K, T (number of rounds), L, σ^2, ζ^2, that determine precisely the regimes of (K, σ^2, ζ^2, L, …) in which performing K > 1 local steps strictly improves convergence over the mini-batch SGD baseline using MK gradients per round, and the regimes in which it strictly hurts.

(b) In the homogeneous (IID) setting where all F_i = F, determine whether the gap between known upper bounds for local SGD and the optimal rate of accelerated mini-batch SGD (with MK gradients per round) can be closed; either exhibit a local-update method (possibly with acceleration, momentum, or control variates) matching the accelerated mini-batch lower bound, or prove a separation showing no local-update method can attain it.

(c) Establish convergence guarantees for asynchronous and straggler-tolerant variants of FedAvg under realistic federated constraints — heterogeneous client availability, arbitrary and possibly adversarial delays, partial participation, communication compression, and statistical heterogeneity — with rates that explicitly account for delay distributions and participation biases, and which degrade gracefully (rather than diverge) as stragglers become extreme.

Substantial progress has been made: tight upper and lower bounds for local SGD in the homogeneous convex setting (Woodworth et al. 2020) identify regimes where local steps help or hurt versus mini-batch SGD, and methods like SCAFFOLD and FedAC give improved or accelerated rates in some regimes. Consider a federated learning setup with $N$ clients, where client $i$ has a local data distribution $\mathcal{D}_i$ over an input-output space $\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}$ and a (possibly client-specific) loss function $\ell_i$. Three families of predictors are available:

(a) a single global model $f_{\theta}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}$ trained to minimize $\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i\,\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}_i}[\ell_i(f_\theta(x),y)]$ for some weights $w_i>0$;

(b) $N$ independent local models $f_{\theta_i}$, each trained only on data drawn from $\mathcal{D}_i$;

(c) personalized models obtained by fine-tuning a globally trained $f_\theta$ on each client's local data, or via multi-task / clustered-client schemes that partition the clients into $K$ groups $\{C_1,\dots,C_K\}$ and train one model $f_{\theta^{(k)}}$ per group.

Personalized architectures may additionally take as input user/context feature vectors $u_i\in\mathcal{U}$, yielding predictors of the form $f_\theta(x,u_i)$.

Address the following three questions:

1. Architectural incorporation of personalization. Specify principled ways of designing the model family $\{f_\theta(x,u)\}$ so that user and context features $u_i$ are exploited to provide personalization while still permitting federated training (i.e., aggregation across clients of the shared parameters of $f_\theta$).

2. Choice of grouping in multi-task / clustered FL. Given the client distributions $\{\mathcal{D}_i\}_{i=1}^N$ (or empirical samples therefrom), give an algorithm and analysis that selects the number of models $K$ and the assignment $\pi:\{1,\dots,N\}\to\{1,\dots,K\}$ minimizing the expected personalized risk $\sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}_i}[\ell_i(f_{\theta^{(\pi(i))}}(x),y)]$, with guarantees relating optimal $(K,\pi)$ to a measure of inter-client distributional similarity.

3. Global vs. local vs. fine-tuned comparison. Identify quantitative conditions on the heterogeneity of $\{\mathcal{D}_i\}$, the per-client sample sizes $n_i$, the hypothesis-class complexity, and any structural assumptions (e.g., shared representations) under which the single global model (a) attains strictly lower expected risk on each client than the corresponding independent local model (b) and than the personalized fine-tuned model (c), and conversely under which (b) or (c) dominate (a).

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The questions remain active research topics. Recent works (2024–2025) propose hybrid and mixture-of-models approaches (e.g., Fed-POE) showing that ensemble/hybrid strategies can simultaneously attain global and personalized regret guarantees, and empirical studies report that local fine-tuning can destabilize globally learned features ("federated feature distortion"). However, no general theory characterizes when the global model dominates independent local or fine-tuned models, nor a definitive algorithm for choosing the number and grouping of models in clustered/multi-task FL. The problem is therefore best classified as open with partial progress.

Consider the federated learning setting in which a central server coordinates training across a population of clients $\{1,2,\dots,N\}$, where each client $i$ holds a local data distribution $\mathcal{D}_i$ over an input-output space $\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}$ and the distributions $\mathcal{D}_i$ may be statistically heterogeneous (non-IID) and may drift over time. A model is parameterized by $\theta\in\mathbb{R}^d$, with a loss $\ell(\theta;x,y)$ and per-client risk $F_i(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}_i}[\ell(\theta;x,y)]$.

In the model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML) / learning-to-learn formulation of personalization, the server seeks an initialization $\theta^\star$ such that, after a small number $k\geq 1$ of local adaptation steps $U_i^k(\theta)$ (e.g., gradient steps on $F_i$), the personalized parameters $\theta_i:=U_i^k(\theta^\star)$ achieve low local risk. A natural objective is
$$\min_{\theta\in\mathbb{R}^d}\ \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N F_i\bigl(U_i^k(\theta)\bigr).$$
More generally, "non-parameter-transfer" personalization replaces $U_i^k$ by transfer mechanisms that do not consist solely of fine-tuning a shared parameter vector (e.g., hypernetworks, modular components, prototype/embedding transfer, or data-dependent personalization maps).

Develop a theory and methodology for federated meta-learning addressing all of the following:

(a) Construct realistic benchmark task distributions and evaluation protocols for federated meta-learning that reflect cross-device and cross-silo deployments, including non-IID clients, system heterogeneity, partial participation, communication constraints, and temporal concept drift in $\{\mathcal{D}_i\}_{i,t}$.

(b) Establish theoretical guarantees (convergence rates, sample/communication complexity, and generalization bounds to held-out and to newly-arriving clients) for federated MAML-type algorithms under realistic assumptions on heterogeneity, stochastic gradients, partial participation, and Hessian access in the inner update.

(c) Define and analyze rigorous personalized-performance metrics that measure post-adaptation accuracy across the client population (including tail/worst-client behavior, fairness across clients, and few-shot adaptation on new clients), and prove their relation to the global meta-objective above.

(d) Provide a mathematical characterization explaining when and why a globally optimal model $\theta_G^\star\in\arg\min_\theta \frac{1}{N}\sum_i F_i(\theta)$ personalizes poorly, i.e., quantify the gap
$$\Delta\;=\;\frac{1}{N}\sum_i F_i(\theta_G^\star)\;-\;\frac{1}{N}\sum_i F_i\bigl(U_i^k(\theta^\star)\bigr)$$
in terms of geometric or statistical properties of $\{F_i\}$ (curvature, task similarity, conditioning).

(e) Extend the framework to handle concept drift, where $\mathcal{D}_i$ is replaced by a time-varying $\mathcal{D}_{i,t}$, with provable tracking/adaptation guarantees.

(f) Design and analyze non-parameter-transfer federated meta-learning algorithms that go beyond a shared initialization, with formal guarantees comparable to (b)–(d).

Determine to what extent each of (a)–(f) admits a complete solution.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Partial progress exists: Fallah–Mokhtari–Ozdaglar (NeurIPS 2020) established convergence and first-order-optimality guarantees for Per-FedAvg, a MAML-based personalized federated learning algorithm, and Jiang et al. (2019) gave empirical MAML-based personalization results. Subsequent work (2023–2025) has produced clustered/co-meta-learning variants, hypernetwork-based personalization (pFedHN/pFedLA), and reinforcement-learning-style personalization addressing heterogeneity. However, comprehensive realistic benchmarks, tight theoretical guarantees under partial participation and concept drift, fairness-aware personalization metrics with provable links to the meta-objective, and provably effective non-parameter-transfer algorithms remain only partially addressed, so the overall program is still open in significant parts.
