A term-rewriting system (TRS) is a finite set R of rewrite rules l → r over terms built from a signature Σ and a countable set of variables, where l is not a variable and every variable of r occurs in l. The TRS is left-linear if no variable occurs more than once in any left-hand side l. The one-step rewrite relation →_R is defined by replacing an instance σ(l) of a left-hand side at some position in a term by σ(r); its reflexive–transitive closure is →_R*, and the parallel rewrite relation ⇒_R rewrites a finite set of pairwise-disjoint redex positions simultaneously in one step. R is Church-Rosser (confluent) if for all terms u, v, w with u →_R* v and u →_R* w there exists t with v →_R* t and w →_R* t.

A critical pair ⟨t, s⟩ of R arises from a non-variable overlap of two (renamed) rules of R: unifying a left-hand side l₁ with a non-variable subterm of another left-hand side l₂ via a most general unifier μ yields the two reducts t and s of μ(l₂).

Problem: Give a decidable criterion on the finite set of critical pairs of an arbitrary left-linear TRS R that is sufficient for R to be Church-Rosser. In particular, determine whether each of the following critical-pair conditions implies Church-Rosserness of every left-linear TRS:

(a) for every critical pair ⟨t, s⟩, s ⇒_R t (one parallel step);
(b) for every critical pair ⟨t, s⟩, s →_R^{=} t (zero or one steps);
(c) for every critical pair ⟨t, s⟩, either s →_R^{=} t or t →_R^{=} s.

Provide proofs or counterexamples, and identify other decidable sufficient critical-pair conditions ensuring the Church-Rosser property of left-linear term-rewriting systems.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Several decidable sufficient critical-pair criteria for Church-Rosser of left-linear TRSs have been established and refined: Huet's strong/parallel closedness, Toyama's parallel-critical-pair (parallel closedness) theorem, Okui's simultaneous-critical-pair criterion, Oyamaguchi–Ohta-style parallel closure criteria, and more recent extensions (e.g., to nominal and higher-order rewriting). Thus partial criteria exist and the cited specific conditions (parallel-step closedness, almost parallel closedness) are known to suffice. However, a complete decidable characterization of Church-Rosserness for arbitrary left-linear systems remains open (and is in general undecidable without further restrictions), so the broader problem of finding the strongest decidable critical-pair criterion remains an active research direction.

representations.normalized:
Background. A term rewriting system (TRS) is a set R of rewrite rules ℓ → r over terms built from a signature and a set of variables. The one-step rewrite relation →_R is defined by ℓσ →_R rσ at any position of a term. The parallel rewrite relation ⇒_R reduces a finite set of pairwise-disjoint (parallel) redex positions simultaneously. A binary relation → is called subcommutative (or has the diamond property) if whenever a → b and a → c there exists d with b → d and c → d. For an orthogonal TRS (left-linear, no critical pairs) the parallel rewrite relation ⇒_R is known to be subcommutative, which gives a strong form of confluence.

A conditional term rewriting system (CTRS) is a set of conditional rules of the form ℓ → r ⇐ s₁ ≈ t₁, …, s_n ≈ t_n, where the conditions s_i ≈ t_i are interpreted (depending on the type of CTRS, e.g., join, oriented, semi-equational, or normal) as requirements that have to hold for a rewrite step using the rule to be valid. The corresponding rewrite relation is defined inductively in levels: →_0 = ∅, and a step at level k+1 uses rules whose conditions are satisfied with respect to →_k. The parallel rewrite relation ⇒_R for a CTRS is defined analogously by contracting pairwise-disjoint parallel redexes (each licensed by the appropriate conditional inference).

Problem. Determine syntactic conditions on a conditional term rewriting system R (such as restrictions on left-linearity, on the variables occurring in the conditions and right-hand sides, on critical pairs of the underlying unconditional system, on the form of the conditions, or on the type of CTRS) under which the parallel rewrite relation ⇒_R is subcommutative, i.e. satisfies: whenever t ⇒_R u and t ⇒_R v, there exists w with u ⇒_R w and v ⇒_R w. Equivalently, characterize the classes of CTRSs for which subcommutativity of parallel rewriting holds, in analogy with the orthogonal (unconditional) case.

Consider Combinatory Logic extended with two Boolean constants $T$ and $F$ and a ternary conditional constant $C$. Terms are built from variables and the constants $I, K, S, T, F, C$ by left-associative application. Define a conditional rewrite system with the following rules:

(1) $I\,x \to x$,
(2) $K\,x\,y \to x$,
(3) $S\,x\,y\,z \to (x\,z)(y\,z)$,
(4) $C\,T\,x\,y \to x$,
(5) $C\,F\,x\,y \to y$,
(6) the semi-equational conditional rule: if $x$ is convertible to $y$ (i.e.\ $x \leftrightarrow^{*} y$ in the system itself), then $C\,z\,x\,y \to x$.

Here ``semi-equational'' means the side condition $x \leftrightarrow^{*} y$ uses the symmetric-transitive closure of the rewrite relation, and the system is nonterminating. Determine whether this rewrite system is confluent: that is, whether for every term $t$ and all reductions $t \to^{*} u$ and $t \to^{*} v$ there exists a term $w$ with $u \to^{*} w$ and $v \to^{*} w$.

A conditional term-rewriting system (CTRS) is a set R of rewrite rules of the form l → r ⇐ c, where c is a conjunction of conditions on terms s, t. Depending on how conditions are interpreted, one distinguishes:

• A semi-equational CTRS R_se, in which a condition s = t in a rule is satisfied when s and t are convertible (s ↔* t) with respect to R_se itself.

• A normal (oriented) CTRS R, in which every condition has the form s →! t with t a ground normal form, and the condition is satisfied when s rewrites in zero or more steps to t using R itself.

Given a normal CTRS R with conditions of the form s →! t (t a ground R-normal form of s), let R_se be the associated semi-equational CTRS obtained by replacing each condition s →! t by the convertibility condition s ↔* t.

A rewrite relation is confluent if whenever u →* v and u →* w, there exists a term q such that v →* q and w →* q.

Problem. Determine general syntactic or semantic conditions on R (e.g., on its rules, conditions, left-linearity, decreasingness, or termination of the underlying rewrite relation) under which confluence of R_se implies confluence of R.

Consider the first-order conditional term-rewriting system R over the signature consisting of constants I, K, S, D, unary symbols D1 and D2, and a binary application operator (written by juxtaposition, left-associative). The unconditional rewrite rules of R are:

  (I)  I x  -> x,
  (K)  K x y -> x,
  (S)  S x y z -> (x z)(y z),
  (P1) D1 (D x y) -> x,
  (P2) D2 (D x y) -> y.

In addition, R has two semi-equational conditional rules using the convertibility (i.e., symmetric-transitive closure of one-step rewriting) relation =_R generated by R itself:

  (C1)  D (D1 z) (D2 w) -> z   if   z =_R w,
  (C2)  D (D1 z) (D2 w) -> w   if   z =_R w.

(This system is the "surjective-pairing linearization" of Combinatory Logic extended with surjective pairing: the nonlinear identity D(D1 t)(D2 t) = t is replaced by the conditional rules (C1) and (C2).)

Questions:
(a) Is R confluent, i.e., does t ->>_R u and t ->>_R v imply that there exists w with u ->>_R w and v ->>_R w?
(b) If R is confluent, does it admit an effective normal-form strategy — that is, a computable function F on terms such that for every term t, F(t) is a one-step R-rewrite reduct of t whenever t is not in R-normal form, and iterating F from t terminates at an R-normal form whenever t has any R-normal form?

A closely related problem — confluence of an extension of Combinatory Logic by Boolean constants (RTA open problem 15, "CL-pc") — was solved by Ł. Czajka (FSCD 2017, arXiv:1306.2069) with a Coq-formalized confluence proof. Let R be an orthogonal term rewriting system (a first-order TRS whose rewrite rules are left-linear and have no critical pairs). Equip the set of finite and infinite terms over the signature of R with the standard metric d, where d(s,t) = 2^{-n} with n the minimal depth at which s and t differ (and d(s,t)=0 if s=t); under this metric the set of (possibly infinite) terms is a complete metric space.

A transfinite reduction sequence is a sequence of rewrite steps (t_α →_R t_{α+1})_{α<λ} indexed by an ordinal λ. Such a sequence is:
 • Cauchy-convergent (weakly convergent) of length λ to a limit t_λ if, for every limit ordinal μ ≤ λ, the sequence (t_α)_{α<μ} converges to t_μ in the metric d;
 • strongly convergent of length λ to t_λ if it is Cauchy-convergent and, in addition, for every limit ordinal μ ≤ λ the depths of the redexes contracted at steps t_α →_R t_{α+1} tend to infinity as α → μ.

Write s ↠_R^{str} t (resp. s ↠_R^{Cau} t) to mean that there is a strongly convergent (resp. Cauchy-convergent) transfinite reduction sequence from s to t.

It is known that orthogonal TRSs satisfy the following "almost-confluence" property for strongly convergent reductions: whenever s ↠_R^{str} t_1 and s ↠_R^{str} t_2, there exist terms u_1, u_2 and a "hypercollapsing" equivalence ≈ (the equivalence on terms generated by identifying any pair of terms that can be reduced to a common term whose only redex activity sits inside hypercollapsing subterms) such that t_1 ↠_R^{str} u_1, t_2 ↠_R^{str} u_2, and u_1 ≈ u_2.

Question: Does the same almost-confluence property hold for every orthogonal TRS when ↠_R^{str} is replaced everywhere by ↠_R^{Cau}? Equivalently: for every orthogonal TRS R and all terms s, t_1, t_2 with s ↠_R^{Cau} t_1 and s ↠_R^{Cau} t_2, do there exist u_1, u_2 with t_i ↠_R^{Cau} u_i (i=1,2) and u_1 ≈ u_2?

Consider the simply typed lambda calculus, whose terms are built from variables, applications, and lambda abstractions, and whose types are built from base types using the function-type constructor →. β-reduction is the rewriting relation generated by (λx:A. M) N → M[x := N]. The system is strongly normalizing: every β-reduction sequence terminates.

(a) Does there exist a "reasonably straightforward" map Φ from well-typed simply typed lambda terms into a well-founded ordering (W, <) with the property that whenever M →_β M' one has Φ(M') < Φ(M), so that strong normalization follows directly from well-foundedness of (W, <)? The challenge is that a β-redex (λx:A. M) N and its contractum M[x := N] may have identical type structure, so Φ cannot simply read off type information in a naive way.

(b) Does the same kind of straightforward mapping into a well-founded ordering yield a strong normalization proof for the polymorphic (second-order) lambda calculus, i.e. System F, where types include universally quantified type variables and reduction includes type-abstraction/type-application β-reduction?

For the simply typed lambda calculus, recent work (Van Oostrom and Wiedijk, "Two Decreasing Measures for Simply Typed λ-Terms", FSCD 2023) gives explicit decreasing measures from typed terms into well-founded orderings (natural numbers and nested multisets), affirmatively answering part (a). Earlier works (e.g. Gandy, de Vrijer, Joachimski–Matthes, Loader) had also developed such measure-based proofs. For System F / second-order polymorphic lambda calculus, no simple measure-based mapping into a well-founded ordering is known; standard proofs rely on Girard's reducibility candidates, and a "reasonably straightforward" ordinal-style mapping remains elusive. Hence part (b) appears still open.

A string-rewriting (semi-Thue) system over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$ consists of a set of rewriting rules of the form $\ell 	o r$ with $\ell, r \in \Sigma^*$. A single rewriting step $u \Rightarrow v$ holds if there exist $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ and a rule $\ell 	o r$ such that $u = x\ell y$ and $v = x r y$. A derivation from a word $w_0$ is a sequence $w_0 \Rightarrow w_1 \Rightarrow \dots \Rightarrow w_m$, and its length is $m$.

Call the system length-preserving if $|\ell| = |r|$ for every rule, and one-rule if it consists of exactly one rule $\ell 	o r$. Define the size of the (unique) rule as $k = |\ell| = |r|$.

Let $D(n, k)$ denote the supremum, over all length-preserving one-rule systems whose rule has size $k$ and all starting words $w_0$ of length $n$, of the length of any terminating derivation from $w_0$.

Determine the best possible upper bound on $D(n,k)$ as a function of $n$ and $k$.

Consider term rewriting systems over a finite signature with variables. A rewrite rule l → r is left-linear if no variable occurs more than once in l, and right-linear if no variable occurs more than once in r; the rule is called linear if it is both left-linear and right-linear. A rewrite system terminates if there is no infinite rewrite sequence t₁ → t₂ → t₃ → ⋯ using its rules.

Question: Is termination decidable for a single linear rewrite rule, i.e., does there exist an algorithm that, given any rule l → r in which every variable occurs at most once on each side, decides whether the one-rule rewrite system {l → r} terminates?

Related questions in the same spirit: Is termination (respectively, confluence) decidable for a single string (semi-Thue) rewrite rule l → r, in either the monadic case (where r has length at most one over the alphabet) or the general non-monadic case?

Termination of one-rule term/string rewriting is a long-standing open problem. Undecidability is known for one rule that is only left-linear (Dauchet's simulation of Turing machines by a left-linear one-rule system), but the linear (both left- and right-linear) one-rule case, as well as the one-rule string rewriting case, remain open. Various partial decidability results exist for restricted subclasses (e.g., single-threaded systems, growing systems, rules with restricted overlaps), but no general algorithm is known.

A conditional term rewriting system (CTRS) is a finite set of conditional rewrite rules of the form l → r ⇐ s₁ = t₁, …, sₙ = tₙ, where l, r, s_i, t_i are terms over a signature, l is not a variable, and the rewrite relation is defined by: t →_R t' iff there is a rule l → r ⇐ s₁ = t₁, …, sₙ = tₙ, a substitution σ, and a position p in t such that t|_p = lσ, t' = t[rσ]_p, and for each i, s_iσ and t_iσ rewrite to a common term using →_R (so-called "standard" or "join" CTRSs of type 3).

Such a system is called terminating if →_R is well-founded. The intrinsic difficulty is that the definition of →_R itself depends on normalization (joinability of the conditions), which in turn depends on termination, making direct termination arguments delicate.

Problem: Develop practical, automatable methods for proving termination of standard conditional term rewriting systems, taking into account this circular interdependence between normalization and termination.

Consider the term rewriting system that encodes the Battle of Hydra and Hercules: hydras are finite rooted trees, Hercules' moves correspond to rewrite rules that delete a leaf and (if the leaf is not adjacent to the root) duplicate a chosen subtree above the leaf's grandparent some number of times, and the system is known to be terminating but not provably terminating in Peano Arithmetic. Recall that a termination ordering proving termination of a rewrite system is a well-founded strict order on terms, compatible with the rewrite relation, and its order type is the ordinal obtained by collapsing the induced well-founded relation on reachable terms. The Howard–Bachmann ordinal is the proof-theoretic ordinal of the theory ID_1 of one inductive definition.

Question: Must every termination ordering that proves termination of this Hydra–Hercules rewrite system have order type at least the Howard–Bachmann (Howard) ordinal?

Let $\Sigma$ be a finite signature of function symbols, each with a fixed arity, and let $\mathcal{X}$ be a countably infinite set of variables. Let $T(\Sigma,\mathcal{X})$ denote the set of first-order terms built from $\Sigma$ and $\mathcal{X}$. A precedence is a strict partial order $>_\Sigma$ on $\Sigma$ (not required to be total). To each $f\in\Sigma$ assign a status $\tau(f)\in\{\mathrm{mul},\mathrm{lex}\}$. The recursive path ordering with status $>_{\mathrm{rpo}}$ induced by $(>_\Sigma,\tau)$ is the relation on $T(\Sigma,\mathcal{X})$ defined recursively by: $s=f(s_1,\dots,s_m) >_{\mathrm{rpo}} t$ iff
1. $t=g(t_1,\dots,t_n)$ with $f >_\Sigma g$ and $s >_{\mathrm{rpo}} t_j$ for every $j$; or
2. $s_i \ge_{\mathrm{rpo}} t$ for some $i$ (where $\ge_{\mathrm{rpo}}$ is $>_{\mathrm{rpo}}$ together with syntactic equality); or
3. $t=f(t_1,\dots,t_m)$, $s >_{\mathrm{rpo}} t_j$ for every $j$, and $(s_1,\dots,s_m)$ is greater than $(t_1,\dots,t_m)$ in the multiset (resp. lexicographic) extension of $>_{\mathrm{rpo}}$ when $\tau(f)=\mathrm{mul}$ (resp. $\mathrm{lex}$).

An RPO ordering constraint is a finite conjunction of atomic constraints of the forms $u>_{\mathrm{rpo}} v$ and $u=v$, with $u,v\in T(\Sigma,\mathcal{X})$. The existential fragment of the first-order theory of $>_{\mathrm{rpo}}$ consists of formulas $\exists \bar{x}\,\varphi(\bar{x})$ where $\varphi$ is a Boolean combination of such atoms; satisfiability asks whether there exists an assignment of the variables to ground terms in $T(\Sigma)$ making the formula true.

Question: Is the existential fragment of the first-order theory of the recursive path ordering with multiset and lexicographic status decidable when the precedence $>_\Sigma$ is allowed to be an arbitrary strict partial order rather than required to be total? Equivalently, is satisfiability of RPO ordering constraints decidable for non-total precedences? (The same question is posed for the lexicographic path ordering LPO, the special case where every symbol has lexicographic status.)

Let $\Sigma$ be a finite signature of function symbols, each with a fixed arity, and let $\mathcal{X}$ be a countably infinite set of variables. Let $T(\Sigma,\mathcal{X})$ denote the set of first-order terms built from $\Sigma$ and $\mathcal{X}$. A precedence is a strict partial order $>_\Sigma$ on $\Sigma$ (not required to be total). To each $f\in\Sigma$ assign a status $\tau(f)\in\{\mathrm{mul},\mathrm{lex}\}$. The recursive path ordering with status $>_{\mathrm{rpo}}$ induced by $(>_\Sigma,\tau)$ is the relation on $T(\Sigma,\mathcal{X})$ defined recursively by: $s=f(s_1,\dots,s_m) >_{\mathrm{rpo}} t$ iff
1. $t=g(t_1,\dots,t_n)$ with $f >_\Sigma g$ and $s >_{\mathrm{rpo}} t_j$ for every $j$; or
2. $s_i \ge_{\mathrm{rpo}} t$ for some $i$ (where $\ge_{\mathrm{rpo}}$ is $>_{\mathrm{rpo}}$ together with syntactic equality); or
3. $t=f(t_1,\dots,t_m)$, $s >_{\mathrm{rpo}} t_j$ for every $j$, and $(s_1,\dots,s_m)$ is greater than $(t_1,\dots,t_m)$ in the multiset (resp. lexicographic) extension of $>_{\mathrm{rpo}}$ when $\tau(f)=\mathrm{mul}$ (resp. $\mathrm{lex}$).

An RPO ordering constraint is a finite conjunction of atomic constraints of the forms $u>_{\mathrm{rpo}} v$ and $u=v$, with $u,v\in T(\Sigma,\mathcal{X})$. The existential fragment of the first-order theory of $>_{\mathrm{rpo}}$ consists of formulas $\exists \bar{x}\,\varphi(\bar{x})$ where $\varphi$ is a Boolean combination of such atoms; satisfiability asks whether there exists an assignment of the variables to ground terms in $T(\Sigma)$ making the formula true.

Question: Is the existential fragment of the first-order theory of the recursive path ordering with multiset and lexicographic status decidable when the precedence $>_\Sigma$ is allowed to be an arbitrary strict partial order rather than required to be total? Equivalently, is satisfiability of RPO ordering constraints decidable for non-total precedences? (The same question is posed for the lexicographic path ordering LPO, the special case where every symbol has lexicographic status.)

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Existing decidability/NP-completeness results for satisfiability of RPO/LPO ordering constraints (e.g., Nieuwenhuis's "RPO constraint solving is in NP" and related work) address the case of total precedences. Available sources indicate that the corresponding question for partial (non-total) precedences has not been resolved in the literature, and indeed the full first-order theory of LPO with partial precedence on a unary signature is known to be undecidable, while the existential fragment with partial precedence appears to remain open.

Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a finite set of function symbols containing at least one designated binary symbol $+$ that is assumed to be associative and commutative; let $AC$ denote the equational theory consisting of the axioms
$$x+(y+z) = (x+y)+z, \qquad x+y = y+x.$$
Let $T(\mathcal{F})$ be the set of ground terms built from $\mathcal{F}$ and let $T(\mathcal{F})/{=_{AC}}$ be its quotient by the congruence generated by $AC$. Consider the first-order structure whose domain is $T(\mathcal{F})/{=_{AC}}$ and whose signature consists of the function symbols of $\mathcal{F}$, interpreted as the operations on $AC$-equivalence classes.

The $\Sigma_2$ fragment of the first-order theory of this structure consists of all closed formulas of the form
$$\exists \bar{x}\, \forall \bar{y}\, \varphi(\bar{x},\bar{y}),$$
where $\varphi$ is a quantifier-free formula in the language of $\mathcal{F}$ (with equality).

Question: Is the $\Sigma_2$ fragment of this first-order theory decidable? In particular, is the following "complement problem" decidable: given terms $t, t_1, \dots, t_n$ over $\mathcal{F}$ (possibly with variables), decide whether there exists a ground instance of $t$ that is not $AC$-equal to any ground instance of any $t_i$?

Let R be a (possibly non-orthogonal) term-rewriting system or combinatory reduction system. A redex in a term is an occurrence of a subterm matching the left-hand side of some rule. Given a one-step reduction t →_u t' contracting a redex u, the standard residual theory associates to every other redex v in t a (possibly empty) set of residual redexes v/u in t', and identifies certain redexes in t' as new (created) redexes that are not residuals of any redex in t.

Suppose there exists a well-founded linear order (D, <) and an assignment of a "degree" d(v) ∈ D to every redex occurrence (in every reachable term), satisfying:
(i) for every redex v and every redex u, every residual v' ∈ v/u satisfies d(v') ≤ d(v); and
(ii) every redex w in t' that is created by the contraction of u in t satisfies d(w) < d(u).

Call such an assignment a decreasing-redexes labelling, and say R has the decreasing-redexes property if such a labelling exists.

Question: Does the existence of a decreasing-redexes labelling imply that R is terminating (strongly normalizing) for arbitrary, not necessarily orthogonal, term-rewriting systems and combinatory reduction systems? If not, identify natural subclasses of non-orthogonal systems for which the decreasing-redexes property does imply termination.

Background. Let $\Sigma$ be a finite signature of function symbols (each with fixed arity) and let $T(\Sigma, X)$ denote the set of first-order terms over $\Sigma$ and a denumerable set of variables $X$. A rewrite ordering on $T(\Sigma, X)$ is a strict partial order $>$ that is stable under contexts (if $s > t$ then $f(\ldots, s, \ldots) > f(\ldots, t, \ldots)$) and under substitutions (if $s > t$ then $s\sigma > t\sigma$). The homeomorphic embedding (term embedding) relation $\trianglerighteq_{emb}$ is the smallest rewrite ordering containing the subterm relation. A simplification ordering is a rewrite ordering containing $\trianglerighteq_{emb}$; by Kruskal's tree theorem every simplification ordering on a finite signature is well-founded.

Lescanne's notion of a well-rewrite-ordering is a strengthening/extension of these concepts: it is a rewrite (quasi-)ordering whose strict part is well-founded and that is compatible with the embedding relation, but which need not require the full simplification property and which is closed under certain natural operations used to build orderings.

Dershowitz's recursive path ordering (RPO) is constructed from a well-founded precedence $>_F$ on $\Sigma$ by the recursive definition: $s = f(s_1, \ldots, s_m) >_{rpo} t = g(t_1, \ldots, t_n)$ iff (i) some $s_i \geq_{rpo} t$, or (ii) $f >_F g$ and $s >_{rpo} t_j$ for all $j$, or (iii) $f = g$ and $\{s_1, \ldots, s_m\} \gg_{rpo} \{t_1, \ldots, t_n\}$ in the multiset extension.

Problem. Define, in a uniform manner, a new family of recursive-path-style orderings on $T(\Sigma, X)$ whose construction is based on an arbitrary given well-rewrite-ordering (in Lescanne's sense) in place of, or in addition to, a precedence on function symbols, in such a way that:

(a) The resulting relation is itself a well-rewrite-ordering on $T(\Sigma, X)$;
(b) When the input well-rewrite-ordering is taken to be the empty ordering (with a precedence on $\Sigma$ supplied separately), the construction specializes to Dershowitz's recursive path ordering;
(c) The construction is closed under the natural lifting operations (multiset and lexicographic status on argument tuples) and yields a strictly larger class of well-founded rewrite orderings than RPO, capable of orienting rewrite systems that no RPO with any precedence can orient.

Give such a definition and prove (a)–(c), or show that no such construction exists.

Let R be a finite term rewriting system over a signature Σ, where each function symbol f ∈ Σ of arity n is interpreted by a function [f] : ℕ^n → ℕ. An interpretation is called exponential if the interpretations [f] are built from constants, projections, addition, multiplication, and exponentiation x ↦ a^x (with base a ≥ 2). Each term t with variables x_1,...,x_k is then assigned a function [t] : ℕ^k → ℕ obtained by composition. The system R is said to decrease with respect to the interpretation if [ℓ](x_1,...,x_k) > [r](x_1,...,x_k) holds for all (x_1,...,x_k) ∈ ℕ^k, for every rewrite rule ℓ → r in R; this implies termination of R.

Problem: Develop an effective and implementable algorithm that, given a finite rewrite system R, decides whether there exists an exponential interpretation (in the above sense) with respect to which R decreases, analogous to the established procedures for deciding the existence of suitable polynomial interpretations. In particular, devise a mechanizable method for comparing expressions built using addition, multiplication, and exponentiation over ℕ that can serve as the core of such a decision procedure.

Work in the setting of first-order term rewriting over a fixed signature, with terms built from function symbols and a countable set of variables. A binary relation $\to$ on terms is called a rewrite relation if it is closed under contexts and under substitutions; it is fully invariant (under instantiation) if $s \to t$ implies $\sigma(s) \to \sigma(t)$ for every substitution $\sigma$. A rewrite relation $\to$ is terminating if there is no infinite chain $t_0 \to t_1 \to t_2 \to \cdots$.

The encompassment relation $\unrhd_\sigma$ is defined by: $s \unrhd_\sigma t$ iff some subterm of $s$ is an instance of $t$ (equivalently, $t$ matches a subterm of $s$).

Determine the coarsest binary relation $R$ on terms such that, for every terminating rewrite relation $\to$, the union $\to \cup\, R$ is terminating and remains fully invariant under instantiation.

Moreover, if the requirement of full invariance is dropped, decide whether the encompassment relation $\unrhd_\sigma$ is the coarsest relation $R$ such that $\to \cup\, R$ is terminating whenever $\to$ is a terminating rewrite relation.

Let Σ be a finite signature of function symbols, each with a fixed arity, and let V be a countable set of variables. Denote by T(Σ,V) the set of (first-order) terms over Σ and V. A precedence on Σ is a (strict) partial order >_Σ on Σ; it is total if it is a linear order.

Given a precedence >_Σ, the recursive path ordering (RPO) >_rpo on T(Σ,V) is defined as the smallest relation such that s = f(s_1,…,s_m) >_rpo t iff one of the following holds:
 (1) t is a variable occurring strictly in s; or
 (2) t = g(t_1,…,t_n) and either
   (a) s_i ≥_rpo t for some i, or
   (b) f >_Σ g and s >_rpo t_j for all j, or
   (c) f = g and {s_1,…,s_m} is greater than {t_1,…,t_n} in the multiset extension of >_rpo.

The lexicographic path ordering (LPO) >_lpo is defined identically except that case (c) is replaced by the lexicographic extension of >_lpo on the tuples (s_1,…,s_m) and (t_1,…,t_n) (together with s >_lpo t_j for all j).

Determine the computational complexity of the following decision problems:

(i) Given Σ, a precedence >_Σ on Σ (not necessarily total), and two terms s, t ∈ T(Σ,V), decide whether s >_rpo t.

(ii) Given Σ, a (possibly non-total) precedence >_Σ on Σ, and two terms s, t ∈ T(Σ,V) (which may contain variables), decide whether s >_lpo t.

In particular, classify each of these problems with respect to standard complexity classes (P, NP, coNP, PSPACE, etc.), determining tight upper and lower bounds.

Background and definitions. Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and let $\Sigma^*$ denote the free monoid of finite words over $\Sigma$. A finite string rewriting system (Thue system) on $\Sigma$ is a finite set $R \subseteq \Sigma^* \times \Sigma^*$ of rewrite rules $\ell \to r$. The single-step relation $\to_R$ is defined by $u\ell v \to_R urv$ for $(\ell,r)\in R$ and $u,v\in\Sigma^*$; let $\leftrightarrow_R^*$ denote its reflexive, symmetric, transitive closure. The uniform word problem for a class $\mathcal{C}$ of finite rewriting systems asks, given as input a finite system $R\in\mathcal{C}$ over some alphabet $\Sigma$ together with two words $u,v\in\Sigma^*$, whether $u\leftrightarrow_R^* v$.

By a "variant of rewriting" we mean any decision procedure based on rewriting in a generalized sense, including but not limited to:
(i) standard rewriting with a finite confluent and terminating (canonical) system,
(ii) rewriting modulo a finitely-generated congruence with a decidable matching problem,
(iii) ordered (or recursive-path-ordering–based) rewriting using a reduction order,
(iv) any combination of the above using only the original alphabet $\Sigma$ (no auxiliary symbols are introduced into the signature).

Question. Does there exist a finitely presented equational/rewriting theory $(\Sigma, E)$ whose uniform word problem is decidable, but for which no variant of rewriting in the above sense, restricted to the alphabet $\Sigma$ (i.e., without enlarging the vocabulary by introducing new auxiliary symbols), yields a decision procedure for the word problem of $(\Sigma, E)$?

Let $\mathrm{FL}(X)$ denote the free lattice generated by a set $X$, regarded as an algebra in the signature $\{\vee, \wedge\}$ subject to the lattice axioms (idempotency, commutativity, associativity of both operations, and the two absorption laws). A term rewriting system over this signature (possibly modulo associativity and commutativity, or in some other suitable framework such as ordered, conditional, or graph rewriting) is called convergent if it is terminating and confluent, so that every term has a unique normal form.

Question: Does there exist a finite term rewriting system, of some appropriate kind, that is convergent for the equational theory of lattices, so that the normal forms of terms over $X$ are in bijection with the elements of $\mathrm{FL}(X)$?

representations.normalized:
Let $\Sigma$ be a signature containing a binary function symbol $+$, and consider the equational theory ACUI consisting of the axioms
- (A) $(x+y)+z = x+(y+z)$,
- (C) $x+y = y+x$,
- (U) $x+0 = x$ for a constant $0\in\Sigma$,
- (I) $x+x = x$.

Given a finite set $E$ of equations between $\Sigma$-terms, the goal of completion modulo ACUI is to transform $E$ into a finite rewrite system $R$ such that the rewrite relation $\to_{R/\mathrm{ACUI}}$ (rewriting on ACUI-equivalence classes) is terminating and Church–Rosser, so that $\mathrm{ACUI}\cup E$-equality of two terms can be decided by reducing each to its $R/\mathrm{ACUI}$-normal form.

Standard Knuth–Bendix–style completion procedures have been extended to handle the AC axioms, and further to ACU (with identity), by adapting orderings, critical-pair computation, and unification modulo the relevant theory. These techniques, however, do not extend directly to systems that additionally include the idempotence axiom (I), because idempotence interacts badly with termination orderings and with extended-rule mechanisms used in AC/ACU completion.

Problem: Devise an effective completion procedure modulo ACUI. Concretely, give:
1. an appropriate notion of rewriting modulo ACUI (including suitable extended rules and a termination ordering compatible with idempotence),
2. a finite, decidable mechanism for computing the critical pairs that must be considered (in particular, a usable form of ACUI-unification within completion), and
3. a completion algorithm that, when it succeeds, produces a finite convergent system $R$ deciding ACUI$\cup E$-equality,

or prove that no such effective procedure exists.

Let $E$ be a set of equations over a set of terms built from a signature $\mathcal{F}$ and variables, and let $>$ be a reduction ordering on terms (i.e., a well-founded strict ordering that is closed under contexts and substitutions). A rewrite system $R$ is said to be convergent (with respect to $>$) if every rule $\ell \to r \in R$ satisfies $\ell > r$, if $R$ is confluent, and if its equational theory coincides with that of $E$ (so that every $E$-equivalence class has a unique $R$-normal form).

Question: Does there exist a set of inference rules for completion that, given any equational theory $E$ and any reduction ordering $>$ for which some convergent rewrite system $R$ contained in $>$ presenting $E$ exists, is guaranteed to compute such an $R$? In particular, must the procedure succeed even when $>$ cannot be extended to a reduction ordering that is total on ground terms?

representations.normalized:
Consider a Knuth–Bendix style completion procedure operating on a set of equations over a term algebra. In the standard setting, a fixed reduction ordering ≻ (a well-founded ordering on terms that is stable under contexts and substitutions) is chosen at the start, and every rule produced during the run is oriented according to ≻; the procedure is known to be correct in the sense that, if it does not fail and does not run forever, the persisting rules form a confluent and terminating term rewriting system equivalent to the input equations.

Now consider the following modification. At each step of the run, the procedure is allowed to choose a (possibly new) reduction ordering, with the only requirement that the chosen ordering orient the rules currently present in the system. Rules that have been deleted in earlier steps need not be oriented by the new ordering. Persisting rules are those rules that, once generated, are never deleted in the remainder of the run.

Question: Can this modified completion procedure be incomplete? That is, can a run of this procedure terminate (or persist) with a set of persisting rules that is terminating but not confluent, even though the run did not fail?

The question has been answered affirmatively: allowing the reduction ordering to change during a Knuth–Bendix completion run (requiring only that the current rules be oriented) renders the procedure incomplete. Even when the modified procedure terminates without failure, the resulting finite terminating term rewriting system can fail to be confluent. This is established in work on "About changing the ordering during Knuth-Bendix completion."

Background. In Boolean-ring based theorem proving, first-order clauses are translated into polynomials over the Boolean ring GF(2)[X]/(x^2 − x : x ∈ X), where conjunction is multiplication, exclusive-or is addition, and atoms become indeterminates. Refutational theorem proving is then carried out by superposition-style inferences on these polynomials: given two polynomials P and Q sharing a (unifiable) atom A, one forms new polynomials by overlapping P and Q on A (after applying a most general unifier), and the goal is to derive the polynomial 1 (representing falsity). Standard completeness proofs allow "multiple overlaps" (superposing on several atoms simultaneously or considering many atom pairs) and impose only mild restrictions on which atoms may be selected.

Problem. Determine whether the following more restrictive inference strategies for Boolean-ring based resolution-like first-order theorem proving are refutationally complete:

(a) A "single-overlap" strategy, in which each inference between two polynomials P and Q is required to superpose on exactly one chosen atom (no simultaneous multi-atom overlap is permitted).

(b) A "maximal-atom unification" strategy, in which, with respect to a fixed admissible ordering on atoms, inferences are restricted to unifications of maximal atoms of the participating polynomials only.

In each case, prove completeness (every unsatisfiable set of clauses admits a derivation of 1 under the restricted strategy) or exhibit a counterexample showing incompleteness. More generally, identify and prove complete the most restrictive natural strategies of these types for Boolean-ring based first-order theorem proving.

Partial progress exists: a method restricting superposition to maximal atoms (extending Hsiang's N-strategy) with a completeness proof via semantic trees has been published, and a linear strategy plus O-linear/pseudo-O-linear strategies based on a partial ordering of atoms have been shown complete. Results on the unnecessity of multiple overlaps in completion theorem proving also exist. However, a definitive resolution of the general question of identifying the most restrictive complete strategies (single-overlap and maximal-atom unification combined) in the Boolean-ring setting does not appear to be fully settled in the literature found.

representations.normalized:
Consider the following clausal reasoning mechanism, called contextual deduction. Clauses are finite disjunctions of literals in first-order logic. Contextual deduction is a rewriting-like inference system on clauses that, unlike resolution, uses pattern matching instead of full unification: a clause C may be used to simplify or reduce another clause D only by instantiating C (via a substitution applied to its variables) so that the instantiated literals of C syntactically match literals already present in D, with no instantiation of D permitted. In particular, no new terms are introduced into the clause set by the inference rule.

The system is to be used as a refutation procedure for ground clauses: given a set S of (possibly non-ground) clauses together with a finite set G of ground clauses, the goal is to derive the empty clause from S ∪ G using contextual deduction whenever S ∪ G is unsatisfiable.

Because contextual deduction never instantiates clauses except to match literals already in the current clause set, it is in general incomplete for first-order refutation. The problem is the following:

Does there exist a useful and non-trivial notion of "complete theory" T (i.e., a class of clause sets, defined by some natural closure or saturation condition) such that, whenever S belongs to this class T and G is any finite set of ground clauses with S ∪ G unsatisfiable, contextual deduction is guaranteed to derive the empty clause from S ∪ G? Identify and characterize such a notion of complete theory, or prove that no useful such notion exists.

Unification modulo the pure two-sided distributivity theory (both left and right distributivity, no associativity, commutativity, or unit) was shown to be decidable by Schmidt-Schauß, who reduced the problem to AC1-unification with linear constant restrictions together with a word-unification problem solvable via Makanin's algorithm. representations.normalized:
Consider a set of inference rules that transform a system of equations in an equational theory toward a "dag-solved form": a conjunction of equations x_1 = t_1, ..., x_n = t_n where the x_i are pairwise distinct variables and there is no cycle in the dependency relation x_i ▷ x_j defined by "x_j occurs in t_i" (so that the system, viewed as a substitution after acyclic ordering, is idempotent).

Among the transformation rules is a Merge rule of the form
    {x = s, x = t} ∪ P  ⟹  {x = t, s = t} ∪ P,
which combines two equations sharing the left-hand variable x. As usually stated, the Merge rule carries the application condition that s is a non-variable term whose size is no larger than the size of t (this restriction is imposed to ensure termination and to interact properly with an occurs-check style rule).

A separate rule, called Check*, is used to detect cycles in the variable-dependency graph of the current system and to signal failure when such a cycle is present.

Question. Can the application condition on the Merge rule "s is a non-variable term and |s| ≤ |t|" be replaced by the strictly more permissive condition "Check* does not apply to the current system" while preserving soundness, completeness and termination of the overall rule set for computing dag-solved forms? Equivalently, is Check* complete for detecting all cycles that would otherwise be prevented by the size/non-variable restriction on Merge?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Known as Lehmer's totient problem (posed by D. H. Lehmer in 1932), the question remains open. No composite n with φ(n) | n−1 has ever been found, and known lower bounds require any such n to have at least 15 distinct prime factors and to exceed 10^30, with further computational improvements over time, but no proof or counterexample exists.

Consider the problem of associative–commutative (AC) unification: given two first-order terms s and t built from a signature containing one or more binary function symbols declared associative and commutative, find a complete set of substitutions σ such that sσ =_AC tσ, where =_AC denotes equality modulo the associativity and commutativity axioms of those symbols.

Standard AC-unification procedures are presented as nondeterministic transformation systems on systems of equations (e.g., variants of Stickel's algorithm and its refinements). For such transformation systems, termination has been established under restrictive control regimes, namely:
  (a) the strategy that performs a variable-replacement (instantiation) step after every transformation step, and
  (b) the strategy that defers variable replacement until the very end of the derivation.

The problem is to determine whether the same (or analogously formulated) transformation rules for AC-unification still terminate when these rigid control disciplines are loosened, i.e., when variable replacement steps may be interleaved arbitrarily with other transformation steps rather than being constrained to occur after every step or only at the end. Concretely: identify a flexible control strategy strictly more permissive than (a) and (b), and prove that every derivation of the AC-unification transformation system under this strategy is finite; or else exhibit a counterexample showing nontermination.

Both theories are known to be decidable (Mal'cev; Maher for infinite/rational trees; Comon and others), and the full first-order theory of finite trees is known to have non-elementary complexity (so it is not in PSPACE), with similar non-elementary lower bounds for the infinite-tree case. Tight complexity characterizations within the non-elementary hierarchy are not fully settled in the literature surveyed, so the precise complexity question is only partially resolved.

Work in the free term algebra (Herbrand universe) of finite trees over a fixed signature of function symbols, with syntactic equality as the only predicate. Consider first-order formulas built from equations s = t between terms using the connectives ∧, ∨, ¬, → and the quantifiers ∀, ∃, interpreted in this algebra. Call a formula positive if it is built without the negation connective ¬.

A substitution σ is a unifier of a formula φ(x₁, …, xₙ) if σ makes φ true in the algebra of finite trees. A finite set Σ of substitutions is a complete set of unifiers of φ if every unifier of φ is an instance of some σ ∈ Σ.

Question: Is there an algorithm that, given a first-order formula φ over finite trees with equality as the only predicate such that φ is semantically equivalent to some positive formula, produces a negation-free formula equivalent to φ? Equivalently, when such a φ admits a finite complete set of unifiers, can that set be effectively computed?

Constraint solving in symbolic computation encompasses a wide variety of procedures, including:

- syntactic and equational unification algorithms (computing solutions to equations s = t modulo a given equational theory E),
- algorithms for systems of equations together with disequations (disunification),
- algorithms over signatures whose theories share certain symbols, such as shared constants or shared free constructors,
- algorithms handling membership constraints (e.g., sort or regular-tree constraints requiring variables to range over specified sets), and
- algorithms over non-free solution domains (algebraic structures that are not initial/free in the corresponding theory).

Each of these classes admits its own combination results (for instance, decision procedures for unifiability in disjoint equational theories can be combined under suitable conditions, and analogous methods exist for disunification with linear constant restrictions).

Problem. Design a single general framework for combining constraint-solving algorithms that simultaneously encompasses all of the above settings. More precisely, formulate a uniform notion of "constraint solver" and a uniform combination procedure such that, given constraint solvers S_1, …, S_n for theories (or constraint languages) L_1, …, L_n satisfying explicitly stated abstract hypotheses, the framework produces a constraint solver for the combined constraint language L_1 ∪ … ∪ L_n, and such that the existing combination results for unification, for equations-plus-disequations, for theories sharing constants or constructors, for membership constraints, and for constraint solving over non-free domains all arise as instances of this single framework.

Let E be a syntactic equational theory over a first-order term signature; that is, an equational theory for which every E-equality s =_E t admits a proof by an equational replacement at the root using an axiom of E followed by paramodulations strictly below the root. Assume further that E is finitary, meaning that for every E-unification problem Γ (a finite set of equations to be solved modulo E) there exists a finite complete set of E-unifiers, i.e. a finite set S of substitutions such that:
  (i) every σ ∈ S is an E-unifier of Γ (σ(s) =_E σ(t) for each equation s = t in Γ), and
  (ii) for every E-unifier τ of Γ there exists σ ∈ S and a substitution ρ with τ =_E ρ ∘ σ on the variables of Γ.

The standard syntactic mutation-based unification calculus for E (the system of transformation rules: Decomposition, Mutate-with-axiom, Variable elimination, etc.) produces, from Γ, a derivation tree whose leaves labelled by solved forms correspond to E-unifiers. In general this derivation tree may be infinite even when E is finitary.

Question: Can one design uniform additional control rules — of "pruning" type (discarding redundant branches that produce only unifiers subsumed elsewhere in the tree) and/or "freezing" type (temporarily blocking the application of mutation steps on certain subterms to prevent non-terminating expansions) — that, when added to the syntactic mutation calculus, guarantee for every finitary syntactic equational theory E and every E-unification problem Γ that the resulting derivation tree is finite and that its solved-form leaves form a finite complete set of E-unifiers for Γ?

Let $\mathcal{T}$ be a $d$-dimensional conformal field theory (CFT), i.e. a quantum field theory invariant under the conformal group $SO(d,2)$ (in Lorentzian signature) or $SO(d+1,1)$ (in Euclidean signature). A conformal boundary condition for $\mathcal{T}$ is a choice of boundary $\partial M \subset M$ together with boundary data preserving the subgroup of the conformal group that fixes $\partial M$ (typically $SO(d-1,2)$ or $SO(d,1)$), equivalently a boundary state in the bulk operator algebra for which the component $T_{\perp\parallel}$ of the stress tensor vanishes on the boundary. A conformal defect of dimension $p < d$ is an extended operator supported on a $p$-dimensional submanifold preserving the analogous defect conformal subgroup $SO(p+1,1)\times SO(d-p)$ (Euclidean).

Question: Using one or more of the following techniques—
  (a) superconformal symmetry and its representation theory,
  (b) the numerical and analytic conformal bootstrap (crossing equations for boundary/defect correlation functions and their associated bounds),
  (c) integrability methods (e.g. boundary Yang–Baxter equations, integrable boundary states, spin-chain techniques),
  (d) coupling to topological quantum field theories (e.g. symmetry topological field theories / SymTFTs and their boundary conditions),
exhibit a new conformal boundary condition or a new conformal defect in a non-trivial unitary CFT in dimension $d \geq 2$ that is not unitarily equivalent to any currently known boundary condition or defect, or alternatively prove that the techniques above suffice to classify all conformal boundary conditions and defects of some specific non-trivial CFT (such as a free scalar, free Maxwell theory in $d=4$, or the 3d Ising CFT).

Let $\mathrm{CFT}_+$ and $\mathrm{CFT}_-$ be two large-$N$ conformal field theories in $d$ dimensions that are related by a relevant double-trace deformation: starting from a CFT containing a single-trace scalar primary $\mathcal{O}$ of scaling dimension $\Delta_-$, the deformation $\int d^d x\, \mathcal{O}^2$ triggers an RG flow whose IR endpoint is a CFT in which the corresponding operator has dimension $\Delta_+ = d - \Delta_-$. A double-trace interface is the planar codimension-one conformal interface $\mathcal{I}$ separating these two theories that is obtained by turning on the double-trace deformation only on a half-space; equivalently, it is described holographically by a bulk scalar in AdS$_{d+1}$ satisfying alternate boundary conditions on the two halves of the conformal boundary.

Given two such double-trace interfaces $\mathcal{I}_1$ and $\mathcal{I}_2$, placed on parallel planes at separation $\varepsilon \to 0$, describe the fusion product
$$\mathcal{I}_1 \star \mathcal{I}_2 := \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} \mathcal{I}_1(x_d = \varepsilon)\, \mathcal{I}_2(x_d = 0),$$
including the renormalization of local interface operators and counterterms, the resulting conformal interface (or composite defect) between the appropriate pair of CFTs, the leading-$1/N$ fusion algebra they generate, the spectrum of operators on the fused interface, and the change in the interface contribution to the sphere partition function (the $g$-factor in $d=2$).

Consider the impartial combinatorial game DUDENEY, defined as follows. Fix a positive integer Y (the upper bound). A position consists of a single heap of n ≥ 0 beans together with a record of the opponent's most recent move (an integer in {1, 2, …, Y}, or "none" at the start). On a turn a player removes between 1 and Y beans from the heap, subject to the restriction that the number removed must differ from the number the opponent removed on the immediately preceding move. A player unable to move loses (normal play convention).

For each Y, the sequence (G_Y(n))_{n≥0} of Sprague–Grundy (Nim) values of the positions with heap size n (after a generic opening) is eventually periodic; the structural patterns of these sequences are called "pearl-strings", with a well-defined period associated to each Y.

(a) Complete the analysis of the Nim-value sequence G_Y for every odd Y, classifying the pearl-string structure in all remaining unresolved odd-Y cases.

(b) Determine whether the pearl-string periods for odd Y are bounded, or whether they become arbitrarily large as Y → ∞ through odd values.

(c) Decide whether there exist odd values of Y for which the analysis is "incompletable" in the sense that no finite description of the Nim-value sequence exists (i.e., G_Y fails to be eventually periodic, or no algorithm computes its structure), and identify the underlying combinatorial structure governing the odd-Y cases.

A tournament is an orientation of a finite complete graph; that is, a directed graph obtained by assigning a direction to every edge of a complete graph. A directed cycle in a tournament is a sequence of distinct vertices v_1, v_2, …, v_k, v_1 (k ≥ 3) such that each consecutive pair forms an arc in the tournament. Given a tournament T that contains at least one directed cycle, the reversal of an arc (u,v) is the operation of replacing (u,v) by (v,u), producing a new tournament T'. Let c(T) denote the total number of directed cycles in T (of all lengths).

Prove or disprove: for every tournament T with c(T) ≥ 1, there exists an arc e of T whose reversal yields a tournament T' with c(T') < c(T).

Call a directed multigraph $D=(V,A)$ an Euler oriented graph if (i) $D$ is connected, (ii) $D$ contains no pair of opposite arcs (i.e., no directed cycle of length 2), and (iii) every vertex $x\in V$ satisfies $d^{+}(x)=d^{-}(x)$, where $d^{+}(x)$ and $d^{-}(x)$ denote the out-degree and in-degree of $x$. A directed cycle in $D$ is a cyclic sequence $v_0,v_1,\dots,v_{k-1},v_0$ of distinct vertices with $(v_i,v_{i+1\bmod k})\in A$ for all $i$. For an arc $a=(u,v)\in A$, the reversal of $a$ replaces $a$ by $(v,u)$, yielding a new directed graph $D^{a}$. Let $c(D)$ denote the total number of directed cycles in $D$.

Prove or disprove: for every Euler oriented graph $D$ with $c(D)\ge 1$, there exists an arc $a\in A$ such that $c(D^{a})<c(D)$.

The Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture remains open in general. The Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture asserts that every finite simple digraph on n vertices in which every vertex has out-degree at least n/k contains a directed cycle of length at most k. Equivalently, for every integer k ≥ 1, if D is a digraph on n vertices with minimum out-degree at least ⌈n/k⌉, then D contains a directed cycle of length at most k.

The conjecture is known to hold for k ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}. The problem is to settle the conjecture for the next fixed value, k = 6: prove or disprove that every digraph on n vertices with minimum out-degree at least ⌈n/6⌉ contains a directed cycle of length at most 6. More generally, settle the conjecture for further fixed small values of k beyond k = 6.

The Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture has been proved for k = 1, 2, 3 (Hamidoune) and k = 4, 5 (Hoàng–Reed), and for all sufficiently large k (k ≥ 224,539 via Shen-type bounds). The case k = 6 is the first unsettled fixed small case and does not appear to have been resolved in the literature; the standard open-problem repositories continue to list it as open.

representations.normalized:
A multipartite tournament is an orientation of a complete multipartite graph; equivalently, it is a digraph whose vertex set can be partitioned into independent sets ("parts") such that between any two vertices in different parts there is exactly one arc, and there are no arcs within a part. For a digraph D and a vertex v, the out-degree of v is the number of arcs leaving v, and the minimum out-degree of D is the minimum of these values over all vertices. The girth of D is the length of a shortest directed cycle in D (or infinity if D is acyclic).

Question: Does every multipartite tournament D on n vertices with minimum out-degree at least k contain a directed cycle of length at most ⌈n/k⌉? Equivalently, prove or disprove that the Caccetta–Häggkvist bound holds in this class: every orientation of a complete multipartite graph on n vertices with minimum out-degree k has girth at most ⌈n/k⌉.

The general Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture is well known to be open, with even the k = n/3 (triangle) case unresolved. Partial results exist for special classes (bipartite tournaments, digraphs with small independence number, forbidden subgraph variants), but no proof or disproof of the conjecture restricted to multipartite tournaments appears in the literature; the restricted statement is posed as an open problem.

Call a directed multigraph $D=(V,E)$ an Euler digraph if $D$ is connected and every vertex $x\in V$ satisfies $d^{+}(x)=d^{-}(x)$, where $d^{+}(x)$ and $d^{-}(x)$ denote the out-degree and in-degree of $x$ respectively. Define the minimum out-degree of $D$ as $\delta^{+}(D)=\min_{x\in V}d^{+}(x)$, and the girth of $D$ as the length of a shortest directed cycle in $D$.

Prove or disprove the following statement: For every Euler digraph $D$ on $n$ vertices with minimum out-degree $k\ge 1$, $D$ contains a directed cycle of length at most $\lceil n/k\rceil$.

(This is the Caccetta–Häggkvist statement restricted to the class of Euler digraphs.)

Let $D=(V,A)$ be a finite directed graph (loops and multiple arcs forbidden) and let $k$ be a positive integer. The minimum out-degree of $D$ is $\delta^{+}(D) := \min_{v \in V} |\{u \in V : (v,u) \in A\}|$. A directed cycle is a sequence $v_1 v_2 \cdots v_\ell v_1$ of distinct vertices ($\ell \geq 2$) such that $(v_i,v_{i+1}) \in A$ for each $i$ (indices mod $\ell$). Two directed cycles are vertex-disjoint if they share no vertex.

Prove or disprove: for every positive integer $k$ and every finite digraph $D$ with $\delta^{+}(D) \geq 2k-1$, $D$ contains $k$ pairwise vertex-disjoint directed cycles.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The conjecture is confirmed for $k=1$ (trivial), $k=2$ (Thomassen, 1983), and $k=3$ (Lichiardopol, Pór, Sereni). It has also been verified for tournaments (Bang-Jensen, Bessy, Thomassé) and for digraphs with minimum semi-degree $\geq 2k-1$ in special classes, but the full conjecture remains open for general digraphs when $k \geq 4$.

For a graph (or digraph) $H$, let $\lambda(H)$ denote the number of vertices in a longest path of $H$ (in the directed case, a longest directed path).

Prove or disprove: For every finite (directed or undirected) graph $G$ and every natural number $q$ with $0<q<\lambda(G)$, there exists a partition $(A,B)$ of $G$ such that
$$\lambda(A)\le q \quad\text{and}\quad \lambda(B)\le \lambda(G)-q.$$

An acyclic digraph is a finite directed graph with no directed cycles. For a digraph $D=(V,A)$ and a partition $V=X\sqcup Y$, the directed cut $(X,Y)$ is the set of arcs of $D$ with tail in $X$ and head in $Y$; its size is $|(X,Y)|$. For an acyclic digraph $D$, let $\mathrm{mc}(D)$ denote the maximum of $|(X,Y)|$ over all partitions $V=X\sqcup Y$. Define
$$h(m)=\min\{\mathrm{mc}(D): D\text{ is an acyclic digraph with exactly }m\text{ arcs}\}.$$
It is known that $h(m)=m/4+o(m)$. Determine
$$\alpha_0=\inf\{\alpha>0 : h(m)=\tfrac{m}{4}+O(m^{\alpha})\text{ as }m\to\infty\}.$$

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The exact value of α₀ remains open. Work of Alon, Bollobás, Gyárfás, Lehel and Scott (J. Graph Theory, 2007) establishes the bounds α₀ ∈ [3/5, 4/5] for acyclic digraphs, but no improvement determining the precise infimum is known.

A directed cut in a digraph $D=(V,A)$ is the set of arcs from $S$ to $V\setminus S$ for some $S\subseteq V$. For an acyclic directed multigraph $D$ with $m$ arcs (parallel arcs allowed), let $\mathrm{mc}(D)$ denote the maximum number of arcs in a directed cut of $D$, and define
$$h_\mu(m) = \min\{\mathrm{mc}(D) : D \text{ is an acyclic directed multigraph with } m \text{ arcs}\}.$$
For a weighted acyclic digraph $D$ with arc weight function $\omega:A\to[1,\infty)$ and total weight $w=\sum_{a\in A}\omega(a)$, let $\mathrm{mc}_\omega(D)$ denote the maximum total weight of a directed cut, and define
$$h_\omega(w) = \min\{\mathrm{mc}_\omega(D) : D \text{ is a weighted acyclic digraph with arc weights} \ge 1 \text{ and total weight } w\}.$$
It is known that
$$\tfrac{m}{4} + \Omega(m^{3/5}) \le h_\mu(m) \le \tfrac{m}{4} + O(m^{3/4}), \qquad \tfrac{w}{4} + \Omega(w^{3/5}) \le h_\omega(w) \le \tfrac{w}{4} + O(w^{3/4}).$$
Determine the exact asymptotic exponent $\alpha\in[3/5,\,3/4]$ such that $h_\mu(m) = m/4 + \Theta(m^\alpha)$ and $h_\omega(w) = w/4 + \Theta(w^\alpha)$.

A sowing game (Mancala-type game) is a two-player combinatorial game played on a finite row or ring of pits, each pit containing a nonnegative number of stones. A move consists of selecting a nonempty pit, removing all its stones, and "sowing" them one by one into successive pits according to a fixed rule (typically moving in a fixed direction around the board, possibly with capture rules depending on the variant). The terminal condition and winning condition are specified by the particular variant (for example, the player unable to move loses, or the player capturing the most stones wins).

Develop a substantive combinatorial-game-theoretic analysis of sowing/Mancala games. Concretely, address one or more of the following:

1. For a natural infinite family of sowing games (parametrized by the number of pits n and/or the number of stones s), determine the Sprague–Grundy values of positions, or prove structural results (e.g., periodicity, polynomial-time computability) about these values.

2. Identify nontrivial classes of sowing positions whose game-theoretic outcome (first-player win, second-player win, or draw) can be determined in closed form or by an efficient algorithm.

3. Provide a rigorous classification of which sowing variants are tractable (e.g., polynomial-time solvable) versus intractable (e.g., PSPACE-hard) as combinatorial games, beyond the small finite instances already settled by computer search.

Any such result, supported by proof, would constitute substantial progress on the combinatorial theory of sowing games.

Develop a substantive combinatorial-game-theoretic analysis of sowing/Mancala games. Concretely, address one or more of the following:

1. For a natural infinite family of sowing games (parametrized by the number of pits n and/or the number of stones s), determine the Sprague–Grundy values of positions, or prove structural results (e.g., periodicity, polynomial-time computability) about these values.

2. Identify nontrivial classes of sowing positions whose game-theoretic outcome (first-player win, second-player win, or draw) can be determined in closed form or by an efficient algorithm.

3. Provide a rigorous classification of which sowing variants are tractable (e.g., polynomial-time solvable) versus intractable (e.g., PSPACE-hard) as combinatorial games, beyond the small finite instances already settled by computer search.

Any such result, supported by proof, would constitute substantial progress on the combinatorial theory of sowing games.

Sowing/Mancala games remain a largely open area in combinatorial game theory. Small variants (Awari, Kalah for some sizes, MiniMancala, Ohvalhu) have been solved by computer search, but more complex variants such as Bao and Omweso are unsolved, and no general combinatorial-game-theoretic framework giving Sprague–Grundy values or structural results for natural infinite families is known.

Exhibit a two-player combinatorial game G satisfying all of the following conditions simultaneously:

1. (Simple, playable rules.) The rules of G can be described concisely and the game is humanly playable.
2. (Bounded branching.) From every position, each player has only finitely many legal moves.
3. (Simple explicit strategy.) There is an explicitly described strategy (i.e., a function from positions to moves) that one of the players can follow.
4. (Bounded play length.) The number of moves in any play of G, as a function of the size n of the input position, is at most exponential in n (i.e., bounded by 2^{p(n)} for some polynomial p).
5. (High decision complexity.) The decision problem "Given an instance/position of G, does the first player have a winning strategy?" is NP-hard, or harder (e.g., PSPACE-hard, EXPTIME-hard).

Construct such a game G, or prove that no such game exists.

A topological algebra is an associative algebra $A$ over $\mathbb{C}$ equipped with a (Hausdorff) vector space topology making the multiplication separately (or jointly) continuous. A (left/two-sided) ideal $I$ of $A$ is called finitely generated if there exist finitely many elements $x_1, \dots, x_n \in A$ such that $I = Ax_1 + \cdots + Ax_n$ (no closure is taken on the right-hand side). The algebra $A$ is said to have the Arens property if $A$ has no dense finitely generated proper ideal.

Question: Suppose $A$ is a topological algebra with the Arens property, and let $A_0 \subseteq A$ be a closed subalgebra of $A$. Must $A_0$ also have the Arens property?

The conjecture was proved by Z. Füredi and D. Kleitman: for any Z_m-edge-coloring (equivalently, integer weights mod m) of K_{m+1}, there exists a spanning tree whose edge-sum is 0 mod m. A simpler proof and a generalization were later given by Schrijver and Seymour. The result is now a standard theorem in zero-sum Ramsey theory.

Let $E$ be an elliptic curve defined over the rational numbers $\mathbb{Q}$. For each place $v$ of $\mathbb{Q}$ (including the archimedean place), let $\mathbb{Q}_v$ denote the corresponding completion, and consider the Galois cohomology groups $H^1(\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q}), E(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}))$ and $H^1(\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}_v}/\mathbb{Q}_v), E(\overline{\mathbb{Q}_v}))$. The Tate–Shafarevich group of $E$ is defined by
$$\mathrm{Sha}(E/\mathbb{Q}) \;=\; \ker\!\left(H^1(\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q}), E(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})) \;\longrightarrow\; \prod_{v} H^1(\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}_v}/\mathbb{Q}_v), E(\overline{\mathbb{Q}_v}))\right),$$
where the map is induced by the restriction maps for each place $v$. Equivalently, $\mathrm{Sha}(E/\mathbb{Q})$ classifies isomorphism classes of principal homogeneous spaces (torsors) for $E$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ that have a $\mathbb{Q}_v$-rational point for every place $v$ of $\mathbb{Q}$.

Question: Is $\mathrm{Sha}(E/\mathbb{Q})$ a finite group for every elliptic curve $E$ over $\mathbb{Q}$?

This is a form of Lang's conjecture on rational points (the "geometric/arithmetic" Lang conjecture), which predicts that rational points concentrate on the special/exceptional locus swept out by images of $\mathbb{P}^1$ and abelian varieties. Let $X$ be a smooth projective algebraic variety over the field $\mathbb{C}$ of complex numbers. Its singular cohomology with rational coefficients admits, for each integer $k \ge 0$, a Hodge decomposition

$$H^{2k}(X,\mathbb{Q}) \otimes_{\mathbb{Q}} \mathbb{C} \;=\; \bigoplus_{p+q=2k} H^{p,q}(X),$$

where $H^{p,q}(X)$ is the space of cohomology classes representable by closed differential forms of type $(p,q)$, and $\overline{H^{p,q}(X)} = H^{q,p}(X)$. A rational cohomology class $\alpha \in H^{2k}(X,\mathbb{Q})$ is called a Hodge class of degree $2k$ if its image in $H^{2k}(X,\mathbb{C})$ lies in the subspace $H^{k,k}(X)$.

For any closed irreducible algebraic subvariety $Z \subset X$ of complex codimension $k$ (more generally, for any algebraic cycle, i.e., a finite formal $\mathbb{Q}$-linear combination of such subvarieties), one has an associated cohomology class $\mathrm{cl}(Z) \in H^{2k}(X,\mathbb{Q})$, and $\mathrm{cl}(Z)$ is a Hodge class.

Question: Is it true that for every smooth projective complex algebraic variety $X$ and every integer $k \ge 0$, every Hodge class of degree $2k$ on $X$ can be written as a $\mathbb{Q}$-linear combination
$$\alpha \;=\; \sum_i q_i \, \mathrm{cl}(Z_i),$$
where $q_i \in \mathbb{Q}$ and each $Z_i$ is an algebraic cycle of codimension $k$ on $X$?

For a smooth projective variety $X$ over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$, the Hasse–Weil zeta function $\zeta(X,s) = \prod_{x \in |X|}(1 - N(x)^{-s})^{-1}$ admits a cohomological interpretation: by the Grothendieck–Lefschetz trace formula, it can be expressed as an alternating product $\zeta(X,s) = \prod_{i=0}^{2\dim X} \det\!\big(1 - q^{-s}\,\mathrm{Frob} \mid H^i_{\ell}(X)\big)^{(-1)^{i+1}}$ where $H^i_\ell(X)$ are the $\ell$-adic étale cohomology groups, and the Riemann Hypothesis for $\zeta(X,s)$ (Deligne's theorem) is a consequence of the existence of a suitable Weil cohomology theory together with the Riemann Hypothesis–type bounds on Frobenius eigenvalues.

Construct, for the classical global setting of the Riemann zeta function $\zeta(s) = \sum_{n \ge 1} n^{-s}$ (and more generally Dirichlet, Hecke, and automorphic $L$-functions over number fields), a cohomological formalism that plays the same role as $\ell$-adic (or other Weil) cohomology plays for zeta functions of varieties over fields of positive characteristic. Concretely: produce a category of "motivic" or geometric objects attached to $\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb{Z}$ and number rings, together with cohomology functors $H^i$ valued in vector spaces over some coefficient field, equipped with an endomorphism (analogue of Frobenius) whose characteristic polynomials yield the completed zeta/$L$-functions as an alternating product, and from which the Riemann Hypothesis for $\zeta(s)$ and related $L$-functions would follow by an analogue of Deligne's positivity/purity argument.

For a smooth projective variety $X$ of dimension $n$ over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$, the geometric Frobenius endomorphism $\mathrm{Frob}_q$ acts on the $\ell$-adic étale cohomology groups $H^i_{\mathrm{ét}}(X_{\overline{\mathbb{F}_q}}, \mathbb{Q}_\ell)$, and the zeta function $Z(X,t)$ of $X$ can be expressed in terms of characteristic polynomials of this action. Deligne's theorem (the Weil conjectures) shows that the eigenvalues of $\mathrm{Frob}_q$ on $H^i$ are algebraic numbers all of whose conjugates have absolute value $q^{i/2}$, which yields the Riemann hypothesis for $Z(X,t)$.

Now consider the classical Riemann zeta function
$$\zeta(s) \;=\; \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^s}, \qquad \Re(s) > 1,$$
extended meromorphically to $\mathbb{C}$, whose nontrivial zeros are conjectured (the Riemann hypothesis) to lie on the line $\Re(s) = 1/2$.

Problem. Construct, in a mathematically meaningful sense, an object playing the role of $\mathrm{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})$ as a variety over a hypothetical "absolute base," together with a cohomology theory and an endomorphism that plays for $\zeta(s)$ the role that the geometric Frobenius plays for zeta functions of varieties over finite fields. More precisely: does there exist a natural operator (a "Frobenius analogue in the classical case") acting on a suitable cohomology of $\mathrm{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})$ (or a suitable completion thereof) whose characteristic-polynomial-type data recovers the completed Riemann zeta function $\xi(s) = \tfrac{1}{2} s(s-1)\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)\zeta(s)$, and whose eigenvalue distribution would directly account for the location of the nontrivial zeros of $\zeta(s)$ on the critical line?

Let $\zeta(s) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n^{-s}$ for $\Re(s) > 1$, extended by analytic continuation to a meromorphic function on $\mathbb{C}$ with a unique simple pole at $s=1$. The classical Riemann Hypothesis (RH) asserts that every non-trivial zero of $\zeta(s)$ (i.e., every zero not at $s = -2, -4, -6, \dots$) lies on the critical line $\Re(s) = 1/2$.

Recall that an index theorem (in the sense of Atiyah–Singer and its generalizations) equates the analytic index of an elliptic (or suitably Fredholm) operator $D$ acting on sections of a vector bundle over a manifold (or a more general geometric/noncommutative space) with a topological index defined in terms of characteristic classes (or K-theoretic data) of the underlying space. A typical use of such a theorem is to express the dimension of an obstruction space, or the signature of a quadratic form, in manifestly non-negative or topologically constrained terms.

Question: Does there exist a general index theorem—that is, an identification of an analytic index of some naturally constructed (possibly Hilbert space, possibly noncommutative geometric) operator with a topological/cohomological invariant—from which the classical Riemann Hypothesis can be deduced? More precisely, exhibit a geometric or noncommutative-geometric framework together with a self-adjoint (or otherwise spectrally constrained) operator $D$ whose spectrum encodes the non-trivial zeros of $\zeta(s)$ via the relation $s = 1/2 + it$ with $t$ ranging over $\mathrm{Spec}(D) \subset \mathbb{R}$, and a corresponding index-theoretic identity that forces the reality of this spectrum, thereby proving RH.

Define
\[\Phi(t) \;=\; 2\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\Bigl(2n^{4}\pi^{2}e^{9t/2} \;-\; 3n^{2}\pi e^{5t/2}\Bigr) e^{-n^{2}\pi e^{2t}}, \qquad t\in\mathbb R,\]
and the completed Riemann xi-function
\[\Xi(z) \;=\; \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\Phi(t)\,e^{izt}\,dt \;=\; 2\int_{0}^{\infty}\Phi(t)\cos(zt)\,dt.\]
A real sequence $\{\gamma_k\}_{k\ge 0}$ is called a multiplier sequence if for every hyperbolic polynomial $p(x)=\sum_{k}a_k x^k$ (a polynomial with only real zeros) the polynomial $\sum_{k}\gamma_k a_k x^k$ is again hyperbolic. Address the following:

(i) What number-theoretic information is encoded in $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\Phi(x)\cos(zx)\,dx$? In particular, is it possible to prove the Prime Number Theorem — which is equivalent to the statement that this function of $z$ has no zeros in the half-plane $\{z\in\mathbb C : \operatorname{Im} z \ge 1/2\}$ — using only this integral representation?

(ii) Characterize the multiplier sequences $\{\gamma_k\}$ whose associated diagonal action evens out the spacings between consecutive real zeros of $\Xi$.

(iii) Does there exist $R>0$ such that $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{R}\Phi(x)\cos(zx)\,dx$ has more than one pair of complex conjugate (non-real) zeros?

(iv) For real entire functions of order $1$ all of whose zeros are real, is differentiation a more effective method for evening out the spacings between consecutive zeros than the midpoint method (the operation that replaces consecutive zeros by their pairwise midpoints)?

A polynomial p(x,y) in two complex variables is called stable if p(x,y) ≠ 0 whenever Im(x) > 0 and Im(y) > 0. Fix a positive integer n. If A is a real skew-symmetric n×n matrix and B₁, B₂ are real positive definite n×n matrices, then the polynomial

  p(x,y) := det(A + i(xB₁ + yB₂))

is stable, and moreover every monomial appearing in p has total degree of the same parity as n (all monomials of even total degree when n is even, all monomials of odd total degree when n is odd).

Question: Is the converse true? That is, suppose p(x,y) is a polynomial of total degree n in which every monomial has total degree of the same parity as n, and suppose p is stable in the sense above. Must there exist a real skew-symmetric n×n matrix A and real positive definite n×n matrices B₁, B₂ such that

  p(x,y) = det(A + i(xB₁ + yB₂)) ?

Determine whether this characterization holds, or exhibit a stable polynomial of the indicated parity that admits no such determinantal representation.

Related results exist on determinantal representations of stable/real-stable polynomials (e.g., Helton–Vinnikov theorem for real zero polynomials in two variables, and Borcea–Brändén type representations), and there is work on definite symmetric determinantal representations. Let n be a positive integer. A polynomial F(x,y,z) in three complex variables is called stable if F(x,y,z) ≠ 0 whenever Im(x) > 0, Im(y) > 0, and Im(z) > 0. A univariate polynomial is called real-rooted if all its roots are real.

Given vectors α, β, γ ∈ ℝⁿ, determine necessary and sufficient conditions on α, β, γ (equivalently, on the real-rooted polynomials f, g, h ∈ ℝ[x] of degree n whose roots are α, β, γ respectively) such that there exists a homogeneous stable polynomial F(x,y,z) of degree n with

  f(x) = F(x, 1, 0),  g(x) = F(0, x, 1),  h(x) = F(1, 0, x).

Background: The classical additive Horn problem (existence of Hermitian matrices A, B, C with A + B + C = 0 having prescribed real spectra α, β, γ) is known to be solvable if and only if the triple (α, β, γ) forms the boundary of a hive (a real-valued function on the triangular grid satisfying certain rhombus concavity inequalities). The logarithms of the coefficients of any such F necessarily determine a hive, but this hive condition alone is not known to be sufficient. Find the precise characterization.

Both questions concern the heat-flow deformation of the Riemann xi-function and the closely related de Bruijn–Newman framework. Part (i) would imply that almost all zeros of the Riemann zeta function lie on the critical line, and remains open: the exact value of the de Bruijn–Newman constant Λ is unknown, with only the bounds 0 ≤ Λ ≤ 0.22 established (Rodgers–Tao 2018 lower bound, Polymath15 upper bound 2019). Part (ii), in its stated generality for arbitrary even real entire functions of order 1 and maximal type with zeros in a horizontal strip, is not known; only the special case of the Riemann xi-function and related L-functions has affirmative partial information.

The closed circular domain and boundary cases were settled by Borcea–Brändén's Pólya–Schur master theorems. The strip case (c) has been addressed by classification theorems for operators preserving zeros in a strip (Brändén–Chasse–Visontai-type results, published in J. d'Analyse Math. 2017). Let $\mathbb{C}[z]$ denote the algebra of complex polynomials in one variable. Every $\mathbb{C}$-linear operator $T\colon \mathbb{C}[z]\to \mathbb{C}[z]$ admits a unique formal differential representation
$$T \;=\; \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} Q_k(z)\,\frac{d^k}{dz^k},\qquad Q_k\in\mathbb{C}[z],$$
in the sense that for every $p\in\mathbb{C}[z]$ only finitely many terms $Q_k(z)\,p^{(k)}(z)$ are nonzero and their sum equals $T(p)$.

For a region $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{C}$, let $\pi_n(\Omega)$ denote the set of polynomials of degree at most $n$ whose zeros all lie in $\Omega$, and let $\pi(\Omega)=\bigcup_{n\ge 0}\pi_n(\Omega)$.

Problem. Given a region $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{C}$, characterize all sequences of polynomials $(Q_k)_{k\ge 0}$ in $\mathbb{C}[z]$ such that the associated operator $T=\sum_{k\ge 0} Q_k(z)\,\dfrac{d^k}{dz^k}$ satisfies
$$T\bigl(\pi_n(\Omega)\bigr)\subseteq \pi(\Omega)\cup\{0\}\qquad\text{for every } n\in\mathbb{N}.$$

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Borcea and Brändén (2009) gave a complete characterization of linear operators preserving stability/non-vanishing on products of prescribed open circular regions, which solves the problem for circular regions Ω and yields the classification of the coefficient polynomials Q_k in those cases. For general regions Ω (e.g. arbitrary open or closed sets in C), no full characterization is known, and subsequent works (e.g., interlacing/real-root preserving results, representation-theoretic explanations) extend but do not fully resolve the general problem.
