Let n, m, ℓ be positive integers. For n×n complex matrices A_1, …, A_m, define
   η(A_1, …, A_m) = Σ det(A_1[S_1]) · det(A_2[S_2]) ··· det(A_m[S_m]),
where the sum is over all ordered partitions (S_1, …, S_m) of {1, …, n} into m (possibly empty) blocks, and A_j[S_j] denotes the principal submatrix of A_j with rows and columns indexed by S_j (with the convention det(A_j[∅]) = 1).

A "positive pencil" in the variables z = (z_1, …, z_ℓ) is a matrix-valued linear form
   L(z) = A_1 z_1 + A_2 z_2 + ⋯ + A_ℓ z_ℓ + B,
where each A_k is an n×n positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix and B is an n×n Hermitian matrix.

A polynomial f ∈ ℝ[z_1, …, z_ℓ] is called real stable if f has real coefficients and f(z_1, …, z_ℓ) ≠ 0 whenever Im(z_i) > 0 for every i = 1, …, ℓ.

Question: Is it true that for every real stable polynomial f of degree n in ℓ variables, there exist a positive integer m and positive pencils L_1, …, L_m (of common size n×n) such that
   f(z) = η(L_1(z), L_2(z), …, L_m(z)) ?

Let $\mathbb{R}[x]$ denote the ring of real polynomials. For a real polynomial $p(x) = \sum_{k=0}^n a_k x^k$, let $Z_C(p)$ denote the number of non-real zeros of $p$, counted with multiplicity. Given a sequence $\{\gamma_k\}_{k=0}^\infty$ of real numbers, define the associated diagonal linear operator $T$ on $\mathbb{R}[x]$ by $T[x^k] = \gamma_k x^k$, extended linearly, so that $T\bigl[\sum a_k x^k\bigr] = \sum \gamma_k a_k x^k$.

A sequence $\{\gamma_k\}$ is called a multiplier sequence (of the first kind) if for every hyperbolic polynomial $p(x) \in \mathbb{R}[x]$ (i.e. every $p$ all of whose zeros are real), the image $T[p]$ is also hyperbolic, equivalently $Z_C(p) = 0 \Rightarrow Z_C(T[p]) = 0$.

The sequence is called a complex zero decreasing sequence (CZDS) if for every $p(x) \in \mathbb{R}[x]$,
$$Z_C(T[p]) \le Z_C(p).$$

It is known that, for each integer $p \geq 3$, the sequence $\{e^{-k^p}\}_{k=0}^\infty$ is a multiplier sequence.

Question: For each integer $p \geq 3$, is the sequence $\{e^{-k^p}\}_{k=0}^\infty$ a complex zero decreasing sequence (CZDS)?

Let \[\Phi(t)=2\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\bigl(2n^{4}\pi^{2}e^{9t/2}-3n^{2}\pi e^{5t/2}\bigr)e^{-n^{2}\pi e^{2t}},\qquad t\in\mathbb{R},\] which is a positive, even, rapidly decaying function on $\mathbb{R}$ whose Fourier cosine transform is (up to normalization) the Riemann xi-function $\Xi(z)=\xi(\tfrac12+iz)$, where $\xi(s)=\tfrac12 s(s-1)\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)\zeta(s)$.

For $k=0,1,2,\dots$ define the moments
\[b_{k}=\int_{0}^{\infty}t^{2k}\Phi(t)\,dt,\qquad \gamma_{k}=\frac{k!}{(2k)!}\,b_{k},\]
and the entire function
\[F(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{b_{k}}{(2k)!}\,x^{k}=\int_{0}^{\infty}\Phi(t)\cosh\!\bigl(t\sqrt{x}\bigr)\,dt.\]

Recall the following definitions.
\begin{itemize}
\item A sequence $\{\lambda_{k}\}_{k\geq 0}$ of real numbers is a \emph{multiplier sequence} if for every real polynomial $p(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_{k}x^{k}$ with only real zeros, the polynomial $\sum_{k=0}^{n}\lambda_{k}a_{k}x^{k}$ also has only real zeros.
\item A sequence $\{c_{k}\}_{k\geq 0}$ of positive reals is \emph{totally positive} if every minor of the infinite Toeplitz matrix $(c_{i-j})_{i,j\geq 0}$ (with $c_{m}=0$ for $m<0$) is nonnegative.
\item A sequence $\{a_{k}\}_{k\geq 0}$ is a \emph{complex zero decreasing sequence} (CZDS) if, for every real polynomial $p(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}c_{k}x^{k}$, the number of nonreal zeros of $\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_{k}c_{k}x^{k}$ does not exceed the number of nonreal zeros of $p$.
\end{itemize}

It is known that the Riemann Hypothesis (that all nontrivial zeros of $\zeta(s)$ lie on the line $\Re s=\tfrac12$) is equivalent to each of the following statements:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(A)] $\{\gamma_{k}\}_{k\geq 0}$ is a multiplier sequence (equivalently $\{\gamma_{k}/k!\}_{k\geq 0}$ is totally positive).
\item[(B)] $\{F(k)\}_{k\geq 0}$ is a CZDS, where one has the closed form
\[F(k)=\frac{\pi^{-1/4}}{64}(k-1)\,\pi^{-\sqrt{k}/4}\,\Gamma\!\Bigl(\tfrac14+\tfrac{\sqrt{k}}{4}\Bigr)\,\zeta\!\Bigl(\tfrac12+\tfrac{\sqrt{k}}{2}\Bigr).\]
\end{enumerate}

Problem: Prove or disprove that $\{\gamma_{k}\}_{k\geq 0}$ is a multiplier sequence, or, equivalently, that $\{F(k)\}_{k\geq 0}$ is a complex zero decreasing sequence, thereby establishing or refuting the Riemann Hypothesis.

Let $F$ be a meromorphic function on $\mathbb{C}$, written as $F(x)=\varphi(x)/\psi(x)$ where $\varphi,\psi$ are entire functions, and assume that $F(k)$ is well-defined (i.e., finite) for every nonnegative integer $k$. Consider the linear operator $T_F$ defined on the space of real univariate polynomials by
$$T_F\!\left(\sum_{k=0}^n a_k x^k\right) \;=\; \sum_{k=0}^n F(k)\,a_k\,x^k.$$
Characterize completely all such meromorphic functions $F$ with the property that, for every integer $n\ge 0$ and every real polynomial $\sum_{k=0}^n a_k x^k$ whose zeros are all real, the polynomial $\sum_{k=0}^n F(k) a_k x^k$ also has all of its zeros real.

Setup and definitions.

(i) A real polynomial is called hyperbolic if all of its zeros are real. A sequence of real numbers $\{\gamma_k\}_{k=0}^{\infty}$ is called a multiplier sequence if for every hyperbolic polynomial $\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k x^k \in \mathbb{R}[x]$, the polynomial $\sum_{k=0}^{n} \gamma_k a_k x^k$ is also hyperbolic (where the zero polynomial is regarded as hyperbolic).

(ii) For a real polynomial $p(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k x^k$, let $Z_c(p)$ denote the number of non-real zeros of $p$ counted with multiplicity. A sequence $\{\gamma_k\}_{k=0}^{\infty}$ of real numbers is called a complex zero decreasing sequence (CZDS) if for every real polynomial $p(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k x^k$,
$$ Z_c\!\left(\sum_{k=0}^{n} \gamma_k a_k x^k\right) \le Z_c(p). $$

(iii) A multiplier sequence $\{\gamma_k\}_{k=0}^{\infty}$ is called a meromorphic Laguerre multiplier sequence if there exists a function $F$ that is meromorphic on $\mathbb{C}$ such that $F$ has no pole at any non-negative integer and $\gamma_k = F(k)$ for every integer $k \ge 0$.

Question. Is every meromorphic Laguerre multiplier sequence $\{F(k)\}_{k=0}^{\infty}$ necessarily a complex zero decreasing sequence?

Recall that a sequence of real numbers $\{\gamma_k\}_{k=0}^\infty$ is called a multiplier sequence if the linear diagonal operator $T$ defined by $T(x^k) = \gamma_k x^k$ has the property that, for every real polynomial $p(x) = \sum a_k x^k$ all of whose zeros are real (a "hyperbolic" polynomial), the image $T[p](x) = \sum \gamma_k a_k x^k$ is again a hyperbolic polynomial (or identically zero).

Define $\gamma_k = k^{\sqrt{k}}$ for $k \geq 1$ (and set $\gamma_0 = 1$ by convention). For each integer $m \geq 1$, consider the shifted sequence $\{\gamma_{k+m}\}_{k=0}^\infty$, and the associated formal power series
$$f_m(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{\gamma_{k+m}}{k!}\, x^k,$$
which defines a real entire function of order $1$ satisfying $f_1^{(m)} = f_{m+1}$.

Question: Does there exist an integer $M$ such that for every $m \geq M$ the sequence $\{\gamma_{k+m}\}_{k=0}^\infty$ is a multiplier sequence?

Let p(x_1, …, x_n) be a symmetric, homogeneous, real stable polynomial of degree d with d ≤ n, having at least one strictly positive coefficient in the monomial basis. (Recall that a polynomial in R[x_1,…,x_n] is real stable if it has no zeros in the open upper half-plane in each variable, i.e. p(z_1,…,z_n) ≠ 0 whenever Im(z_j) > 0 for all j.) Since p is symmetric and homogeneous of degree d, expand it in the basis of Schur polynomials in n variables:
   p = Σ_{λ ⊢ d} a_λ s_λ(x_1,…,x_n),
where the sum is over partitions λ of d and s_λ denotes the Schur polynomial. For a partition λ ⊢ d, let f^λ denote the number of standard Young tableaux of shape λ, and let (1^d) denote the single-column partition of d (so s_{(1^d)} = e_d is the elementary symmetric polynomial of degree d).

Question: Does the inequality
   a_λ ≤ f^λ · a_{(1^d)}
hold for every partition λ ⊢ d and every such polynomial p?

An affirmative answer to this Stable Permanent-On-Top inequality would imply Lieb's Permanent-On-Top conjecture for positive semi-definite Hermitian matrices. The Permanent-On-Top conjecture was disproved by Shchesnovich (2016) and a simpler counterexample was given by Wanless (2021/2022). Consequently the proposed implication forces the Stable POT inequality to fail in general as well, so the answer to the question as stated is negative. However, the literature treats the closely related Lieb permanental dominance conjecture (a different statement, often confused with POT) as still open, and no paper was located that explicitly writes out an explicit real-stable counterexample to the stable version above.

Call a square real matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ a P-matrix if all of its principal minors are strictly positive. For variables $z_1,\dots,z_n$, set
$$f_A(z_1,\dots,z_n) = \det(A + \operatorname{diag}(z_1,\dots,z_n)).$$
A polynomial $f\in\mathbb{R}[z_1,\dots,z_n]$ is called multi-affine if it has degree at most $1$ in each $z_i$. For such a polynomial with nonnegative coefficients, $f$ is said to satisfy the Rayleigh correlation inequalities if for all $i\neq j$ and all $z\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{n}$,
$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial z_i}(z)\cdot \frac{\partial f}{\partial z_j}(z) \;\geq\; f(z)\cdot \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial z_i \partial z_j}(z).$$
A Rayleigh polynomial is a multi-affine polynomial with nonnegative coefficients satisfying these Rayleigh inequalities. A P-matrix $A$ is called a Rayleigh matrix if $f_A$ is a Rayleigh polynomial.

Given a multi-affine polynomial $f(z_1,\dots,z_n)=\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}} c_S \prod_{i\in S} z_i$, its diagonal specialization is the univariate polynomial $g(t) = f(t,t,\dots,t) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k t^k$, where $a_k = \sum_{|S|=k} c_S$. We say $f$ has log-concave diagonal specialization if the sequence $(a_0,a_1,\dots,a_n)$ is log-concave, i.e.\ $a_k^2 \geq a_{k-1}a_{k+1}$ for all $1\leq k\leq n-1$.

Question: Does $f_A(z) = \det(A + \operatorname{diag}(z_1,\dots,z_n))$ have log-concave diagonal specialization for every Rayleigh matrix $A$?

For a real parameter $\alpha>0$, consider the Schrödinger operator
$$A_\alpha \;=\; -\frac{d^2}{dx^2} + i\,|x|^\alpha$$
acting either on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$, or on $L^2(\mathbb{R}_+)$ with Dirichlet boundary condition at $0$ (in the latter case the potential reduces to $i x^\alpha$). The operator is defined via its maximal/minimal accretive realization; under standard assumptions, $A_\alpha$ has compact resolvent and a discrete spectrum, hence a countable set of eigenfunctions in $L^2$.

Say that the system of eigenfunctions of $A_\alpha$ is complete if its linear span is dense in the underlying $L^2$ space.

It is known that this completeness holds for every $\alpha > 2/3$.

Question: Does the system of eigenfunctions of $A_\alpha$ remain complete for every exponent in the range $0 < \alpha \le 2/3$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Subsequent works have extended completeness results for the complex Schrödinger operator $-d^2/dx^2 + c x^\alpha$ on the half-line with Dirichlet boundary, including a dedicated treatment of the borderline case $\alpha = 2/3$ (Mityagin–Siegl, 2019) and an extension to $\alpha \in (0,2)$ under the angular condition $|\arg c| < 2\pi\alpha/(\alpha+2) + \Delta_t(\alpha)$ with $\Delta_t(\alpha)>0$ (2021/2022). At $c = i$ (i.e. $\arg c = \pi/2$) and $\alpha = 2/3$, one has $2\pi\alpha/(\alpha+2) = \pi/2$, so the case $\alpha = 2/3$ is covered, but for $0 < \alpha < 2/3$ the angular condition is delicate and not obviously satisfied for $c=i$ from the published statements, so the full range $0 < \alpha \le 2/3$ does not appear to be unconditionally resolved.

For each positive integer $n$, let $e_n(x) = \sqrt{2}\,\sin(n\pi x)$ on $(0,1)$, so that $\{e_n\}_{n\ge 1}$ is the standard orthonormal sine basis of $L^2(0,1)$. Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{C}$ be a $2$-periodic function that is odd, $f(-x)=-f(x)$, and symmetric about $1/2$, $f(\tfrac12+x)=f(\tfrac12-x)$. Such an $f$ admits a sine Fourier expansion
$$f(x)=\sum_{k\ge 1} c_k\,\sqrt{2}\,\sin(k\pi x),\qquad x\in\mathbb{R},$$
with coefficients $c_k\in\mathbb{C}$ supported on odd $k$ (by the symmetry assumptions).

For $n\ge 1$ define $f_n(x):=f(nx)$ and, on $L^p(0,1)$ with $1<p<\infty$, $p\neq 2$, let $A$ be the densely defined linear operator obtained as the linear extension of
$$A e_n = f_n,\qquad n\ge 1.$$
Equivalently, in terms of the "multiplier" operators $M_k$ defined by $M_k e_n = e_{kn}$ (interpreting $e_{kn}$ via its sine-series representative), one has the formal expansion
$$A = \sum_{k\ge 1} c_k\, M_k.$$

Problem. Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on the sequence $\{c_k\}_{k\ge 1}$ ensuring that, for every $p\in(1,\infty)$ with $p\neq 2$, the operator $A$ extends to a bounded operator on $L^p(0,1)$ whose spectrum does not contain $0$ (equivalently, $A$ is boundedly invertible on $L^p(0,1)$).

Let H be a separable complex Hilbert space and let A = L + B be a closed densely-defined linear operator on H with purely discrete spectrum {λ_n} ⊂ C (here L is a "background" operator and B a perturbation, so A is in general non-self-adjoint). Assume that the generalized eigenfunctions and associated root vectors {φ_{nν}} of A form a complete system in H, with corresponding biorthogonal system {ψ_{nν}} (so ⟨φ_{nν}, ψ_{mμ}⟩ = δ_{nm}δ_{νμ}). Consider the abstract Cauchy problem

   u'(t) = A u(t),    u(0) = f ∈ H,

whose formal solution admits the expansion
   u(t) = Σ_n e^{λ_n t} Σ_ν c_{nν}(f) p_{nν}(t) φ_{nν},
where c_{nν}(f) = ⟨f, ψ_{nν}⟩ and p_{nν}(t) are polynomials in t arising from Jordan blocks. An observation is made through a fixed vector g ∈ H by recording
   ω(t) = ⟨u(t), g⟩,    t ≥ 0.

Problem. Characterize, in terms of the biorthogonal system {ψ_{nν}}, the initial conditions f ∈ H such that every exponential mode e^{λ_n t} is excited; that is, give necessary and sufficient conditions on f ensuring that
   c_{nν}(f) = ⟨f, ψ_{nν}⟩ ≠ 0  for every n and every ν.
In particular, construct explicit choices of f for which this nonvanishing holds for general classes of non-self-adjoint operators A = L + B.

where the c_{nν}(f) are scalar coefficients depending linearly on f, and each p_{nν}(t) is a polynomial in t (of degree at most ν) arising from the Jordan-chain structure attached to λ_n.

Devise a constructive procedure that, from the knowledge of the single function ω restricted to a finite time interval [0, T], recovers
 (a) every eigenvalue λ_n ∈ ℂ that contributes to the sum, and
 (b) its algebraic multiplicity m_n,
together with quantitative stability estimates in the presence of measurement noise. The difficulty over the self-adjoint case lies in the fact that the λ_n are genuinely complex (so the exponentials oscillate as well as decay) and that the expansion contains polynomial-in-t factors coming from non-trivial Jordan blocks.

whose solution is $u(t) = e^{tA} f$. Given an observation functional $g \in H^*$ (or $g \in H$ via the Riesz identification) and finitely many times $0 < t_1 < t_2 < \cdots < t_N < \infty$, the available data consist of the $N$ scalar measurements
$$ y_k = \langle g, e^{t_k A} f \rangle, \qquad k = 1,\dots,N. $$

Within a prescribed admissible class $\mathcal{A}$ of operators on $H$ (specifying domain, spectrum, or structural constraints), the inverse problem is to recover $A \in \mathcal{A}$ from the data $\{(t_k, y_k)\}_{k=1}^{N}$.

Determine, for the admissible class $\mathcal{A}$:
(a) the choices of initial state $f \in H$ and observation functional $g$ for which identification of $A$ from finitely many observations in finite time is possible (uniqueness of $A$ given the data);
(b) among such admissible pairs $(f, g)$, those that minimize the number $N$ of observations needed to guarantee unique identification of every $A \in \mathcal{A}$, and the corresponding minimal value of $N$ together with optimal choices of the observation times $t_1, \dots, t_N$.

Let $L$ be a (generally non-self-adjoint) linear differential operator acting on a dense domain of a Hilbert space $H$ of functions on a bounded interval, equipped with periodic boundary conditions. Assume that the spectrum of $L$ consists of isolated eigenvalues of finite algebraic multiplicity. Define the instability index of $L$ to be
$$\mathrm{ind}(L) \;=\; \sum_{\lambda \in \sigma(L),\ \mathrm{Re}\,\lambda > 0} m_a(\lambda),$$
where $m_a(\lambda)$ denotes the algebraic multiplicity of the eigenvalue $\lambda$ (so $\mathrm{ind}(L)$ counts, with multiplicity, the total number of eigenvalues with positive real part).

Let $\{\varphi_k\}_{k\in\mathbb Z}$ be the orthonormal trigonometric basis of $H$, let $P_N$ denote the orthogonal projection onto the finite-dimensional subspace $V_N = \mathrm{span}\{\varphi_k : |k|\le N\}$ of trigonometric polynomials of degree at most $N$, and consider the finite-dimensional matrix truncation
$$L_N \;=\; P_N\, L\, P_N \;:\; V_N \to V_N.$$

Determine sufficient (and, ideally, necessary) conditions on $L$ under which there exists $N_0$ such that for all $N \ge N_0$ one has
$$\mathrm{ind}(L_N) \;=\; \mathrm{ind}(L),$$
i.e., the instability index of the infinite-dimensional operator $L$ can be computed exactly from the finite matrix $L_N$.

Let $X$ be a complex Banach space and let $\mathcal{B}(X)$ denote the algebra of bounded linear operators on $X$. For $A \in \mathcal{B}(X)$, let $\|A\|$ denote the operator norm and let
$$\mathrm{spr}(A) = \lim_{n\to\infty} \|A^n\|^{1/n} = \sup\{|\lambda| : \lambda \in \sigma(A)\}$$
denote the spectral radius of $A$. Define the gap of $A$ by
$$\mathrm{gap}(A) = \|A\| - \mathrm{spr}(A) \geq 0.$$

Characterize, as Banach space $X$ varies, the classes of bounded linear operators $A \in \mathcal{B}(X)$ for which $\mathrm{gap}(A) > 0$ (strict gap) and the classes for which $\mathrm{gap}(A) = 0$ (the operator norm coincides with the spectral radius). In particular, give intrinsic structural conditions on $A$ (and possibly on $X$) that are equivalent to $\mathrm{gap}(A) = 0$.

No complete characterization of the classes of bounded operators on Banach spaces for which the operator norm equals the spectral radius (resp. exceeds it) appears in the literature. Standard sufficient conditions (e.g., normal operators on Hilbert space, more generally hyponormal or spectraloid operators) yield gap zero, and partial results exist for tensor products and positive operators, but a general intrinsic characterization is not known. Let H be a complex Hilbert space and let A: H → H be a bounded linear operator. Define the numerical range of A by
   W(A) = { ⟨Ax, x⟩ : x ∈ H, ‖x‖ = 1 },
which is a bounded convex subset of the complex plane. For any function f that is analytic on a neighborhood of the closure of W(A), the operator f(A) is defined via the holomorphic functional calculus.

Crouzeix's conjecture asserts that there exists a universal constant C ≥ 2 (independent of H and A) such that
   ‖f(A)‖ ≤ C · sup_{z ∈ W(A)} |f(z)|
for every bounded linear operator A and every function f analytic on W(A) and continuous on its closure.

Prove or disprove this conjecture, and in particular determine whether one may take C = 2 (the conjectured optimal value), or at least C ≤ 11.08.

(a) Give general criteria on $W$ under which $\lambda$ persists as an eigenvalue of $H_\varepsilon$, dissolves into the continuous spectrum, or moves off the real axis into the complex plane (becoming a complex eigenvalue or a resonance).
(b) When $\lambda$ does perturb to a (possibly complex) eigenvalue $\lambda(\varepsilon)$ of $H_\varepsilon$, derive the leading-order asymptotic expansion of $\lambda(\varepsilon)$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$, including the sign/direction of $\operatorname{Im} \lambda(\varepsilon)$ in terms of $W$ and the eigenfunction(s) of $H_0$ associated with $\lambda$.
(c) Identify the codimension (in a suitable space of perturbations $W$) of the set for which the embedded eigenvalue persists on the real axis.

The question of the general behavior of embedded eigenvalues of self-adjoint Schrödinger operators under non-self-adjoint perturbations remains an active area of research. Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a separable Hilbert space and let $A$ be a bounded self-adjoint operator on $\mathcal{H}$ with spectrum $\sigma(A) \subset \mathbb{R}$. Let $K$ be a trace-class operator on $\mathcal{H}$, with trace norm $\|K\|_1$, and consider the (not necessarily self-adjoint) perturbation $A+K$. Denote by $\sigma_d(A+K)$ the discrete spectrum of $A+K$, i.e. the set of isolated eigenvalues of finite algebraic multiplicity, counted with their algebraic multiplicities, and for $\lambda \in \mathbb{C}$ write $\mathrm{dist}(\lambda, \sigma(A))$ for the distance from $\lambda$ to $\sigma(A)$.

Assume that the following non-endpoint estimate holds: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists a constant $C(\varepsilon) > 0$ such that for all trace-class $K$,
$$\sum_{\lambda \in \sigma_d(A+K)} \mathrm{dist}(\lambda, \sigma(A))^{1+\varepsilon} \le C(\varepsilon)\, \|K\|_1^{1+\varepsilon}.$$

Question: Does it follow that there exists a constant $C > 0$, independent of $K$, such that the endpoint estimate
$$\sum_{\lambda \in \sigma_d(A+K)} \mathrm{dist}(\lambda, \sigma(A)) \le C\, \|K\|_1$$
holds for every trace-class operator $K$?

Let n ≥ 1 and let p(x,ξ) be a smooth symbol on the cotangent bundle T*R^n with Re p(x,ξ) ≥ 0, belonging to a standard semiclassical symbol class so that its Weyl quantization
   P = p^w(x, hD_x),  0 < h ≤ 1,
defines a closed densely-defined operator on L^2(R^n). For z ∉ Spec(P) lying in a region where general (Hörmander/Davies/Dencker–Sjöstrand–Zworski type) abstract arguments apply, there is an upper bound of the form
   ‖(P − z)^{−1}‖_{L^2 → L^2} ≤ C_1 exp(C_2 h^{−n})
with constants C_1, C_2 > 0 independent of h. On the other hand, lower bounds obtained from pseudospectral (quasimode) constructions are typically much smaller than this, except in special cases such as elliptic quadratic differential operators.

Question: Is the upper bound ‖(P − z)^{−1}‖ ≤ C_1 exp(C_2 h^{−n}) sharp as h → 0? More precisely, does there exist a symbol p as above (and a point z outside the spectrum in a suitable region) for which the resolvent norm satisfies a matching lower bound of order exp(c h^{−n}) for some c > 0, particularly in dimensions n ≥ 2?

representations.normalization_method: unicode-preserving newline and trailing-whitespace normalization v1
representations.normalized:
Consider the one-dimensional semiclassical Schrödinger operator
$$H_h = -h^2 \frac{d^2}{dx^2} + V(x), \qquad h \to 0^+,$$
acting in $L^2(\mathbb{R})$, where $V : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ is a (possibly complex-valued) potential. For a point $z \in \mathbb{C}$, a semiclassical pseudomode at energy $z$ is a family $\{\psi_h\}_{h>0} \subset \mathrm{Dom}(H_h)$ with $\|\psi_h\|=1$ such that
$$\|(H_h - z)\psi_h\| = \mathcal{O}(h^N) \quad \text{as } h\to 0^+,$$
for every $N \in \mathbb{N}$ (or for a prescribed rate). For smooth potentials $V$, there is a general WKB/microlocal construction producing such pseudomodes at every $z$ in the interior of the numerical range whose preimage satisfies a non-self-adjoint bracket (Hörmander) condition.

Problem. Develop an analogous general construction of semiclassical pseudomodes for Schrödinger operators $H_h = -h^2 \partial_x^2 + V$ when the potential $V$ is merely discontinuous (e.g., piecewise smooth with jump discontinuities, or step-like complex potentials). Specifically, determine to what extent the smooth-potential pseudomode construction can be adapted so as to yield, for $z$ in an appropriate spectral/numerical region determined by $V$, families $\psi_h$ with $\|(H_h-z)\psi_h\|/\|\psi_h\| \to 0$ at a quantitative rate as $h \to 0^+$, and identify the geometric/analytic conditions on the jumps of $V$ under which this is possible.

representations.normalization_method: unicode-preserving newline and trailing-whitespace normalization v1
representations.normalized:
Consider on the real line the generalized indefinite Sturm–Liouville eigenvalue problem
  ( -d²/dx² + V(x) ) ψ(x) = λ · sgn(x) · ψ(x),   x ∈ ℝ,
where sgn(x) denotes the sign function (with sgn(0)=0), ψ lies in a suitable Sobolev space on ℝ, and λ ∈ ℂ is the (possibly non-real) spectral parameter. The associated operator A = sgn(x)(-d²/dx² + V(x)) is self-adjoint in the Krein space (L²(ℝ), [·,·]) with indefinite inner product [f,g] = ∫_ℝ sgn(x) f(x) \overline{g(x)} dx.

For the special potential V(x) = c/(1+|x|) with c ∈ ℝ, it is known that the non-real eigenvalues of A accumulate to 0, and that the growth of the resolvent (A−z)^{-1} near 0 is not of finite order; moreover associated conjectures (e.g. the precise rate of accumulation and resolvent estimates) have been established.

Problem. Determine the largest class of real-valued potentials V : ℝ → ℝ (for instance, satisfying V(x) → 0 as |x| → ∞ at some prescribed rate, or belonging to weighted L^p spaces) for which the analogous spectral results remain valid: namely, characterize precisely the conditions on V under which
 (i) the non-real eigenvalues of A = sgn(x)(-d²/dx² + V(x)) accumulate to 0,
 (ii) the rate of accumulation of these eigenvalues can be quantified, and
 (iii) the resolvent of A near 0 fails to be of finite order,
extending the results known for V(x) = c/(1+|x|) to this more general setting.

A Nevanlinna function (Herglotz function) is an analytic function m : C \ R → C satisfying m(\bar z) = \overline{m(z)} and Im m(z) ≥ 0 for Im z > 0. Such a function admits a meromorphic continuation across any open interval of R on which it is real-analytic, and its singularities on R consist of simple poles with negative residues, together with possible interlaced real zeros.

Let (m_j)_{j≥1} be a sequence of Nevanlinna functions, and let I ⊂ R be a nonempty open interval with the following property: for every nonempty open subinterval J ⊆ I, the number of poles of m_j contained in J tends to infinity as j → ∞. Let g be a function analytic in some open complex neighborhood of I.

Prove or disprove: for every nonempty open subinterval J ⊆ I and every open complex neighborhood U ⊆ C of J (contained in the common domain of analyticity of g and of the meromorphic continuations of the m_j across I),
   lim_{j → ∞} #{ z ∈ U : m_j(z) − g(z) = 0 } = ∞,
where zeros are counted with multiplicity.

Differential Equations, 2012; arXiv:1104.4846) gives general criteria for the root-vector system to form a Schauder or Riesz basis, expressed in terms of asymptotic deviations of eigenvalues. A complete explicit characterization purely in terms of the coefficients $\{v_k\}$ of a trigonometric polynomial potential does not appear to be fully established; only special families (e.g., certain PT-symmetric cases, single-harmonic Mathieu-type potentials) have been resolved. The problem appears to be partially solved.

The question is posed as an open problem at an AIM workshop on non-self-adjoint operators. Related literature establishes results for polynomial (e.g., PT-symmetric) potentials where eigenvalues are real with at most finitely many exceptions, and constructions of decaying complex potentials with infinitely many non-real eigenvalues, but no source found explicitly resolves the non-polynomial case requested. representations.normalized:
Let A₀ = −d²/dx² + x² be the self-adjoint harmonic oscillator on L²(ℝ), with its standard domain. For a complex-valued potential V ∈ L^∞(ℝ), define the operator A := A₀ + V on L²(ℝ) (as a bounded perturbation of A₀, with the same domain as A₀). It is known that A has compact resolvent and that for |Re λ| large enough the eigenvalues of A are simple, so that one can form an eigensystem consisting of (normalized) eigenfunctions associated to these eigenvalues, together with finitely many root vectors corresponding to the remaining (possibly nonsimple) eigenvalues.

Question: For every complex-valued V ∈ L^∞(ℝ), does the eigensystem of A form a Riesz basis of L²(ℝ)? Equivalently, does there exist a bounded invertible operator on L²(ℝ) mapping the eigensystem of A onto an orthonormal basis?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Positive results are known under additional assumptions on V: if V ∈ L^p(ℝ) for some 2 ≤ p < ∞, or if V ∈ L^∞(ℝ) with sufficiently small norm, the eigensystem is an unconditional (Riesz) basis (Mityagin–Siegl and others; local form-subordination framework of Mityagin–Siegl–Viola). General results for arbitrary complex V ∈ L^∞(ℝ) without smallness or decay assumptions do not appear to be established, so the problem in full generality appears to remain open.

representations.normalized:
Let $L$ be a linear differential operator on a bounded interval with linear boundary conditions, possibly non-self-adjoint, such that the associated initial-boundary value problem
$$\partial_t u + L u = 0, \qquad u(0,\cdot) = u_0, \qquad \text{(boundary conditions)}$$
is well-posed. An augmented eigenfunction of $L$ is a spectral functional $F_\lambda$, indexed by a spectral parameter $\lambda$ lying on a contour in the complex plane, with the properties that (i) the solution $u(t,x)$ admits a representation as a contour integral of $e^{-\lambda t}$ against $F_\lambda(u_0)$ evaluated at $x$, and (ii) the family $\{F_\lambda\}$ diagonalizes the inverse $L^{-1}$ (when it exists) in the sense that $L^{-1}$ acts as multiplication by $1/\lambda$ in the transform defined by $F_\lambda$.

Beyond the two known applications described above — namely (a) expressing solutions of initial-boundary value problems via spectral contour integrals, and (b) diagonalizing the inverse of the differential operator — exhibit further mathematical or physical applications of augmented eigenfunctions. Specifically, identify additional classes of problems (for instance in spectral theory, in functional-analytic decompositions, in transform methods for PDEs, or in physical models involving non-self-adjoint operators) for which augmented eigenfunctions provide a useful analytical tool, and justify rigorously that they do so.

representations.normalized:
Background. Consider linear evolution partial differential equations posed on domains with boundary (for example, initial–boundary value problems on the half-line or on a finite interval) whose spatial differential operator L is not self-adjoint, so that classical eigenfunction expansions (Fourier, Sturm–Liouville) do not produce a transform pair adapted to the problem. For such problems one may construct, via contour-deformation/unified-transform techniques, families of "augmented eigenfunctions": functionals depending on a spectral parameter k that satisfy L f(·,k) = λ(k) f(·,k) only in a generalized (distributional or contour) sense, together with an associated direct/inverse transform pair that diagonalizes the time evolution and solves the boundary value problem.

Problem. Develop an intrinsic spectral theory whose primary objects are augmented eigenfunctions, rather than treating them merely as auxiliary devices for solving differential equations. Concretely, give:

(a) An abstract definition of an augmented eigenfunction and of the associated transform pair for a closed (in general non-self-adjoint) linear operator L on a suitable function space, that recovers the constructions known for concrete initial–boundary value problems as special cases.

(b) Notions corresponding to spectrum, resolvent set, completeness, and a Plancherel/inversion theorem, formulated directly in terms of augmented eigenfunctions, and theorems characterizing when such a complete family exists for a given L.

(c) Functional-analytic conditions on L (relating to its symbol, boundary conditions, pseudospectrum, or numerical range) that guarantee existence, uniqueness, and analytic dependence of the augmented eigenfunctions, together with a comparison theorem showing that, when L is self-adjoint or normal, the theory reduces to the classical spectral theorem.

The question is whether such a self-contained spectral theory, with augmented eigenfunctions as the fundamental objects, can be constructed.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Augmented eigenfunctions were introduced by Fokas–Pelloni and collaborators to handle initial–boundary value problems where classical spectral expansions fail; subsequent works (e.g., Smith and others on half-line and interval problems) extend their use, but the literature continues to treat them primarily as a tool for solving PDEs. No comprehensive intrinsic spectral theory built around augmented eigenfunctions appears to have been established; recent workshop reports on non-self-adjoint operators still list this as a programmatic direction.

representations.normalized:
Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a complex separable Hilbert space and let $J:\mathcal{H}\to\mathcal{H}$ be a conjugation, that is, an antilinear involution satisfying $\langle Jx,Jy\rangle=\langle y,x\rangle$ for all $x,y\in\mathcal{H}$. A densely defined closed linear operator $T:\mathrm{dom}(T)\subset\mathcal{H}\to\mathcal{H}$ is called $J$-self-adjoint if $T^{*}=JTJ$. Such operators are generally non-self-adjoint, and their spectrum need not be real, but it is symmetric with respect to the real axis.

Develop a numerical projection scheme that, given a $J$-self-adjoint operator $T$ (presented through its action and the conjugation $J$), produces rigorous coarse enclosures of the spectrum $\sigma(T)$. That is: construct a family of finite-dimensional subspaces $\{V_n\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subset\mathrm{dom}(T)$ and associated finite-dimensional matrix problems whose computable output $E_n\subset\mathbb{C}$ provably satisfies
$$\sigma(T)\subset E_n\quad\text{or}\quad \mathrm{dist}_{\mathrm{Hausdorff}}(E_n\cap K,\sigma(T)\cap K)\to 0\ \text{ for compact } K\subset\mathbb{C},$$
in a way that explicitly uses the structure of the conjugation $J$ in the design of the projection (for instance by requiring $JV_n=V_n$, or by replacing the standard Galerkin condition by a $J$-compatible bilinear form), so that spurious eigenvalues (spectral pollution) characteristic of naive Galerkin methods for non-self-adjoint operators are controlled. Provide convergence guarantees and explicit error bounds for the enclosures.

A web search returns work on spectral enclosures for J-self-adjoint operators and on rigorous projection-based spectral computations (e.g., Galerkin/SpecSolve-type methods, perturbation approaches that push eigenvalues off the real line), but no source was found that specifically delivers rigorous coarse enclosures for general J-self-adjoint operators with the conjugation J explicitly built into the projection scheme. Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $J:\mathcal{H}\to\mathcal{H}$ be a conjugate-linear involution (i.e., $J$ is antilinear, $J^2=I$, and $\langle Jx,Jy\rangle=\langle y,x\rangle$ for all $x,y\in\mathcal{H}$). A closed densely defined linear operator $T$ on $\mathcal{H}$ is called $J$-self-adjoint if $JTJ = T^*$, equivalently $T = JT^*J$. Such an operator is in general non-self-adjoint, but its spectrum is symmetric with respect to the real axis.

Develop methods that produce sharp, numerically useful enclosures for the spectrum $\sigma(T)$ of a $J$-self-adjoint operator $T$. Concretely:

(a) Find, for specific physically motivated models (e.g., non-self-adjoint Schrödinger operators $-\Delta + V$ on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$ with complex potential $V$ satisfying $\overline{V(\bar{x})} = V(x)$, PT-symmetric operators, or $J$-self-adjoint block operator matrices), explicit two-sided enclosures $E \subset \mathbb{C}$ with $\sigma(T) \subset E$ that are sharp in the sense that they capture eigenvalues (in particular isolated, possibly clustered or degenerate eigenvalues) and resonances with provable rate of convergence as discretization parameters are refined.

(b) Establish a general framework, valid for broad classes of $J$-self-adjoint operators (including operators unbounded above and below), giving computable sharp enclosures together with rigorous a posteriori error bounds, analogous to the Lehmann–Maehly–Goerisch and Davies–Plum methods in the self-adjoint case.

A densely defined closed linear operator $A$ on $\mathcal{H}$ is called $J$-self-adjoint if $JAJ=A^*$. Consider one-dimensional Schrödinger operators $H_V = -\frac{d^2}{dx^2} + V$ on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$, where $V\colon \mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{C}$ is a compactly supported complex-valued potential. For such $V$, the resolvent $(H_V-\lambda^2)^{-1}$ admits a meromorphic continuation from the upper half-plane $\{\operatorname{Im}\lambda>0\}$ to the whole complex plane $\mathbb{C}$ as an operator from $L^2_{\mathrm{comp}}(\mathbb{R})$ to $L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R})$; its poles, together with their multiplicities, are the resonances of $H_V$. Two potentials $V_1, V_2$ are called isoresonant if the resonance sets of $H_{V_1}$ and $H_{V_2}$ coincide with multiplicities. It is known that nontrivial families $\mathcal F$ of pairwise distinct compactly supported complex-valued potentials can be mutually isoresonant.

(a) Find further invariants—necessarily not encoded in the resonance set with multiplicities—that are derived from spectral or pseudospectral data (for example: the resolvent norm function $\lambda\mapsto \|(H_V-\lambda)^{-1}\|$, $\varepsilon$-pseudospectra, semigroup norms, scattering phase, numerical range, or analogous quantities) and that separate distinct elements of an isoresonant family $\mathcal F$.

(b) Formulate and answer the analogous question for isospectral families of Schrödinger operators $-\frac{d^2}{dx^2} + V$ acting on $L^2(S^1)$ with complex-valued potential $V$ on the unit circle $S^1$: find spectral or pseudospectral data that distinguish the distinct potentials inside such an isospectral family.

Let $X$ be a complex Banach space and let $A: \mathrm{dom}(A) \subseteq X \to X$ be a (possibly unbounded) closed linear operator with spectrum $\sigma(A) \subset \mathbb{C}$ and resolvent set $\rho(A) = \mathbb{C} \setminus \sigma(A)$. For $\lambda \in \rho(A)$, let $R(\lambda, A) = (\lambda I - A)^{-1}$ denote the resolvent and $\|R(\lambda, A)\|$ its operator norm. Say that $A$ has polynomially bounded resolvent near its spectrum if there exist constants $C > 0$ and $\alpha \geq 0$ such that
$$\|(\lambda I - A)^{-1}\| \;\leq\; \frac{C}{\mathrm{dist}(\lambda, \sigma(A))^{\alpha}}$$
for all $\lambda$ in some neighborhood of $\sigma(A)$ in $\rho(A)$.

Give an intrinsic classification of all closed linear operators $A$ on a Banach space $X$ which possess this property; equivalently, characterize the class of operators whose resolvent norm grows at most polynomially in $1/\mathrm{dist}(\lambda, \sigma(A))$ as $\lambda$ approaches the spectrum.

Let X be a complex Banach space and let A be a (possibly unbounded) closed linear operator on X with spectrum σ(A), resolvent set res(A) = ℂ ∖ σ(A), and spectral radius spr(A) = sup{|λ| : λ ∈ σ(A)}. For λ ∈ res(A), denote by (λ − A)^{-1} ∈ B(X) the resolvent and by dist(λ, σ(A)) the Euclidean distance from λ to σ(A).

Give an intrinsic classification (in terms of the operator A and the geometry of X) of those operators A for which there exists a constant M ≥ 1 such that
   (a) ‖(λ − A)^{-1}‖ ≤ M / dist(λ, σ(A))  for every λ ∈ res(A),
and, separately, of those A for which there exists M ≥ 1 such that
   (b) ‖(λ − A)^{-1}‖ ≤ M / (|λ| − spr(A))  for every λ with |λ| > spr(A).

In each case, characterize the class of operators (and identify, where possible, the optimal constant M) for which the stated resolvent estimate holds.

Let $n\ge 1$ and let $M$ be either $\mathbb{R}^n$ or a smooth compact manifold of dimension $n$. For $h\in(0,1]$ a semiclassical parameter, consider an $h$-pseudodifferential operator
\[
P = p^w(x, hD_x),
\]
that is, the Weyl quantization of a (possibly complex-valued) symbol $p \in S(m)$ in a suitable symbol class on $T^*M$ with order function $m$, where
\[
p^w(x,hD_x)u(x) = \frac{1}{(2\pi h)^n}\iint e^{i(x-y)\cdot\xi/h}\, p\!\left(\tfrac{x+y}{2},\xi\right) u(y)\, dy\, d\xi.
\]
Assume $p$ admits an asymptotic expansion $p \sim p_0 + h p_1 + h^2 p_2 + \cdots$ as $h\to 0$, and that $P$ has discrete spectrum (or, in the case of resonances, a meromorphic continuation of its resolvent with a well-defined set of resonances) in some prescribed spectral window depending on $h$.

Problem. Determine which features of the classical symbol $p$ (in particular of its principal symbol $p_0:T^*M\to\mathbb{C}$ and, where possible, the subprincipal symbol $p_1$ and the full asymptotic expansion modulo symplectic invariants) can be recovered from the semiclassical spectrum (respectively the set of resonances) of $P$ in the limit $h\to 0$. Specifically, address the case when $P$ is non-self-adjoint, and in particular:

(a) For $P$ with discrete spectrum in a fixed spectral window, identify the symplectic invariants of $p_0$ (e.g.\ action integrals, periods of Hamiltonian flows on regular level sets, Birkhoff normal forms near non-degenerate critical points or near elliptic/hyperbolic closed orbits) that are determined by the eigenvalue asymptotics.

(b) For operators arising from resonance problems (e.g.\ semiclassical Schrödinger operators $-h^2\Delta + V$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with complex absorbing potentials or with potentials supporting trapped trajectories), determine to what extent the trapped set, the dynamics on it, and the symbol $p$ in a neighborhood of it are recovered from the distribution of resonances as $h\to 0$.

(c) For the damped wave equation on a compact Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$,
\[
(\partial_t^2 - \Delta_g + 2a(x)\partial_t)u = 0, \qquad a\in C^\infty(M;\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}),
\]
whose high-frequency spectral problem is governed by a non-self-adjoint $h$-pseudodifferential operator, determine which information about the damping function $a$ and the geodesic flow on $T^*M$ is encoded in the asymptotic distribution of the (complex) eigenfrequencies as the frequency tends to infinity.

Provide either positive recovery (uniqueness) results or explicit counterexamples (isospectral non-isomorphic symbols) in each of these settings.

Let $H$ be a (generally non-self-adjoint) closed densely defined linear operator on a complex Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$, with spectrum $\sigma(H) \subset \mathbb{C}$. Consider the following three classes of symmetry structures that $H$ may possess:

(i) Reflection symmetry: there exists a bounded involution $R$ on $\mathcal{H}$ (i.e. $R^2 = I$) such that $R H R = H^*$ (or, in a variant, $RHR = H$ with $R$ antilinear). A prototype example is the class of Kramers–Fokker–Planck operators of the form
$$P = y\cdot\partial_x - \partial_x V(x)\cdot\partial_y + \tfrac{1}{2}(y - \partial_y)\cdot(y+\partial_y)$$
on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^{2n})$, where $V\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n,\mathbb{R})$ is a Morse potential, and the reflection symmetry implies that the exponentially small eigenvalues lie on the real axis.

(ii) PT symmetry: there exist a linear involution $P$ (parity) and an antilinear involution $T$ (time reversal) with $[P,T]=0$ such that $(PT) H (PT)^{-1} = H$. A standard family of examples is $H = -\partial_x^2 + x^2(ix)^\varepsilon$ on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ for $\varepsilon\ge 0$.

(iii) Supersymmetric structure: there exist closed operators $d, d^\#$ on $\mathcal{H}$ (not necessarily adjoints of one another) such that $d^2 = (d^\#)^2 = 0$ and $H = d\,d^\# + d^\#\,d$, so that $H$ admits a Hodge-type decomposition tied to a $\mathbb{Z}_2$-graded chain complex.

Problem: Develop a general theory describing how symmetries of types (i), (ii), and (iii) constrain or determine the spectrum $\sigma(H)$ of a non-self-adjoint operator $H$. In particular, identify natural geometric/algebraic conditions on each symmetry under which one can prove:

(a) reality (or reality up to complex conjugate pairing) of all eigenvalues, or of a distinguished subset such as eigenvalues that are exponentially small in a semiclassical parameter;
(b) localization of $\sigma(H)$ on prescribed curves or in prescribed sectors of $\mathbb{C}$;
(c) explicit identification or counting of eigenvalues via a supersymmetric/Hodge decomposition;
(d) stability of these spectral features under perturbations that preserve the symmetry but possibly break self-adjointness.

State and prove theorems realizing (a)–(d) at a level of generality that covers Kramers–Fokker–Planck operators with reflection symmetry, PT-symmetric Schrödinger operators, and Witten-type supersymmetric non-self-adjoint operators in a unified framework.

The question is a broad research direction rather than a single conjecture. Partial results exist in specific settings (reality of exponentially small eigenvalues for Kramers–Fokker–Planck operators with reflection symmetry; reality of PT-symmetric Schrödinger spectra in unbroken regimes proved by Dorey–Dunkel–Tateo and others; Witten/supersymmetric methods for non-self-adjoint operators). Let Ω ⊂ ℝ^d be an open connected set, and let H_+ and H_0 be nonnegative self-adjoint operators on L²(Ω), associated to second-order elliptic differential expressions, with inf σ(H_+) = inf σ(H_0) = 0. Assume:

(i) H_+ is subcritical, in the sense that there exists a smooth strictly positive function ρ on Ω with H_+ ≥ ρ as quadratic forms (equivalently, H_+ admits a positive minimal Green function);

(ii) H_0 is critical, in the sense that for every nonnegative, nontrivial V ∈ C_0^∞(Ω) one has inf σ(H_0 − V) < 0 (equivalently, H_0 admits no positive Green function, but there exists a positive (Agmon) ground state φ_0 with H_0 φ_0 = 0).

Let e^{−tH_+} and e^{−tH_0} denote the corresponding heat semigroups on L²(Ω), and let p_+(t,x,y) and p_0(t,x,y) denote their respective heat kernels.

Establish, or else refute by counterexample, each of the following two assertions:

(A) (Semigroup ratio limit.) There exists a positive measurable weight w : Ω → (0,∞) such that for every nonnegative f ∈ C_0^∞(Ω) (with the appropriate normalization involving w and the ground state φ_0),
   lim_{t→∞} ( e^{−tH_+} f ) / ( e^{−tH_0} f ) = 0,
pointwise (or in the appropriate sense determined by the weight w).

(B) (Heat-kernel ratio limit.) For every x, y ∈ Ω,
   lim_{t→∞} p_+(t,x,y) / p_0(t,x,y) = 0,
and the convergence is locally uniform on Ω × Ω.

Let Ω ⊂ ℝ^d be an open connected set, and let H_+ and H_0 be nonnegative self-adjoint operators on L²(Ω), associated to second-order elliptic differential expressions, with inf σ(H_+) = inf σ(H_0) = 0. Assume:

(i) H_+ is subcritical, in the sense that there exists a smooth strictly positive function ρ on Ω with H_+ ≥ ρ as quadratic forms (equivalently, H_+ admits a positive minimal Green function);

(ii) H_0 is critical, in the sense that for every nonnegative, nontrivial V ∈ C_0^∞(Ω) one has inf σ(H_0 − V) < 0 (equivalently, H_0 admits no positive Green function, but there exists a positive (Agmon) ground state φ_0 with H_0 φ_0 = 0).

Let e^{−tH_+} and e^{−tH_0} denote the corresponding heat semigroups on L²(Ω), and let p_+(t,x,y) and p_0(t,x,y) denote their respective heat kernels.

Establish, or else refute by counterexample, each of the following two assertions:

(A) (Semigroup ratio limit.) There exists a positive measurable weight w : Ω → (0,∞) such that for every nonnegative f ∈ C_0^∞(Ω) (with the appropriate normalization involving w and the ground state φ_0),
   lim_{t→∞} ( e^{−tH_+} f ) / ( e^{−tH_0} f ) = 0,
pointwise (or in the appropriate sense determined by the weight w).

(B) (Heat-kernel ratio limit.) For every x, y ∈ Ω,
   lim_{t→∞} p_+(t,x,y) / p_0(t,x,y) = 0,
and the convergence is locally uniform on Ω × Ω.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The two conjectures originate in works by Krejčiřík–Zelenko and by Fraas–Krejčiřík–Pinchover (around 2010) on strong ratio limit theorems for heat kernels of subcritical versus critical second-order elliptic operators. Subsequent literature (e.g., arXiv:math/0504344 on Davies' conjecture, and recent 2022–2023 work on heat/Martin kernel estimates for critical Hardy potentials) addresses related ratio asymptotics in particular settings, but no general proof of the conjectures in the stated generality (nor a counterexample) appears to have been published. The problem is listed as open at the AIM workshop and the status remains open as of available sources.

Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ be a bounded domain partitioned as $\Omega = \Omega_+ \cup \Sigma \cup \Omega_-$, where $\Omega_+$ and $\Omega_-$ are disjoint open subdomains and $\Sigma$ is a smooth hypersurface separating them. Define the sign function $\operatorname{sgn}(x) = +1$ for $x \in \Omega_+$ and $\operatorname{sgn}(x) = -1$ for $x \in \Omega_-$, and consider the formal differential expression
$$L u := \operatorname{div}\bigl(\operatorname{sgn}(x)\,\nabla u\bigr),$$
acting on functions $u : \Omega \to \mathbb{C}$ (with, say, Dirichlet boundary conditions on $\partial\Omega$). Because the coefficient $\operatorname{sgn}(x)$ changes sign across $\Sigma$, the associated sesquilinear form $\int_\Omega \operatorname{sgn}(x) |\nabla u|^2\,dx$ is indefinite and the standard form-theoretic construction does not apply.

Problem: Construct a self-adjoint realization of $L$ as an unbounded operator on $L^2(\Omega)$. Precisely, identify a dense domain $\mathcal{D}(L) \subset L^2(\Omega)$ — together with appropriate transmission/interface conditions on $\Sigma$ (and boundary conditions on $\partial\Omega$) — such that the operator $L$ acting on $\mathcal{D}(L)$ is self-adjoint in $L^2(\Omega)$, and analyze its spectral properties.

Let $q\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R})$ be a complex-valued $a$-periodic potential, $q(x+a)=q(x)$. Consider the Hill operator $L=-\dfrac{d^2}{dx^2}+q(x)$ on the line, and for each $\lambda\in\mathbb{C}$ define the following multiplicities associated with boundary value problems on $[0,a]$:

(i) $d(\lambda)$ is the algebraic multiplicity of $\lambda$ as an eigenvalue of the periodic problem ($y(a)=y(0)$, $y'(a)=y'(0)$) or, when applicable, of the semi-periodic (antiperiodic) problem ($y(a)=-y(0)$, $y'(a)=-y'(0)$); equivalently, $d(\lambda)$ is the order of $\lambda$ as a zero of $\Delta(\lambda)\mp 2$, where $\Delta$ is the Hill discriminant.

(ii) For $i\in\{0,a\}$, $p_i(\lambda)$ is the algebraic multiplicity of $\lambda$ as a Dirichlet eigenvalue on $[i, i+a]$ (boundary conditions $y(i)=y(i+a)=0$).

(iii) For $i\in\{0,a\}$, $r_i(\lambda)$ is the algebraic multiplicity of $\lambda$ as a Neumann eigenvalue on $[i,i+a]$ (boundary conditions $y'(i)=y'(i+a)=0$).

Assume $\lambda$ is a periodic (or semi-periodic) eigenvalue of geometric multiplicity $2$, so that the corresponding monodromy matrix is a multiple of the identity at $\lambda$.

Question. In this non-self-adjoint setting, can the strict inequality
$$ d(\lambda) - p_i(\lambda) - r_i(\lambda) > 0 $$
hold for some choice of $q$, $a$, $\lambda$ and $i\in\{0,a\}$? Either prove that $d(\lambda)-p_i(\lambda)-r_i(\lambda)>0$ forces $p_i(\lambda)+r_i(\lambda)=0$, or construct an explicit complex periodic potential exhibiting $d(\lambda)-p_i(\lambda)-r_i(\lambda)>0$ together with $p_i(\lambda)+r_i(\lambda)>0$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem of producing fully explicit closed-form bounds for integer points on plane curves in terms only of degree and coefficient height remains an open problem in Diophantine geometry. Effective bounds are known in several cases (e.g., via Baker's method for curves of genus ≥ 1, Bilu–Tichy, Bombieri–Pillay, Bugeaud–Győry, and more recent work on polynomial systems over the rationals), but a single explicit closed-form bound covering all polynomials f ∈ Z[X,Y] with finitely many integer zeros, depending only on degree and height, has not been established.

A Markoff triple is a triple $(m, m_1, m_2)$ of positive integers satisfying the Markoff equation
$$m^2 + m_1^2 + m_2^2 = 3\, m\, m_1\, m_2.$$
A positive integer $m$ is called a Markoff number if there exist positive integers $m_1, m_2$ with $0 < m_1 \le m_2 \le m$ such that $(m, m_1, m_2)$ is a Markoff triple.

Prove or disprove: for every Markoff number $m$, the pair $(m_1, m_2)$ of positive integers with $0 < m_1 \le m_2 \le m$ satisfying $m^2 + m_1^2 + m_2^2 = 3 m m_1 m_2$ is unique.

Let $P(T,Y) \in \mathbb{Z}[T,Y]$ be a polynomial that is irreducible as an element of $\mathbb{Q}[T,Y]$ and has positive degree in $Y$. Denote by $d$ the total degree of $P$ and by $H = H(P)$ the (naive) height of $P$, i.e. the maximum of the absolute values of its integer coefficients. By Hilbert's irreducibility theorem, there exists $t \in \mathbb{Z}$ such that the specialized polynomial $P(t,Y) \in \mathbb{Z}[Y]$ remains irreducible in $\mathbb{Q}[Y]$. Let
$$N(P) = \min\{\,|t| : t \in \mathbb{Z},\ P(t,Y)\text{ is irreducible in }\mathbb{Q}[Y]\,\}.$$
Question: does there exist an absolute constant $C > 0$ and absolute exponents $a, b \geq 0$ such that for every such polynomial $P$,
$$N(P) \;\leq\; C\, d^{a}\, (\log H)^{b}\,,$$
i.e. a bound for the smallest hilbertian integer specialization that is polynomial in the degree $d$ and in $\log H$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Quantitative versions of Hilbert's irreducibility theorem have been obtained by Dèbes–Walkowiak, Zywina, Castillo–Dietmann and others, yielding bounds polynomial in log H but typically with exponential or super-polynomial dependence on the degree d (or with extra group-theoretic factors). Let $m$, $n$, $k$ be positive integers, and let $(a_{ij\kappa})$ be an array of rational integers indexed by $1 \le i \le n$, $1 \le j \le m$, $1 \le \kappa \le k$. Denote by $\mathbb{R}_{+}^{\times}$ the multiplicative group of positive real numbers. For each $x = (x_1, \ldots, x_k) \in (\mathbb{R}_{+}^{\times})^k$, define the finitely generated subgroup $\Gamma(x) \subset (\mathbb{R}_{+}^{\times})^n$ by
$$\Gamma(x) = \left\{ \left( \prod_{j=1}^{m} \prod_{\kappa=1}^{k} x_{\kappa}^{a_{ij\kappa} s_j} \right)_{1 \le i \le n} : s = (s_1, \ldots, s_m) \in \mathbb{Z}^m \right\}.$$
Recall that real numbers $\gamma_1, \ldots, \gamma_k$ are called multiplicatively independent if the only tuple $(n_1, \ldots, n_k) \in \mathbb{Z}^k$ with $\gamma_1^{n_1} \cdots \gamma_k^{n_k} = 1$ is the zero tuple.

Prove or disprove: if there exists some $x \in (\mathbb{R}_{+}^{\times})^k$ such that $\Gamma(x)$ is dense in $(\mathbb{R}_{+}^{\times})^n$, then for every $\gamma = (\gamma_1, \ldots, \gamma_k) \in (\mathbb{R}_{+}^{\times})^k$ whose coordinates are algebraic numbers that are multiplicatively independent, the subgroup $\Gamma(\gamma)$ is also dense in $(\mathbb{R}_{+}^{\times})^n$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The existence of a flexible closed C² surface in ℝ³ is a long-standing open problem going back to Euler (1776) and Maxwell (1819). While Connelly (1977) constructed flexible closed polyhedral surfaces, and Nash–Kuiper showed flexibility is abundant in class C¹, no example is known in class C² (or even C^{1,1}), and no proof of rigidity is known either. The problem remains open as of recent surveys on the geometry of curves and surfaces.

A smooth closed surface $M \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ is called tight if its total absolute curvature equals $4\pi$, equivalently if the integral of positive Gaussian curvature over $M$ equals $2\pi$. Such surfaces are natural higher-genus analogues of smooth closed convex surfaces (which correspond to genus $0$); for instance, smooth tori of revolution are tight. A smooth immersed closed surface $M \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ is called rigid if every smooth one-parameter family of isometric immersions $f_t : M \to \mathbb{R}^3$ with $f_0$ the inclusion consists, for $t$ near $0$, only of rigid motions of $M$ (i.e., the only isometric deformations are trivial).

Question: Is every smooth tight surface in $\mathbb{R}^3$ rigid in this sense?

Let $A \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ be a smooth compact embedded annulus (a surface with two boundary components, homeomorphic to $S^1 \times [0,1]$) of class $C^\infty$. Assume:

(i) the Gaussian curvature of $A$ is negative at every interior point, and
(ii) the boundary of $A$ consists of two disjoint convex planar curves $\gamma_0, \gamma_1$ (each $\gamma_i$ lies in some plane $\Pi_i \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ and bounds a convex region in $\Pi_i$).

An isometric deformation of $A$ is a continuous one-parameter family $A_t \subset \mathbb{R}^3$, $t \in [0,1]$, of $C^\infty$ embedded annuli with $A_0 = A$, such that each $A_t$ is isometric to $A$ (with the induced metric) and the boundary of $A_t$ coincides with $\gamma_0 \cup \gamma_1$ for all $t$.

Question: Is $A$ necessarily rigid under such isometric deformations, in the sense that every isometric deformation $A_t$ fixing the boundary curves $\gamma_0, \gamma_1$ must consist of rigid motions of $A$ (equivalently, $A_t = A$ for all $t$, up to ambient isometries of $\mathbb{R}^3$ fixing $\gamma_0 \cup \gamma_1$)?

The problem is stated as an open problem in Ghomi's collection of open problems on curves and surfaces. Let $\Gamma\colon S^1 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ be a smooth closed immersed curve. Suppose there exists a continuous vector field $B\colon S^1 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ along $\Gamma$ such that:

(i) for every $t \in S^1$, $B(t)$ is a unit vector orthogonal to the osculating plane of $\Gamma$ at $t$ (i.e., orthogonal to both $\Gamma'(t)$ and $\Gamma''(t)$ whenever these are linearly independent), so that $B$ is a continuous binormal vector field; and

(ii) $B\colon S^1 \to S^2$ is one-to-one (injective as a map to the unit sphere).

For sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$, consider the offset curve $\Gamma_\varepsilon(t) := \Gamma(t) + \varepsilon B(t)$, which is disjoint from $\Gamma$. The pair $(\Gamma, B)$ determines a ribbon, and its twisting is measured by the linking number $\mathrm{lk}(\Gamma, \Gamma_\varepsilon) \in \mathbb{Z}$.

Question: Must $\mathrm{lk}(\Gamma, \Gamma_\varepsilon) \neq 0$? Equivalently, must the ribbon $(\Gamma, B)$ be twisted whenever the binormal field $B$ is one-to-one?

Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on the space curve $\gamma$ (in terms of its extrinsic geometric invariants such as length, curvature, torsion, knotting, total curvature, etc., possibly together with compatibility conditions relating $\gamma$ to the boundary data of $g$) under which there exists an isometric embedding $f : (D,g) \hookrightarrow \mathbb{R}^3$ such that $f|_{\partial D} = \gamma$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem, posed by S.-T. Yau in 1990, asks for conditions on a space curve to bound an isometric embedding of a positively curved disk into R^3. While the closed-surface case (Weyl problem) was settled by Nirenberg, and a free-boundary analogue (boundary meeting the unit sphere orthogonally, with geodesic curvature 1) has been studied more recently, the general prescribed-boundary problem for positively curved disks does not appear to have a known complete answer and is still listed among open problems in the geometry of curves and surfaces.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Ghomi (in "Boundary torsion and convex caps of locally convex surfaces") proved that if a closed space curve bounds a bounded locally convex topological disk in $\mathbb{R}^3$ with nonvanishing curvature, then either its torsion vanishes identically or it changes sign at least four times, which addresses important cases of Rosenberg's question. However, the problem in full generality (arbitrary positively curved surfaces bounded by the curve, including non-disk topologies) is still listed as an open problem.

A smooth surface $S \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ is called rigid if every isometric immersion $f: S \to \mathbb{R}^3$ (i.e., every immersion preserving the intrinsic Riemannian metric induced from $\mathbb{R}^3$) is the restriction to $S$ of a rigid motion of $\mathbb{R}^3$. A closed surface in $\mathbb{R}^3$ is called tight if every plane cuts it into at most two connected pieces; equivalently, the total absolute Gauss curvature equals the infimum among all immersions of the surface into $\mathbb{R}^3$. A surface is nonconvex if it is not the boundary of a convex body.

(a) Does there exist a smooth nonconvex closed surface $S \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ together with a finite set of points $P \subset S$ such that $S \setminus P$ is rigid?

(b) In particular, let $T \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ be a real-analytic tight surface (for example, a standard torus of revolution). For any finite subset $P \subset T$, is $T \setminus P$ rigid?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

No published resolution of this rigidity question for punctured nonconvex surfaces (in particular for punctured analytic tight surfaces such as a torus of revolution) was found. It is listed as an open problem on Ghomi's problem list, and related work (e.g., on Nirenberg's problem on rigidity of tight surfaces) addresses neighboring but distinct questions. Status appears to remain open.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem, posed by Yau (1993) and Gromov, is widely regarded as open. Local results (Poznyak 1973) show smooth local isometric embeddings of 2-manifolds in R^4 exist, and global embeddings in much higher codimension follow from Nash–Günther, but the global existence in R^4 for arbitrary smooth 2-dimensional Riemannian manifolds is not known.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The smooth local isometric embedding problem for 2-dimensional Riemannian manifolds into R^3, equivalent to local solvability of a Monge-Ampère (Darboux) equation, remains open in general. Partial results exist when the Gaussian curvature does not change sign, is analytic, or vanishes to finite order along curves with controlled structure, but no general C^∞ result is known. The problem traces back to Schlaefli (1873).

Let $S^n \subset \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ denote the unit sphere. For any $C^1$ immersion $f\colon M^n \to \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ of a closed oriented smooth $n$-manifold $M$, there is a well-defined Gauss map $G_f\colon M \to S^n$ assigning to each point of $M$ the unit normal vector to $f(M)$ determined by the orientation; its image $G_f(M) \subset S^n$ is called the spherical image of $f$. Given a subset $A \subset S^n$, an immersion $f$ is called $A$-directed if $G_f(M) \subset A$.

Characterize the subsets $A \subset S^n$ for which there exists a closed oriented smooth $n$-manifold $M$ and an $A$-directed immersion $f\colon M \to \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The general characterization problem, posed by Gromov, remains open. Partial results are known: h-principle and convex integration techniques yield existence in many cases, and explicit constructions show that for any finite set X ⊂ S^n (n ≥ 2) containing no pair of antipodal points, there are closed orientable immersed hypersurfaces whose Gauss map avoids X (answering a specific question of Gromov). A full characterization of admissible A ⊂ S^n is not available.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

For surfaces in 3-space (n=2), the problem was resolved by M. Ghomi (Annals of Mathematics, 2002), who proved that connectedness of every shadow does not imply convexity: every closed orientable surface admits a smooth embedding into R^3 with all shadows connected. If, however, each shadow is required to be simply connected, then the image is convex.

representations.normalized:
Let P be a convex polytope in three-dimensional Euclidean space, that is, the convex hull of a finite set of points with non-empty interior. Its boundary ∂P is a piecewise-flat surface consisting of finitely many convex polygonal faces meeting along edges and at vertices. A spanning tree of edges of P is a subset T of the 1-skeleton of P that is connected, acyclic, and contains every vertex of P. Cutting ∂P along T yields a simply connected piecewise-flat surface that can be developed (isometrically mapped) into the Euclidean plane, by unfolding adjacent faces one at a time across their shared edges; the result is called an edge unfolding of P with respect to T. The polytope P is said to be unfoldable if there exists a spanning tree T of its edges such that the resulting edge unfolding is a simple (non-self-overlapping) planar polygon, i.e., the developing map is injective on the interior of ∂P \ T.

Question: Is every convex polytope in three-dimensional Euclidean space unfoldable?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question—known as Dürer's unfolding problem or Shephard's conjecture—remains open. It is listed as an open problem in standard problem collections (Open Problem Garden, TOPP). Notable partial results include Ghomi's 2014 theorem that every convex polyhedron admits an edge unfolding after a suitable affine transformation, and the 2019 Barvinok–Ghomi result showing the natural generalization to pseudo-edge graphs fails.

representations.normalized:
Let $K \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ be a convex polyhedron, regarded as a closed convex surface equipped with its intrinsic (path) metric induced from the Euclidean metric. The vertices of $K$ are the points where $K$ has positive cone angle defect, and they form a finite set determined purely by the intrinsic geometry of $K$. An edge of $K$ is a maximal straight segment lying on $\partial K$ along which two flat faces meet at a nonzero dihedral angle; every edge is a distance-minimizing geodesic between two vertices, but in general not every minimizing geodesic between two vertices is an edge.

Question: Does there exist a reasonably simple algorithm that, given only the intrinsic metric structure of $K$ (its development, i.e. the abstract polyhedral metric on a sphere together with the cone points and their angle defects) and not its embedding in $\mathbb{R}^3$, decides for each pair of vertices and each minimizing geodesic between them whether that geodesic is realized as an edge of the polyhedron?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

No intrinsic algorithm for detecting the edges of a convex polyhedron is known. Work of Barvinok and Ghomi on "pseudo-edge graphs" shows that there exist 3-connected graphs of distance-minimizing geodesics on convex polyhedra whose vertices coincide with the polyhedron's vertices and whose faces are intrinsically convex, but which differ from the true edge graph; moreover such pseudo-edge unfoldings can fail to be valid unfoldings. This suggests local intrinsic data cannot distinguish edges from pseudo-edges, and the problem of finding a simple intrinsic edge-detection algorithm remains open.

Let $K \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ be a convex polyhedron with vertex set $V(K)$. A *pseudo edge graph* of $K$ is a 3-connected graph $G$ embedded in the boundary $\partial K$ such that:
(i) the vertex set of $G$ equals $V(K)$;
(ii) each edge of $G$ is a distance-minimizing geodesic segment in the intrinsic metric of $\partial K$; and
(iii) each face of $G$ (i.e., each connected component of $\partial K \setminus G$) is intrinsically convex.

A pseudo edge graph $G$ is said to be *unfoldable* if, after cutting $\partial K$ along $G$, the resulting collection of (intrinsically flat) faces can be developed isometrically into the plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ as a connected non-overlapping polygonal region.

Question: Does there exist a convex polyhedron $K \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ which admits a pseudo edge graph $G$ that is not unfoldable (i.e., every such planar development produces overlaps)?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The question has been answered in the affirmative. Barvinok and Ghomi (Discrete & Computational Geometry, 2019; arXiv:1709.04944) constructed an explicit convex polyhedron with 340 vertices admitting a pseudo edge graph that is not unfoldable, building on earlier work of Tarasov and using Pogorelov's theorem on convex caps. This shows Dürer's conjecture fails in the pseudo-edge setting.

Let $S \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ be a closed convex surface, i.e., the boundary of a compact convex body with nonempty interior. Equip $S$ with its induced intrinsic (length) metric $d_S$, where $d_S(p,q)$ is the infimum of lengths of rectifiable curves on $S$ connecting $p$ and $q$. Define the intrinsic diameter of $S$ as $\operatorname{diam}_{\mathrm{int}}(S) = \sup_{p,q \in S} d_S(p,q)$, and let $A(S)$ denote the surface area of $S$. A "doubled disk" of radius $r$ is the (degenerate) convex surface obtained by gluing two flat closed Euclidean disks of radius $r$ along their common boundary circle; its intrinsic diameter equals $2r$ and its area equals $2\pi r^2$.

Question: Among all closed convex surfaces $S \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ with a prescribed intrinsic diameter $D > 0$, is the maximum of $A(S)$ attained by the doubled disk of radius $D/2$? Equivalently, does every closed convex surface $S$ satisfy
$$A(S) \le \frac{\pi}{2}\,\operatorname{diam}_{\mathrm{int}}(S)^2,$$
with equality only for a doubled disk?

Alexandrov's conjecture that the maximum area of a closed convex surface with given intrinsic diameter $D$ is $\pi D^2/2$, attained by the doubled disk, remains open in general. Special cases have been confirmed: tetrahedra (Makai, Zalgaller), rectangular parallelepipeds (Nikonorov–Nikonorova), and surfaces of revolution. There is no known proof or counterexample in full generality.

A closed surface $S \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ is said to have constant width $w > 0$ if the distance between any pair of parallel supporting planes of the convex body bounded by $S$ equals $w$. Such a surface bounds a convex body, and we denote by $\mathrm{area}(S)$ the surface area of $S$ and by $\mathrm{vol}(S)$ the volume of the convex body it bounds.

Fix a constant $A > 0$. Among all closed surfaces $S \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ of constant width (of any value $w > 0$) such that $\mathrm{area}(S) = A$, determine the infimum of $\mathrm{vol}(S)$, and characterize the surfaces (if any) that attain it.

Let γ : [a,b] → ℝ³ be a (rectifiable) space curve, and let L(γ) denote its length. Define:

• The width w(γ) of γ is the infimum, over all pairs of parallel planes Π₁, Π₂ ⊂ ℝ³ such that γ lies in the closed slab bounded by Π₁ and Π₂, of the Euclidean distance between Π₁ and Π₂.

• The inradius r(γ) of γ is the supremum of the radii of all open round balls B ⊂ ℝ³ such that B is contained in the convex hull of the image of γ and B is disjoint from the image of γ.

(a) For each fixed w₀ > 0, determine the infimum of L(γ) over all space curves γ in ℝ³ with width w(γ) = w₀, and describe (up to rigid motion and reparametrization) the curves that achieve, or asymptotically achieve, this infimum.

(b) For each fixed r₀ > 0, determine the infimum of L(γ) over all space curves γ in ℝ³ with inradius r(γ) = r₀, and describe the extremal curves.

Equivalently, find the sharp constants

c_w = inf { L(γ)/w(γ) : γ a space curve with w(γ) > 0 },   c_r = inf { L(γ)/r(γ) : γ a space curve with r(γ) > 0 },

together with the curves attaining these infima.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem, posed by Zalgaller in 1994, remains open. Zalgaller constructed a curve achieving L/w ≤ 3.9215 (still conjectured optimal for the width problem) and a spiral with L/r ≤ 9.5767 for the inradius problem. Subsequent work has confirmed some of Zalgaller's conjectures up to within 99% of their stated values and disproved one, but the sharp constants and extremizers have not been determined. A minimal surface in Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^3$ is a smooth immersed surface whose mean curvature vanishes identically. A planar curve is a simple closed curve contained in some affine plane of $\mathbb{R}^3$, and it is called convex if it bounds a convex region within that plane.

Suppose $M \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ is a compact, connected minimal surface (smoothly immersed, possibly with self-intersections in the interior) whose boundary $\partial M$ consists of exactly two disjoint convex planar curves (each lying in its own affine plane).

Prove or disprove: $M$ is necessarily topologically an annulus (i.e., homeomorphic to $S^1 \times [0,1]$).

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The question, due to W. Meeks (circa 1978), appears to remain open in full generality. Partial results are known: A. Ros established the annulus conclusion when one of the boundary curves is a parallel translate of the other, and the conclusion is known when the two parallel boundary planes are sufficiently close. Classical work of Shiffman (1956) gives strong geometric properties (e.g., convex level sets) for minimal annuli with such boundary, but does not resolve the topological conjecture.

Let $M \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ be a smooth (at least $C^2$) surface, isometrically immersed in Euclidean 3-space, which is complete with respect to the induced Riemannian metric. At each point of $M$, let $\kappa_1, \kappa_2$ denote the principal curvatures, so that the Gauss curvature is $K = \kappa_1 \kappa_2$. Assume that $K < 0$ everywhere on $M$ (i.e., $M$ has strictly negative Gauss curvature), and that the principal curvatures are bounded away from zero, in the sense that there exists a constant $c > 0$ such that $\min(|\kappa_1(p)|, |\kappa_2(p)|) \geq c$ for every $p \in M$.

Does such a surface $M$ exist?

Let $B^3 \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ denote the open unit ball. A smooth surface $S \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ is said to be embedded in $B^3$ if it is the image of a smooth injective immersion of a $2$-manifold into $B^3$ (no self-intersections). The surface $S$ is called complete if it is complete as a Riemannian manifold with respect to the metric induced from the Euclidean metric on $\mathbb{R}^3$, and negatively curved if its Gaussian curvature satisfies $K<0$ at every point.

Question: Does there exist a complete, smoothly embedded surface $S \subset B^3$ with $K<0$ everywhere?

Equivalently, is there an embedding of a complete Riemannian $2$-manifold of strictly negative Gaussian curvature into the open unit ball of $\mathbb{R}^3$?

The corresponding problem for immersed (non-embedded) surfaces was solved affirmatively by Nadirashvili (1996), who constructed complete negatively curved minimal surfaces contained in a ball; however, such examples have self-intersections. By a result of Colding–Minicozzi, complete embedded minimal surfaces in $\mathbb{R}^3$ must be unbounded, ruling out minimal embedded examples. The general embedded Hadamard problem (without the minimality assumption) is listed as still open in current surveys of open problems in geometry of curves and surfaces.

Let $S \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ be a smooth surface, and at each non-umbilic point of $S$ consider the two principal directions (the eigendirections of the shape operator corresponding to the two distinct principal curvatures). These directions define a pair of (unoriented) line fields on the complement of the umbilic set, called the principal line fields of $S$. An isolated umbilic point $p \in S$ is an isolated singularity of these line fields, and to such a singularity one can associate an index (the Poincaré–Hopf index of the line field, equal to one-half of the winding number of the line field along a small loop around $p$).

Prove that for any smooth surface $S \subset \mathbb{R}^3$, the index of every isolated singularity of a principal line field on $S$ is at most one.

representations.normalized:
Let $d \geq 3$ be a fixed integer and let $N \geq 2$. Consider the discrete $d$-dimensional torus $\mathbb{Z}_N^d = (\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^d$, viewed as a graph in which two vertices are joined by an edge whenever they differ by $\pm 1$ in exactly one coordinate (with wrap-around). Replace each undirected edge by two oppositely directed edges, obtaining a directed graph in which every vertex has in-degree and out-degree equal to $2d$. An Eulerian circuit is a directed closed walk that uses every directed edge exactly once. Fix a vertex $0 \in \mathbb{Z}_N^d$ as origin. Any Eulerian circuit, started at $0$, naturally decomposes into $2d$ directed loops based at $0$ (the $i$-th loop is the portion of the circuit between its $(i-1)$-th and $i$-th returns to $0$); let $L_1, \dots, L_{2d}$ denote the lengths of these loops.

Let the Eulerian circuit be chosen uniformly at random from the (finite) set of all Eulerian circuits of this directed graph starting at $0$. Prove that as $N \to \infty$ (with $d$ fixed), with probability tending to $1$, some of the lengths $L_1, \dots, L_{2d}$ are $O(1)$ while each of the remaining ones is of order $N^d$. Equivalently, show that for any sequence $\omega_N \to \infty$,
$$\mathbb{P}\!\left(\exists\, i:\ \omega_N < L_i < N^d/\omega_N \right) \longrightarrow 0 \quad \text{as } N \to \infty.$$

Let $U_{k+1},U_{k+2},\dots$ be independent and identically distributed uniform random points in $[0,1]^2$. Inductively, for each $j\ge k+1$, color $U_j$ with the color of the point in $\{U_1,\dots,U_{j-1}\}$ that is closest to $U_j$ in Euclidean distance (ties having probability zero). Let $\partial$ denote the union of the boundaries between distinct colored regions of this limit partition. Determine whether the Hausdorff (fractal) dimension of $\partial$ is equal to $1$, or strictly greater than $1$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

A 2023 preprint by Aïdékon, Berestycki, and others ("Fractal properties of the frontier in Poissonian coloring", arXiv:2302.07254) shows that in [0,1]^d the frontier between colored regions has Hausdorff dimension strictly between d-1 and d, in particular strictly greater than 1 in the planar case, resolving Aldous's open question.

representations.normalized:
Consider random dynamic models that produce a sequence of coalescing partitions of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$. In a baseline model, fix a locally finite configuration of distinguished points ("capital cities"), one for each cell ("country") of an initial partition; each country is absorbed at rate $1$ (independently, as an exponential clock), and upon absorption it is merged into the country whose capital is the Euclidean-nearest other capital. This particular construction (from a space-time Poisson point process) possesses an exact statistical self-similarity under simultaneous spatial and temporal rescaling.

Construct or analyze rigorously any other natural stochastic model of randomly coalescing partitions of the plane (for instance, models in which neighboring cells merge at rates depending on geometric features such as shared boundary length, area, or distance, rather than on nearest-capital rules), and prove for at least one such model that, as time tends to infinity, the partition exhibits one of the following two dichotomous behaviors:

(a) asymptotic self-similarity: after appropriate space-time rescaling, the law of the partition converges to a nondegenerate scale-invariant random partition of $\mathbb{R}^2$; or

(b) emergence of a unique infinite cluster (country) of positive density, analogous to the supercritical phase of bond percolation.

Establish rigorously which of (a) or (b) occurs for the chosen model.
