In the setting of the untyped lambda calculus, let $\Lambda$ denote the set of lambda terms and let $\mathrm{NF} \subseteq \Lambda$ denote the set of (beta) normal forms. Assume given a set $\mathcal{D}$ of objects called deeds together with an injective map
$$ \mathrm{NF} \longrightarrow \mathcal{D}, \qquad M \longmapsto D_M, $$
which associates to each normal form $M$ its deed $D_M$, and a notion of equation $D_M X = D_N X$ in $\mathcal{D}$ (with $X$ a variable ranging over an appropriate domain) that is compatible with the lambda-calculus equation $M X = N X$ in the sense that any solution of $M X = N X$ in $\Lambda$ induces a solution of $D_M X = D_N X$ in $\mathcal{D}$.

Problem. Given arbitrary normal forms $M, N \in \mathrm{NF}$, determine what information about the set of solutions $X$ of the lambda-calculus equation
$$ M X = N X $$
can be extracted from, or reduced to, the analysis of the associated deed equation
$$ D_M X = D_N X. $$
In particular, characterize precisely the equational content captured by the passage from $M, N$ to their deeds $D_M, D_N$, and identify which properties of solutions (existence, uniqueness, structure) of $M X = N X$ are reflected by, or can be inferred from, $D_M X = D_N X$.

Work in the pure untyped λβ-calculus. A combinator is a closed λ-term (a λ-term with no free variables). A fixed point of a combinator F is a λ-term X such that F X =_β X; two fixed points are identified when they are β-convertible, and otherwise considered distinct. It is known that if a combinator F has a fixed point in β-normal form, then either F has exactly one fixed point (up to β-conversion) or F has infinitely many pairwise β-distinct fixed points.

Determine, for an arbitrary combinator F in λβ, all possible cardinalities of the set of its fixed points up to β-conversion. In particular, decide whether every combinator has either exactly one fixed point or infinitely many pairwise β-distinct fixed points (the "fixed point property" for λβ), or exhibit a combinator whose number of fixed points is a finite integer greater than one.

Let $\Lambda_\to$ denote the set of terms of the simply typed lambda calculus (with $\beta$-reduction $\to_\beta$). Construct an "easy" map
$$\# : \Lambda_\to \longrightarrow \mathrm{Ord}$$
from simply typed $\lambda$-terms to ordinals (possibly transfinite) such that
$$\forall M, N \in \Lambda_\to,\quad M \to_\beta N \;\Longrightarrow\; \#M > \#N.$$

For each integer $k \geq 3$, let $k\text{-SAT}$ denote the decision problem of determining whether a given Boolean formula in conjunctive normal form, in which every clause has at most $k$ literals, is satisfiable. For an instance with $n$ Boolean variables, let $T_k(n)$ denote the infimum over all deterministic algorithms solving $k\text{-SAT}$ of the worst-case running time exponent, and define
$$ s_k \;=\; \inf\{\, \delta \geq 0 \;:\; k\text{-SAT on } n \text{ variables can be decided in time } 2^{\delta n} \cdot \mathrm{poly}(n)\,\}. $$
The Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH) is the statement that $s_3 > 0$; equivalently, that there exists a constant $c > 0$ such that no deterministic algorithm decides $3\text{-SAT}$ on $n$ variables in time $2^{cn}$ in the worst case (more strongly, that $3\text{-SAT}$ cannot be solved in subexponential time $2^{o(n)}$).

Determine whether the Exponential Time Hypothesis is true: prove that $s_3 > 0$, or exhibit (or prove the existence of) a deterministic algorithm deciding $3\text{-SAT}$ on $n$ variables in time $2^{o(n)}$.

A function $f : \{0,1\}^* \to \{0,1\}^*$ is called a one-way function if the following two conditions hold:

1. (Easy to compute) There exists a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm $A$ such that for every $x \in \{0,1\}^*$, $A(x) = f(x)$.

2. (Hard to invert) For every probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm $B$, every positive polynomial $p(\cdot)$, and all sufficiently large $n$,
$$\Pr_{x \leftarrow \{0,1\}^n}\bigl[\,B(f(x), 1^n) \in f^{-1}(f(x))\,\bigr] < \frac{1}{p(n)},$$
where the probability is taken over the uniform choice of $x \in \{0,1\}^n$ and the internal coin tosses of $B$.

Determine whether a one-way function (in the above sense) exists. Equivalently, prove or disprove the existence of a polynomial-time computable function that is hard to invert on average by every probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm.

A deterministic (or probabilistic) classical algorithm runs in polynomial time if there exists a constant $c \geq 0$ such that, on every input of bit-length $n$, the algorithm halts after at most $O(n^c)$ elementary steps on a standard Turing machine model (no quantum operations allowed).

The integer factorization problem is: given a positive integer $N \geq 2$ encoded in binary (so the input length is $n = \lceil \log_2(N+1) \rceil$ bits), output the complete multiset of prime factors of $N$ (equivalently, output a nontrivial factor of $N$ whenever $N$ is composite).

Question: Does there exist a classical algorithm that solves the integer factorization problem in polynomial time in the bit-length $n$ of the input?

Let $G$ be a finite cyclic group given by a generator $g$ of order $n$, where group elements are represented by binary strings of length $O(\log n)$ and the group operations (multiplication and inversion) can be performed in time polynomial in $\log n$. The discrete logarithm problem asks: given $g$ and an element $h \in \langle g \rangle$, find the unique integer $x \in \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ such that $g^x = h$.

Question: Does there exist a deterministic (or probabilistic) classical algorithm that, for every such cyclic group $G$ (in particular, for the multiplicative groups $(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^\times$ for prime $p$, and for the groups of rational points of elliptic curves over finite fields), solves the discrete logarithm problem in time polynomial in $\log n$?

No polynomial-time classical algorithm for the discrete logarithm problem is known in general. Two finite simple graphs $G_1=(V_1,E_1)$ and $G_2=(V_2,E_2)$ are said to be isomorphic if there exists a bijection $\varphi\colon V_1	o V_2$ such that for all $u,v\in V_1$, $\{u,v\}\in E_1$ if and only if $\{\varphi(u),\varphi(v)\}\in E_2$.

The Graph Isomorphism Problem is the following decision problem: given two finite simple graphs $G_1$ and $G_2$ as input (encoded, e.g., by adjacency matrices), decide whether $G_1$ and $G_2$ are isomorphic.

An algorithm runs in polynomial time if there exists a constant $c\ge 0$ and a polynomial-time deterministic Turing machine that decides the problem in time $O(n^c)$, where $n$ is the total bit-length of the input.

Question: Does there exist a deterministic algorithm that solves the Graph Isomorphism Problem in polynomial time? Equivalently, is the Graph Isomorphism Problem in the complexity class $\mathsf{P}$?

A graph G = (V, E) is called a k-leaf power (for an integer k ≥ 2) if there exists a tree T whose set of leaves is exactly V, such that for all distinct u, v ∈ V, one has uv ∈ E if and only if the distance between u and v in T is at most k. A graph is called a leaf power if it is a k-leaf power for some k ≥ 2.

Questions:
(1) Is there an algorithm that, given a graph G on n vertices, decides in time polynomial in n whether G is a leaf power?
(2) For each fixed integer k ≥ 2, is there an algorithm that, given a graph G on n vertices, decides in time polynomial in n whether G is a k-leaf power?
(3) More strongly, is there an algorithm with running time polynomial in both n and k that, given (G, k), decides whether G is a k-leaf power?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Lafond (2021/2023) gave an algorithm that recognizes k-leaf powers in time n^f(k) for every fixed k, resolving the recognition problem for each constant k in polynomial time. However, the dependence on k is a tower function, so the parameterized/uniform version (polynomial in both n and k) and the recognition of leaf powers in general (without fixing k) remain not fully resolved by a single uniform polynomial-time algorithm. Earlier polynomial-time results existed only up to k = 6.

A parity game is an infinite-duration two-player game played on a finite directed graph G = (V, E) with the following data: the vertex set V is partitioned into V_0 (positions of Player 0, also called Even) and V_1 (positions of Player 1, also called Odd); every vertex has at least one outgoing edge; and there is a priority function p: V → {0, 1, ..., d} assigning a nonnegative integer priority to each vertex. A play of the game is an infinite sequence v_0, v_1, v_2, ... of vertices such that (v_i, v_{i+1}) ∈ E for every i ≥ 0; at each step, if v_i ∈ V_σ then Player σ chooses the successor v_{i+1}. Player 0 wins the play if the largest priority that occurs infinitely often along the play is even; otherwise Player 1 wins. It is known that parity games are positionally determined: from every starting vertex v ∈ V, exactly one of the two players has a positional (memoryless) winning strategy. The decision problem "Parity Game" is: given a finite parity game (V_0, V_1, E, p) and a vertex v ∈ V, decide whether Player 0 has a winning strategy from v.

Question: Does there exist an algorithm that solves the Parity Game decision problem in time polynomial in |V| + |E| + d?

A rooted binary tree is a finite rooted tree in which every internal node has exactly two ordered children (a left child and a right child). A rotation at an internal edge of such a tree is the standard local restructuring operation: if y is the left child of x and y has children A (left) and B (right), then the rotation replaces the configuration in which x has left child y (with children A, B) and right child C by the configuration in which y becomes the parent of the subtree, with left child A and right child x, while x has left child B and right child C; the symmetric operation is defined for a right child. The rotation distance d(T, T') between two rooted binary trees T and T' with the same number of nodes is the minimum number of rotations needed to transform T into T'.

Question: Is there an algorithm that, given two rooted binary trees T and T' on n nodes, computes d(T, T') in time polynomial in n?

A rooted binary tree is a finite rooted tree in which every internal node has exactly two ordered children (a left child and a right child). A rotation at an internal edge of such a tree is the standard local restructuring operation: if y is the left child of x and y has children A (left) and B (right), then the rotation replaces the configuration in which x has left child y (with children A, B) and right child C by the configuration in which y becomes the parent of the subtree, with left child A and right child x, while x has left child B and right child C; the symmetric operation is defined for a right child. The rotation distance d(T, T') between two rooted binary trees T and T' with the same number of nodes is the minimum number of rotations needed to transform T into T'.

Question: Is there an algorithm that, given two rooted binary trees T and T' on n nodes, computes d(T, T') in time polynomial in n?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem of computing rotation distance between two binary trees in polynomial time remains open. It is known to be in NP (since rotation sequences of length at most 2n−6 always exist), is fixed-parameter tractable (Cleary–St. John), and admits polynomial-time algorithms in restricted variants, but it is neither known to be NP-hard nor known to be solvable in polynomial time.

Let $P \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ be a convex polyhedron given by its combinatorial structure and the coordinates of its vertices. A closed curve $\gamma$ on the surface of $P$ is called a closed quasigeodesic if $\gamma$ is locally straight in the interior of every face and on the relative interior of every edge, and at each vertex of $P$ that $\gamma$ passes through, the total surface angle on each of the two sides of $\gamma$ is at most $\pi$. The curve is called simple if it has no self-intersections. By a theorem of Pogorelov (1949), every convex polyhedron carries at least one simple closed quasigeodesic.

Question: Does there exist an algorithm that, given as input a convex polyhedron $P$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ (with rational vertex coordinates), computes a simple closed quasigeodesic on $P$ in time polynomial in the bit-size of the input?

Demaine, Hesterberg, and Ku (2020) gave the first finite algorithm computing a closed quasigeodesic on a convex polyhedron, but it runs in pseudo-polynomial time. Chartier and de Mesmay (2022) provided a finite algorithm computing a weakly simple closed quasigeodesic on polyhedral spheres. No worst-case polynomial-time algorithm is known, and obtaining one would resolve or interact with the sum-of-square-roots problem, suggesting a polynomial-time algorithm on the word RAM is unlikely with current techniques. The problem remains open.

The k-server problem is defined as follows. Let $(M,d)$ be a metric space and let $k \geq 1$ be an integer. An algorithm controls $k$ mobile servers occupying points of $M$. At each time step $t=1,2,\dots$, a request point $r_t \in M$ is revealed, and the algorithm must move at least one server to $r_t$. The cost of an algorithm on a request sequence is the total distance traveled by all servers. An online algorithm processes requests one at a time without knowledge of future requests. An online algorithm $\mathrm{ALG}$ is said to be $c$-competitive if there is a constant $\alpha$ such that for every metric space $(M,d)$, every initial configuration of $k$ servers, and every finite request sequence $\sigma$,
$$\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{ALG}}(\sigma) \le c\cdot \mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{OPT}}(\sigma) + \alpha,$$
where $\mathrm{OPT}$ denotes the optimal offline cost.

Question: Does there exist a deterministic $k$-competitive online algorithm for the $k$-server problem on every metric space?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The k-server conjecture, posed by Manasse, McGeoch, and Sleator (1988), remains open in general. The best known deterministic competitive ratio is $2k-1$ via the Work Function Algorithm (Koutsoupias–Papadimitriou, 1995). The conjecture is verified for special cases (k=2, tree metrics, (k+1)-point metrics, line metrics, weighted star metrics, k=3 in the Manhattan plane, and recently the circle), but no $k$-competitive algorithm is known for general metrics.

Background and definitions:
- The complexity class NC consists of decision problems (or, more generally, function problems) solvable on a parallel random-access machine (or by uniform families of Boolean circuits) using polynomially many processors (resp. polynomial-size circuits of polylogarithmic depth) in time polylogarithmic in the input size.
- Given a connected undirected graph G = (V, E) with a designated root vertex r ∈ V, a depth-first search (DFS) tree of G rooted at r is a spanning tree T of G such that for every edge {u, v} ∈ E, one of u, v is an ancestor of the other in T. Equivalently, T is the spanning tree produced by some execution of the standard sequential depth-first search procedure starting at r.

Problem: Does there exist a deterministic NC algorithm that, given as input an arbitrary undirected graph G with a specified root r, outputs (the adjacency representation of) a depth-first search tree of G rooted at r? Equivalently, is the problem of constructing a DFS tree of a general undirected graph in the complexity class NC?

The parallel complexity of constructing a depth-first search tree remains unsettled as of 2026. A randomized NC (RNC) algorithm is known (Aggarwal–Anderson), and deterministic NC algorithms exist for restricted graph classes (planar, bounded genus, H-minor-free with one-crossing H, bounded treewidth in Logspace), but no deterministic NC algorithm for general graphs is known. Recent work (arXiv:2506.14974) explicitly states the parallel complexity of DFS "is still not settled."

For a positive integer $n$, the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) of a vector $x = (x_0, x_1, \dots, x_{n-1}) \in \mathbb{C}^n$ is the vector $\hat x = (\hat x_0, \dots, \hat x_{n-1}) \in \mathbb{C}^n$ defined by
$$\hat x_k \;=\; \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} x_j \, e^{-2\pi i j k / n}, \qquad k = 0,1,\dots,n-1.$$
The Cooley–Tukey fast Fourier transform (FFT) computes this transformation using $O(n \log n)$ arithmetic operations on a model of computation with exact arithmetic over $\mathbb{C}$ (or, equivalently, in the standard RAM/arithmetic-circuit model with constant-time operations $+,-,\times,\div$ on complex numbers, where roots of unity are available as inputs).

Question: Does there exist an algorithm that computes the discrete Fourier transform of every input $x \in \mathbb{C}^n$ using $o(n \log n)$ arithmetic operations? Equivalently, is the arithmetic complexity of the $n$-point DFT strictly $o(n \log n)$, or is $\Theta(n \log n)$ optimal?

No general arithmetic lower bound matching the $O(n \log n)$ upper bound of the Cooley–Tukey FFT is known, and no algorithm running in $o(n \log n)$ time has been discovered. The question of unconditional $o(n \log n)$ computability of the DFT is widely regarded as open.

Shellsort is a comparison-based sorting algorithm parameterized by a finite sequence of positive integers h_1 > h_2 > ... > h_p = 1, called the gap sequence. Given an array of N elements, for each k = 1, ..., p the algorithm performs an h_k-sort: it sorts (via insertion sort) every subarray consisting of elements whose indices are congruent modulo h_k. The average-case running time T(N) of Shellsort with a given gap sequence is the expected number of element comparisons (equivalently, key operations) when the input is a uniformly random permutation of N distinct keys.

A gap sequence is called deterministic and fixed if, for every N, the gaps h_1(N) > h_2(N) > ... > h_{p(N)}(N) = 1 are determined by a deterministic rule depending only on N (and not on the input).

Determine the infimum, over all deterministic fixed gap sequences, of the asymptotic average-case time complexity of Shellsort on inputs of size N. In particular, decide whether there exists a deterministic fixed gap sequence achieving average-case complexity Θ(N log N), and otherwise determine the best achievable asymptotic order.

Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet. For two strings $x, y \in \Sigma^*$, the edit distance (Levenshtein distance) $\mathrm{ed}(x,y)$ is the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions, and substitutions required to transform $x$ into $y$. The classical dynamic-programming algorithm computes $\mathrm{ed}(x,y)$ in time $O(n^2)$ when $|x|=|y|=n$, and only mild $\mathrm{polylog}(n)$ improvements are known.

A problem on inputs of size $n$ is said to be solvable in strongly subquadratic time if there exists a constant $\delta > 0$ and an algorithm running in time $O(n^{2-\delta})$ on a standard word-RAM machine with $O(\log n)$-bit words.

The Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH) asserts that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $k \geq 3$ such that $k$-SAT on $N$ variables cannot be solved in time $O(2^{(1-\varepsilon)N})$.

Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet. For two strings $x, y \in \Sigma^*$, the edit distance (Levenshtein distance) $\mathrm{ed}(x,y)$ is the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions, and substitutions required to transform $x$ into $y$. The classical dynamic-programming algorithm computes $\mathrm{ed}(x,y)$ in time $O(n^2)$ when $|x|=|y|=n$, and only mild $\mathrm{polylog}(n)$ improvements are known.

The Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH) asserts that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $k \geq 3$ such that $k$-SAT on $N$ variables cannot be solved in time $O(2^{(1-\varepsilon)N})$.

Backurs and Indyk (STOC 2015; SICOMP) proved that an exact $O(n^{2-\delta})$ algorithm for edit distance would refute SETH, giving a conditional negative answer. Let $G=(V,E,w)$ be a directed graph on $n=|V|$ vertices with real edge weights $w:E\to\mathbb{R}$ (and no negative cycles). The all-pairs shortest paths (APSP) problem asks, for every ordered pair $(u,v)\in V\times V$, to compute the length $d(u,v)$ of a shortest path from $u$ to $v$ in $G$ (where $d(u,v)=+\infty$ if $v$ is unreachable from $u$).

An algorithm is said to run in truly (strongly) sub-cubic time if there exists a constant $\varepsilon>0$ such that its worst-case running time on $n$-vertex inputs is $O(n^{3-\varepsilon})$ in the standard word-RAM model (with word size $O(\log n)$).

Question: Does there exist an algorithm that solves the all-pairs shortest paths problem on arbitrary $n$-vertex real-weighted directed graphs in truly sub-cubic time $O(n^{3-\varepsilon})$ for some constant $\varepsilon>0$?

Polynomial Identity Testing (PIT) is the following decision problem: given an arithmetic circuit C over a field F that computes a multivariate polynomial p(x_1, ..., x_n) of total degree at most d, decide whether p is identically zero.

The Schwartz–Zippel lemma states that if p is a nonzero polynomial of total degree d over F, and S ⊆ F is a finite set, then the number of points (a_1, ..., a_n) ∈ S^n with p(a_1, ..., a_n) = 0 is at most d·|S|^{n−1}. Choosing the evaluation point uniformly at random from S^n with |S| > d therefore yields a randomized polynomial-time algorithm for PIT with one-sided error.

Problem: Construct a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for Polynomial Identity Testing. Equivalently, exhibit, for every n and d (and a circuit size bound s), an explicit "hitting set" H ⊆ F^n of size polynomial in n, d, and s such that every nonzero polynomial computable by an arithmetic circuit of size at most s has at least one nonzero evaluation on H, and such that H can be produced in deterministic polynomial time. Either provide such a deterministic algorithm/hitting-set construction or prove that none exists under standard complexity-theoretic assumptions.

Consider the problem of envy-free cake cutting in the standard Robertson–Webb query model. The "cake" is the interval [0,1], and there are n agents, each having a non-atomic, additive valuation measure V_i on [0,1] with V_i([0,1]) = 1. A protocol may interact with the agents only via two types of queries:
  • Eval_i(x, y): the agent i reports V_i([x, y]).
  • Cut_i(x, α): the agent i reports the smallest y ≥ x such that V_i([x, y]) = α.
A protocol is envy-free if, upon termination, it produces a partition of [0,1] into n disjoint pieces P_1, …, P_n (one per agent) such that V_i(P_i) ≥ V_i(P_j) for all i, j. A protocol is discrete and bounded if there is a function f(n) such that on every instance with n agents the protocol halts after at most f(n) queries.

Let Q(n) denote the minimum, over all discrete and bounded envy-free protocols for n agents in the Robertson–Webb model, of the worst-case number of queries used. Determine the asymptotic behavior of Q(n). In particular, close the gap between the known lower bound Q(n) = Ω(n^2) and the best known upper bound, which is a tower of exponentials in n.

Consider the following procedural maze-generation rule. A maze is built column by column on a rectangular grid in which each cell is either a wall or open. The cells are filled in a fixed scan order. To determine the value of the next cell to be generated, one inspects the values (wall/open) of exactly five already-generated neighbouring cells in a fixed pattern relative to the current position; this 5-bit pattern (32 possible inputs) is used as an index into a fixed lookup table whose entries specify the next cell to be "wall", "open", or "random" (in which case a pseudorandom bit is used).

The empirical fact is that there exists a specific 32-entry lookup table with this property: when used in the above procedure (together with appropriate boundary conditions and the indicated random fallback), it consistently produces mazes that are "playable", meaning each generated maze contains a navigable path through it without dead-end blockage of the player's traversal.

Problem: Determine a principled algorithm or mathematical derivation that explains how to construct such a 32-entry lookup table from first principles — i.e., describe a method that, given only the local 5-cell neighbourhood rule and the playability requirement, derives a lookup table guaranteed to consistently generate playable mazes, and prove that the resulting procedure indeed produces playable mazes for all admissible random choices.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Existing syllabification systems for English (rule-based, dictionary-based, and machine-learning approaches such as those by Marchand–Adsett–Damper, Bartlett et al., and more recent neural models) report word-level accuracies well below 100%, and English syllabification remains contested even among linguists due to ambisyllabicity and dialectal variation. No system has been demonstrated to be perfect, and the very notion of a "correct" syllabification of every English word is not uniquely defined. The problem is therefore generally regarded as still open / ill-posed in the strict sense.

Consider a wireless communication network consisting of $n$ nodes placed in a region of the plane. Each node may act as a source, destination, and/or relay. Communication between nodes takes place over a shared wireless medium modeled by additive Gaussian noise together with a path-loss attenuation function and (possibly) multipath fading: when nodes $\{T_i\}$ simultaneously transmit signals $\{X_i(t)\}$, each receiver $j$ observes
$$Y_j(t) = \sum_{i \neq j} g_{ij}\, X_i(t) + Z_j(t),$$
where $g_{ij}$ are channel gains determined by the geometry and the propagation law, and $Z_j(t)$ are independent white Gaussian noise processes. Each transmitter is subject to an average power constraint $P$. A rate tuple $(R_{s,d})$ indexed by source-destination pairs $(s,d)$ is said to be achievable if there exist block coding schemes (allowing arbitrary cooperation, relaying, multi-hopping, network coding, feedback, and unbounded delay) such that the probability of decoding error at each destination tends to zero as the block length tends to infinity, with source $s$ delivering data to destination $d$ at rate at least $R_{s,d}$. The capacity region $\mathcal{C}$ of the network is the closure of the set of all achievable rate tuples.

Problem: Determine the capacity region $\mathcal{C}$ of an arbitrary wireless network of the above form. Equivalently, give a single-letter information-theoretic characterization of $\mathcal{C}$ for general node placements, general source-destination demand sets, general fading statistics, and arbitrary numbers of nodes $n \geq 2$, that recovers the known capacity formulas in special cases (such as the point-to-point AWGN channel and the point-to-point fading channel).

The capacity region of a general wireless network is a longstanding open problem in network information theory. While capacity is known for isolated cases such as the point-to-point AWGN and fading channels, no single-letter characterization is known even for small multi-terminal building blocks like the general interference channel or the general relay channel. Recent work (scaling laws, degrees-of-freedom bounds, deterministic-channel approximations) provides partial results and asymptotic characterizations, but a full information-theoretic characterization of the capacity region remains unsolved.

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be a finite input alphabet and let $\mathcal{Y}_1,\ldots,\mathcal{Y}_K$ be finite output alphabets. A discrete memoryless broadcast channel is specified by a transition probability kernel $p(y_1,\ldots,y_K\mid x)$ with $x\in\mathcal{X}$ and $y_k\in\mathcal{Y}_k$. A single transmitter wishes to send $K$ independent messages $M_1,\ldots,M_K$ (with $M_k$ uniformly distributed on $\{1,\ldots,\lceil 2^{nR_k}\rceil\}$) to $K$ separate receivers: a $(2^{nR_1},\ldots,2^{nR_K},n)$ code consists of an encoder $f_n:\prod_k\{1,\ldots,2^{nR_k}\}\to\mathcal{X}^n$ and decoders $g_{k,n}:\mathcal{Y}_k^n\to\{1,\ldots,2^{nR_k}\}$, with average probability of error $P_e^{(n)}=\Pr\{(g_{1,n}(Y_1^n),\ldots,g_{K,n}(Y_K^n))\neq(M_1,\ldots,M_K)\}$. A rate tuple $(R_1,\ldots,R_K)$ is achievable if there exists a sequence of codes with $P_e^{(n)}\to 0$. The capacity region $\mathcal{C}$ is the closure of the set of achievable rate tuples.

Problem: Determine, as an explicit single-letter information-theoretic characterization, the capacity region $\mathcal{C}$ of an arbitrary discrete memoryless broadcast channel $p(y_1,\ldots,y_K\mid x)$ (for general $K\ge 2$, and in particular for the two-receiver case $K=2$ with private messages and no degradedness or other structural assumptions).

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The capacity region of the general (discrete memoryless) broadcast channel remains an open problem. It is known in several special cases — degraded broadcast channels (Cover, Bergmans, Gallager), less noisy and more capable channels, and the Gaussian MIMO broadcast channel (where dirty-paper coding with Gaussian codebooks is capacity-achieving) — but no single-letter characterization is known for the general case. Marton's inner bound and the UV outer bound remain the best general bounds; their equality is unresolved.

Consider a discrete memoryless two-user interference channel, defined by an input alphabet pair (X_1, X_2), an output alphabet pair (Y_1, Y_2), and a transition probability kernel p(y_1, y_2 | x_1, x_2). Two transmitter-receiver pairs share the channel: transmitter i encodes an independent message M_i (uniformly distributed on {1, ..., 2^{nR_i}}) into a length-n codeword X_i^n, and receiver i must decode M_i from Y_i^n, for i = 1, 2. The capacity region C is the closure of the set of all rate pairs (R_1, R_2) for which there exist sequences of codes whose average probability of decoding error tends to zero as n → ∞.

Give a single-letter (computable) characterization of the capacity region C for an arbitrary two-user interference channel p(y_1, y_2 | x_1, x_2). Equivalently, determine whether the Han–Kobayashi inner bound coincides with the capacity region, or otherwise provide a matching outer bound that is tight in general.

The same question may be specialized to the Gaussian case, in which
  Y_1 = h_{11} X_1 + h_{12} X_2 + Z_1,   Y_2 = h_{21} X_1 + h_{22} X_2 + Z_2,
with fixed real channel gains h_{ij}, independent Gaussian noises Z_i ~ N(0,1), and per-block average power constraints (1/n) Σ_{t=1}^{n} X_{i,t}^2 ≤ P_i.

The exact capacity region of the two-user interference channel remains a long-standing open problem in network information theory. Consider a discrete memoryless two-way channel with finite input alphabets $\mathcal{X}_1, \mathcal{X}_2$ and finite output alphabets $\mathcal{Y}_1, \mathcal{Y}_2$, specified by a transition probability kernel $p(y_1, y_2 \mid x_1, x_2)$. Two terminals communicate simultaneously in both directions: at each time $t = 1, 2, \ldots, n$, terminal 1 transmits $X_{1,t}$ and terminal 2 transmits $X_{2,t}$; each terminal $i$ may choose $X_{i,t}$ as an arbitrary (possibly randomized) function of its own message $M_i$ and its previously received outputs $Y_{i,1}, \ldots, Y_{i,t-1}$. The capacity region $\mathcal{C}$ is the closure of the set of all rate pairs $(R_1, R_2)$ such that, for every $\epsilon > 0$ and all sufficiently large $n$, there exist encoders and decoders permitting the reliable transmission of a message $M_1$ uniform on $\{1, \ldots, 2^{nR_1}\}$ from terminal 1 to terminal 2 and a message $M_2$ uniform on $\{1, \ldots, 2^{nR_2}\}$ from terminal 2 to terminal 1, with average error probability at most $\epsilon$.

Determine a computable single-letter characterization of the capacity region $\mathcal{C}$ for an arbitrary discrete memoryless two-way channel $p(y_1, y_2 \mid x_1, x_2)$.

Finding a computable single-letter characterization of the capacity region for the general discrete memoryless two-way channel remains a long-standing open problem in information theory. Consider a multiple-access communication channel of ALOHA type. There are $N$ transmitters sharing a common channel to a single receiver. Time is slotted, and in each slot every transmitter is independently either active (has a packet to send) or idle. Each active transmitter transmits its packet without coordinating with the other transmitters; if two or more transmitters transmit simultaneously, a collision occurs and (in the basic model) none of the colliding packets is received correctly, while if exactly one transmitter transmits, its packet is received successfully. More generally, one may consider the information-theoretic model in which transmitters use codes of arbitrary block length over a memoryless channel with input from each active user, and where the set of active users in each slot is random and unknown to the transmitters but known (or unknown) to the receiver.

Define the capacity (or capacity region) of the ALOHA channel as the closure of the set of rate tuples $(R_1, \dots, R_N)$ that are simultaneously achievable with arbitrarily small probability of error, under this uncoordinated random-access protocol.

Problem: Determine the capacity region of the ALOHA random-access channel in full generality. Equivalently, give a single-letter characterization of the set of achievable rates for the ALOHA multiple-access scheme for arbitrary numbers of users and arbitrary activity statistics.

Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_m$ be $m \ge 2$ jointly distributed discrete memoryless sources with a known joint distribution $p(x_1, \ldots, x_m)$ on a finite alphabet $\mathcal{X}_1 \times \cdots \times \mathcal{X}_m$. Each source $X_i$ is observed only by encoder $i$; the encoders cannot communicate with each other. Encoder $i$ maps blocks $X_i^n = (X_{i,1}, \ldots, X_{i,n})$ to an index $f_i^{(n)}(X_i^n) \in \{1, \ldots, 2^{nR_i}\}$ at rate $R_i$. A joint decoder receives all indices $(f_1^{(n)}(X_1^n), \ldots, f_m^{(n)}(X_m^n))$ and produces reconstructions $(\hat X_1^n, \ldots, \hat X_m^n)$ in target alphabets $\hat{\mathcal{X}}_i$, subject to per-letter distortion constraints
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty} \mathbb{E}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^n d_i(X_{i,t}, \hat X_{i,t})\right] \le D_i, \qquad i = 1, \ldots, m,$$
for given bounded distortion measures $d_i:\mathcal{X}_i \times \hat{\mathcal{X}}_i \to [0,\infty)$ and target distortion levels $(D_1, \ldots, D_m)$.

Determine, as an explicit single-letter characterization, the rate-distortion region
$$\mathcal{R}(D_1, \ldots, D_m) = \{(R_1, \ldots, R_m) : (R_1, \ldots, R_m, D_1, \ldots, D_m) \text{ is achievable}\}$$
for an arbitrary joint source distribution and arbitrary distortion measures. Equivalently, give a computable formula for the minimum total rate (or full Pareto boundary) required to compress $m$ correlated sources, observed and encoded separately without cooperation, so that a joint decoder can reconstruct them within prescribed distortions.

The lossless case (Slepian–Wolf, 1973) and the case with decoder side information (Wyner–Ziv, 1976) are solved. The Gaussian two-terminal case has been resolved by Wagner, Tavildar, and Viswanath, and several helper variants are known. However, a single-letter characterization of the rate-distortion region for the general multiterminal lossy distributed source coding problem (m ≥ 2 correlated sources, arbitrary distributions and distortion measures) remains open, as reflected in current survey and research literature.

The problem of detecting and correcting systematic errors when random errors dominate (Tukey's "uncomfortable science") is a longstanding open methodological challenge in statistics; no general solution exists, although domain-specific techniques (meta-analysis bias adjustments, instrumental variables, sensitivity analysis, blinded analyses) address special cases. No authoritative source claims a general resolution.

The Graybill–Deal estimator of $\mu$ is
$$\hat\mu_{GD}=\frac{S_1^{-2}\,\bar X+S_2^{-2}\,\bar Y}{S_1^{-2}+S_2^{-2}}.$$

Determine whether $\hat\mu_{GD}$ is admissible in the class of all estimators of $\mu$ under squared-error loss.

Let $X_1,\dots,X_m$ be i.i.d. samples from a normal distribution $\mathcal{N}(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2)$ and let $Y_1,\dots,Y_n$ be i.i.d. samples from a normal distribution $\mathcal{N}(\mu_2,\sigma_2^2)$, with the two samples independent. The parameters $\mu_1,\mu_2\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\sigma_1^2,\sigma_2^2>0$ are all unknown, and in particular $\sigma_1^2$ and $\sigma_2^2$ are not assumed to be equal (so the variances are nuisance parameters). Fix a significance level $\alpha\in(0,1)$. Consider testing the null hypothesis $H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2$ against the alternative $H_1:\mu_1\neq\mu_2$.

A test (a measurable function of the data with values in $\{0,1\}$, where $1$ means rejection of $H_0$) is called exact at level $\alpha$ if, whenever $\mu_1=\mu_2$, its rejection probability equals exactly $\alpha$ for every choice of $(\sigma_1^2,\sigma_2^2)$. Such a test is called uniformly most powerful (UMP) within a given class of exact level-$\alpha$ tests if, for every alternative $(\mu_1,\mu_2,\sigma_1^2,\sigma_2^2)$ with $\mu_1\neq\mu_2$, its rejection probability is at least as large as that of any other exact level-$\alpha$ test in the class.

Problem: Construct an exact level-$\alpha$ test of $H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2$ that is uniformly most powerful (or, more generally, an exact procedure with optimal power properties) against all alternatives and uniformly over all values of the unknown variances $(\sigma_1^2,\sigma_2^2)$, or prove that no such procedure with the desired optimality property can exist beyond what is already known.

The Behrens–Fisher problem is a classical statistical problem dating back to Behrens (1929) and Fisher (1935). Linnik (1966) proved that no uniformly most powerful exact test exists, and many approximate solutions (Welch's t-test, Welch–Satterthwaite, fiducial and Bayesian approaches) are widely used. The problem is generally regarded as still open in the sense that no fully satisfactory exact solution with optimal power exists; it continues to be studied as a classical open problem in statistics.

Let $H_1, H_2, \dots, H_m$ be a (possibly very large) collection of null hypotheses tested simultaneously on a common data set, producing raw $p$-values $p_1, \dots, p_m$. Let $V$ denote the (random) number of true null hypotheses that are rejected and $R$ the total number of rejections; define the family-wise error rate as $\mathrm{FWER} = \Pr(V \ge 1)$ and the false discovery rate as $\mathrm{FDR} = \mathbb{E}[V/\max(R,1)]$. Suppose the joint distribution of $(p_1, \dots, p_m)$ exhibits arbitrary, unknown dependence among the test statistics.

Develop a procedure $\mathcal{P}$ that adjusts the $p$-values (or equivalently selects a rejection set) so as to:
(a) control a prescribed overall Type-I error criterion (such as $\mathrm{FWER} \le \alpha$ or $\mathrm{FDR} \le \alpha$) at level $\alpha \in (0,1)$ uniformly over all admissible joint distributions;
(b) maximize statistical power, i.e. the expected proportion of false null hypotheses correctly rejected; and
(c) explicitly incorporate the dependence structure among the test statistics into the adjustment, rather than relying on worst-case independence-based bounds.

In particular, characterize the optimal trade-off between (a)–(c) in the regime $m 	o \infty$ relevant to high-dimensional applications such as DNA microarray analysis, and exhibit a procedure attaining (or approaching) this trade-off.

Sampling of species problem (Bayesian updating under unanticipated outcomes). Consider a population consisting of an unknown, possibly infinite collection of distinct "species" (categories) with unknown relative frequencies. Suppose a statistician models the population by a prior distribution over discrete probability measures on a measurable space of species labels, and suppose a sample X_1, X_2, ..., X_n has been drawn i.i.d. from the population. Assume that when the prior is specified, only a finite list of species labels is assigned positive prior mass, and that a new observation X_{n+1} then takes a value (a "new species") that was not anticipated by the prior, i.e., a label that the prior assigned zero mass.

Formulate and justify a coherent rule for updating the posterior probability distribution over (i) the species composition of the population and (ii) the probability of observing any further previously unanticipated species in future draws, given the appearance of the unanticipated outcome. Equivalently: provide a fully general principled mechanism by which Bayesian conditioning can be extended or replaced so as to incorporate observations whose occurrence had been assigned prior probability zero, and characterize the resulting predictive distribution for subsequent samples.

The problem of updating probabilities in light of unanticipated species/categories is a long-standing foundational issue. It has been substantially addressed (though not fully resolved as a foundational question about conditioning on prior-null events) via Bayesian nonparametric approaches such as the Dirichlet process, Pitman–Yor process, and related species-sampling priors, which give explicit predictive rules accommodating new, previously unseen species. Recent works (e.g., 2022–2024) continue to develop and refine such methods, indicating an active but partially resolved research area.

Let N denote the total number of human beings who will ever have been born by the end of the human species' existence, and let n denote the rank (birth order) of a randomly chosen human among all humans ever to live. Assume the Self-Sampling Assumption: conditional on N, the rank n is uniformly distributed on {1, 2, ..., N}. Suppose we are given an estimate n_0 of the total number of humans born up to the present time, interpreted as the observed rank of a typical currently living person.

The Doomsday argument asserts that, using Bayesian reasoning from a suitable prior on N together with the uniform-rank assumption, one can derive a non-trivial posterior distribution on the remaining future lifetime (or remaining total number of births) N - n_0 of the human race from knowledge of n_0 alone.

Question: Assess the validity of this probabilistic argument. Specifically, determine under what choice of prior on N, and under what precise formulation of the reference class of observers and of the Self-Sampling (or Self-Indication) Assumption, the inference from n_0 to a posterior distribution on N is mathematically and probabilistically justified, and characterize whether and in what sense the resulting prediction of future human lifetime is a legitimate consequence of probability theory rather than an artifact of the chosen prior or reference class.

Consider the following two decision-theoretic puzzles, formulated within the subjectivistic (Bayesian) interpretation of probability theory.

(1) Two envelopes problem. Two indistinguishable envelopes each contain a positive amount of money; one contains exactly twice the amount of the other. An agent selects one envelope at random and, before opening it, is offered the option to switch to the other envelope. Let X denote the amount in the chosen envelope and Y the amount in the other. A naive computation gives E[Y | X = x] = (1/2)(2x) + (1/2)(x/2) = (5/4)x > x, suggesting the agent should always switch, and by symmetry always switch back, which is absurd.

(2) Necktie paradox. Two persons each receive a necktie as a gift and compare their (unknown) prices. They agree that whoever has the more expensive tie must give it to the other. Each reasons: "If my tie is more expensive I lose its value v; if my tie is cheaper I gain something worth more than v; since by symmetry each outcome has probability 1/2, the bet is favorable." Both agents thus regard the wager as advantageous, which is impossible.

Task: Within Bayesian decision theory — that is, taking the agent's beliefs to be encoded by a (possibly improper) prior probability distribution over the relevant monetary quantities, and decisions to be made by maximizing subjective expected utility — formulate a single coherent resolution of both paradoxes. Specifically, identify precisely which step in the naive expected-value reasoning fails (e.g., the use of an improper prior, non-integrability, illegitimate conditioning, nonlinearity of utility, or misuse of the principle of indifference), and provide a general normative principle, agreed upon by subjectivists, that prevents such paradoxical conclusions in all exchange-type problems.

representations.normalized: The Sunrise Problem. Suppose one has observed that a certain binary event (call it "the sun rises") has occurred on each of the past $n$ consecutive days, with no observed failures. Treating the daily occurrences as exchangeable Bernoulli trials with unknown success probability $p$, determine, in a principled and well-justified way, the probability that the event will occur on day $n+1$ given the observed history. In particular: (a) Specify a prior distribution on $p$ (or, more generally, a probabilistic model on the infinite sequence of outcomes) that can be defended as "uninformative" or otherwise canonical, and compute the resulting predictive probability $P(X_{n+1}=1 \mid X_1=\dots=X_n=1)$. (b) Compare and reconcile the answers obtained under different reasonable choices of model and prior (e.g., the uniform prior on $[0,1]$ giving Laplace's rule of succession $(n+1)/(n+2)$, improper Haldane priors, hierarchical priors, or non-exchangeable models that allow for catastrophic failure). (c) Decide whether there is a uniquely "correct" answer to the question of the probability that a long-running uninterrupted event will continue for one more trial, or whether the answer is irreducibly dependent on subjective modeling assumptions.
representations.original: The Sunrise Problem. Suppose one has observed that a certain binary event (call it "the sun rises") has occurred on each of the past $n$ consecutive days, with no observed failures. Treating the daily occurrences as exchangeable Bernoulli trials with unknown success probability $p$, determine, in a principled and well-justified way, the probability that the event will occur on day $n+1$ given the observed history. In particular: (a) Specify a prior distribution on $p$ (or, more generally, a probabilistic model on the infinite sequence of outcomes) that can be defended as "uninformative" or otherwise canonical, and compute the resulting predictive probability $P(X_{n+1}=1 \mid X_1=\dots=X_n=1)$. (b) Compare and reconcile the answers obtained under different reasonable choices of model and prior (e.g., the uniform prior on $[0,1]$ giving Laplace's rule of succession $(n+1)/(n+2)$, improper Haldane priors, hierarchical priors, or non-exchangeable models that allow for catastrophic failure). (c) Decide whether there is a uniquely "correct" answer to the question of the probability that a long-running uninterrupted event will continue for one more trial, or whether the answer is irreducibly dependent on subjective modeling assumptions.

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

The "sunrise problem" is a classical philosophical/statistical question dating back to Laplace, often listed among unsolved problems because no single "correct" answer exists independent of modeling assumptions. It is widely discussed but not considered a problem with a definitive mathematical resolution; its status is best described as unknown/ill-posed in the strict sense.

representations.normalized: In star-formation theory, the stellar initial mass function (IMF) is the probability distribution describing the masses with which stars are formed in a stellar population. Empirically, observations of star-forming regions across vastly different environments (varying metallicity, gas density, turbulence level, magnetic field strength, and redshift) yield IMFs that are remarkably similar, often well approximated by a Salpeter-like power law dN/dM ∝ M^(−2.35) for M ≳ 1 M☉ together with a turnover near ~0.2–0.5 M☉ (e.g., the Kroupa or Chabrier forms). Provide a first-principles physical theory that derives the observed stellar initial mass function from the fundamental processes governing the gravitational collapse, fragmentation, accretion, and feedback of molecular cloud gas, and explain why this mass distribution appears to be approximately universal—i.e., largely independent of the initial conditions of the parent molecular cloud.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The origin and apparent universality of the stellar initial mass function remains an open problem in astrophysics. Reviews and recent simulations (e.g., Krumholz 2014, Hopkins 2018, Guszejnov et al. 2022, and ongoing work in 2024–2025) acknowledge that no complete first-principles theory yet explains the IMF shape and its near-invariance, although turbulent fragmentation, protostellar feedback, and radiative heating models offer partial accounts. Some evidence (e.g., from massive ellipticals and high-redshift observations) suggests the IMF is not strictly universal, further complicating a definitive theory.

Cosmic rays are charged particles (predominantly protons and atomic nuclei) reaching Earth from space. Above an energy threshold of approximately 5 × 10^19 eV (the Greisen–Zatsepin–Kuzmin, or GZK, cutoff), protons traveling cosmological distances are expected to lose energy rapidly through interactions with cosmic microwave background photons (chiefly via pion photoproduction), so that the mean free path becomes only on the order of 50–100 Mpc. Nevertheless, ultra-high-energy cosmic ray events with energies at or above this threshold—most famously the so-called "Oh-My-God" particle at roughly 3 × 10^20 eV—have been observed.

Identify and characterize the physical processes (astrophysical sources, acceleration mechanisms, and propagation effects, possibly including the role of heavier nuclei) that produce cosmic rays with energies exceeding the GZK cutoff. In particular: determine the class(es) of astrophysical accelerators capable of producing such particles, the mechanism by which the requisite energies are attained, and a quantitative explanation consistent with observed arrival directions, energy spectrum, and mass composition at Earth.

As of 2025, the origin and acceleration mechanisms of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays exceeding the GZK cutoff remain unresolved. Although the Pierre Auger Observatory and Telescope Array have observed flux suppression near the predicted GZK energy, the source populations, acceleration processes, and the heavy-nuclei composition reported by Auger leave the question open. Next-generation observatories such as the Global Cosmic Ray Observatory (GCOS) are being proposed specifically to settle this problem.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Multi-wavelength observations show that the dimming is wavelength-dependent (stronger in UV than IR), which strongly favors circumstellar dust — likely from exocomet debris or a tidally disrupted exomoon — as the cause, and rules out opaque solid objects such as alien megastructures. However, no single dust model has yet fully reproduced all features of the short-term dips and the long-term secular fading, so the problem is considered partially solved.

Observations of spiral galaxies show that the orbital (tangential) speed v(r) of stars and gas as a function of distance r from the galactic center remains approximately flat at large r, rather than decreasing as r^{-1/2} as predicted by Newtonian (or general-relativistic) dynamics applied to the visible (luminous) mass distribution. Concretely, given a galaxy with observed luminous-mass surface density Σ(r) (and inferred enclosed mass M_lum(r) = ∫ 2π r' Σ(r') dr'), Newtonian dynamics predicts a circular speed v_N(r) = sqrt(G M_lum(r)/r) which falls off at large r, while measured rotation curves yield v_obs(r) ≈ const for r large.

Problem: Identify the cause of the discrepancy between v_obs(r) and v_N(r). Specifically, determine whether this discrepancy is fully accounted for by an additional non-luminous matter component (dark matter) distributed in a halo around each galaxy — in which case one must establish the nature, particle content, and density profile ρ_DM(r) of that component — or whether the discrepancy instead requires a modification of the gravitational/inertial dynamics on galactic scales (such as a modification of Newton's second law or of the gravitational law at low accelerations), in which case one must give the correct dynamical law and demonstrate that it reproduces observed rotation curves of galaxies as well as other gravitational phenomena.

The singularity theorems of Penrose and Hawking guarantee, under suitable energy and causality conditions, that solutions describing gravitational collapse (e.g. the maximally extended Schwarzschild and Kerr spacetimes) contain incomplete causal geodesics, indicating that the classical description breaks down in the interior region bounded by an event horizon.

Determine whether classical general relativity actually fails to provide a valid description of the geometry in the interior of a black hole, in the sense that the singular behavior predicted by the classical Einstein equations is resolved or modified once additional physical effects are incorporated. Specifically, decide whether any of the following mechanisms (or another such mechanism) yields a singularity-free, geodesically complete effective geometry replacing the classical interior:

(i) quantum-gravitational corrections (for instance via a consistent theory of quantum gravity such as loop quantum gravity, string theory, or asymptotic safety) modifying the effective field equations at high curvature;

(ii) inclusion of spacetime torsion, as in Einstein–Cartan theory, where the connection is metric-compatible but not symmetric and torsion couples to intrinsic spin;

(iii) other classical or semiclassical phenomena (e.g. higher-curvature corrections, nonlinear electrodynamics, or backreaction of quantum fields).

Provide either a rigorous derivation showing that classical general relativity remains valid all the way to a true singularity inside black holes, or a mathematically consistent modification under which the interior geometry is regular.

In general relativity, a stationary, asymptotically flat, electrovacuum black hole solution of the Einstein–Maxwell equations is conjectured (the no-hair theorem) to be characterized completely by three externally observable classical parameters: mass M, electric charge Q, and angular momentum J, with the exterior geometry given by the Kerr–Newman family. Beyond this exterior characterization, address the following:

(a) Do black holes possess a nontrivial internal structure — that is, a physically meaningful geometric, quantum, or information-theoretic substructure inside the event horizon that is not fully determined by (M, Q, J)?

(b) If such an internal structure exists, formulate and describe explicit physical or mathematical procedures (e.g., gravitational wave ringdown spectroscopy, quasinormal mode deviations, tidal Love numbers, near-horizon probes, quantum information signatures) by which an external observer could probe and detect it.

Provide either a proof that the exterior parameters uniquely determine all relevant interior structure, or a construction exhibiting additional internal degrees of freedom together with a feasible probing mechanism.

In the semiclassical treatment of quantum fields on a curved spacetime background, a Schwarzschild black hole of mass M is predicted to emit a flux of particles with a spectrum that, to leading order, is thermal at the Hawking temperature T_H = ℏ c^3 / (8 π G M k_B). If this radiation persists, the black hole loses mass and is expected to evaporate completely in finite time. Under unitary quantum mechanical evolution, the von Neumann entropy of a pure initial state is preserved, so information about the initial state forming the black hole cannot be destroyed.

Resolve the following:

(a) Do black holes, treated within a consistent theory of quantum gravity, in fact emit radiation whose total state (over the full history of formation and evaporation) is exactly thermal, or does the outgoing radiation carry correlations that purify it?

(b) Assuming complete evaporation, give a precise mechanism by which the quantum information encoded in the matter that formed the black hole is either (i) recovered in the outgoing Hawking radiation in a manner consistent with unitarity, (ii) preserved in a stable or long-lived remnant after radiation ceases at some mass scale, or (iii) genuinely lost, requiring a modification of quantum mechanics.

Provide a definitive determination of which of these alternatives is realized, together with a derivation from first principles of quantum gravity.

In the semiclassical treatment of an evaporating black hole, consider an old black hole that has radiated for longer than the Page time. The standard postulates of black hole complementarity assert simultaneously: (i) unitarity of the evaporation process as seen by a distant observer, (ii) validity of effective quantum field theory outside the stretched horizon, and (iii) the equivalence principle, which requires that an observer freely falling through the event horizon encounters no high-energy excitations ("the horizon is a smooth, regular region of spacetime"). An argument based on the monogamy of quantum entanglement shows that these three postulates cannot all hold: after the Page time, the late Hawking radiation must be maximally entangled with the early Hawking radiation (by unitarity), yet the equivalence principle requires that modes just outside the horizon be maximally entangled with their interior partners. This forces one to abandon at least one postulate; one proposed resolution is that the infalling observer encounters a "firewall" — a high-energy region of excited quanta — at or near the horizon, violating the equivalence principle.

Problem: Determine whether such a firewall is actually present at the horizon of an old black hole. Equivalently, identify which of the postulates of black hole complementarity must be modified or abandoned in order to obtain a consistent quantum description of black hole evaporation, and provide a complete and self-consistent account that either establishes the existence of a firewall or demonstrates a mechanism preserving the smoothness of the horizon for the infalling observer.

The black hole firewall paradox (AMPS, 2012) remains an open problem in theoretical physics. While many partial resolutions have been proposed — including the ER=EPR conjecture (Maldacena–Susskind), state-dependence (Papadodimas–Raju), and more recently work on the Page curve via replica wormholes and quantum extremal surfaces (Penington; Almheiri et al., 2019–2020) — no fully consensus resolution exists, and discussion of whether a firewall actually exists at the horizon continues to be active.

representations.normalized:
Consider a binary system of two supermassive black holes (each with mass of order $10^6$–$10^{10}$ solar masses) orbiting one another in a galactic nucleus. Standard dynamical arguments establish the following: at large separations, dynamical friction against stars and gas drives the pair inward; at very small separations (well below one parsec), emission of gravitational waves drives the pair to coalescence on timescales much shorter than the age of the universe. However, at intermediate separations of order one parsec, the loss cone of stars whose orbits intersect the binary is depleted, dynamical friction becomes inefficient, and gravitational-wave emission is still too weak, so the residual hardening timescale exceeds the Hubble time $t_H \approx 1.4\times 10^{10}$ years.

Provide a physical mechanism, together with quantitative estimates, by which a generic supermassive black-hole binary in a realistic galactic-nucleus environment loses sufficient orbital energy and angular momentum at separations near one parsec to reach the gravitational-wave-dominated regime and merge within a time $\lesssim t_H$. The mechanism must be consistent with current observational constraints, including the observation of close supermassive black-hole pairs and the stochastic gravitational-wave background detected at nanohertz frequencies.

A 2024 paper in Physical Review Letters by Alonso-Álvarez, Cline, and Dewar argues that dynamical friction from a self-interacting dark matter spike around supermassive black holes provides the missing energy-loss mechanism, allowing binaries to bridge the final parsec within a Hubble time, and is consistent with the NANOGrav stochastic gravitational-wave background. Other proposed mechanisms (triaxial stellar potentials refilling the loss cone, gas-disk torques, interactions with a third black hole) remain under active investigation. The problem is considered to have plausible candidate solutions but no single, observationally confirmed resolution.

Planck satellite analyses (2013–2018) found no statistically significant evidence favoring the Poincaré dodecahedral space or any other nontrivial topology over a simply connected flat model, but they also do not exclude topologies on scales larger than or comparable to the observable universe. Recent work (e.g., the COMPACT collaboration, 2023–2024) continues to search for cosmic topology signatures without a definitive detection.

Prominent works (e.g., Haspelmath's "The indeterminacy of word segmentation and the nature of morphology and syntax," 2011) argue that no coherent universal definition has been found, while others continue to propose competing criteria. There is no settled consensus, so the problem remains open.

Determine whether there exist any universal grammatical categories: that is, decide whether there is at least one grammatical category C such that every natural human language has C as part of its grammar. If such universal categories exist, characterize them; if not, prove that for every candidate grammatical category there exists a natural language whose grammar lacks it.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The existence of universal grammatical categories remains an open and contested question in linguistics, debated between universalist traditions (e.g., generative grammar, Universal Grammar) and typologists/functionalists (e.g., Haspelmath, Evans & Levinson) who argue that no grammatical category is found in all languages. There is no consensus answer.

representations.normalized:
In theoretical syntax, two foundational frameworks compete to describe the architecture of sentence structure. The constituency (phrase-structure) view holds that syntactic structure is built from part–whole relations among syntactic constituents: words group into phrases, phrases group into larger phrases, and a sentence is a hierarchy of nested constituents. The dependency view holds that syntactic structure consists of asymmetrical binary head–dependent relations between individual words, so that a sentence is a directed tree on its word tokens with no intermediate phrasal nodes.

Determine which of these two formalisms correctly characterizes the underlying nature of syntactic structure in natural language: is syntactic structure fundamentally constituted by part–whole relations among syntactic constituents, or is it fundamentally constituted by asymmetrical dependency relations between words?

2. Determine whether there exist universal patterns or invariants in the development of idiolects and dialects across different languages, communities, and historical periods, and if so characterize these patterns precisely.

3. Decide whether idiolects and dialects can be measured both quantitatively (e.g., via numerical metrics on linguistic features, distances between varieties, or rates of change) and qualitatively (e.g., via structural or typological descriptions). An extant undeciphered writing system is a system of written symbols, attested in surviving inscriptions or manuscripts, whose underlying language and/or sign values have not been reconstructed in a manner that allows consistent reading of the texts. Known examples include (but are not limited to) the Indus script, Linear A, Proto-Elamite, the Rongorongo script of Easter Island, the Cypro-Minoan syllabary, the Voynich manuscript script, the Singapore Stone inscription, and the Olmec/Isthmian (Epi-Olmec) script. A decipherment of such a system consists of: (i) identification of the language (or language family) it encodes, (ii) determination of the phonetic, logographic, or other values of its signs, and (iii) a reading procedure that produces coherent and reproducible translations of the surviving corpus, verifiable against independent evidence (e.g., bilinguals, onomastics, internal consistency, or external linguistic data).

Problem: Produce, for at least one currently undeciphered extant writing system, a decipherment in the above sense — that is, exhibit the encoded language, assign values to the signs, and provide a reading method yielding consistent and independently verifiable translations of the surviving inscriptions in that system.

In historical linguistics, the comparative method is the standard technique for reconstructing ancestral (proto-)languages by systematically comparing cognate words and sound correspondences across attested daughter languages, thereby inferring the phonology, morphology, and lexicon of an unattested common ancestor. Empirically, the method has been applied successfully to language families with a time depth of roughly 6,000–10,000 years (e.g., Proto-Indo-European), but its applicability to deeper time horizons is contested because regular sound change, lexical replacement, and borrowing tend to erode cognate signal over time.

Address the following questions:

(a) Determine whether the comparative method, in principle, can be used to reconstruct features of a proto-language at an arbitrary time depth in the past, or whether fundamentally new methods are required to access the distant linguistic past beyond the reach of the standard comparative method.

(b) Determine whether there exists an inherent time-depth horizon T (measured in years before present) beyond which reliable reconstruction of an ancestral language from its modern descendants is impossible, and if so, characterize T and the factors (rate of lexical replacement, phonological erosion, contact-induced change, etc.) that determine it.

Consider the following two related questions in the comparative study of animal communication and human language:

1. To what extent can non-human animals (e.g., great apes, parrots, dolphins, cetaceans) be taught to acquire and productively use elements of human language, including vocabulary, grammar, and recursive or compositional structure? Characterize the limits of such acquisition across species and modalities (vocal, gestural, lexigram-based).

2. To what extent do natural animal communication systems share formal properties with human language? In particular, determine whether features such as compositionality (e.g., combinatorial structure in bird calls or primate alarm calls), displacement, productivity, or syntactic recursion are genuinely present in any non-human communication system, and provide rigorous criteria for distinguishing such properties from simpler signaling behavior.

Provide a principled account of which properties of human language are uniquely human and which are shared with other species' communicative systems.

Consider human natural language as it is actually used, where speakers and groups exhibit systematic variation along several dimensions: idiolects (the speech patterns of an individual), dialects (regional or community varieties), sociolects (varieties tied to social class or group), jargons (specialized vocabularies of professions or disciplines), and argots (in-group or secretive vocabularies). Such variation can cause misunderstandings when individuals or groups attempt to communicate.

Determine principles, strategies, or methods by which speakers and groups can handle this variation so as to achieve effective and successful communication with minimal misunderstanding. Specifically, identify the best practices for ensuring efficient communication across linguistic varieties in: (i) everyday interpersonal interaction, (ii) educational settings, (iii) scientific discourse, and (iv) philosophical discussion.

Develop a rigorous framework for the quantitative and qualitative comparison of linguistic competence (the underlying tacit knowledge of a language's grammar, lexicon, phonology, and semantics possessed by a speaker) and linguistic performance (the actual production and comprehension of language in concrete situations, including errors, hesitations, and contextual variation) across individuals and across groups of speakers. Specifically, propose and justify:

1. A formal definition of measurable quantities that capture aspects of competence (e.g., grammaticality judgments, productive rule mastery, lexical breadth and depth) distinct from performance (e.g., fluency, accuracy in real-time production, comprehension under load).
2. Methods (statistical, information-theoretic, or otherwise) for aggregating these measurements into comparable scores for individuals and for groups, including how to handle inter-rater variability, sample size effects, and confounds such as dialect, register, and proficiency.
3. Qualitative analytic procedures that complement the quantitative measures and allow meaningful cross-individual and cross-group comparison without conflating competence with performance.
4. Criteria by which one such method can be judged superior to another for the purposes of cross-individual and cross-group comparison.

Identify the best such methods according to these criteria.

An argot is a specialized, often secretive, vocabulary and idiom used by a particular group (such as a profession, subculture, or criminal network) to communicate within the group while concealing meaning from outsiders. Provide a rigorous account of the following three interrelated questions about argots as a linguistic and sociolinguistic phenomenon:

1. Formation: By what social, psychological, and linguistic mechanisms do argots come into being within a community? Describe the processes (lexical borrowing, semantic shift, phonological disguise, metaphor, code-mixing, etc.) and the social conditions that give rise to them.

2. Function: What communicative, identity-marking, exclusionary, and pragmatic roles do argots play for their speakers and for outsiders? Characterize how an argot operates as a system within a host language, including its interaction with grammar, register, and group identity.

3. Acquisition: What are the most effective methods by which an outsider, or a new member of the in-group, can become proficient in a given argot? Identify principles of immersion, lexical learning, contextual inference, and social validation that lead to genuine competence.

The task is to give a comprehensive, evidence-based, and predictive theory addressing all three questions.

representations.normalized: In translation studies, several competing paradigms have been proposed for guiding the production of high-quality translations between natural languages. Two classical axes of opposition are: (i) fidelity (a translation that adheres closely to the literal form, wording, and structure of the source text) versus transparency (a translation that reads as if it had been originally composed in the target language and idiom); and (ii) formal equivalence (preserving the lexical, syntactic, and structural features of the source) versus dynamic (functional) equivalence (preserving the effect on the reader and the communicative function rather than the form). Determine, with principled justification, what the best general strategy is for producing high-quality translations: should translators prioritize fidelity or transparency, formal equivalence or dynamic equivalence, or some other framework or hybrid? Provide criteria under which one approach is preferable to another.

Each step introduces a "translation loss," understood as a discrepancy in meaning, nuance, register, or information content between the source and target texts. When a text is translated from an already-translated text (rather than from the original), these losses can accumulate across the chain of translations, in the manner of the game commonly known as "Chinese whispers."

Develop a principled methodology — together with appropriate formal definitions, quantitative measures, and procedures — for: (i) precisely defining and quantifying the translation loss incurred at a single translation step; (ii) modeling how such losses compose and accumulate across a chain of successive translations T_1, T_2, ..., T_n; and (iii) determining strategies that minimize the cumulative loss when one must translate from a translation rather than from the original source.

Provide a framework that addresses these three points and discuss conditions under which cumulative translation loss can be bounded or reduced.

Model a monolingual dictionary as a finite directed graph D = (W, E), where W is the set of headwords (the dictionary's lexicon) and, for each word w ∈ W, its definition is a finite nonempty multiset of words drawn from W, inducing directed edges from w to each word used in its definition. Say that D contains a definitional cycle if the directed graph D has a directed cycle. Given that natural languages exhibit features such as vagueness (definitions admit borderline cases) and polysemy (a single headword may carry multiple distinct senses, each with its own definition), address the following:

(1) Identify a set of structural principles (good practices) under which a dictionary D, intended to cover a natural language L, can be constructed so as to minimize the number and length of definitional cycles in D while still providing, for every headword, a definition composed only of words in W.

(2) Determine whether it is possible, in principle, to construct such a dictionary D for a natural language L that contains no definitional cycles at all — i.e., such that D is a directed acyclic graph — and justify the answer in light of the finiteness of W and the semantic phenomena (vagueness, polysemy) intrinsic to natural languages.

This is a foundational question in lexicography and the philosophy of language rather than a settled mathematical theorem. Studies of dictionary "definition graphs" (e.g., work by Picard, Blondel, Levary, and others on kernels and strongly connected components of definitional digraphs) have shown that every finite monolingual dictionary necessarily contains definitional cycles, since a finite vocabulary cannot be fully defined acyclically without external grounding. Approaches such as defining vocabularies (e.g., Longman's ~2000-word defining vocabulary) and semantic primitives (Wierzbicka's NSM) are partial mitigations, but full elimination is generally regarded as impossible. The general question of best practices remains an active area of lexicographic research.

In the field of lexicography (the theory and practice of compiling dictionaries), a "lexicographic error" refers to any inaccuracy, omission, inconsistency, or misleading representation in a dictionary entry (e.g., in spelling, pronunciation, grammatical labels, definitions, translation equivalents, usage examples, or cross-references). A "lexicographic information cost" refers to the cognitive, temporal, and practical effort a user must invest to consult a dictionary and retrieve the information they need; it includes search costs (locating an entry), comprehension costs (understanding the entry's structure and content), and interpretation costs (mapping the retrieved data to the user's actual information need in a specific situation of use, such as text reception, text production, translation, or knowledge acquisition).

Develop a general methodology, together with measurable criteria and concrete design principles, that simultaneously achieves both of the following goals for a dictionary (in either printed or electronic form):

(a) Minimize the rate and severity of lexicographic errors across all entries and information categories.

(b) Minimize the lexicographic information costs incurred by users in each identified situation of use.

Specifically, give: (i) precise definitions and quantitative measures of lexicographic errors and of the various components of lexicographic information costs; (ii) a procedure for systematically detecting and correcting errors during dictionary compilation and maintenance; and (iii) design rules for macrostructure, microstructure, access structure, and (for electronic dictionaries) interactive features that provably reduce the user's information costs, with a demonstrated trade-off analysis between (a) and (b).

Word-sense disambiguation (WSD) is the computational task of determining, for each occurrence of an ambiguous word in a natural-language text, which of its possible senses (drawn from a fixed sense inventory such as a dictionary or lexical database) is intended in that context. A WSD system is a software procedure that takes as input a finite text together with a designated target word occurrence and outputs a single sense label from the inventory. Call such a system "perfect" if, for every input text and every target occurrence, its output coincides with the sense intended by a competent native speaker (equivalently, the gold-standard human-annotated sense), in every natural language and across all domains.

Question: Does there exist a software procedure (in the sense of a Turing-computable algorithm, possibly with arbitrarily large but finite resources of memory and training data) that achieves perfect computational word-sense disambiguation as defined above? If such a procedure exists, exhibit a method by which it can be constructed and justify its correctness. If no such procedure exists, provide a proof of impossibility.

Word-sense induction (WSI) is the unsupervised computational task of automatically discovering the distinct senses (meanings) of a given word from its usage in a large, unannotated text corpus, without recourse to any predefined sense inventory (such as a dictionary or WordNet). Formally, one is given a target word w together with a collection of contexts C(w) = {c_1, c_2, ..., c_n} in which w occurs, and the goal is to produce a partition (or soft clustering) of C(w) into groups such that contexts in the same group correspond to the same underlying sense of w, and contexts in different groups correspond to distinct senses. An algorithm for WSI is said to be "accurate" if, for an arbitrary target word drawn from natural language, its induced clustering agrees (up to relabeling) with a gold-standard human sense partition to within a prescribed tolerance under a standard evaluation measure (e.g., paired F-score, V-measure, or B-cubed).

Question: Is accurate computational word-sense induction, in the above sense, feasible? That is, does there exist an algorithm that, for any target word in a natural language and a sufficiently large corpus of its contexts, outputs a clustering that matches the gold-standard human sense partition to within the prescribed tolerance? If such an algorithm exists, exhibit it and explain why it succeeds; if no such algorithm can exist, prove a corresponding impossibility result and explain the obstruction.
