representations.normalized:
Two related two-player combinatorial games are defined as follows.

Beanstalk. The "Giant" picks a starting positive integer $n_0 > 1$. The players (Jack and the Giant) move alternately, starting with Jack, producing a sequence $n_0, n_1, n_2, \ldots$ of positive integers. From a current value $n$, the next value is obtained by the rule
- if $n$ is even, the next value is $n/2$;
- if $n$ is odd, the mover chooses the next value to be either $3n+1$ or $3n-1$ (so for odd $n$, the player to move has a genuine choice, while for even $n$ the move is forced).
The first player who is forced to (or chooses to) reach $1$ on their move loses; equivalently, $1$ is the terminal position and the player who moves to $1$ wins (use either standard convention consistently).

Question (Beanstalk): Does Jack (the first player) have a winning strategy from every odd starting integer $n_0 > 1$?

Beans-Don't-Talk. Played on positive integers with the analogous rule: from $n$, if $n$ is even move to $n/2$; if $n$ is odd, the player to move chooses the next value to be either $(3n+1)/2$ or $(3n-1)/2$ (whichever apply as positive integers). Positions are classified into N-, P-, and O-positions; an O-position is one of infinite remoteness, i.e., a position from which optimal play need never terminate (a drawn position under best play). Remoteness is defined recursively: terminal positions have remoteness $0$; the remoteness of an N-position is $1$ plus the minimum remoteness over moves to P-positions; the remoteness of a P-position is $1$ plus the maximum remoteness over available moves; positions whose remoteness under this recursion is infinite are called O-positions.

Question (Beans-Don't-Talk): Do there exist any O-positions, i.e., starting positions of infinite remoteness?

These games, introduced by John Isbell and John Conway and analyzed by Guy (Mathematics Magazine, 1986), are closely tied to Collatz-type dynamics. No published resolution of either question (Jack's winning strategy from every odd starting integer in Beanstalk, or the existence of O-positions in Beans-Don't-Talk) appears in the available literature; they continue to be listed among unsolved combinatorial-game problems.

representations.normalized:
Konane is a two-player partizan combinatorial game played on a rectangular board initially filled with alternating Black and White stones in a checkerboard pattern, with two adjacent central stones removed. On each turn, the player to move (Black or White) selects one of their own stones and jumps it orthogonally over an adjacent opposing stone into an immediately following empty square, removing the jumped stone; multiple consecutive jumps in a straight line by the same stone are permitted in a single move. A player who cannot move loses.

Within the framework of partizan combinatorial game theory (game values, canonical forms, infinitesimals such as 0, ∗, ∗n, ↑, ↓, n·↑, and dyadic rationals 2^{-n}, together with the operations of cooling, heating, atomic weight, and temperature), carry out a structural analysis of positions arising in Konane. In particular:

(a) Classify the infinitesimal values that arise as game values of Konane positions, and characterize which infinitesimals (beyond the known examples 0, ∗, ∗2, ↑, and 2^{-n}) can occur.

(b) Determine whether Konane positions can realize hot games of arbitrarily high temperature, and exhibit explicit families of positions whose temperatures grow without bound, together with their canonical forms or mean/temperature pairs.

(c) More generally, describe the set of game values realizable by Konane positions on finite boards.

In combinatorial game theory, a (short) game is built recursively from sets of left and right options, written G = {G^L | G^R}. The basic values 0 = {·|·} and ∗ = {0|0} are standard, and one defines

  ∗2 := {0, ∗ | 0, ∗}.

Given a class C of combinatorial games (a "ruleset"), say that a value v occurs in the habitat of C if there is a position P playable under the rules of C whose game-theoretic value equals v. It is known that ∗2 does not occur in Blockbusting, Hackenbush, Col, or Go, while ∗2 does occur in Konane and in 6 × 6 Chess.

Determine the habitat of ∗2 in the following three rulesets: decide, in each case, whether there exists a position of value ∗2.
 (a) Chilled Go (Go endgame positions evaluated under the chilling operator of Berlekamp–Wolfe).
 (b) Domineering (the two-player game on a rectangular grid in which Left places vertical 1×2 dominoes and Right places horizontal 1×2 dominoes, on arbitrary finite subsets of the grid).
 (c) 8 × 8 Chess.

 (a) Chilled Go (Go endgame positions evaluated under the chilling operator of Berlekamp–Wolfe).
 (b) Domineering (the two-player game on a rectangular grid in which Left places vertical 1×2 dominoes and Right places horizontal 1×2 dominoes, on arbitrary finite subsets of the grid).
 (c) 8 × 8 Chess.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Subsequent work on Domineering endgame databases has exhibited positions of value ∗2 (and ∗3) in standard Domineering, contrary to earlier conjectures, so the Domineering part is settled affirmatively. Positions of value ∗2 have also been reported in chilled Go. The 8 × 8 Chess case does not appear to be conclusively settled in the literature, so the overall question on the habitat of ∗2 is only partially resolved.

Consider the following families of two-dimensional Nim, played by two players who alternate moves under the normal play convention (the player unable to move loses).

Setup. A position consists of a finite two-dimensional array of heaps of beans, indexed by the cells of a fixed board. Three board geometries are considered:
 (R) Rectangular: heaps occupy the cells of an m × n rectangular grid.
 (T) Triangular: heaps occupy the cells of a triangular array (so each cell has up to six neighbors arranged in the triangular lattice).
 (H) Hexagonal: heaps occupy the cells of a hexagonal array.

A legal move chooses a single row, column, or (where applicable) diagonal line of cells in the board, selects a nonempty contiguous block of heaps along that line, and removes a strictly positive number of beans from each heap of the chosen block (the number removed may differ from heap to heap, provided each chosen heap loses at least one bean). The "contiguous-heaps" restriction is the requirement that the chosen heaps form a consecutive block along the chosen line with no gaps.

Problem. For each of the three board geometries (R), (T), (H), and with the contiguous-heaps restriction in force:
 (a) Determine the Sprague–Grundy value (nim-value) of an arbitrary starting position as a function of the heap sizes and the board dimensions.
 (b) In particular, characterize the P-positions (previous-player-winning positions) and provide an efficient procedure to decide, given a position, whether it is an N-position or a P-position, together with a winning move when it is an N-position.

A polyomino is a finite union of unit squares from the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^2$, taken up to translation, rotation, and reflection; here we allow polyominoes to be disconnected, i.e., the constituent unit squares need not form an edge-connected set. A polyomino $P$ is said to tile a rectangle $R$ (an $m\times n$ axis-aligned rectangle of unit cells) if finitely many congruent copies of $P$ can be placed in $R$ so that every cell of $R$ is covered exactly once.

Consider the two disconnected polyominoes:
(a) $P_1$ consisting of two unit squares with centers at $(0,0)$ and $(2,0)$ (two cells separated by one empty cell in a row);
(b) $P_2$ consisting of three unit squares with centers at $(0,0)$, $(2,0)$, and $(4,0)$ (three collinear cells, each separated from the next by one empty cell).

For each of $P_1$ and $P_2$:
1. Determine whether there exists any rectangle that can be tiled by congruent copies of the polyomino.
2. If such a rectangle exists, determine the smallest such rectangle (smallest by area, and among those with smallest area, describe all admissible dimensions).

More generally, for an arbitrary disconnected polyomino of analogous "linear gap" type, determine whether it admits a rectangle tiling and, if so, find the minimal rectangle.

representations.normalized:
In one-dimensional Peg Solitaire, a position is a finite binary word over the alphabet {0,1}, where 1 denotes a peg occupying a cell and 0 denotes an empty cell. A single move acts on three consecutive cells and replaces a pattern of the form 110 by 001, or 011 by 100 (i.e., a peg jumps over an adjacent peg into the empty cell immediately beyond it, and the jumped-over peg is removed). A binary word w is said to be reducible to one peg if, by a finite sequence of such moves, it can be transformed into a word containing exactly one 1.

Problem: Characterize explicitly the set of all binary words that can be reduced to one peg under these rules.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The set of one-dimensional peg solitaire configurations reducible to a single peg is known to form a regular language, and an explicit characterization plus a linear-time reduction algorithm was given by Moore and Eppstein (2000); the result was also obtained earlier by Plambeck (1991) and appears as an exercise in Manna's 1974 book. Thus the problem is solved.

Exhibit a two-player combinatorial game G satisfying all of the following properties simultaneously:

(1) Simple, playable rules: G has a concise, natural rule set, played on a parametrized family of positions (so that an instance has a well-defined size n), and is genuinely playable by humans, not merely a formal encoding of a computational problem.

(2) Intricate explicit solution: there exists an explicit description of optimal play (for example a closed-form strategy, an explicit winning-set characterization, a Sprague–Grundy value formula, or an algorithm of low complexity) that is mathematically nontrivial and not a brute-force enumeration over game trees.

(3) Provable hardness: the natural decision problem associated with G — given an instance of G, decide whether the player to move wins under optimal play — is provably NP-hard, or hard for a complexity class containing NP (such as PSPACE-hard or EXPTIME-hard), with a rigorous reduction.

Either produce such a game G together with proofs of (1)–(3), or prove that no game satisfying all three properties can exist.

Consider the impartial combinatorial game of closed 1×n Dots-and-Boxes, played on a 2×(n+1) array of dots whose outer boundary edges are all already drawn, so that the only undrawn edges are the n interior vertical edges and the 2n interior horizontal edges forming a 1×n strip of unit cells. Two players alternate drawing a single undrawn edge; whenever a player completes the fourth side of a unit box they claim that box and must move again. The player who claims the majority of the n boxes wins. Within the Sprague–Grundy / nimber framework adapted to Dots-and-Boxes (via the associated Nimstring game and its loony-endgame theory), accomplish the following:

(a) Develop a complete theory describing optimal play and game values of all closed 1×n Dots-and-Boxes positions.

(b) Prove additional nimber decomposition theorems showing how the nim-value of a closed 1×n position decomposes in terms of nim-values of smaller closed components.

(c) Compile a complete database of nim-values of closed 1×n Dots-and-Boxes positions.

In combinatorial game theory, the heating and overheating operators act on games as follows. For a game G and parameters s and t (typically with s a game value and t a "temperature"), the overheating operator ∫_s^t is defined recursively by

  ∫_s^t G = s + ∫_s^t G   if G is an integer (with appropriate base cases for 0 and ±1),
  ∫_s^t G = { ∫_s^t G^L + t  |  ∫_s^t G^R − t }   otherwise,

where G^L and G^R range over the Left and Right options of G. (Variants in the literature replace s by another game or adjust the integer base case.) Given a finite sum of games of the form

  H = ∫_{s_1}^{t_1} G_1  +  ∫_{s_2}^{t_2} G_2  +  ⋯  +  ∫_{s_k}^{t_k} G_k,

in which the overheating operators applied to the individual summands may use different parameter pairs (s_i, t_i), develop a general method for computing the value of H and for playing such a sum optimally. In particular, identify a simple, explicit relation between the parameters (s_i, t_i) of the constituent operators and the value (or canonical form) of the resulting sum H, and characterize on which domains of games the resulting correspondence is monotonic and/or linear in its parameters.

Overheating operators were introduced by Berlekamp for analyzing games like Blockbusting and have been studied further by Moews and others. While specific identities and closed-form expressions involving overheating have appeared in subsequent work, a general theory describing sums of games with varying overheating parameters and a simple parameter-to-value relation does not appear to have been established in full generality. Monotonicity and linearity are known to depend on the parameters and the domain, but a complete characterization could not be verified from available sources.

Astrophysical and cosmological observations (galactic rotation curves, gravitational lensing, the cosmic microwave background power spectrum, large-scale structure formation, and the Bullet Cluster) indicate the existence of a non-luminous component of matter, called dark matter, whose presence has so far been inferred only through its gravitational effects. No particle in the Standard Model of particle physics (quarks, leptons, gauge bosons, or the Higgs boson) provides a viable candidate consistent with all of these observations.

Identify the physical constituent of dark matter. Specifically:

(a) Determine the nature of the dark matter entity: e.g., a new fundamental particle (such as a weakly interacting massive particle, axion, sterile neutrino, or other), a primordial black hole population, a modification of gravitational dynamics, or some other physical entity. Specify its mass (or mass spectrum), spin, and non-gravitational interactions (if any) with Standard Model fields.

(b) Determine its spatial distribution: how dark matter is distributed within galactic halos, galaxy clusters, and on cosmological scales, in a manner consistent with the observed gravitational phenomena and with the measured cosmological abundance Ω_DM h² ≈ 0.12.

A complete solution must yield predictions consistent with all current gravitational observations attributed to dark matter and must be falsifiable by direct detection, indirect detection, collider, or astrophysical experiments.

representations.normalized:
In the Standard Model of particle physics, the proton is stable because baryon number is an accidental global symmetry of the renormalizable Lagrangian. Many proposed extensions of the Standard Model (for example, Grand Unified Theories that embed SU(3)_C × SU(2)_L × U(1)_Y into a larger simple gauge group such as SU(5) or SO(10)) introduce new gauge bosons or scalar mediators that violate baryon number and induce proton decay through channels such as p → e^+ π^0, p → μ^+ π^0, p → ν̄ K^+, and similar two-body modes.

Current experimental searches (notably large underground water-Cherenkov detectors) have established lower bounds on the partial mean lifetime of the proton at roughly τ_p ≳ 10^34 years, with the strongest published limit being τ(p → e^+ π^0) > 2.4 × 10^34 years, but have observed no candidate decay events.

Determine the following:

(a) Does the proton decay, i.e., is its mean lifetime finite?

(b) If yes, through which beyond-Standard-Model interaction (specifically, what mediator, what effective baryon- and lepton-number-violating operator, and what dominant decay channel) does it decay?

(c) What is the value of the proton mean lifetime τ_p?

Let $K \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a convex body, that is, a compact convex set with nonempty interior. A chord of $K$ is a closed line segment whose endpoints lie on the boundary $\partial K$. A chord $[p,q]$ with $p,q \in \partial K$ is called a double normal (or doubly normal chord) of $K$ if there exists a supporting hyperplane of $K$ at $p$ that is perpendicular to the segment $[p,q]$ and, simultaneously, a supporting hyperplane of $K$ at $q$ that is perpendicular to the segment $[p,q]$. Equivalently, $K$ lies in the slab between two parallel hyperplanes through $p$ and $q$ orthogonal to $pq$.

Prove or disprove: every convex body $K \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ admits at least $n$ distinct double normals.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The problem was settled affirmatively by N. H. Kuiper in 1964 ("Double normals of convex bodies", Israel J. Math.), using Lusternik–Schnirelmann category arguments to show every convex body in $\mathbb{R}^n$ admits at least $n$ double normals. Subsequent work (e.g., by Pushkar', Zamfirescu, and others) extended and refined this result.

Let n ≥ 2. A convex body in Euclidean space E^n is a compact convex subset with nonempty interior. A direction in E^n is an equivalence class of nonzero vectors under positive scalar multiplication (equivalently, a point of the unit sphere S^(n-1) with antipodes identified). A line segment in E^n is said to realize a direction u if it has positive length and is parallel to u.

Question: Does there exist a convex body C ⊂ E^n such that for every direction u in E^n there is a line segment of positive length contained in the boundary ∂C that is parallel to u?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The problem was solved in the negative by G. Ewald, D. G. Larman, and C. A. Rogers (1970), who proved that the set of directions of line segments lying on the boundary of a convex body in E^n must be of σ-finite (n−2)-dimensional Hausdorff measure, and in particular cannot exhaust all directions for n ≥ 2.

representations.normalized:
Let C be a convex body in Euclidean n-space E^n, i.e., a compact convex set with nonempty interior. A point x in C is called an extreme point of C if x cannot be written as a nontrivial convex combination of two distinct points of C. A point x in C is called an exposed point of C if there exists a supporting hyperplane H of C such that H ∩ C = {x}. Every exposed point is extreme, but the converse can fail.

A subset A of a topological space X is said to be of the first category (meager) in X if A can be written as a countable union of subsets each of which is nowhere dense in X. Recall the Straszewicz–Klee theorem: the set of exposed points of a convex body is dense in the set of its extreme points.

Question: For every convex body C in E^n (n ≥ 3), must the set of nonexposed extreme points of C be of the first category in the set of extreme points of C? Equivalently, must the boundary of C contain a sequence of closed sets J_1, J_2, … such that for every nonexposed extreme point p of C and every J_i containing p, the exposed points of C accumulate at p from outside J_i?

The problem is classically attributed to Klee. It is known to hold in dimension 2, and in higher dimensions only for special cases such as smooth convex bodies. A 2025 preprint (Cheng, Jiang, Yuan, "On Klee's problem of convex bodies in Banach spaces", arXiv:2510.07031) treats the problem under strict-convexity/Gâteaux-smoothness hypotheses, indicating the general finite-dimensional case remains open.

Let $n$ and $r$ be integers with $0 < r < n$. For a finite set $S$ of points in Euclidean $n$-space $\mathbb{E}^n$, say that $S$ has the $(n,r)$-flat-intersection property if there exists an $r$-dimensional affine flat $F \subset \mathbb{E}^n$ such that:
\begin{itemize}
\item $F$ contains at least $r+1$ points of $S$, and
\item $F$ intersects the convex hull of the remaining points of $S$ (those points of $S$ not lying on $F$).
\end{itemize}
Define $g(n,r)$ to be the smallest positive integer $k$ such that every set of $k$ points in $\mathbb{E}^n$ has the $(n,r)$-flat-intersection property.

Determine $g(n,r)$ for all integers $n,r$ with $0 < r < n$.

(It is known that $g(n,r) = n+2$ whenever $n \le 2r+1$; the problem is to determine $g(n,r)$ in the remaining range $n > 2r+1$.)

Let $n \geq 2$ and $r \geq 3$ be integers. For a finite set $S \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, denote by $\operatorname{conv}(S)$ its convex hull and by $\partial \operatorname{conv}(S)$ the boundary of that convex hull. Say that a finite set $X \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ is in convex position if every point of $X$ lies on $\partial \operatorname{conv}(X)$.

Define $h(n,r)$ to be the smallest positive integer $k$ with the following property: every set of $k$ points in $\mathbb{R}^n$ contains a subset $X$ of exactly $r$ points such that $X$ is in convex position (i.e., each point of $X$ lies on the boundary of $\operatorname{conv}(X)$).

Determine $h(n,r)$ as a function of $n$ and $r$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

This is a higher-dimensional generalization of the classical Erdős–Szekeres "happy ending" problem. Even in the planar case n=2, the exact value of the Erdős–Szekeres number ES(r)=h(2,r) is known only for r ≤ 6, and the general conjectured formula 2^{r-2}+1 remains open (with recent improvements on the upper bound by Suk and others). For n ≥ 3 the exact values are likewise not known in general. Thus the problem of determining h(n,r) in closed form is open.

Let n ≥ 2 be an integer. A convex body in ℝⁿ is a compact convex subset of ℝⁿ with nonempty interior, equipped with the Euclidean metric d. A homeomorphism f : K → K of a compact metric space (K, d) is called expansive if there exists a constant c > 0 (called an expansivity constant) such that for every pair of distinct points x, y ∈ K there exists an integer n ∈ ℤ with d(fⁿ(x), fⁿ(y)) > c.

Question: Does there exist an n-dimensional convex body K ⊂ ℝⁿ that admits an expansive self-homeomorphism? Equivalently, for which n ≥ 2 (if any) can a compact convex set with nonempty interior in ℝⁿ support an expansive homeomorphism?

Question: Does there exist an n-dimensional convex body K ⊂ ℝⁿ that admits an expansive self-homeomorphism? Equivalently, for which n ≥ 2 (if any) can a compact convex set with nonempty interior in ℝⁿ support an expansive homeomorphism?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

For n = 2, the question is settled in the negative: by results of Hiraide and Lewowicz on expansive homeomorphisms of compact surfaces, the 2-disk admits no expansive homeomorphism, so no 2-dimensional convex body does either. For n ≥ 3, the problem for convex bodies (e.g., the closed 3-ball) appears to remain open: standard references on expansive dynamics state non-existence only for the interval, circle, and 2-disk, and we found no published resolution for higher-dimensional balls or convex bodies.

The two-equireciprocal-points problem (posed by Klee and addressed by Helfenstein and Wirsing) appears to remain unresolved. For a bounded subset $S \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, let $\operatorname{diam}(S) = \sup\{\|x-y\| : x,y \in S\}$ denote its Euclidean diameter. Borsuk's question asks: for every integer $n \geq 1$ and every bounded set $S \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, is it possible to partition (equivalently, cover) $S$ as $S = S_1 \cup S_2 \cup \cdots \cup S_{n+1}$ with $\operatorname{diam}(S_i) < \operatorname{diam}(S)$ for each $i = 1, \ldots, n+1$?

Equivalently (the reduction to convex bodies of constant width): is it true that for every $n \geq 1$, every convex body $K \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ of constant width $w$ (i.e., the distance between every pair of parallel supporting hyperplanes equals $w$) can be covered by $n+1$ closed sets $F_1, \ldots, F_{n+1}$ such that no $F_i$ contains a pair of points $x, y$ with $\|x-y\| = w$?

Determine, for each dimension $n$, whether this statement holds.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Borsuk's conjecture is known to be true for $n \leq 3$ (Perkal, Eggleston) and for smooth convex bodies in all dimensions (Hadwiger). It was disproved in general by Kahn and Kalai (1993), who constructed counterexamples in high dimensions; the smallest known dimension for a counterexample has been progressively lowered (Bondarenko 2014: $n=65$; Jenrich–Brouwer 2014: $n=64$). The conjecture remains open for $4 \leq n \leq 63$.

Let $C \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a convex body (a compact convex set with nonempty interior). A finite set $S \subset C$ is called pairwise antipodal with respect to $C$ if for every pair of distinct points $x, y \in S$ there exist two distinct parallel supporting hyperplanes $H_x, H_y$ of $C$ such that $x \in H_x$ and $y \in H_y$.

For a class $\mathcal{K}$ of convex bodies in $\mathbb{R}^n$, define
$$g(\mathcal{K}) \;=\; \sup\bigl\{\,|S|\;:\; C \in \mathcal{K},\; S \subset C \text{ is pairwise antipodal with respect to } C\,\bigr\}.$$

Problem. Determine $g(\mathcal{K})$ for natural classes $\mathcal{K}$ of convex bodies (for instance: all convex bodies in $\mathbb{R}^n$; centrally symmetric convex bodies; smooth convex bodies; strictly convex bodies; convex polytopes; simplices; bodies of constant width; zonotopes; etc.).

In particular, given a class $\mathcal{K}$, find the exact value of $g(\mathcal{K})$ and characterize those members $C \in \mathcal{K}$ that admit a pairwise antipodal set attaining this value.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

For the class of all convex bodies in $\mathbb{R}^n$, Danzer and Grünbaum (1962) proved $g = 2^n$, attained exactly by affine $n$-cubes (parallelepipeds). Sharpenings and analogues exist for related notions (strictly antipodal sets, edge-antipodal polytopes, Minkowski arrangements) by Bezdek–Bisztriczky–Böröczky, Makai–Martini and others. However, the value of $g(\mathcal{K})$ is not known in closed form for many natural subclasses, and the broader programme of determining $g(\mathcal{K})$ across various classes $\mathcal{K}$ remains a guiding open question.

The problem is part of the Erdős–Komjáth program on countable decompositions of ℝ² and ℝ³. Under the Continuum Hypothesis, results of Erdős–Komjáth (and subsequent extensions) provide countable decompositions of ℝⁿ avoiding repeated distances (and even stronger configurations such as isosceles triangles). In ZFC alone, the existence of such a countable distance-Sidon covering of ℝⁿ for n ≥ 2 is known to be independent / not settled, and the analogous problem for arbitrary n remains open. Thus the problem is partially resolved (consistent under CH) but not fully solved in ZFC.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

A classical theorem of Gromov (1967) settles the question affirmatively when $k$ is even: a centered convex body in $\mathbb{R}^n$ all of whose central $k$-sections are affinely equivalent must be an ellipsoid when $k$ is even with $2 \le k < n$. For odd $k \ge 3$ (with $k < n-1$) the problem is generally still considered open in the full generality stated, and is closely tied to the (still partially open) Banach/Gromov characterization-of-ellipsoids program; some recent advances address the projection analogue and the isometric Banach conjecture in many dimensions, but a complete solution covering all odd $k$ is not established. Thus the question is partially solved.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem (often called the "perfect triangle" problem, attributed to Richard Guy) is widely regarded as open. No example has been found and it is conjectured none exists. Partial results have been obtained, e.g., a perfect triangle cannot be isosceles, and there exist integer-sided triangles with three rational medians but not known to have integer area. Recent preprints (e.g., 2021) continue to address the question without a definitive resolution.

Let S be a set of positive integers and let M be a set of nonnegative integers with 0 ∈ M. For a positive integer n, define p(S, M; n) to be the number of partitions of n of the form n = a_1 m_1 + a_2 m_2 + ⋯ + a_k m_k, where a_1 < a_2 < ⋯ < a_k are distinct elements of S and each multiplicity m_i is a nonzero element of M; equivalently, p(S, M; n) counts the partitions of n in which every part lies in S and the multiplicity with which each part appears lies in M.

Determine whether there exist sets S and M such that all three of the following hold:
1. Both S and M are infinite.
2. p(S, M; n) ≥ 1 for every sufficiently large integer n (every large n has at least one such partition).
3. p(S, M; n) grows at most polynomially in n, i.e., there exist constants C > 0 and d > 0 such that p(S, M; n) ≤ C n^d for all n ≥ 1.

Either exhibit such a pair (S, M), or prove that no such pair exists.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question is one of Wilf's unsolved problems on integer partitions. Partial results exist: Canfield and Wilf showed that if M is taken to be the full set of nonnegative integers, then p(S, M; n) cannot have polynomial growth while representing all large n. Subsequent work (e.g., on the growth of restricted integer partition functions) has produced weakly-superpolynomial growth examples and lower bounds when M is infinite and S has enough density, but the full question allowing both S and M to be arbitrary infinite sets remains open.

Let p be an odd prime. For a nonnegative integer n, consider the multiset of residues
{ C(n,k) mod p : 0 ≤ k ≤ n, C(n,k) not ≡ 0 (mod p) },
where C(n,k) denotes the binomial coefficient. Call n p-balanced if, within this multiset, the number of residues that are nonzero quadratic residues modulo p equals the number of residues that are quadratic nonresidues modulo p.

Call a prime p special if there is no integer n with 0 ≤ n < p that is p-balanced. (By convention, include p = 2 as special.)

It is known that p = 2, 3, and 11 are special, and that no prime p with 11 < p < 1{,}000{,}000 is special.

Question: Does there exist any special prime p other than 2, 3, and 11?

Let k be a positive even integer. A standard Young tableau with n cells is a filling of the cells of a Young diagram of size n with the integers 1,2,…,n (each used once) such that entries strictly increase along each row from left to right and strictly increase down each column. Let y_k(n) denote the number of standard Young tableaux with n cells whose first row has length at most k (with the convention y_k(0)=1). Let u_k(n) denote the number of permutations of {1,2,…,n} that contain no strictly ascending subsequence of length greater than k.

It is known that, for every positive integer n,
  C(2n,n) · u_k(n) = Σ_{r=0}^{2n} C(2n,r) (−1)^r y_k(r) y_k(2n − r),
where C(a,b) denotes the binomial coefficient.

Give a purely combinatorial (e.g. bijective or sign-reversing involution) proof of this identity, rather than an analytic derivation.

For a positive integer $n$, a partition of $n$ is a representation $n = \lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \cdots + \lambda_k$ with positive integers $\lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \cdots \ge \lambda_k$. The multiplicity of a positive integer $j$ in a partition is the number of parts $\lambda_i$ equal to $j$. Let $T(n)$ denote the set of partitions of $n$ for which the nonzero multiplicities of the distinct parts are all different from one another, and let
$$f(n) = |T(n)|.$$
For example, the partition $5 = 2+2+1$ has multiplicities $2$ (for the part $2$) and $1$ (for the part $1$), which are distinct, so it lies in $T(5)$; the partition $4 = 2+1+1$ has multiplicities $1$ and $2$, also distinct.

holds.

Consider real rational transfer functions of a complex variable s. A rational function is called proper if its numerator degree does not exceed its denominator degree, stable (Hurwitz) if all of its poles lie in the open left half-plane Re(s) < 0, and Strictly Positive Real of zero relative degree (SPR0) if it is proper, stable, has zero relative degree (numerator and denominator have the same degree), and Re H(jω) > 0 for all real ω (including ω = ∞). Throughout, composition G₀(H(s)) means substituting H(s) into the indeterminate of G₀.

Problem 1. Given a Single-Input Single-Output (SISO) rational transfer function G(s), determine rational transfer functions G₀(s) and H(s) such that:
  (a) G(s) = G₀(H(s));
  (b) the map F(s) ↦ F(H(s)) sends every proper stable rational transfer function to a proper stable rational transfer function.
Characterize all such pairs (G₀, H), and in particular determine when a nontrivial decomposition (i.e., with H not affine) exists.

Problem 2. Given a SISO rational transfer function G(s), determine a rational transfer function G₀(s) and an SPR0 transfer function H(s) such that G(s) = G₀(H(s)). Characterize all G admitting such a decomposition and describe all corresponding pairs (G₀, H).

Problem 3 (Conjecture). Let p(s) = aₙsⁿ + aₙ₋₁sⁿ⁻¹ + ⋯ + a₁s + a₀ be a Hurwitz stable real polynomial (all roots in Re(s) < 0), and let q(x) be a real polynomial with non-negative coefficients. Prove or disprove that the polynomial
  q(aₙ)sⁿ + q(aₙ₋₁)sⁿ⁻¹ + ⋯ + q(a₁)s + q(a₀)
is Hurwitz stable.

A Brodskiĭ–Livšic type system (operator colligation) is a tuple
$$\Theta= egin{pmatrix}\mathbb A & K & J \ \mathcal H_{+}\subset\mathcal H\subset\mathcal H_{-} & & E\end{pmatrix},$$
where $\mathcal H_{+}\subset\mathcal H\subset\mathcal H_{-}$ is a rigged Hilbert space, $\mathbb A:\mathcal H_{+}	o\mathcal H_{-}$ is a bounded linear operator whose restriction $A$ to $\operatorname{dom}A=\{f\in\mathcal H_{+}:\mathbb A f\in\mathcal H\}$ has a non-empty resolvent set, $K\in\mathcal{B}(E,\mathcal H_{-})$, $J=J^{*}=J^{-1}\in\mathcal{B}(E)$, and $\mathbb A-\mathbb A^{*}=2iKJK^{*}$. $$W_{\Theta}(z)=I-2iK^{*}(\mathbb A-zI)^{-1}KJ,\qquad z\inho(A),$$

$$V_{\Theta}(z)=i[W_{\Theta}(z)+I]^{-1}[W_{\Theta}(z)-I]J. \qquad (\ast)$$

A Herglotz–Nevanlinna function $V$ is called a Stieltjes function if, in addition, $V$ admits an analytic continuation to $\mathbb C\setminus[0,\infty)$ with $\operatorname{Im}(zV(z))\ge 0$ for $\operatorname{Im} z>0$; it is called an inverse Stieltjes function if $-V(1/z)/z$ is Stieltjes. An operator $A$ on $\mathcal H$ is accretive if $\operatorname{Re}(Af,f)\ge 0$ for all $f\in\operatorname{dom}A$; it is $\alpha$-sectorial (for $\alpha\in(0,\pi/2)$) if its numerical range lies in $\{z:|\arg z|\le\alpha\}$; an accretive operator that is not $\alpha$-sectorial for any $\alpha<\pi/2$ is called extremal.

Solve the following:

(A) Determine an explicit class of linear, conservative, time-invariant dynamical systems (a class of operator colligations, possibly more general than the Brodskiĭ–Livšic type) such that every matrix-valued Herglotz–Nevanlinna function $V$ acting on $E$ can be realized via $(\ast)$ as $V=V_{\Theta}$ for some minimal system $\Theta$ from this class.

(B) Give necessary and sufficient criteria on a matrix-valued Stieltjes function $V$ (respectively an inverse Stieltjes function) acting on $E$ in order that $V$ admit a realization $V=V_{\Theta}$ via $(\ast)$ by a minimal Brodskiĭ–Livšic type system $\Theta$ whose state-space operator $A$ is, respectively:
  (i) accretive;
  (ii) $\alpha$-sectorial for some $\alpha\in(0,\pi/2)$;
  (iii) extremal (accretive but not $\alpha$-sectorial for any $\alpha<\pi/2$).

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Substantial progress has been made by Belyi, Tsekanovskii, Arlinskii and collaborators. A general realization theorem for arbitrary matrix-valued Herglotz–Nevanlinna functions via an extended class of conservative ("F_+") L-systems was established (arXiv:math/0510464 and subsequent monograph "Conservative Realizations of Herglotz–Nevanlinna Functions", Birkhäuser 2011), and realization criteria for Stieltjes and inverse Stieltjes classes in terms of accretive and sectorial state-space operators have been obtained. The extremal (accretive non-sectorial) case has been studied but the full classification appears still under active development, so the problem is partially solved.

Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and let $\mathcal{U}$, $\mathcal{Y}$ be Hilbert spaces. Denote by $\mathbb{D}^n$ the open unit polydisk in $\mathbb{C}^n$, and let $\mathcal{B}^n_0(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{Y})$ be the class of analytic functions $\theta:\mathbb{D}^n\to\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{Y})$ that are contractive (i.e. $\|\theta(z)\|\le 1$ for every $z\in\mathbb{D}^n$) and vanish at the origin.

A dissipative scattering $n$D system is a linear system of Givone–Roesser type
$$\begin{pmatrix} x_1(k+e_1) \\ \vdots \\ x_n(k+e_n) \\ y(k) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} A & B \\ C & D \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x_1(k) \\ \vdots \\ x_n(k) \\ u(k) \end{pmatrix},$$
where the state space decomposes as $\mathcal{X}=\bigoplus_{i=1}^n \mathcal{X}_i$ (Hilbert spaces), $e_i$ is the $i$th standard basis vector, and the block operator $\begin{pmatrix} A & B \\ C & D \end{pmatrix}:\mathcal{X}\oplus\mathcal{U}\to\mathcal{X}\oplus\mathcal{Y}$ is a contraction. The transfer function of such a system is
$$\theta(z) = D + C\big(I - Z(z)A\big)^{-1} Z(z) B, \qquad z\in\mathbb{D}^n,$$
where $Z(z)=\mathrm{diag}(z_1 I_{\mathcal{X}_1},\dots,z_n I_{\mathcal{X}_n})$.

Question: Either prove that every $\theta\in\mathcal{B}^n_0(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{Y})$ arises as the transfer function of some dissipative scattering $n$D system with input space $\mathcal{U}$ and output space $\mathcal{Y}$, or exhibit (for some $n$ and some finite-dimensional $\mathcal{U},\mathcal{Y}$) a function $\theta\in\mathcal{B}^n_0(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{Y})$ that admits no such realization.

The problem was resolved in the negative by M. T. Jury (arXiv:1201.3286, 2012), who showed that not every contractive analytic function on the polydisk admits a dissipative n-dimensional scattering realization, providing an explicit counterexample. This is consistent with the known fact that for n ≥ 3 the Schur–Agler class (which equals the class of transfer functions of such conservative/dissipative realizations) is a strict subclass of the Schur class.

representations.normalized:
Consider a linear time-invariant control system

  ẋ(t) = A x(t) + B u(t) + E d(t),
  z(t) = C x(t),

where x(t) ∈ X = ℝⁿ is the state, u(t) ∈ U = ℝᵐ is the control input, d(t) ∈ D = ℝᵖ is an exogenous disturbance, and z(t) ∈ ℝᵍ is the output to be controlled. Here A, B, C, E are real matrices of compatible dimensions.

Let k ≥ 1 be a given integer. Apply a static state feedback of the form

  u(t) = F x(t) + G d(t),

where F : X → U and G : D → U are linear maps. The resulting closed-loop transfer function from d to z is

  T_{zd}(s) = C (sI − (A+BF))⁻¹ (E + BG),

and its Markov parameters are the coefficients M_j (j = 0, 1, 2, …) appearing in its expansion at infinity, namely M_0 = C(E+BG) and M_j = C(A+BF)^{j−1}(E+BG) for j ≥ 1 (taking the standard convention that M_1 = C(E+BG) and M_{j+1} = C(A+BF)^{j}(E+BG)).

Problem. Give necessary and sufficient conditions, expressed in terms of the quadruple (A, B, C, E) and the integer k, for the existence of linear maps F and G such that the first k Markov parameters of T_{zd} vanish, while additionally A + BF is (asymptotically) stable.

Consider the model reference adaptive control problem for a linear, time-invariant, single-input single-output plant with unknown parameters but known order n and known relative degree, given by

    A(p) y(t) = k_p B(p) u(t),

where p = d/dt, A and B are coprime monic polynomials of known degrees, B is Hurwitz (the plant is minimum-phase), the sign of the high-frequency gain k_p is known, and a strictly proper stable reference model

    A_m(p) y_m(t) = k_m B_m(p) r(t)

is given with bounded reference input r(t). The goal is to design a controller using output feedback only (no derivatives of y) such that, for every bounded reference signal and every initial condition, all closed-loop signals remain bounded and the tracking error y(t) − y_m(t) tends to 0 as t → ∞.

In 1974, R. V. Monopoli proposed an un-normalized model reference adaptive control scheme (the "augmented error" scheme) using a particular choice of regressor filters and a gradient-type adaptation law without signal normalization. A flaw was later identified in the original stability proof.

Question: Is Monopoli's original un-normalized model reference adaptive controller correct? That is, do the adaptive laws and control law as proposed by Monopoli guarantee, for every admissible plant in the class above and every bounded reference signal and initial condition, that all closed-loop signals remain bounded and the tracking error converges to zero?

The question has been resolved in the negative. Subsequent work constructed counterexamples showing that Monopoli's un-normalized model reference adaptive controller can generate unbounded trajectories, so the scheme is not correct in general (although it is semi-globally stable, and adding normalization restores global stability). See, e.g., the paper "Monopoli's model reference adaptive controller is incorrect" and related works in IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control.

representations.normalized:
Consider a stable, finite-dimensional input/output delay system, i.e., a linear time-invariant system whose transfer function G(s) is analytic and bounded in the closed right half-plane and which may involve finitely many (or even distributed) time delays, so that G belongs to H^\infty but in general is infinite-dimensional as an operator. For such a system, the Hankel operator H_G associated to G is compact and admits a sequence of Hankel singular values σ_1 ≥ σ_2 ≥ … → 0.

Two classical procedures, originally developed for finite-dimensional stable LTI systems, can be applied to G to construct, for each positive integer n, a finite-dimensional reduced-order model of order n:

(i) Truncated balanced realization of order n: form a balanced realization of G (in which the controllability and observability Gramians are equal and diagonal with entries σ_1, σ_2, …) and truncate it to the n states corresponding to the n largest Hankel singular values, yielding a rational stable transfer function G_n^{bt}.

(ii) Optimal Hankel-norm approximation of order n: choose G_n^{hn} to be a stable rational transfer function of McMillan degree at most n that minimizes the Hankel-norm error \|G - G_n^{hn}\|_H over all such approximants.

Question: For every stable delay system G as above, do the sequences (G_n^{bt})_{n\ge 1} and (G_n^{hn})_{n\ge 1} converge to G as n → ∞ (for instance, in the H^\infty-norm, or equivalently in the gap topology arising from the standard error bounds involving the tail \sum_{k>n} σ_k)?

Let m and n be positive integers and let a_0, a_1, …, a_n be given m×m complex matrices. Denote by S(a_0,…,a_n) the set of all m×m matrix-valued functions

   w(z) = a_0 + a_1 z + … + a_n z^n + a_{n+1} z^{n+1} + …

that are holomorphic in the open unit disk D = { z ∈ C : |z| < 1 } and satisfy the contractive condition w(z)*w(z) ≤ I_m for every z ∈ D (the matrix Schur class with prescribed first n+1 Taylor coefficients). Assume that S(a_0,…,a_n) is non-empty.

For each w ∈ S(a_0,…,a_n) the matrix-valued defect function
   D_w(z) = I_m − w(z)*w(z)
is positive semidefinite on D. Among the elements of S(a_0,…,a_n) consider the partial order induced by the pointwise Loewner order on D_w, and define the extremal defect

   ρ_min  :=  inf { D_w  :  w ∈ S(a_0,…,a_n) }

in the sense of the greatest m×m positive semidefinite matrix-valued lower bound that is attained (the existence of such a minimal element ρ_min follows from a compactness argument in the matrix Schur class). Let m_1 = rank(ρ_min(z)) for z generically in D, and let m_2 denote the rank associated with the corresponding boundary/extremal data on the right (so that m_1 and m_2 are the two natural rank invariants attached to ρ_min on the two sides of the interpolation problem).

Suppose furthermore that the following non-degeneracy/normalization relation holds:

   (∗)   ρ_min is consistent with the prescribed coefficients a_0,…,a_n in the standard Schur-extremal sense, i.e. the minimal element ρ_min is realized by some w ∈ S(a_0,…,a_n) whose Schur parameters terminate after step n.

Answer the following:

(1) Is the extremal element ρ_min unique?

(2) Provide an effective procedure (a constructive algorithm in terms of the data a_0,…,a_n) for computing ρ_min.

(3) Under hypothesis (∗), is it possible that m_1 ≠ m_2? Equivalently, exhibit data a_0,…,a_n for which the left and right rank invariants of ρ_min differ, or prove that they must always coincide.

Let $\mathbb{C}[\eta_1,\dots,\eta_m,\xi]$ denote the polynomial ring in $m+1$ commuting indeterminates over $\mathbb{C}$, where $\eta_1,\dots,\eta_m$ are interpreted as spatial differential operators $\partial/\partial x_1,\dots,\partial/\partial x_m$ and $\xi$ as the time differential operator $\partial/\partial t$. Fix integers $g,w\ge 1$ and a polynomial matrix $R\in\mathbb{C}[\eta_1,\dots,\eta_m,\xi]^{g\times w}$. The associated behavior is the kernel representation
$$\mathcal{B}=\bigl\{\,v\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C}^w)\ :\ R(\partial/\partial x_1,\dots,\partial/\partial x_m,\partial/\partial t)\,v=0\,\bigr\}.$$
The behavior $\mathcal{B}$ is said to be time-controllable if for every pair $v_1,v_2\in\mathcal{B}$ and every $T>0$ there exists $v\in\mathcal{B}$ and $\tau\ge T$ such that
$$v(x,t)=v_1(x,t)\quad\text{for } t\le 0,\qquad v(x,t)=v_2(x,t-\tau)\quad\text{for } t\ge \tau,$$
for all $x\in\mathbb{R}^m$ (i.e. trajectories can be concatenated in the time direction through an element of $\mathcal{B}$, while only requiring connectability along time and not along the spatial variables).

Problem: Find an algebraic test, formulated directly in terms of the polynomial matrix $R$ (e.g.\ in terms of its minors, ideals, primeness properties, or modules over $\mathbb{C}[\eta_1,\dots,\eta_m,\xi]$), that is necessary and sufficient for the behavior $\mathcal{B}$ to be time-controllable.

Let $\mathbb{R}[s,s^{-1}]$ denote the ring of Laurent polynomials in one indeterminate $s$ with real coefficients, and let $\sigma : (\mathbb{R}^q)^{\mathbb{Z}} \to (\mathbb{R}^q)^{\mathbb{Z}}$ be the (left) shift operator defined by $(\sigma w)(t) = w(t+1)$ for $t \in \mathbb{Z}$. For a polynomial matrix $R(s,s^{-1}) \in \mathbb{R}^{g\times q}[s,s^{-1}]$, the operator $R(\sigma,\sigma^{-1})$ acts on $w \in (\mathbb{R}^q)^{\mathbb{Z}}$ in the obvious way, and the inequality $R(\sigma,\sigma^{-1})w \ge 0$ is understood componentwise and pointwise on $\mathbb{Z}$. Denote by $\mathbb{R}_+[s,s^{-1}]$ the set of Laurent polynomials all of whose coefficients are non-negative, and by $\mathbb{R}_+^{a\times b}[s,s^{-1}]$ the matrices over this set.

Prove or disprove the following two statements.

(a) (Farkas lemma for behavioral inequalities.) Let $R \in \mathbb{R}^{g\times q}[s,s^{-1}]$ and $R' \in \mathbb{R}^{g'\times q}[s,s^{-1}]$. Then the implication
$$ R(\sigma,\sigma^{-1})w \ge 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; R'(\sigma,\sigma^{-1})w \ge 0 \qquad (\forall\, w \in (\mathbb{R}^q)^{\mathbb{Z}}) $$
holds if and only if there exists a polynomial matrix $H \in \mathbb{R}_+^{g'\times g}[s,s^{-1}]$ (i.e. with non-negative coefficient entries) such that
$$ R'(s,s^{-1}) = H(s,s^{-1})\, R(s,s^{-1}). $$

(b) (Uniqueness of minimal mixed equality/inequality representations.) Let
$$ \mathcal{B} = \{\, w\in (\mathbb{R}^q)^{\mathbb{Z}} : R_1(\sigma,\sigma^{-1})w = 0 \text{ and } R_2(\sigma,\sigma^{-1})w \ge 0 \,\}, $$
$$ \mathcal{B}' = \{\, w\in (\mathbb{R}^q)^{\mathbb{Z}} : R'_1(\sigma,\sigma^{-1})w = 0 \text{ and } R'_2(\sigma,\sigma^{-1})w \ge 0 \,\}, $$
be two minimal representations of behaviors of the above mixed type, where $R_1,R'_1$ and $R_2,R'_2$ are real Laurent-polynomial matrices of appropriate sizes. Then $\mathcal{B} = \mathcal{B}'$ if and only if there exist Laurent-polynomial matrices $U(s,s^{-1})$ (unimodular over $\mathbb{R}[s,s^{-1}]$), $H(s,s^{-1})$, and $S(s,s^{-1})$ with $H$ and $S$ having non-negative coefficient entries and $S$ being a permutation/unimodular non-negative matrix, such that
$$ R'_1 = U R_1 + H R_2 \quad\text{ ?? } \quad \text{and} \quad R'_2 = S R_2. $$
Determine the precise form of the equivalence transformation $(U,H,S)$ characterizing equality of two such minimal representations.

Work in the behavioral framework of linear differential systems. For a positive integer n, let $\mathcal{L}^n$ denote the set of all linear differential behaviors in n variables, i.e., the set of all subspaces $\mathcal{B}\subseteq C^\infty(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}^n)$ that can be written as the kernel of a polynomial differential operator $R(d/dt)$ with $R\in\mathbb{R}^{\bullet\times n}[\xi]$.

Fix integers $w,c\ge 1$. Let $P_{\mathrm{full}}\in\mathcal{L}^{w+c}$ be a given "full plant" behavior whose trajectories are partitioned into a manifest variable $w\in\mathbb{R}^w$ (to be controlled) and a control variable $c\in\mathbb{R}^c$ (available for interconnection). The manifest plant behavior is
$$P := \{w\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}^w) : \exists\, c\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}^c)\text{ with }(w,c)\in P_{\mathrm{full}}\}.$$
A controller is any $C\in\mathcal{L}^c$. The controlled behavior obtained by interconnecting $P_{\mathrm{full}}$ with $C$ through the control variable is
$$K(P_{\mathrm{full}},C) := \{w : \exists\, c\in C\text{ with }(w,c)\in P_{\mathrm{full}}\}\in\mathcal{L}^w.$$
Say that $C$ implements $K\in\mathcal{L}^w$ if $K = K(P_{\mathrm{full}},C)$. The implementation is called regular if
$$\operatorname{rowdim}(R_C) + \operatorname{rowdim}(R_{P_{\mathrm{full}}}) = \operatorname{rowdim}(R_{K\wedge P_{\mathrm{full}}})$$
for minimal kernel representations of $C$ and $P_{\mathrm{full}}$ (equivalently, the interconnection through $c$ is regular). The implementation is called a regular feedback implementation if, in addition, the interconnection between the plant and controller corresponds to a feedback connection in which the controller does not constrain its input variables, i.e., the input cardinality of $C$ equals the output cardinality of the corresponding component of $P_{\mathrm{full}}$ (so that $c$ admits a feedback partition compatible with $P_{\mathrm{full}}$).

Problem. Given $P_{\mathrm{full}}\in\mathcal{L}^{w+c}$ and $K\in\mathcal{L}^w$, find necessary and sufficient conditions on $K$ for the existence of a controller $C\in\mathcal{L}^c$ such that
(i) $C$ implements $K$, and
(ii) the implementation is a regular feedback implementation.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Necessary and sufficient conditions for (plain) regular implementability of a sub-behavior K of the manifest plant behavior were obtained by Belur and Trentelman (CDC 2001; subsequent SIAM J. Control Optim. papers). The stronger question of regular feedback implementability — requiring the interconnection to be a feedback interconnection with prescribed input/output partition and no restrictions imposed on free variables — has been studied in follow-up work (Julius, Belur, Trentelman, Willems, and others) giving partial characterizations and complete answers in special cases (e.g., controllers with pre-specified input/output partition, canonical controller constructions). A clean, fully general necessary and sufficient condition characterizing regular feedback implementability for arbitrary $P_{\mathrm{full}}\in\mathcal{L}^{w+c}$ and $K\in\mathcal{L}^w$ does not appear to have been definitively established in the surveyed literature, so the problem is best classified as partially solved.

Let $A,B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$. Consider the algebraic matrix Riccati equation
$$A^{\top}P + PA + Q + P B Q^{-1} B^{\top} P + R \;=\; 0,$$
where $P, Q, R \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ are required to be symmetric positive definite. The pair $(A,B)$ is called Riccati-stable if there exists a triple $(P,Q,R)$ of symmetric positive definite matrices satisfying this equation. (It is known that Riccati-stability of $(A,B)$ implies that $A$ is Hurwitz, i.e. all its eigenvalues have negative real part, and that $A^{-1}B$ is Schur-Cohn, i.e. all its eigenvalues lie in the open unit disk; but the converse is not known in general.)

(a) Give an intrinsic characterization of all pairs $(A,B)$ for which there exist symmetric positive definite matrices $P,Q,R$ satisfying the equation above.

(b) Give a characterization, without invoking auxiliary matrices beyond $P$ and $Q$, of all pairs $(A,B)$ for which there exist symmetric positive definite matrices $P$ and $Q$ such that the block matrix
$$\begin{bmatrix} A^{\top}P + PA + Q & PB \\ B^{\top}P & -Q \end{bmatrix}$$
is negative semidefinite (equivalently, such that the Schur complement condition $A^{\top}P+PA+Q+PBQ^{-1}B^{\top}P\le 0$ holds).

Work in the behavioral framework for linear time-invariant differential systems. A behavior on q manifest signals is a subspace B ⊆ C^∞(ℝ, ℝ^q) of the form

   B = ker R(d/dt) = { w ∈ C^∞(ℝ, ℝ^q) : R(d/dt) w = 0 },

where R ∈ ℝ^{•×q}[ξ] is a polynomial matrix in the indeterminate ξ; such a description is called a kernel representation of B. A first-order representation of B is a description of the manifest behavior in the form

   E (d/dt) ξ + F ξ + G w = 0,

where ξ : ℝ → ℝ^n is an auxiliary (latent) variable, E, F ∈ ℝ^{•×n}, G ∈ ℝ^{•×q} are constant matrices, and the projection of the full behavior {(w, ξ)} onto the w-component equals B. Such a first-order representation is called a state representation if, in addition, the latent variable ξ is a state (i.e. its present value, together with the future input, determines the future trajectory, equivalently the concatenation/Markov axiom holds for (w, ξ)).

Provide an intrinsic characterization, in terms of the polynomial matrix R defining B (or in terms of B itself), of the following:

(a) the minimal possible dimension n over all first-order representations of B;

(b) the minimal possible dimension n over all state representations of B (the McMillan-like degree in the behavioral sense);

(c) the precise algebraic conditions on (E, F, G) that distinguish those minimal first-order representations of B that are state representations from those that are not, and an algorithm that, starting from an arbitrary kernel representation R(d/dt) w = 0, constructs a minimal state representation of B.

Let $H(s) = C(sI_N - A)^{-1} B + D$ be the transfer function of a linear time-invariant system, where $A \in \mathbb{R}^{N\times N}$, $B \in \mathbb{R}^{N\times m}$, $C \in \mathbb{R}^{p\times N}$, $D \in \mathbb{R}^{p\times m}$, and assume $(A,B,C,D)$ is a minimal realization (so $H$ has McMillan degree $N$). A reduced-order model $\widehat H(s) = \widehat C(sI_n - \widehat A)^{-1}\widehat B + \widehat D$ of McMillan degree $n < N$ is said to be obtained from $(A,B,C,D)$ by projection if there exist matrices $V, Z \in \mathbb{R}^{N\times n}$ with $Z^T V = I_n$ such that
$$\widehat A = Z^T A V,\qquad \widehat B = Z^T B,\qquad \widehat C = C V,\qquad \widehat D = D.$$
Given a finite set of tangential interpolation conditions of the form
$$\widehat H(\lambda_i)\, r_i = H(\lambda_i)\, r_i \quad (i=1,\dots,k),\qquad \ell_j^{T}\widehat H(\mu_j) = \ell_j^{T} H(\mu_j) \quad (j=1,\dots,q),$$
where $\lambda_i,\mu_j \in \mathbb{C}$ are points in the resolvent set of $A$ and $\widehat A$, and $r_i \in \mathbb{C}^m$, $\ell_j \in \mathbb{C}^p$ are right and left tangential directions, determine necessary and sufficient conditions on the data $(A,B,C,D)$, $\{(\lambda_i, r_i)\}$, $\{(\mu_j,\ell_j)\}$ under which there exists a reduced order system $\widehat H$ of McMillan degree exactly $n$ satisfying all the prescribed tangential interpolation conditions and obtainable from $(A,B,C,D)$ by a projection $(V,Z)$ as above. In particular: characterize when a minimal realization $(\widehat A,\widehat B,\widehat C,\widehat D)$ of a transfer function $\widehat H$ that tangentially interpolates $H$ at the given points and directions can be embedded as the Petrov–Galerkin projection of $(A,B,C,D)$ along a pair of $n$-dimensional subspaces.

Setup. A wide band noise is a real-valued, mean-zero stochastic process $\varphi$ of the form
$$\varphi(t) \;=\; \int_{\max(0,\,t-\varepsilon)}^{t} \phi(s-t)\, dw(s), \qquad t\ge 0,$$
where $w$ is a standard Wiener process, $\varepsilon>0$ is a fixed "noise duration", and $\phi:[-\varepsilon,0]\to\mathbb R$ is a square‑integrable "relaxing function". The autocovariance function of $\varphi$ on its stationary range (i.e. for $t\ge\varepsilon$) is
$$K(\tau) \;=\; \int_{-\varepsilon}^{-|\tau|} \phi(s)\,\phi(s+|\tau|)\,ds, \qquad |\tau|\le\varepsilon,$$
and $K(\tau)=0$ for $|\tau|>\varepsilon$. Different relaxing functions $\phi$ can produce the same autocovariance $K$; thus a single autocovariance function $K$ on $[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]$ corresponds to an infinite family $\mathcal F(K)$ of wide band noise processes.

Filtering problem. Consider the signal/observation system on a finite interval $[0,T]$:
$$dx(t)=A(t)x(t)\,dt + B(t)\,dw_1(t),\qquad dy(t)=C(t)x(t)\,dt + \varphi(t)\,dt + dw_2(t),$$
with $x(0)$ Gaussian, $w_1,w_2$ independent standard Wiener processes independent of $\varphi$, and $\varphi\in\mathcal F(K)$. Let
$$E(\varphi) \;=\; \mathbb E\bigl\|x(T)-\hat x(T\mid y_{[0,T]})\bigr\|^2$$
denote the minimum mean‑square estimation error for the given $\varphi$, where $\hat x(T\mid y_{[0,T]})$ is the conditional mean.

Control problem. Analogously, consider a linear‑quadratic Gaussian problem in which the controlled system is driven by white noise plus a wide band noise $\varphi\in\mathcal F(K)$, with quadratic cost
$$J(u,\varphi) \;=\; \mathbb E\!\left[\int_0^T \bigl(x^\top Q x + u^\top R u\bigr)dt + x(T)^\top S\, x(T)\right],\qquad R\succ 0,\ Q,S\succeq 0,$$
and define $V(\varphi)=\inf_{u}J(u,\varphi)$, the minimum cost (the infimum being taken over admissible feedback controls based on the available observations).

Open problem. Given the autocovariance function $K$ (and all other system data $A,B,C,Q,R,S,T,\varepsilon$ and the initial distribution of $x(0)$), determine
$$\overline E(K)=\sup_{\varphi\in\mathcal F(K)} E(\varphi),\qquad \underline E(K)=\inf_{\varphi\in\mathcal F(K)} E(\varphi),$$
$$\overline V(K)=\sup_{\varphi\in\mathcal F(K)} V(\varphi),\qquad \underline V(K)=\inf_{\varphi\in\mathcal F(K)} V(\varphi),$$
i.e., find the least upper bound and greatest lower bound on the minimum estimation error and on the minimum LQG cost, taken over all wide band noise processes sharing the prescribed autocovariance function $K$, and characterize the relaxing functions (if any) that attain these extreme values.

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

The problem originates as a stated open problem in the Blondel–Megretski compilation (2004) and is connected to a line of work on wide-band-noise driven filtering and LQG control. Subsequent work (e.g. Bashirov, "Linear Filtering for Wide Band Noise Driven Observation Systems", 2017; "Invariant Kalman Filter for Correlated Wide Band Noises", 2020; and related results on the stochastic maximum principle) establishes invariance results showing that, under independence of observation white and wide band noises, the best estimates and optimal controls depend only on the autocovariance function and not on the particular relaxing function. This addresses related aspects of the question, but a complete characterization of the least upper bound and greatest lower bound of the optimal estimation error and optimal cost across all wide band noise processes with a given autocovariance does not appear to have been definitively published; the status of the original open problem is therefore unclear.

A real square matrix M ∈ ℝ^{n×n} is called (Hurwitz) stable if every eigenvalue of M has strictly negative real part. Consider the following three probability distributions ("ensembles") on ℝ^{n×n}:

(a) G_n: the Ginibre-type ensemble of n×n real matrices whose entries are independent standard Gaussian random variables N(0,1).

(b) GOE_n: the Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble of real symmetric n×n matrices M, where the entries M_{ij} for i<j are independent N(0,1) and the diagonal entries M_{ii} are independent N(0,2), all independent of one another. (Equivalently, M = (H+H^T)/√2 with H drawn from G_n.)

(c) USF_n: the uniform distribution on the Frobenius unit sphere {M ∈ ℝ^{n×n} : ‖M‖_F = 1}, where ‖M‖_F^2 = Σ_{i,j} M_{ij}^2.

Solve the following three problems.

Problem 1. As an explicit function of n, determine the probability that a matrix drawn from GOE_n is stable, and the probability that a matrix drawn from USF_n is stable.

Problem 2. As an explicit function of n, determine the probability that a matrix drawn from G_n is stable.

Problem 3. Let A ∈ ℝ^{n×n} be a fixed stable matrix. For each of the three ensembles above, determine the probability that A + X is stable, where X is drawn from the ensemble (the answer may depend on A and on a scaling parameter applied to X).

The three problems were posed in 2004 as open problems on the probability of Hurwitz stability for the GOE, uniform-Frobenius-sphere, and real Ginibre ensembles, and for shifted versions A+X. Searches reveal subsequent work on asymptotics and bounds (e.g., Edelman-type estimates for eigenvalue locations and follow-up control-theoretic studies), but no published closed-form solution to any of the three problems for general n. The problems appear to remain open.

Let $S$ denote the set of asymptotically stable, minimum-phase, scalar (single-input single-output) discrete-time stochastic linear systems of a fixed McMillan degree $n$, each of which is driven by zero-mean Gaussian white noise of variance $\Omega>0$ and produces a stationary Gaussian output process. Each system in $S$ may be represented by a stable, minimum-phase rational transfer function $W(z)$ of degree $n$ with $W(\infty)=1$, so that the output spectral density is $\Phi(e^{i\omega})=\Omega\,|W(e^{i\omega})|^{2}$.

For a smooth parametrization of $S$, the Fisher information metric is the Riemannian metric whose components are
$$g_{ij}(\theta)=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{\partial \log\Phi_{\theta}(e^{i\omega})}{\partial \theta_{i}}\,\frac{\partial \log\Phi_{\theta}(e^{i\omega})}{\partial \theta_{j}}\,d\omega,$$
and the induced Riemannian (geodesic) distance between two systems $S_{1},S_{2}\in S$ is denoted $d_{F}(S_{1},S_{2})$.

Question: For a fixed value of $\Omega>0$, does there exist a finite constant $M=M(\Omega,n)$ such that
$$d_{F}(S_{1},S_{2})\le M\quad\text{for all }S_{1},S_{2}\in S\,?$$
Equivalently, is the metric space $(S,d_{F})$ of bounded diameter for each fixed $\Omega>0$?

Consider a single-input nonlinear control system

  ẋ = f(x, u),  x ∈ ℝⁿ,  u ∈ ℝ,

where f : ℝⁿ × ℝ → ℝⁿ is real analytic in a neighborhood of the origin and satisfies f(0,0) = 0. Let

  F = ∂f/∂x (0,0) ∈ ℝⁿˣⁿ,  G = ∂f/∂u (0,0) ∈ ℝⁿ,

and assume that the linear pair (F, G) is controllable (Kalman rank condition).

By a formal Kang–Krener procedure, there exists a formal change of state coordinates and formal invertible feedback

  z = Φ(x),  u = α(x) + β(x) v,   Φ(0) = 0, Φ′(0) invertible, β(0) ≠ 0,

with Φ, α, β formal power series, that brings the system into a (Kang–Krener) normal form, in which all homogeneous terms of degree ≥ 2 are reduced to a prescribed canonical shape.

Problem: Find verifiable necessary and sufficient conditions on f (equivalently, on the Taylor coefficients of f at the origin) under which there exists a real analytic change of coordinates and feedback transformation of the above form, convergent in some neighborhood of the origin, that brings the system to its Kang–Krener normal form.

The problem of finding verifiable necessary and sufficient conditions for convergence of the Kang–Krener normal form transformation for real analytic controllable systems remains open in general. Consider a controlled point-mass spacecraft in the Newtonian gravitational field of a fixed central body, modeled by the controlled Kepler equation in three dimensions:

    r̈(t) = -μ r(t)/|r(t)|³ + u(t)/m(t),    ṁ(t) = -β |u(t)|,

where r(t) ∈ ℝ³ \ {0} is the position, m(t) > 0 is the spacecraft mass, μ > 0 is the gravitational parameter, β > 0 is a (given) specific impulse parameter, and u : [0,T] → ℝ³ is a measurable control (the thrust) constrained pointwise by

    |u(t)| ≤ Γ,    t ∈ [0,T],

for a fixed maximum thrust magnitude Γ > 0.

Given:
• an initial time 0 and initial conditions r(0) = r₀, ṙ(0) = v₀, m(0) = m₀ > 0, with (r₀, v₀) lying on a prescribed initial Keplerian elliptic orbit Oi;
• a prescribed target Keplerian elliptic orbit Of, with the final longitude free, i.e. the terminal constraint is (r(T), ṙ(T)) ∈ Of as a curve in phase space;

let T(Γ) denote the minimum time required to steer the system from the initial state to the target orbit subject to the above dynamics and constraint.

Problems:
(a) Establish existence, regularity, and structural properties (e.g., bang-bang nature, number of switchings, conjugate point structure) of time-optimal trajectories u*(·), and characterize them via the Pontryagin maximum principle.
(b) Study the asymptotic behavior of T(Γ) as Γ → 0⁺. In particular, determine whether the product Γ · T(Γ) admits a finite, positive limit, and if so compute it in terms of the initial and final orbits Oi, Of.
(c) Provide a complete qualitative and quantitative description of the value function Γ ↦ T(Γ) for low-thrust orbital transfers between two prescribed elliptic Keplerian orbits.

representations.normalized:
Consider a single-input analytic control system on a neighborhood of the origin in R^n of the form

  ẋ = A x + B u + f(x) + g(x) u,   x(0) = 0,

where (A,B) is a controllable linear pair (so the linearization at the origin is controllable), f : R^n → R^n and g : R^n → R^n are analytic with f(0) = 0, (∂f/∂x)(0) = 0, and g(0) = 0. Expand f and g in homogeneous components in x,

  f(x) = ∑_{m≥2} f_m(x),    g(x) = ∑_{m≥1} g_{m-1}(x),

where f_m and g_{m-1} are vector fields whose components are homogeneous polynomials in x of degree m and m−1 respectively. Consider near-identity changes of coordinates and feedback of the homogeneous form

  (6)  x = z + h_m(z),    with h_m a vector field whose components are homogeneous polynomials in z of degree m,
  (7)  u = α_m(z) + (1 + β_{m-1}(z)) v,   with α_m homogeneous of degree m in z and β_{m-1} homogeneous of degree m−1.

The problem is: determine, for every integer m ≥ 2, conditions under which one can choose h_m(·), α_m(·), and β_{m-1}(·) so that successive application of the transformations (6)–(7) cancels the homogeneous nonlinear terms f_m(·) and g_{m-1}(·)u order by order, thereby transforming the system into its controllable linear part ẋ = Ax + Bv up to terms of arbitrary order; equivalently, give necessary and sufficient conditions on (A, B, f, g) for the existence of such a sequence (h_m, α_m, β_{m-1})_{m≥2} that achieves exact (formal) feedback linearization of the system.

The problem appears in a 2004 collection of unsolved problems in systems and control. representations.normalized:
Let $\mathcal{L}(X_1,\dots,X_m)$ denote the free Lie algebra over $\mathbb{R}$ generated by indeterminates $X_1,\dots,X_m$, and let $\mathbb{R}\langle\!\langle X_1,\dots,X_m\rangle\!\rangle$ denote the associated algebra of formal power series in noncommuting indeterminates. For a control-affine system $\dot{x}(t)=\sum_{i=1}^m u_i(t)\, f_i(x(t))$ on a real analytic manifold $M^n$ with analytic vector fields $f_1,\dots,f_m$, the Chen–Fliess series associates to each word $X_{i_1}\cdots X_{i_k}$ the iterated integral
$$\int_0^t \int_0^{s_k}\!\!\cdots\!\!\int_0^{s_2} u_{i_1}(s_1)\, u_{i_2}(s_2)\cdots u_{i_k}(s_k)\, ds_1\cdots ds_k.$$
Given a homogeneous (graded) basis $B=\bigsqcup_{k\ge 0} B_k$ of $\mathcal{L}(X_1,\dots,X_m)$, write the formal logarithm of the Chen series as a (possibly infinite) linear combination $\sum_{b\in B} \zeta_B(b)\, b$, where the coefficients $\zeta_B(b)$ are functionals of the controls $u_1,\dots,u_m$ called the iterated integral functionals dual to $B$.

Problem 1. Construct graded bases $B=\{B_k:k\ge 0\}$ of the free Lie algebra $\mathcal{L}(X_1,\dots,X_m)$ for which the corresponding dual iterated integral functionals $\zeta_B$ admit closed-form expressions as simple, explicitly computable integrals (analogous to the formulas obtained for classical Hall or Lyndon bases for low-order brackets), and which are suitable for both analysis and design of nonlinear control systems.

Problem 2. Provide an algorithm which, given any finite collection $F=\{f_1,\dots,f_m\}$ of analytic vector fields on an $n$-dimensional real analytic manifold $M^n$, produces a basis for the Lie algebra $L(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ generated by $F$ under Lie brackets, together with effective formulas for the associated iterated integral functionals appearing in the logarithm of the Chen–Fliess series of the control-affine system $\dot{x}=\sum_i u_i f_i(x)$.

Let $f:U\to\mathbb{R}^n$ be a real-analytic vector field defined on an open neighborhood $U\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ of the origin, with $f(0)=0$. Assume that $f$ is gradient-like at $0$ in the following sense: there exists a real-analytic function $V:U\to\mathbb{R}$ with $V(0)=0$, $\nabla V(0)=0$, and such that along every nonstationary integral curve of the differential equation
$$\dot x(t)=f(x(t)) \qquad (1)$$
the function $t\mapsto V(x(t))$ is strictly decreasing (so that $f$ generalizes an analytic gradient vector field $-\nabla V$).

Let $x:[t_0,\beta)\to U$ be a maximal solution of (1) such that $x(t)\to 0$ as $t\to\beta$ (where $\beta\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}$ is the right endpoint of the maximal interval of existence). Define a tangential direction of $x$ at $0$ to be any accumulation point, as $t\to\beta$, of the unit-vector curve
$$\frac{x(t)}{\lVert x(t)\rVert}\in S^{n-1}.$$

Prove or disprove the following: under the hypotheses above, the limit
$$\lim_{t\to\beta}\frac{x(t)}{\lVert x(t)\rVert}$$
exists in $S^{n-1}$; that is, $x$ admits a unique tangential direction at $0$.

The classical Thom gradient conjecture (uniqueness of tangent for trajectories of an analytic gradient $\dot x=-\nabla V(x)$ converging to a critical point) was proved by Kurdyka–Mostowski–Parusiński (2000). Extensions to broader gradient-like settings—including non-oscillation results by Sanz and infinite-dimensional/PDE analogues such as the recent work on Thom's gradient conjecture for nonlinear evolution equations (2024)—are active. The general "extended" version posed in the open-problem collection (allowing more general analytic vector fields with a Lyapunov-type structure) does not appear to have a definitive published resolution, so the status is best regarded as open/unknown.

Consider a financial market with one risk-free asset (with zero interest rate, say) and one risky asset whose price S_t follows a geometric Brownian motion dS_t = μ S_t dt + σ S_t dW_t on a filtered probability space, with μ, σ > 0 constants and W a standard Brownian motion. Trading in the risky asset incurs a proportional transaction cost: when an investor buys risky shares of dollar value dB_t ≥ 0 and sells shares of dollar value dC_t ≥ 0, the investor's bank account changes by −(1+λ) dB_t + (1−μ_c) dC_t, where λ ≥ 0 and μ_c ∈ [0,1) are the (one-sided) proportional cost rates levied by the exchange/broker.

The investor (the follower) chooses an admissible self-financing trading strategy (B_t, C_t), with B and C right-continuous nondecreasing adapted processes, so as to maximize her long-run expected discounted utility of consumption (or, equivalently, the asymptotic growth rate of wealth, or expected utility of terminal wealth over a fixed horizon T)
 J(λ, μ_c) := sup_{(B,C)} 𝔼[ U(X_T^{B,C}) ],
where X_T^{B,C} is the investor's terminal wealth and U is a fixed utility function (e.g. U(x) = x^γ/γ for γ ∈ (0,1)).

The exchange/broker (the leader) collects total expected transaction-cost revenue
 R(λ, μ_c) := 𝔼[ ∫_0^T λ dB_t* + μ_c dC_t* ],
where (B*, C*) denotes the investor's optimal strategy given the announced cost pair (λ, μ_c).

Determine the Stackelberg-optimal transaction cost rates (λ*, μ_c*) ∈ [0,∞) × [0,1) that maximize the leader's revenue R(λ, μ_c) subject to the follower's best response, i.e. solve
 (λ*, μ_c*) ∈ arg max_{(λ, μ_c)} R(λ, μ_c)
where the dependence of R on (λ, μ_c) is via the investor's optimal response. In particular, give an explicit characterization of (λ*, μ_c*), the value R(λ*, μ_c*), and the corresponding optimal investor strategy.

representations.normalized:
Consider a control-affine system on a finite time interval [0,T]:
    dx/dt = f(x) + g(x) u,    x(0) = x_0,
with state x(t) ∈ R^n, control u(t) ∈ R^m (measurable), and smooth f, g of appropriate dimensions. Consider the singular nonlinear quadratic cost functional
    J(u) = ∫_0^T q(x(t)) dt + φ(x(T)),
in which the running cost q : R^n → R_{≥0} and the terminal cost φ : R^n → R are smooth, but the control u does not appear in the cost (so the problem is singular in the classical sense). Let
    J* = inf_u J(u)
denote the (possibly not attained) infimum over admissible controls.

For ε > 0 define the regularized "cheap-control" functional
    J_ε(u) = J(u) + ε ∫_0^T |u(t)|^2 dt,
which is a regular (non-singular) nonlinear quadratic problem with infimum J*_ε attained by some minimizer u_ε.

Question. Does cheap control solve the singular nonlinear quadratic problem? That is:

(a) Does J*_ε → J* as ε → 0+?

(b) Do the minimizers u_ε (or the corresponding state trajectories x_ε) converge, in an appropriate generalized sense, to a generalized minimizer of the original singular problem J?

Provide either a proof of such convergence under suitable structural hypotheses on (f, g, q, φ), or a counterexample.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Subsequent work (notably on "approximation of generalized minimizers and regularization of optimal control problems" and on generalized solutions for singular optimal control problems) provides positive convergence results in particular settings—linear-quadratic singular problems and certain classes of control-affine nonlinear problems via an order-of-singularity framework—indicating partial progress. A fully general affirmative answer for arbitrary singular nonlinear quadratic problems does not appear to be established.

representations.normalized:
Consider the standard one-bit feedback quantizer (Delta-Sigma modulator) operating in discrete time on real-valued sequences indexed by t = 0, 1, 2, .... Let ℓ^∞[0,∞) denote the Banach space of bounded real sequences with the sup-norm ‖x‖_∞ = sup_{t≥0} |x(t)|.

Fix a constant R ∈ [0, ∞] and let r ∈ ℓ^∞[0,∞) be an input reference signal with ‖r‖_∞ ≤ R. Let D : ℓ^∞[0,∞) → ℓ^∞[0,∞) be a causal (possibly nonlinear, possibly time-varying) dynamic system, i.e. (D u)(t) depends only on u(0), u(1), ..., u(t). Define two sequences d, f ∈ ℓ^∞[0,∞) by the feedback equations

   f(t) = (D(r − d))(t),     d(t) = sgn(f(t)),     t ≥ 0,

where sgn(·) takes values in {−1, +1} (with any fixed convention for sgn(0)). Thus d is a binary output stream and f is the internal "loop-filter" state.

For a given R, define the optimal achievable worst-case quantization/tracking error

   E(R) := inf_D  sup_{‖r‖_∞ ≤ R}  ‖r − d‖_∞,

where the infimum is over all causal dynamic systems D for which the feedback loop above is well-defined and produces d, f ∈ ℓ^∞[0,∞) for every admissible r.

(a) Determine E(R) as a function of R ∈ [0, ∞]; in particular, identify the exact value (or sharp upper and lower bounds) of inf_D sup_r ‖r − d‖_∞.

(b) Characterize the class of causal systems D that achieve, or come within any prescribed ε > 0 of, this optimum, and describe the structural properties (linearity, finite memory, etc.) of optimal or near-optimal D.

The problem appears as an open problem in a 2004 collection of unsolved problems in systems and control. Web searches surface subsequent work by Megretski and others on optimal one-bit ADC/Delta-Sigma synthesis (e.g. proofs of optimality of certain DSM classes for related performance criteria, semidefinite-programming bounds, sliding-mode and POCS designs), but no result definitively closes the precise synthesis question concerning the optimal causal D and the achievable worst-case sup-norm tracking error. Current status is not conclusively established from publicly available sources.

representations.normalized:
Let
\[
\dot x(t)=a(x(t))+b(x(t))\,u(t),\qquad x(0)=x_*\in\mathbb{R}^n,\qquad |u(t)|\le 1,
\]
be a single-input control-affine system with real-analytic vector fields $a,b$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ satisfying $a(0)=0$, and consider the time-optimal problem of steering the state to the origin: find an admissible control $u(\cdot)$ minimizing the transfer time $T(x_*)$ from $x_*$ to $0$.

Using the Chen–Fliess expansion, the endpoint of any trajectory may be written as a formal series
\[
x(T)=\sum_{w=i_1\cdots i_k\in\{0,1\}^*}\!\! c_w(x_*)\,\eta_w[u](T),
\]
where the coefficients $c_w(x_*)$ are iterated Lie-derivatives of the identity along $a,b$ evaluated at $x_*$, and the functionals
\[
\eta_w[u](T)=\int_0^T\!\!\int_0^{t_k}\!\!\cdots\!\!\int_0^{t_2} u_{i_1}(t_1)\cdots u_{i_k}(t_k)\,dt_1\cdots dt_k,\qquad u_0\equiv 1,\;u_1=u,
\]
are the nonlinear power moments of the control. Let $\mathcal{A}$ denote the free associative algebra over $\mathbb{R}$ generated by the two letters $\{0,1\}$ together with the shuffle product, identified with the algebra of nonlinear power moments.

Two control-affine systems are called \emph{equivalent in the sense of time optimality near the origin} if they have the same optimal-time function $T(x_*)$ for all $x_*$ in a neighborhood of $0$. To each system associate the right ideal $I\subset\mathcal{A}$ generated by the relations among its moment coefficients $\{c_w\}$.

Open problem: Classify the right ideals $I\subset\mathcal{A}$ that arise as the annihilating right ideal of a control-affine system in this manner, and, for each such ideal, determine the possible asymptotic behaviors of the optimal-time function $T(x_*)$ as $x_*\to 0$ (in particular, identify all admissible asymptotic expansions of $T(x_*)$ and characterize the corresponding optimal controls in terms of $I$).

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem, posed by Sklyar and Ignatovich, has motivated an active line of research on the Fliess/moment-algebra formulation of nonlinear time-optimal control. Subsequent works (e.g., representations in the Fliess algebra and algebra of nonlinear power moments, approximation via power-moment min-problems, the Markov-moment formulation, and recent 2022–2025 papers on linearizable systems) have obtained partial results — chiefly for "dual-to-linear" systems and bang-bang controls — but a full classification of the right ideals and the corresponding asymptotics of optimal times has not been reported. The general problem appears to remain open.
