Consider finite collections of axis-parallel closed squares in the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ whose union has Lebesgue measure (area) equal to $1$. For such a collection $F$, let
$$m(F) = \sup\bigl\{\, \mathrm{area}(\textstyle\bigcup_{S \in I} S) \;:\; I \subseteq F,\ \text{the squares in } I \text{ are pairwise disjoint}\,\bigr\}.$$
Determine the largest constant $c$ such that $m(F) \ge c$ for every finite collection $F$ of axis-parallel squares in the plane whose union has unit area; equivalently, determine
$$c^* \;=\; \inf_{F} m(F),$$
where the infimum is taken over all such finite collections $F$.
representations.original:
Consider finite collections of axis-parallel closed squares in the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ whose union has Lebesgue measure (area) equal to $1$. For such a collection $F$, let
$$m(F) = \sup\bigl\{\, \mathrm{area}(\textstyle\bigcup_{S \in I} S) \;:\; I \subseteq F,\ \text{the squares in } I \text{ are pairwise disjoint}\,\bigr\}.$$
Determine the largest constant $c$ such that $m(F) \ge c$ for every finite collection $F$ of axis-parallel squares in the plane whose union has unit area; equivalently, determine
$$c^* \;=\; \inf_{F} m(F),$$
where the infimum is taken over all such finite collections $F$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem remains open. Rado (1928) conjectured the optimal constant is 1/4, but Ajtai (1973) disproved this for axis-parallel squares with a counterexample. The greedy bound 1/9 has been improved over time (to 1/8.75 by R. Rado and 1/8.6 by Zalgaller), with later improvements by Bereg, Dumitrescu, and Jiang, but the exact value of the optimal constant is not known.

Let $M$ be a Cartan–Hadamard manifold of dimension $n \ge 2$, i.e., a complete, simply connected Riemannian manifold whose sectional curvatures satisfy $K \le 0$ everywhere. For a bounded domain $\Omega \subset M$ with sufficiently regular boundary, let $\mathrm{Vol}(\Omega)$ denote its $n$-dimensional Riemannian volume and $\mathrm{Vol}(\partial\Omega)$ the $(n-1)$-dimensional volume of its boundary. Let $\omega_n$ denote the volume of the unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^n$.

Prove or disprove the following sharp isoperimetric inequality: for every such $\Omega \subset M$,
$$\mathrm{Vol}(\partial \Omega)^n \;\ge\; n^n\, \omega_n\, \mathrm{Vol}(\Omega)^{n-1},$$
with equality if and only if $\Omega$ is isometric to a Euclidean ball of the corresponding volume. Equivalently, show that the classical Euclidean isoperimetric inequality extends to all Cartan–Hadamard manifolds in every dimension $n \ge 2$.
representations.original:
Let $M$ be a Cartan–Hadamard manifold of dimension $n \ge 2$, i.e., a complete, simply connected Riemannian manifold whose sectional curvatures satisfy $K \le 0$ everywhere. For a bounded domain $\Omega \subset M$ with sufficiently regular boundary, let $\mathrm{Vol}(\Omega)$ denote its $n$-dimensional Riemannian volume and $\mathrm{Vol}(\partial\Omega)$ the $(n-1)$-dimensional volume of its boundary. Let $\omega_n$ denote the volume of the unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^n$.

Prove or disprove the following sharp isoperimetric inequality: for every such $\Omega \subset M$,
$$\mathrm{Vol}(\partial \Omega)^n \;\ge\; n^n\, \omega_n\, \mathrm{Vol}(\Omega)^{n-1},$$
with equality if and only if $\Omega$ is isometric to a Euclidean ball of the corresponding volume. Equivalently, show that the classical Euclidean isoperimetric inequality extends to all Cartan–Hadamard manifolds in every dimension $n \ge 2$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The conjecture is known in dimensions 2 (Weil/Beckenbach–Radó), 3 (Kleiner, 1992) and 4 (Croke, 1984, under K ≤ 0). In 2019 Ghomi and Spruck announced a proof in all dimensions, but a gap was identified in 2020. As of recent work, they have shown Kleiner's approach succeeds whenever a certain total curvature inequality holds, and related results on total curvature of convex hypersurfaces in Cartan–Hadamard manifolds continue to appear. The general n-dimensional conjecture is not yet fully established.

Let $S \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a closed planar region of known shape and size (for instance, a convex body, polygon, or infinite strip). Suppose a point starts at an unknown location inside $S$ with an unknown orientation, and follows a planned path (a rectifiable curve in $\mathbb{R}^2$) chosen in advance, knowing only the shape $S$ but not the starting position or initial heading. The path is said to "escape" $S$ as soon as it first reaches the boundary $\partial S$.

For a given path $\gamma$, define its worst-case escape length as the supremum, over all possible starting positions in $S$ and all initial orientations, of the arclength traveled along $\gamma$ until $\partial S$ is first reached (after applying the corresponding rigid motion of $\gamma$ inside $S$).

Determine, for a general shape $S$, a path $\gamma^*$ that minimizes this worst-case escape length, and compute the value of this minimum. Equivalently, find the shortest curve in the plane that, when placed inside $S$ at any position and orientation, is guaranteed to touch the boundary of $S$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Bellman's lost-in-a-forest problem, posed in 1956, remains open in general. Optimal escape paths are known only for certain specific shapes (e.g., infinite strips, circles, some rectangles), while for many natural shapes such as the equilateral triangle the optimum is unknown. Recent preprints (e.g., a 2024 arXiv preprint proposing a discretization-based general framework) have not yet established a peer-reviewed general solution.

A tiling of the Euclidean plane by congruent copies (allowing rotations and reflections) of a single closed topological disk T (called the prototile) is a covering of the plane by such copies with pairwise disjoint interiors. A tiling is periodic if it is invariant under translation by some non-trivial lattice; otherwise it is non-periodic. A prototile T is called aperiodic if copies of T admit at least one tiling of the plane but admit no periodic tiling.

Question: Does there exist a two-dimensional shape T (a single connected closed topological disk in the plane) that is an aperiodic prototile, i.e., copies of T (under isometries of the plane) tile the plane but no such tiling is periodic?
representations.original:

A tiling is periodic if it is invariant under translation by some non-trivial lattice; otherwise it is non-periodic. A prototile T is called aperiodic if copies of T admit at least one tiling of the plane but admit no periodic tiling.

Question: Does there exist a two-dimensional shape T (a single connected closed topological disk in the plane) that is an aperiodic prototile, i.e., copies of T (under isometries of the plane) tile the plane but no such tiling is periodic?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The einstein problem was resolved in 2023 by David Smith, Joseph Myers, Craig Kaplan, and Chaim Goodman-Strauss, who exhibited a 13-sided polygonal "hat" tile that admits only non-periodic tilings of the plane (using reflections), and subsequently the "spectre" tile which is a strictly chiral aperiodic monotile requiring no reflections.

Let $S^2 = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^3 : \|x\| = 1\}$ denote the unit sphere in $\mathbb{R}^3$. For an integer $N \geq 2$ and a configuration of $N$ distinct points $x_1, \ldots, x_N \in S^2$, define the (Coulomb) energy
\[
E(x_1, \ldots, x_N) = \sum_{1 \le i < j \le N} \frac{1}{\|x_i - x_j\|},
\]
where $\|\cdot\|$ is the Euclidean norm in $\mathbb{R}^3$.

For each $N \geq 2$, determine the minimum value
\[
E_N = \min_{x_1, \ldots, x_N \in S^2} E(x_1, \ldots, x_N)
\]
and describe, up to rotations and reflections, all configurations $(x_1, \ldots, x_N)$ that attain this minimum.

A graph $G=(V,E)$ is called biplanar if its edge set $E$ can be partitioned into two sets $E_1$ and $E_2$ such that both spanning subgraphs $(V, E_1)$ and $(V, E_2)$ are planar. Equivalently, $G$ is biplanar if its thickness is at most $2$. The chromatic number $\chi(G)$ of $G$ is the smallest positive integer $k$ for which there exists a function $c: V \to \{1, 2, \dots, k\}$ with $c(u) \neq c(v)$ whenever $uv \in E$.

Determine the exact value of
$$\chi_2 \;=\; \sup\{\chi(G) : G \text{ is a biplanar graph}\}.$$

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The Earth–Moon problem remains open. It is known that the maximum chromatic number of biplanar graphs lies in {9, 10, 11, 12}: a lower bound of 9 is established by explicit constructions, and Heawood-type arguments give an upper bound of 12. Ringel originally conjectured the answer is 8 (later shown to be too low), and Gethner (2018) conjectured the true value is 11. The exact value has not been determined.

Two distinct letters $x,y \in A$ are said to alternate in $w$ if, after deleting from $w$ all letters other than $x$ and $y$, the resulting word is of the form $xyxy\cdots$ or $yxyx\cdots$ (of either even or odd length). A word $w$ is called $k$-uniform if every letter of $A$ occurs exactly $k$ times in $w$. A simple graph $G=(V,E)$ is said to be word-representable if there exists a finite word $w$ over the alphabet $V$ such that, for every pair of distinct vertices $x,y \in V$, the letters $x$ and $y$ alternate in $w$ if and only if $xy \in E$. The representation number of a word-representable graph $G$ is the smallest positive integer $k$ such that $G$ admits a $k$-uniform word representing it.

Question: Does there exist a (word-representable) graph $G$ on $n$ vertices whose representation number is strictly greater than $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$?

The Zarankiewicz problem remains unsolved in general. The Kővári–Sós–Turán theorem provides a general upper bound, and matching constructions are known only for limited cases (e.g., $K_{2,2}$, $K_{3,3}$, and a few others, often via finite geometry constructions). Recent surveys and notes (e.g., Conlon's notes and the 2024 survey on Zarankiewicz problems in geometry) confirm tight asymptotics for general $(s,t)$ are still open.

Hilbert's tenth problem over a number field K asks whether there exists an algorithm that, given a polynomial equation f(x_1, ..., x_n) = 0 with coefficients in the ring of integers O_K, decides whether f has a solution with x_1, ..., x_n in O_K. One says that "Hilbert's tenth problem holds" (or has a negative answer) for K when no such algorithm exists, equivalently when the set of integer solutions of polynomial equations over O_K is sufficiently rich that Diophantine definability of Z inside O_K is established.

Problem: Determine, for every number field K (i.e., every finite extension of Q), whether Hilbert's tenth problem has a negative answer over the ring of integers O_K. In other words, prove or disprove that for every number field K there is no algorithm deciding the solvability of polynomial Diophantine equations over O_K.

One says that "Hilbert's tenth problem holds" (or has a negative answer) for K when no such algorithm exists, equivalently when the set of integer solutions of polynomial equations over O_K is sufficiently rich that Diophantine definability of Z inside O_K is established.

Problem: Determine, for every number field K (i.e., every finite extension of Q), whether Hilbert's tenth problem has a negative answer over the ring of integers O_K. In other words, prove or disprove that for every number field K there is no algorithm deciding the solvability of polynomial Diophantine equations over O_K.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

In December 2024, Peter Koymans and Carlo Pagano (and, independently, another team using Mordell curves) announced proofs that Hilbert's tenth problem has a negative answer for the ring of integers of every number field. The argument constructs elliptic curves with full rational 2-torsion whose rank is stable in chosen quadratic extensions, combining 2-descent with additive combinatorics. This resolves the long-standing question affirmatively in the sense that Hilbert's tenth problem is undecidable for all number fields.

The best partial result is a 3×3 magic square with seven of nine entries being perfect squares (Bremner, 1997). Work in ZFC. Recall that an uncountable cardinal κ is strongly compact if every κ-complete filter on any set can be extended to a κ-complete ultrafilter; equivalently, every κ-complete filter on a set I can be extended, or every product of compact spaces of any size is κ-compact. The Generalized Continuum Hypothesis (GCH) is the statement that 2^λ = λ^+ for every infinite cardinal λ. We say GCH holds below κ if 2^λ = λ^+ for every infinite cardinal λ < κ.

Question: Is it provable in ZFC that, whenever κ is a strongly compact cardinal and GCH holds below κ, then GCH holds at every infinite cardinal (i.e., 2^λ = λ^+ for all infinite λ)?

Work in Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory ZF (without the Axiom of Choice). Let V denote the class of all sets, viewed as a structure in the language of set theory. A class function j : V → V is called a nontrivial elementary embedding if:

(i) j is not the identity (there exists a set x with j(x) ≠ x), and
(ii) for every formula φ(x_1, ..., x_n) in the language of set theory and all sets a_1, ..., a_n, one has φ(a_1, ..., a_n) if and only if φ(j(a_1), ..., j(a_n)).

Kunen's theorem shows that in ZFC no such nontrivial elementary embedding j : V → V exists. The question is whether this conclusion still holds when the Axiom of Choice is dropped:

Is it consistent with ZF that there exists a nontrivial elementary embedding j : V → V?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The general classification problem for higher-dimensional asymptotically flat stationary black holes remains open. Uniqueness fails for vacuum 5D solutions (Myers–Perry and black rings can share the same asymptotic charges; helical black rings give infinite non-uniqueness). Partial uniqueness theorems exist: for static vacuum cases (Gibbons–Ida–Shiromizu and later extensions), and for 5D stationary bi-axisymmetric solutions characterized by interval/rod data (Hollands–Yazadjiev and others). Recent work (2024) extends static uniqueness results with photon surfaces. No complete classification is known.

Let $(X,Y)$ be a standard planar Brownian motion on a probability space, and let $\mathcal{F}^{(X,Y)} = (\mathcal{F}^{(X,Y)}_t)_{t\ge 0}$ denote the usual augmentation of its natural filtration. Let $X'$ be a one-dimensional Brownian motion (started at $0$) adapted to $\mathcal{F}^{(X,Y)}$, and write $\mathcal{F}^{X'} = (\mathcal{F}^{X'}_t)_{t\ge 0}$ for the usual augmentation of its natural filtration.

Say that $X'$ is complementable in $\mathcal{F}^{(X,Y)}$ if there exists a one-dimensional Brownian motion $Y'$ adapted to $\mathcal{F}^{(X,Y)}$ such that $X'$ and $Y'$ are independent and the usual augmentation of the natural filtration of the pair $(X',Y')$ coincides with $\mathcal{F}^{(X,Y)}$.

Say that $X'$ is maximal in $\mathcal{F}^{(X,Y)}$ if, for every one-dimensional Brownian motion $X''$ adapted to $\mathcal{F}^{(X,Y)}$ with $\mathcal{F}^{X'} \subset \mathcal{F}^{X''}$, one necessarily has $\mathcal{F}^{X'} = \mathcal{F}^{X''}$.

It is known that any complementable $X'$ is maximal. Question: is the converse true? That is, must every maximal one-dimensional Brownian motion $X'$ in $\mathcal{F}^{(X,Y)}$ be complementable?

Let $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be an unknown smooth $T$-periodic function whose derivative satisfies the a priori bound $\|f'\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R})} \le m_1 < \infty$. Suppose that instead of $f$ we are given a noise level $\delta > 0$ and a function $f_\delta \in L^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ with $\|f_\delta - f\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R})} < \delta$. A method is called a stable approximation of the derivative based on the data $\{\delta, f_\delta, m_1\}$ if it produces, from these data alone, a function $R(f_\delta, \delta, m_1) \in L^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ such that
$$\sup_{f}\, \|R(f_\delta,\delta,m_1) - f'\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R})} \longrightarrow 0 \quad \text{as } \delta \to 0,$$
where the supremum is taken over all admissible pairs $(f, f_\delta)$ with $f$ smooth, $T$-periodic, $\|f'\|_\infty \le m_1$, and $\|f_\delta - f\|_\infty < \delta$.

Question: Does such a stable approximation procedure exist? That is, can $f'$ be recovered in the $L^\infty$ norm with error tending to $0$ as $\delta \to 0$, using only the information $\{\delta, f_\delta, m_1\}$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The problem is solved with a negative answer: it is proved (by A. G. Ramm and collaborators) that one cannot stably approximate $f'$ in $L^\infty$ given only noisy data $f_\delta$ together with bounds on $f$ and $f'$. Stable approximation becomes possible if instead an a priori bound on a derivative of order strictly greater than one (e.g. $m_2$, a bound on $f''$, or a fractional derivative of order $>1$) is assumed.

Let $D \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ with $n \geq 3$ be a bounded domain. For $m = 1,2$, let $L_m$ be a formal linear partial differential operator with sufficiently regular coefficients defined on $D$, and let
$$N(L_m) = \{w : L_m w = 0 \text{ in } D\}$$
denote its null-space in $D$ (in a suitable distributional or classical sense in which the operator acts).

A pair $(L_1, L_2)$ is said to have Property C in $L^p(D)$ (for $p \geq 1$) if the set of finite linear combinations of products $u_1 u_2$, with $u_m \in N(L_m)$ for $m = 1,2$ and such that the product $u_1 u_2$ is well defined and lies in $L^p(D)$, is dense in $L^p(D)$.

Question: Characterize the pairs of formal linear partial differential operators $(L_1, L_2)$ for which Property C holds in $L^2(D)$, and more generally in $L^p(D)$ for $p \geq 1$. In particular, determine whether every pair of such operators (under reasonable hypotheses) enjoys this completeness-of-products property.

Suppose that the values of $\hat f$ are known only on some subset $\widetilde D \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ of positive Lebesgue measure (or, more generally, a set having an accumulation point in $\mathbb{C}^n$ once $\hat f$ is viewed as an entire function via the Paley–Wiener theorem).

(a) Prove or disprove that $f$ is uniquely determined by the restriction $\hat f|_{\widetilde D}$.

(b) If unique recovery holds, give an explicit analytic inversion formula that reconstructs $f(x)$ for $x \in D$ from the data $\{\hat f(\xi) : \xi \in \widetilde D\}$, equivalently a constructive procedure for extrapolating $\hat f$ from $\widetilde D$ to all of $\mathbb{R}^n$.

Since the Fourier transform of a compactly supported function is entire of exponential type (Paley–Wiener), it is uniquely determined by its values on any set with an accumulation point, so uniqueness of recovery is classical. Explicit analytic extrapolation/inversion procedures (e.g., Gerchberg–Papoulis iterations, prolate spheroidal wave function expansions of Slepian–Pollak–Landau, and Tikhonov-regularized analytic continuation) are well established, although the problem is severely ill-posed in practice.

Let N denote the σ-ideal of Lebesgue null subsets of the real line, and let add(N) be its additivity, i.e. the least cardinality of a family F ⊆ N whose union is not in N.

For a topological space X, let O(X) denote the collection of all open covers of X. The Rothberger selection principle S_1(O, O) is the statement that for every sequence (U_n : n ∈ ω) of open covers of X there exists a choice U_n ∈ U_n such that {U_n : n ∈ ω} is an open cover of X. A space satisfying S_1(O, O) is called a Rothberger space. Define the (uniform) critical cardinality
   add(S_1(O, O)) = min{ |F| : F is a family of sets of reals, each satisfying S_1(O, O), whose union does not satisfy S_1(O, O) }.

Question: Is it consistent with ZFC that
   add(N) < add(S_1(O, O)) ?

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple undirected graph on $n$ vertices. A partial Hermitian matrix with graph $G$ is an $n\times n$ array $A=(a_{ij})$ in which the diagonal entries $a_{ii}$ are specified real numbers and an off-diagonal entry $a_{ij}$ is specified (with $a_{ji}=\overline{a_{ij}}$) if and only if $\{i,j\}\in E$; the remaining entries are free. Such a partial matrix is called partial positive (semidefinite) if every principal submatrix all of whose entries are specified is Hermitian positive semidefinite. A Hermitian completion of $A$ is any Hermitian matrix $M$ obtained by assigning complex values to the unspecified entries. For a Hermitian matrix $M$, let $i_-(M)$ denote the number of its negative eigenvalues (counted with multiplicity).

Define the completion number $c(G)$ of $G$ to be the smallest nonnegative integer $k$ such that every partial positive matrix $A$ with graph $G$ admits a Hermitian completion $M$ with $i_-(M)\le k$.

It is known that $c(G)=0$ if and only if $G$ is a chordal graph (every cycle of length at least four has a chord).

Problem: For each integer $k\ge 1$, give a purely graph-theoretic characterization of the class of graphs $G$ satisfying $c(G)=k$.

representations.original:
For a real number $x$, let $\{x\} = x - \lfloor x \rfloor$ denote its fractional part. Determine whether there exists a nonzero real number $\alpha$ with the property that for every positive integer $n$,
$$0 \le \left\{\alpha \left(\tfrac{3}{2}\right)^n\right\} < \tfrac{1}{2}.$$
Such a number is called a $Z$-number. The problem is to decide whether any $Z$-number exists.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The existence of $Z$-numbers, posed by Mahler in 1968, remains an open problem. Mahler showed that each unit interval contains at most one $Z$-number and conjectured none exist. Partial results include bounds by Flatto–Lagarias–Pollington on the diameter of the orbit closure of $\{\alpha(3/2)^n\}$ for rational $\alpha$, and a 2024 preprint ruling out $Z$-numbers among positive integers, but the general existence question is still unresolved.

Let $\mathcal{A}_g(\mathbb{C})$ denote the moduli space of principally polarized complex abelian varieties of dimension $g$. A point of $\mathcal{A}_g(\mathbb{C})$ is called a complex multiplication (CM) point if it corresponds to an abelian variety whose endomorphism algebra (tensored with $\mathbb{Q}$) contains a commutative semisimple $\mathbb{Q}$-algebra of dimension $2g$. An irreducible closed algebraic subvariety $Z \subseteq \mathcal{A}_g(\mathbb{C})$ is said to be of Hodge type if it is an irreducible component of the image in $\mathcal{A}_g(\mathbb{C})$ of a Shimura subvariety associated to a Shimura sub-datum of the Siegel Shimura datum defining $\mathcal{A}_g$.

Prove or disprove: if $Z \subseteq \mathcal{A}_g(\mathbb{C})$ is an irreducible algebraic subvariety such that the set of CM points contained in $Z$ is Zariski-dense in $Z$, then $Z$ is of Hodge type.

The André-Oort conjecture for the Siegel modular variety $\mathcal{A}_g$ was proved by Jacob Tsimerman (arXiv:1506.01466, published in Annals of Mathematics, 2018), conditional at the time on the averaged Colmez conjecture, which was subsequently established unconditionally by Yuan–Zhang and independently by Andreatta–Goren–Howard–Madapusi-Pera. The general André-Oort conjecture for all Shimura varieties was completed by Pila–Shankar–Tsimerman (2021).

Let $\alpha$ be a nonzero algebraic number with minimal polynomial $a_d \prod_{i=1}^{d}(x-\alpha_i) \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$, where $a_d>0$, $\gcd$ of coefficients is $1$, and $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_d$ are the Galois conjugates of $\alpha$ over $\mathbb{Q}$. Define the Mahler measure of $\alpha$ by
$$M(\alpha) = a_d \prod_{i=1}^{d} \max(1,|\alpha_i|),$$
and the absolute logarithmic Weil height by
$$h(\alpha) =  rac{1}{d}\log M(\alpha).$$

Prove or disprove: there exists an absolute constant $c > 0$ such that for every nonzero algebraic number $\alpha$ of degree $d$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ that is not a root of unity, one has
$$h(\alpha) \geq  rac{c}{d}.$$

Equivalently, does there exist an absolute constant $c'>0$ such that $M(\alpha) \geq 1 + c'$ for every algebraic integer $\alpha$ that is not a root of unity?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Lehmer's problem, posed in 1933, remains a famous open problem in number theory. The best known unconditional lower bound is due to Dobrowolski (1979), giving $h(\alpha) \gg (\log\log d/\log d)^3 / d$, with subsequent refinements (Voutier, Louboutin, etc.), but no absolute lower bound of order $1/d$ is known. The conjectured smallest Mahler measure greater than 1 is Lehmer's number $\approx 1.17628$, but this has not been proven.

Must $Z$ necessarily be a union of connected components of $V(\mathbb{R})$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The question (due to Mazur) has been answered negatively. Colliot-Thélène, Skorobogatov, and Swinnerton-Dyer ("Double fibres and double covers: paucity of rational points," Acta Arithmetica 79 (1997), 113–135) constructed smooth projective surfaces X over Q with X(Q) Zariski dense, where X(R) has two connected components: rational points are dense in the real topology in one component, but in the other their closure lies in finitely many curves. Hence Z need not be a union of connected components of V(R).

Let $(n_i)_{i\geq 0}$ be a strictly increasing sequence of positive integers. Suppose there exists a prime number $p$ such that the formal power series
$$f(z) = \sum_{i \geq 0} z^{n_i} \in \mathbb{F}_p[[z]]$$
is algebraic over the field of rational functions $\mathbb{F}_p(z)$. Prove or disprove: the real number
$$\alpha = \sum_{i \geq 0} 10^{-n_i}$$
is either rational or transcendental.
representations.original:
Let $(n_i)_{i\geq 0}$ be a strictly increasing sequence of positive integers. Suppose there exists a prime number $p$ such that the formal power series
$$f(z) = \sum_{i \geq 0} z^{n_i} \in \mathbb{F}_p[[z]]$$
is algebraic over the field of rational functions $\mathbb{F}_p(z)$. Prove or disprove: the real number
$$\alpha = \sum_{i \geq 0} 10^{-n_i}$$
is either rational or transcendental.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

By Christol's theorem, the hypothesis that $\sum z^{n_i}$ is algebraic over $\mathbb{F}_p(z)$ is equivalent to the indicator sequence of $\{n_i\}$ being $p$-automatic, which makes $\alpha$ an automatic real number in base 10. The conjecture is thus the Cobham–Loxton–van der Poorten conjecture, which was proved by B. Adamczewski and Y. Bugeaud (Annals of Mathematics, 2007) using the Schmidt subspace theorem and combinatorial properties of stammering sequences. Hence the statement holds.

A flat virtual link diagram is a 4-valent planar graph whose vertices are decorated either as flat (unoriented, undercrossing/overcrossing information removed) classical crossings or as virtual crossings; two such diagrams are considered equivalent if they are related by a finite sequence of the flat versions of the three classical Reidemeister moves together with the virtual Reidemeister moves (including the mixed move). A doodle link is a closed immersed collection of curves in the plane (or 2-sphere) whose only singularities are transverse double points, considered up to the analogues of Reidemeister moves I and II only; in particular, no Reidemeister III move is allowed (a crossing cannot "slide over itself"). One may likewise define virtual doodles by adding virtual crossings together with the virtual Reidemeister moves but again forbidding the (classical) third Reidemeister move.

Develop a precise comparison between the theory of flat virtual knots and links and the theory of (virtual) doodles. Specifically:

(a) Construct a well-defined map from the set of equivalence classes of (virtual) doodle diagrams to the set of equivalence classes of flat virtual link diagrams induced by interpreting each doodle crossing as a flat crossing, and determine whether this map is injective and/or surjective.

(b) Identify which invariants of flat virtual links descend to invariants of (virtual) doodles, and which invariants of (virtual) doodles fail to extend to flat virtual links because of the third Reidemeister move.

(c) Decide whether there exist non-trivial (virtual) doodles that become trivial as flat virtual links, and conversely whether there exist non-trivial flat virtual links all of whose doodle lifts are trivial.

The comparison between flat virtual knot theory and (virtual) doodle theory is an active research direction. Recent work (e.g., on semiquandles and flat virtual knots, affine flat biquandles, polynomial invariants of virtual doodles and virtual knots, and colorings/doubled colorings of virtual doodles) develops invariants on both sides and notes that virtual doodles correspond to flat virtual diagrams without the third Reidemeister move, but no comprehensive structural comparison theorem appears to have been established. The general comparison question remains open.

Background. A biquandle is a set X equipped with two binary operations ▷, ▷* : X×X → X satisfying axioms derived from the generalized Reidemeister moves for virtual links: each operation makes X into a quandle (idempotent, right-invertible, self-distributive in the appropriate sense), and the two operations satisfy the mixed exchange relation that encodes invariance under all virtual Reidemeister moves. To every oriented virtual link diagram D one associates the fundamental biquandle BQ(D), defined by generators corresponding to semi-arcs of D and relations at each classical crossing using ▷ and ▷*; BQ(D) is an invariant of the virtual link L = [D]. A biquandle is called strong if certain additional compatibility relations between ▷ and ▷* hold (so that the two quandle structures interact in the manner of a fully realized biquandle), and weak otherwise.

Consider also the associative algebra A over a commutative ring with two generators A and B subject to the single relation
   [ B , (A − 1)(A, B) ] = 0,
where [·,·] is the commutator and (A,B) denotes the (multiplicative) commutator of A and B. This algebra arises from the linear (Alexander-type) biquandle case.

Problems.
(i) Does the fundamental biquandle classify oriented virtual links up to mirror image? Equivalently, if two oriented virtual links L₁ and L₂ have isomorphic fundamental biquandles, must L₂ be equivalent either to L₁ or to its mirror image?
(ii) Exhibit informative examples of weak biquandles that are not strong, illustrating in what ways the strong axioms genuinely restrict the class of biquandles relevant to virtual link theory.
(iii) Determine further algebraic structure (e.g. center, representation theory, growth, normal form for elements, ideal structure, or relations to known algebras) of the two-generator one-relation algebra defined by [B,(A − 1)(A,B)] = 0.

The completeness of the fundamental biquandle as an invariant of virtual links up to mirror image is still stated as a conjecture in recent literature on biquandle invariants (e.g., 2025 papers on biquandle quivers and virtual bridge indices). It is known to be complete up to reflection for classical knots, but the virtual case remains an active open conjecture. No published resolution of the algebra question or a definitive catalog of weak-not-strong biquandles was found.

Work in the category of virtual long knots, where a long knot is a properly embedded copy of the real line (more precisely an immersed/virtually-diagrammed long strand) considered up to the usual generalized Reidemeister moves for virtual knots, and where the connected sum K # K' of two long knots is defined by concatenation along the distinguished endpoints. A long knot is called classical if it admits a diagram with no virtual crossings. It is known that every classical long knot commutes (under #) with every virtual long knot.

Question: Suppose K and K' are virtual long knots such that K # K' is isotopic (as virtual long knots) to K' # K. Must there exist a virtual long knot L, classical long knots Q and Q', and non-negative integers m, n such that
   K = L^{# m} # Q   and   K' = L^{# n} # Q' ,
where L^{# k} denotes the k-fold connected sum of L with itself (with L^{# 0} interpreted as the trivial long knot)?

In other words, is classicality (together with sharing a common connected-sum power) the only source of commutativity in the monoid of virtual long knots under connected sum?

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

Web searches confirm the well-known fact that connected sum of virtual long knots is non-commutative while classical long knots commute with all long knots, and that this question appears on standard lists of unsolved problems in virtual knot theory. No published resolution (proof or counterexample) characterizing all commuting pairs of virtual long knots in this form was found, so the status appears to remain open, but this could not be verified definitively.

Work in the complex projective plane $\mathbb{CP}^2$ equipped with its standard Fubini–Study symplectic form $\omega_{FS}$. A symplectic curve $C \subset \mathbb{CP}^2$ is a (possibly singular) two-dimensional subset which is a smooth symplectic submanifold away from a finite set of singular points, and which near each singular point is locally modeled (up to a symplectomorphism of a neighborhood in $\mathbb{CP}^2$) on the image of a holomorphic map from a disk in $\mathbb{C}$ exhibiting a prescribed singularity type. The degree of $C$ is its homology class in $H_2(\mathbb{CP}^2;\mathbb{Z}) \cong \mathbb{Z}$. A node is a singularity locally modeled on $\{xy=0\}\subset\mathbb{C}^2$, and an (ordinary) cusp is a singularity locally modeled on $\{y^2=x^3\}\subset\mathbb{C}^2$. Two symplectic curves $C_0, C_1$ with the same singularity data are called symplectically isotopic if there exists a continuous family $\{C_t\}_{t\in[0,1]}$ of symplectic curves in $\mathbb{CP}^2$, each having exactly the same number of nodes and cusps and no other singularities, interpolating between them.

Fix integers $d \ge 1$, $\nu \ge 0$, and $\kappa \ge 0$. Classify, up to symplectic isotopy preserving the singularity data, all symplectic curves of degree $d$ in $\mathbb{CP}^2$ having exactly $\nu$ nodes and $\kappa$ cusps and no other singularities.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The general classification remains open. Partial results are known: smooth symplectic curves (no singularities) of small degree are isotopic to complex curves (Gromov, Sikorav, Shevchishin, Siebert–Tian); for irreducible rational symplectic curves of degree $d$ with $\nu$ nodes and $\kappa<d$ cusps, isotopy to a complex curve was established (Francisco), and all rational cuspidal curves of degree at most 5, as well as those with a single torus-knot-type cusp, have been classified (Golla–Starkston, 2022). No full classification for arbitrary $(d,\nu,\kappa)$ is known.

representations.normalized:
Let $F_n$ denote the Hirzebruch surface (a rational ruled complex surface) equipped with its natural projection to $\mathbb{CP}^1$ whose generic fiber is a rational curve. A Hurwitz curve in $F_n$ is a (possibly singular) closed real surface $D \subset F_n$ whose only singularities are nodes (transverse double points) and cusps, and such that the restriction of the ruling $F_n \to \mathbb{CP}^1$ to $D$ is a branched covering whose only critical points are simple branch points (away from the singular points of $D$) and the singular points themselves. Two Hurwitz curves are said to be isotopic if there is an isotopy through Hurwitz curves carrying one onto the other. Given a Hurwitz curve $D \subset F_n$ and a complex curve $C \subset F_{n'}$ that has the same intersection number with a fiber as $D$, the fiber sum $D \# C$ is the Hurwitz curve in $F_{n+n'}$ obtained by removing a regular fiber neighborhood from each ambient surface and gluing along the boundary, matching the intersection points of $D$ and $C$ with the chosen fibers.

A monodromy morphism for a Hurwitz curve $D \subset F_n$ is a homomorphism $\theta : \pi_1(F_n \setminus D) \to S_N$ (the symmetric group on $N$ letters) that sends each meridian around $D$ to a transposition; such a $\theta$ is called compatible (with the cuspidal/nodal structure of $D$) when the standard local relations at nodes and cusps are satisfied. Compatibility extends in the obvious way to fiber sums, so that $\theta$ on $D$ and a chosen monodromy datum on $C$ together yield a monodromy on $D \# C$.

Now let $D_1, D_2 \subset F_n$ be Hurwitz curves that represent the same homology class in $H_2(F_n;\mathbb{Z})$ and that have equal numbers of cusps and equal numbers of nodes. Suppose that for $i = 1, 2$ there are compatible monodromy morphisms $\theta_i : \pi_1(F_n \setminus D_i) \to S_N$, and that there exists a fiber $F \subset F_n$ of the ruling with
$$F \cap D_1 \;=\; F \cap D_2 \qquad \text{and} \qquad \theta_1\big|_{F \setminus D_1} \;=\; \theta_2\big|_{F \setminus D_2}.$$

Decide whether there always exists an integer $n' \geq 0$ and a smooth complex curve $C \subset F_{n'}$, compatible with the given monodromy data, such that the fiber sums $D_1 \# C$ and $D_2 \# C$ are isotopic as Hurwitz curves.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

A Kharlamov–Kulikov theorem establishes the analogous statement without monodromy data: any two Hurwitz curves in $F_n$ with equal homology class and equal numbers of cusps and nodes become isotopic after fiber sum with a sufficiently positive smooth complex curve in $F_0$. Let $B_d$ denote the Artin braid group on $d$ strands, with standard generators $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_{d-1}$, and let $\Delta^2 \in B_d$ be the full twist (the generator of the center of $B_d$). A half-twist in $B_d$ is any element conjugate to a standard generator $\sigma_i$. A factorization of $\Delta^2$ is an ordered tuple $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ of elements of $B_d$ with $x_1 x_2 \cdots x_n = \Delta^2$. Two factorizations are declared equivalent if one can be obtained from the other by a finite sequence of:

(i) Hurwitz moves: replacing two consecutive entries $(x_i, x_{i+1})$ by $(x_i x_{i+1} x_i^{-1}, x_i)$ or by $(x_{i+1}, x_{i+1}^{-1} x_i x_{i+1})$;

(ii) global conjugation: replacing every $x_i$ simultaneously by $g x_i g^{-1}$ for some $g \in B_d$.

Fix integers $d \ge 2$, $\nu \ge 0$, and $\kappa \ge 0$ satisfying $\tau := d(d-1) - 2\nu - 3\kappa \ge 0$.

Classify, up to the equivalence above, all factorizations of $\Delta^2$ in $B_d$ as an ordered product of exactly $\tau + \nu + \kappa$ factors, of which $\tau$ are half-twists, $\nu$ are squares of half-twists, and $\kappa$ are cubes of half-twists.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The classification problem for Hurwitz-equivalence classes of factorizations of the full twist $\Delta^2$ into powers of half-twists is a long-standing question in the theory of braid monodromy factorizations of singular plane curves. Only partial results are known: e.g., Hurwitz equivalence has been established for special "semi-frame" factorizations and in small braid groups such as $B_3$. No general classification for arbitrary $(d,\nu,\kappa)$ appears in the literature, and the problem remains open.

Let $B_d$ denote the braid group on $d$ strands. A factorization of length $r$ of an element $\Delta \in B_d$ is an ordered tuple $F = (\rho_1, \ldots, \rho_r)$ of elements of $B_d$ such that $\rho_1 \rho_2 \cdots \rho_r = \Delta$. Two factorizations are said to have the same numbers of factors of each conjugacy type if there is a bijection between their factors that pairs each $\rho_i$ with a $B_d$-conjugate of itself.

The Hurwitz moves act on factorizations of length $r$ by, for each $1 \le i \le r-1$,
$$(\rho_1, \ldots, \rho_i, \rho_{i+1}, \ldots, \rho_r) \longmapsto (\rho_1, \ldots, \rho_i \rho_{i+1} \rho_i^{-1}, \rho_i, \ldots, \rho_r),$$
together with their inverses.

A partial conjugation is defined as follows. Given a factorization $F = (\rho_1, \ldots, \rho_r)$, indices $1 \le p \le q \le r$, and an element $b \in B_d$ such that $b$ commutes with the product $\rho_p \rho_{p+1} \cdots \rho_q$, one forms the new factorization
$$F' = (\rho_1, \ldots, \rho_{p-1}, b^{-1}\rho_p b, b^{-1}\rho_{p+1} b, \ldots, b^{-1}\rho_q b, \rho_{q+1}, \ldots, \rho_r).$$

Now fix a finite subset $\theta \subset \mathbb{C}$ of cardinality $n$, and let $\mathrm{LB}_d(\theta) \subseteq B_d$ denote the corresponding liftable braid subgroup, i.e.\ the subgroup of those braids whose induced permutation of the punctures lifts to an automorphism of the relevant $n$-fold branched cover.

Question: Suppose $F$ and $F'$ are two factorizations of the same element of $B_d$ (respectively of $\mathrm{LB}_d(\theta)$) that contain the same numbers of factors of each conjugacy type. Must $F$ and $F'$ always be equivalent under a finite sequence of Hurwitz moves and partial conjugations by elements of $B_d$ (respectively of $\mathrm{LB}_d(\theta)$)?

Let $n\ge 3$ and let $G\subseteq S_n$ be a transitive permutation group. Fix an $r$-tuple $\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_r)$ of elements of $G$ that generate $G$ and satisfy $\sigma_1\sigma_2\cdots\sigma_r=1$. Let $\mathcal H(\sigma)$ denote the Hurwitz space over $\mathbb{Z}$ parametrizing tamely ramified degree-$n$ covers $f\colon X\to \mathbb{P}^1$ (with $X$ a smooth projective curve) whose branch cycle description is $\sigma$ (i.e., the local inertia generators at the branch points, taken in some standard order, are conjugate to $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_r$ in $G$). Let $g$ be the genus of $X$ determined by $\sigma$ via the Riemann–Hurwitz formula, and let
$$\varphi_\sigma\colon \mathcal H(\sigma)\longrightarrow \mathcal M_g$$
be the morphism sending a cover $(f\colon X\to\mathbb{P}^1)$ to the isomorphism class of $X$.

For a prime number $p$:

(1) Determine whether $\mathcal H(\sigma)\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{F}_p$ is nonempty.

(2) When $\mathcal H(\sigma)\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{F}_p$ is nonempty, compute the dimension of the image of $\varphi_\sigma\otimes\mathbb{F}_p$ in $\mathcal M_g\otimes \mathbb{F}_p$.

Available literature on Hurwitz spaces in positive characteristic (e.g., Romagny–Wewers' survey and related work) treats this as a general open problem: while existence and dimension results are known in many special cases (e.g., when p does not divide |G|, or via lifting/specialization arguments), no general answer is known describing nonemptiness of H(σ)⊗F_p and the dimension of the image in M_g for arbitrary (G, σ) and arbitrary primes p. Let $p$ be a prime number and $k$ a field of characteristic $p$. For a profinite group $G$ and a finite-dimensional continuous $k$-linear representation $V$ of $G$ with $\operatorname{End}_{k[G]}(V)=k$, consider deformations of $V$ to complete Noetherian local commutative rings with residue field $k$: a deformation to such a ring $R$ is an equivalence class of continuous $R[G]$-modules that are free over $R$ and reduce to $V$ modulo the maximal ideal. Under the hypothesis $\operatorname{End}_{k[G]}(V)=k$, the deformation functor is (pro-)representable by a complete local Noetherian ring $R(G,V)$ (the universal deformation ring) provided the functor satisfies the required finiteness; in general $R(G,V)$ is the inverse limit representing the functor on Artinian quotients (a versal/universal deformation ring).

Question: Do there exist a profinite group $G$, a field $k$ of characteristic $p>0$, and a finite-dimensional continuous $k$-linear representation $V$ of $G$ with $\operatorname{End}_{k[G]}(V)=k$ such that the universal deformation ring $R(G,V)$ is Noetherian but is not a local complete intersection (i.e., cannot be written as a quotient of a power series ring $W(k)[[x_1,\dots,x_n]]$ by a regular sequence)?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The question (posed by M. Flach) has been answered in the affirmative. Bleher and Chinburg constructed explicit examples of profinite groups and representations whose universal deformation ring is Noetherian but not a complete intersection (e.g., rings of the form $W[[t]]/(p^n t, t^2)$), published in Mathematische Annalen (2007) and a C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris note (2006). Later work ("Inverse Problems for deformation rings", 2010) extended this in all characteristics.

Let $k$ be the algebraic closure of a finite field, and let $X$ be a connected smooth projective curve over $k$. A stratified vector bundle on $X$ is a quasi-coherent $\mathcal{O}_X$-module equipped with a compatible action of the sheaf of differential operators $\mathcal{D}_{X/k}$, which is finitely generated and locally free as an $\mathcal{O}_X$-module. The category $\mathrm{Strat}(X)$ of stratified vector bundles is a neutral Tannakian category over $k$ (after choosing a $k$-rational fiber functor at a point $x \in X(k)$), and its Tannakian dual is an affine group scheme $\pi_1^{\mathrm{strat}}(X,x)$. For each integer $r \geq 1$, let $\pi_1^{(r)}(X,x)$ denote the Tannakian quotient group scheme corresponding to the full Tannakian subcategory of $\mathrm{Strat}(X)$ generated by stratified bundles of rank at most $r$.

Determine to what extent the curve $X$ is determined by the collection of group schemes $\{\pi_1^{(r)}(X,x)\}_{r \geq 1}$. More precisely: if $X$ and $X'$ are two connected smooth projective curves over $k$ such that $\pi_1^{(r)}(X,x) \cong \pi_1^{(r)}(X',x')$ as affine group schemes over $k$ for every $r \geq 1$ (compatibly in $r$), what can be concluded about the relation between $X$ and $X'$?

For a fixed rational point $x\in X(k)$, let $\pi_1^{\mathrm{strat}}(X,x)$ denote the affine $k$-group scheme arising as the Tannakian fundamental group of $\mathrm{Strat}(X)$ with the fiber functor at $x$. For each integer $r\ge 1$, let $\mathrm{Strat}^{(r)}(X)$ denote the full Tannakian subcategory generated by stratified bundles of rank $\le r$, and let
$$\pi_1^{(r)}(X,x)$$
denote the corresponding Tannakian fundamental group (a quotient of $\pi_1^{\mathrm{strat}}(X,x)$).

Question: For every $r\ge 1$, is $\pi_1^{(r)}(X,x)$ an extension of a finite (étale) group scheme by a pro-$p$ group scheme? Equivalently, does $\pi_1^{(r)}(X,x)$ admit a normal closed pro-$p$ subgroup scheme with finite quotient?

The question appears in a 2004 problem list on automorphisms of curves and concerns the structure of the rank-$r$ stratified/F-divided fundamental group $\pi_1^{(r)}(X)$ of a smooth projective curve over $\overline{\mathbb{F}_p}$. representations.normalized:
Let $X$ be a smooth connected scheme over an algebraically closed field $k$ of characteristic $p>0$. For each integer $r\ge 0$, consider the category $\mathrm{Strat}^{(r)}(X)$ of "stratified vector bundles of level $r$" on $X$: objects are finite-rank locally free $\mathcal{O}_X$-modules $E$ equipped with an action of the sheaf of differential operators of order $\le p^r-1$ (equivalently, sequences $(E_0,E_1,\ldots,E_r)$ together with $\mathcal{O}_X$-linear isomorphisms $\sigma_i\colon F^{*}E_{i+1}\xrightarrow{\sim} E_i$, where $F$ denotes the absolute Frobenius). Equipped with the obvious tensor product and a fiber functor at a rational point $x\in X(k)$, $\mathrm{Strat}^{(r)}(X)$ is a neutral Tannakian category, and one defines the level-$r$ stratified fundamental group scheme
$$\pi_1^{(r)}(X,x) \;:=\; \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}\!\bigl(\omega_x\colon \mathrm{Strat}^{(r)}(X)\to \mathrm{Vect}_k\bigr),$$
an affine group scheme over $k$, whose inverse limit over $r$ recovers the stratified fundamental group $\pi_1^{\mathrm{strat}}(X,x)$.

Problem: Establish whether the groups $\pi_1^{(r)}(X,x)$ carry intrinsic geometric or arithmetic information beyond their formal Tannakian construction. Concretely, exhibit applications, structural theorems, or invariants of $X$ that are genuinely controlled by $\pi_1^{(r)}(X,x)$ for some finite $r$ (for example, relations to the étale fundamental group, to crystalline or $F$-isocrystal data, to lifting/specialization phenomena, or to classification of bundles with bounded $p$-curvature), and which are not visible from $\pi_1^{\mathrm{strat}}(X,x)$ alone.

The question is a meta-question about the usefulness of finite-level stratified fundamental group schemes $\pi_1^{(r)}$. Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic $p>0$ (with $p$ odd in the standard setting). Let $\pi: C \to \mathbb{P}^1_k$ be a hyperelliptic cover, i.e., $C$ is a smooth projective connected curve of genus $g \geq 1$ admitting a degree-$2$ morphism $\pi$ to the projective line, branched at a finite set $B \subset \mathbb{P}^1_k$. Recall that a smooth projective curve $X$ of genus $g$ over $k$ is called ordinary if its $p$-rank equals $g$, equivalently if the Jacobian of $X$ has $p$-rank $g$.

Question: Does there exist a flat family $\mathcal{C} \to S$ of smooth hyperelliptic curves over a connected base $S$ with two distinguished points $0, \eta \in S$ such that:
(i) the fiber $\mathcal{C}_0$ is isomorphic to $C$ (as a hyperelliptic cover of $\mathbb{P}^1_k$);
(ii) the fiber $\mathcal{C}_\eta$ is an ordinary hyperelliptic curve; and
(iii) along the family, the branch locus deforms by moving only one of the branch points (the other branch points remaining fixed in $\mathbb{P}^1$)?

Equivalently, can every hyperelliptic cover of $\mathbb{P}^1_k$ be deformed to an ordinary hyperelliptic cover via a one-parameter deformation of its branch divisor that displaces exactly one branch point?

representations.normalized:
Fix an odd prime $p$ and work over an algebraically closed field $k$ of characteristic $p$. For a finite commutative group scheme $G$ over $k$ killed by $p$ (a BT_1 group scheme), let $F$ and $V$ denote its Frobenius and Verschiebung. The $p$-rank of $G$ is $\dim_{\mathbb F_p} \operatorname{Hom}(\mu_p, G)$, and the $a$-number of $G$ is $\dim_k \operatorname{Hom}(\alpha_p, G)$ where $\alpha_p = \ker(F:\mathbb G_a\to\mathbb G_a)$. For a smooth projective curve $X$ over $k$, write $\operatorname{Jac}(X)[p]$ for the $p$-torsion group scheme of its Jacobian; this is a self-dual BT_1 group scheme of rank $p^{2g(X)}$.

Let $Q$ denote the $p$-torsion group scheme of some abelian variety of dimension $3$ over $k$ having $p$-rank $0$ and $a$-number $1$ (so $Q$ is a self-dual BT_1 group scheme of rank $p^6$). Let $L = \mathbb Z/p \oplus \mu_p$ denote the $p$-torsion group scheme of an ordinary elliptic curve.

Decide each of the following:

(a) Does there exist a smooth hyperelliptic curve $X$ of genus $4$ over $k$ such that $\operatorname{Jac}(X)[p] \cong Q \oplus L$?

(b) Does there exist a smooth hyperelliptic curve $X$ of genus $5$ over $k$ such that $\operatorname{Jac}(X)[p] \cong Q \oplus L^{\oplus 2}$?

Recent work by Pries and collaborators, and by others (e.g., Devalapurkar–Halliday, Elkin–Pries) has produced explicit computations of Dieudonné modules / Ekedahl-Oort types of Jacobians of hyperelliptic curves in genus up to 4 or 5, and several existence questions about specific Ekedahl-Oort types on hyperelliptic loci have been addressed. However, no source found explicitly resolves the specific existence question for the group schemes $Q \oplus (\mathbb Z/p \oplus \mu_p)$ in genus 4 or $Q \oplus (\mathbb Z/p \oplus \mu_p)^2$ in genus 5 with $Q$ as described. The status of this particular question appears to be unresolved in the literature reviewed.

The classification of "big actions" — pairs $(C,G)$ satisfying the Nakajima-type bound $|G|/g_C > 2p/(p-1)$ — remains an active research topic. Work by Lehr–Matignon, Matignon–Rocher, and later authors has produced partial classifications, structural restrictions, and new families (e.g., big actions with non-abelian derived subgroup), but a complete classification has not been achieved. In particular, no examples of big actions with non-abelian second ramification group $G_2$ are known, and the general classification is open.

Let $p$ be a prime and let $K$ be a complete discrete valuation field of characteristic $0$ with algebraically closed residue field $k$ of characteristic $p$. Let $X_K \to \mathbb{P}^1_K$ be a $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$-Galois cover (a $p$-cyclic cover) defined over $K$, where $X_K$ is a smooth projective geometrically connected curve of genus $g = (p-1)(m-1)/2$ for some integer $m \geq 2$.

There exists a minimal finite Galois extension $L/K$ such that $X_K \times_K L$ admits a stable model $\mathcal{X}_L$ over the ring of integers of $L$; the Galois group $\mathrm{Gal}(L/K)$ is called the monodromy group of the cover, and its wild inertia subgroup $\mathrm{Gal}(L/K)_w$ (the $p$-Sylow of the inertia) is called the wild monodromy group. The special fiber $X_k := \mathcal{X}_L \otimes k$ carries a natural action of $\mathrm{Gal}(L/K)_w$, inducing an injection into the group of wild automorphisms $\mathrm{Aut}_k(X_k)$ (those automorphisms whose order is a power of $p$).

For a fixed combinatorial "degeneration type" of the stable reduction (the type of the dual graph together with the genera and ramification data on each component), there is a known upper bound $B(\text{type})$ on the order of $\mathrm{Aut}_k(X_k)$ in terms of the genera of the components, hence an upper bound on $|\mathrm{Gal}(L/K)_w|$.

Question: For every degeneration type that arises from a $p$-cyclic cover $X_K \to \mathbb{P}^1_K$ of genus $g = (p-1)(m-1)/2$, does there exist such a cover for which the wild monodromy group $\mathrm{Gal}(L/K)_w$ attains the upper bound $B(\text{type})$?

$$ y^q - y = c\, x^{q+1}, $$
where $c \in K$ satisfies $v_p(c) = 1/(q+1)$, i.e. $c = p^{1/(q+1)}$ (up to a unit). Under this hypothesis, $C$ has potentially good reduction, and the Galois group of the wild monodromy extension (the minimal extension over which $C$ acquires good reduction, modulo its tame part) is isomorphic to the extraspecial $p$-group of order $p\,q^2$ and exponent $p$.

Let $L/K^{\mathrm{ur}}$ denote this wild monodromy extension and let $G = \mathrm{Gal}(L/K^{\mathrm{ur}})$ be the extraspecial group above. For each real number $u \geq -1$, let $G_u$ (in lower numbering) and $G^u$ (in upper numbering, via the Herbrand function) denote the ramification subgroups of $G$ acting on $L$.

Determine the ramification filtration $(G_u)_{u \geq -1}$ (equivalently $(G^u)_{u \geq -1}$) of $G$: specify the jumps (breaks) of the filtration and the subgroups occurring at each break.

Let $K$ be a complete discretely valued field with algebraically closed residue field of characteristic $p \geq 0$, and let $K^{\mathrm{tame}}$ denote a maximal tamely ramified extension of $K$ inside a fixed algebraic closure. Fix an integer $g \geq 2$ and consider the moduli space $M_g$ of smooth projective curves of genus $g$, together with its Deligne–Mumford compactification $\overline{M}_g$. A "type of degeneration" is a topological/combinatorial type of stable curve of genus $g$; each such type determines a locally closed stratum in $\overline{M}_g$ whose formal/analytic neighborhood (an analytic open in the appropriate sense) parametrizes deformations of that type. For a $K$-point of $M_g$ corresponding to a smooth curve $C/K$ acquiring a stable reduction of the prescribed degeneration type, one associates the finite monodromy extension $L/K^{\mathrm{tame}}$: the smallest finite extension of $K^{\mathrm{tame}}$ over which the $\ell$-adic (or, equivalently in this setting, geometric) monodromy of $C$ becomes trivial. By Krasner's lemma, this finite extension $L/K^{\mathrm{tame}}$ depends only on the analytic-open neighborhood, i.e. is locally constant on the stratum of the chosen degeneration type.

Problem: For a fixed degeneration type of stable genus-$g$ curves, characterize the finite extensions of $K^{\mathrm{tame}}$ that arise as the finite monodromy extension $L/K^{\mathrm{tame}}$ attached in this way. Equivalently, describe the set of isomorphism classes of finite extensions of $K^{\mathrm{tame}}$ realized by curves whose stable reduction has the prescribed degeneration type.

Let S_n denote the set of permutations of {1,2,…,n}. For a pattern τ, let s_n(τ) denote the number of permutations in S_n that avoid τ (i.e., contain no subsequence whose relative order matches τ).

A permutation is called layered if it can be written as the direct sum of finitely many decreasing permutations; equivalently, it consists of consecutive descending runs whose values are increasing across runs.

Given a permutation π ∈ S_k and permutations σ_1, σ_2, …, σ_k (of arbitrary sizes), the inflation π[σ_1, σ_2, …, σ_k] is the permutation obtained by replacing the i-th entry of π with a block order-isomorphic to σ_i, shifting values so that all entries of the block replacing the i-th smallest entry of π lie below all entries of the block replacing the (i+1)-st smallest entry, and similarly for positions.

In particular, 12…k[σ_1, σ_2, …, σ_k] denotes the inflation of the increasing permutation 12…k ∈ S_k by the blocks σ_1, …, σ_k.

Prove or disprove: For every nonlayered permutation π ∈ S_k, every choice of permutations σ_1, σ_2, …, σ_k, and every natural number n,
   s_n(π[σ_1, σ_2, …, σ_k]) < s_n(12…k[σ_1, σ_2, …, σ_k]).

Background and definitions. The stack-sorting operation $s$ on permutations is defined recursively as follows. Given a permutation $\pi = LnR$ written as a word over distinct entries, where $n$ is its largest entry and $L,R$ are the (possibly empty) factors to the left and right of $n$, set $s(\pi) = s(L)\, s(R)\, n$, with $s(\varepsilon) = \varepsilon$. A permutation $\pi \in S_n$ is called West 2-stack sortable if $s(s(\pi))$ is the identity permutation $12\cdots n$.

It is a known theorem (originally conjectured by Julian West and proved by Zeilberger) that the number $W_n$ of West 2-stack sortable permutations of $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ equals
$$W_n \;=\; \frac{2\,(3n)!}{(n+1)!\,(2n+1)!}.$$
From this formula one can verify that for every nonnegative integer $k$, the integer $W_{4k+3}$ is even.

Problem. Provide a combinatorial proof that $W_{4k+3}$ is even for every nonnegative integer $k$. That is, exhibit an explicit fixed-point-free involution on the set of West 2-stack sortable permutations of $\{1,2,\dots,4k+3\}$ (or an equivalent combinatorial pairing argument) that establishes the evenness of its cardinality without recourse to the closed-form enumeration formula.

Consider a sorting machine consisting of three stacks connected in series. Permutations of $\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$ are input from the right onto the first stack; at each step one may either push the next input element onto the first stack, pop the top of stack $i$ and push it onto stack $i+1$ (for $i=1,2$), or pop the top of the third stack to the output. A permutation $\pi$ is said to be sortable by this machine if there exists some sequence of such legal operations that outputs $1,2,\ldots,n$ in increasing order. (No restriction is placed on the contents of any stack; this is the "general," non-deterministic three-stack machine.)

Determine the smallest integer $n$ such that there exists a permutation of $\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$ which cannot be sorted by this machine, and exhibit such a permutation of minimum length.

Let $(X_k)_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}$ be a strictly stationary sequence of real-valued random variables on a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P)$. For a sub-$\sigma$-field $\mathcal{A}\subset\mathcal{F}$, let $L^2(\mathcal{A})$ denote the space of square-integrable $\mathcal{A}$-measurable random variables. For sub-$\sigma$-fields $\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}\subset\mathcal{F}$ define the maximal-correlation coefficient
$$\rho(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}) := \sup\{|\operatorname{Corr}(f,g)| : f\in L^2(\mathcal{A}),\ g\in L^2(\mathcal{B})\}$$
and the $\varphi$-mixing coefficient
$$\varphi(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}) := \sup\{|P(B\mid A)-P(B)| : A\in\mathcal{A},\ B\in\mathcal{B},\ P(A)>0\}.$$
For $S\subset\mathbb{Z}$ write $\mathcal{F}_S := \sigma(X_k : k\in S)$. For each integer $n\geq 1$ define
$$\varphi(n) := \sup_{j\in\mathbb{Z}}\varphi\bigl(\mathcal{F}_{(-\infty,j]},\,\mathcal{F}_{[j+n,\infty)}\bigr),$$
$$\rho^*(n) := \sup\bigl\{\rho(\mathcal{F}_S,\mathcal{F}_T) : S,T\subset\mathbb{Z},\ S,T\neq\emptyset,\ S\cap T=\emptyset,\ \operatorname{dist}(S,T)\geq n\bigr\},$$
where $\operatorname{dist}(S,T) := \min_{s\in S,\,t\in T}|s-t|$. (Note that $S$ and $T$ are not required to be separated by a single integer; they may be "interlaced".) Say that the sequence is $\varphi$-mixing if $\varphi(n)\to 0$ as $n\to\infty$, and $\rho^*$-mixing if $\rho^*(n)\to 0$ as $n\to\infty$.

Question: Does $\varphi$-mixing of $(X_k)_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}$ imply $\rho^*$-mixing of $(X_k)_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}$?

$$\rho(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}) := \sup\{|\operatorname{Corr}(f,g)| : f\in L^2(\mathcal{A}),\ g\in L^2(\mathcal{B})\}$$
and the $\varphi$-mixing coefficient
$$\varphi(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}) := \sup\{|P(B\mid A)-P(B)| : A\in\mathcal{A},\ B\in\mathcal{B},\ P(A)>0\}.$$
For $S\subset\mathbb{Z}$ write $\mathcal{F}_S := \sigma(X_k : k\in S)$. For each integer $n\geq 1$ define
$$\varphi(n) := \sup_{j\in\mathbb{Z}}\varphi\bigl(\mathcal{F}_{(-\infty,j]},\,\mathcal{F}_{[j+n,\infty)}\bigr),$$
$$\rho^*(n) := \sup\bigl\{\rho(\mathcal{F}_S,\mathcal{F}_T) : S,T\subset\mathbb{Z},\ S,T\neq\emptyset,\ S\cap T=\emptyset,\ \operatorname{dist}(S,T)\geq n\bigr\},$$
where $\operatorname{dist}(S,T) := \min_{s\in S,\,t\in T}|s-t|$. (Note that $S$ and $T$ are not required to be separated by a single integer; they may be "interlaced".) Say that the sequence is $\varphi$-mixing if $\varphi(n)\to 0$ as $n\to\infty$, and $\rho^*$-mixing if $\rho^*(n)\to 0$ as $n\to\infty$.

Question: Does $\varphi$-mixing of $(X_k)_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}$ imply $\rho^*$-mixing of $(X_k)_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}$?

Let $X = (X_k)_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}$ be a strictly stationary random sequence defined on some probability space $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)$, taking values in a finite set $S$. For $-\infty \le J \le L \le \infty$, let $\mathcal{F}_J^L := \sigma(X_k : J \le k \le L)$. Define Rosenblatt's strong mixing coefficient
$$\alpha(n) := \sup\{|P(A \cap B) - P(A)P(B)| : A \in \mathcal{F}_{-\infty}^0,\; B \in \mathcal{F}_n^{\infty}\}, \quad n \ge 1,$$
and call $X$ strongly mixing if $\alpha(n) \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$.

Also define the maximal correlation coefficients
$$\rho(n) := \sup\bigl\{ |\mathrm{Corr}(f,g)| : f \in L^2(\mathcal{F}_{-\infty}^0),\; g \in L^2(\mathcal{F}_n^{\infty})\bigr\},$$
$$\rho^*(n) := \sup\bigl\{ |\mathrm{Corr}(f,g)| : f \in L^2(\mathcal{F}_S),\; g \in L^2(\mathcal{F}_T),\; S,T \subset \mathbb{Z},\; \mathrm{dist}(S,T) \ge n\bigr\},$$
where $\mathcal{F}_E := \sigma(X_k : k \in E)$. Say that $X$ is $\rho$-mixing if $\rho(n) \to 0$, and $\rho^*$-mixing if $\rho^*(n) \to 0$.

A Bernoulli shift is the measure-preserving dynamical system $(A^{\mathbb{Z}}, \mathcal{B}, \mu^{\mathbb{Z}}, T)$ where $A$ is a (finite or countable) set, $\mu$ is a probability measure on $A$, and $T$ is the left shift; two stationary processes are isomorphic if their associated measure-preserving systems are isomorphic in the sense of ergodic theory.

Question: Must every strictly stationary, finite-state, strongly mixing sequence $X$ be isomorphic to a Bernoulli shift? Does the conclusion hold under the stronger hypothesis that $X$ is $\rho$-mixing, or under the still stronger hypothesis that $X$ is $\rho^*$-mixing?

Setup. Let $X := (X_k, k \in \mathbb{Z})$ be a strictly stationary sequence of real-valued random variables defined on some probability space. Say that $X$ is representable as an instantaneous function of a strictly stationary, Harris recurrent Markov chain if there exist (i) a strictly stationary Markov chain $Y := (Y_k, k \in \mathbb{Z})$ taking values in a measurable space that is Harris recurrent (i.e., there exists a $\sigma$-finite measure $\varphi$ on the state space such that for every measurable set $A$ with $\varphi(A) > 0$ and every starting point, the chain visits $A$ infinitely often almost surely), and (ii) a Borel measurable function $f : \mathbb{R}' \to \mathbb{R}$ from the state space of $Y$ to $\mathbb{R}$, such that the sequence $(f(Y_k), k \in \mathbb{Z})$ has the same finite-dimensional distributions as $X$.

For a strictly stationary sequence $X$ and integers $-\infty \le J \le L \le \infty$, let $\mathcal{F}_J^L := \sigma(X_k : J \le k \le L)$. Define the $\psi$-mixing coefficients
$$\psi(n) := \sup \left\{ \left| \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(A) P(B)} - 1 \right| : A \in \mathcal{F}_{-\infty}^{0},\ B \in \mathcal{F}_n^{\infty},\ P(A) > 0,\ P(B) > 0 \right\}.$$
The sequence $X$ is called $\psi$-mixing if $\psi(n) \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$. The sequence $X$ is called $1$-dependent if for every integer $k$, the $\sigma$-fields $\sigma(X_j : j \le k)$ and $\sigma(X_j : j \ge k+2)$ are independent.

Question. Does there exist a strictly stationary $\psi$-mixing sequence (or, even more restrictively, a strictly stationary $1$-dependent sequence) that cannot be represented as an instantaneous function of any strictly stationary, Harris recurrent Markov chain in the sense above?

Let $X = (X_k, k \in \mathbb{Z})$ be a centered complex weakly stationary sequence, i.e., a sequence of complex-valued random variables with $E|X_k|^2 < \infty$, $E X_k = 0$, and covariance $E(X_j \overline{X_k})$ depending only on $j-k$. By Herglotz's theorem, there exists a finite nonnegative Borel measure $\mu$ on $[-\pi,\pi]$ (the spectral measure) such that $E(X_{j+k}\overline{X_j}) = \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} e^{ik\lambda}\,d\mu(\lambda)$. Assume $\mu$ is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure, with spectral density $f:[-\pi,\pi] \to [0,\infty)$.

For nonempty finite disjoint subsets $Q, S \subset \mathbb{Z}$, and any finite families of complex numbers $\{a_k : k \in Q\cup S\}$, define
$$r^*(Q,S) = \sup \frac{\left| \operatorname{Cov}\!\left(\sum_{k\in Q} a_k X_k,\ \sum_{k\in S} a_k X_k\right)\right|}{\left(\operatorname{Var} \sum_{k\in Q} a_k X_k\right)^{1/2}\left(\operatorname{Var} \sum_{k\in S} a_k X_k\right)^{1/2}},$$
where the supremum is over all nonzero choices of the $a_k$. For each integer $n \ge 1$, define the interlaced maximal correlation-type coefficient
$$r^*(n) = \sup\, r^*(Q,S),$$
where the supremum is taken over all pairs of nonempty finite disjoint subsets $Q, S \subset \mathbb{Z}$ satisfying $\operatorname{dist}(Q,S) := \min_{j\in Q, k\in S} |j-k| \ge n$ (note that $Q$ and $S$ are allowed to be "interlaced" rather than separated into past and future).

Find a necessary and sufficient condition on the spectral density $f$ for $r^*(n) \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$.

Fix an integer $d \geq 2$. A random field $X = (X_k : k \in \mathbb{Z}^d)$ is called strictly stationary if its finite-dimensional distributions are invariant under all translations of $\mathbb{Z}^d$, finite-state if each $X_k$ takes values in a fixed finite set, and nondegenerate if it is not almost surely constant.

For a vector $v = (v_1,\ldots,v_d) \in \mathbb{Z}^d$, write $v \prec 0$ in the lexicographic order if either $v_1 < 0$, or $v_1 = 0$ and $v$ is lexicographically negative in the remaining coordinates (equivalently, fix any total ordering of $\mathbb{Z}^d$ compatible with a half-space). The lattice half-space at site $k$ is $H_k = \{j \in \mathbb{Z}^d : j - k \prec 0\}$, and its "thickened" complement is the set of sites at lattice distance $\geq 1$ from $H_k$. The field $X$ is called lattice half-space 1-dependent if for every $k \in \mathbb{Z}^d$, the $\sigma$-field generated by $\{X_j : j \in H_k\}$ is independent of the $\sigma$-field generated by $\{X_j : j \notin H_k,\ \|j - H_k\|_\infty \geq 1\}$ (i.e., independence holds between the half-space and the part of the complementary half-space separated from it by a unit gap).

The tail $\sigma$-field of $X$ is $\mathcal{T} = \bigcap_{n \geq 1} \sigma(X_j : \|j\|_\infty \geq n)$.

Question: For the given $d \geq 2$, does there exist a nondegenerate strictly stationary finite-state (or even two-state) random field $X = (X_k : k \in \mathbb{Z}^d)$ such that
(a) $X$ is lattice half-space 1-dependent, and
(b) modulo null sets, every $X_k$ is measurable with respect to $\mathcal{T}$ (equivalently, $\sigma(X) = \mathcal{T}$ modulo null sets)?

Let $n$ be a positive integer and let $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}$ be arbitrary real parameters. Denote by $P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)}$ the Jacobi polynomial of degree $n$ associated to the parameters $\alpha,\beta$, defined by the standard hypergeometric/Rodrigues formula

$$P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)}(x)=\frac{(-1)^n}{2^n n!}(1-x)^{-\alpha}(1+x)^{-\beta}\frac{d^n}{dx^n}\bigl\{(1-x)^{n+\alpha}(1+x)^{n+\beta}\bigr\}.$$

For a continuum (a compact connected set) $K\subset\overline{\mathbb{C}}$ and an $n$-tuple $X=\{x_1,\dots,x_n\}\subset K$ of distinct points, define the (weighted) discrete energy

$$E(X)=\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}\log\frac{1}{|x_i-x_j|}+\frac{\alpha}{2}\sum_{i=1}^n\log\frac{1}{|1-x_i|}+\frac{\beta}{2}\sum_{i=1}^n\log\frac{1}{|1+x_i|},$$

with the convention that points at $\infty$ are handled in the usual chordal/logarithmic capacity sense. For a family $\mathcal{F}$ of admissible continua, set

$$E^*(\mathcal{F})=\sup_{K\in\mathcal{F}}\;\inf_{X\subset K,\,|X|=n}E(X).$$

In the classical regime ($\alpha,\beta>-1$), taking $\mathcal{F}$ to be the family of continua in $\mathbb{C}$ containing $\{-1,+1\}$, one has $E^*<\infty$ and the supremum/infimum is attained at the unique $n$-tuple $X^*=\{x_1^*,\dots,x_n^*\}$ consisting of the zeros of $P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)}$.

Prove or disprove the following conjecture extending this max–min characterization to arbitrary real $\alpha,\beta$. Define the family $\mathcal{F}=\mathcal{F}(n,\alpha,\beta)$ of admissible continua $K\subset\overline{\mathbb{C}}$ by the rules:

1. If $2n+\alpha+\beta<-1$, then $K$ must extend to infinity and separate $-1$ from $+1$ in $\overline{\mathbb{C}}$.
2. If $\alpha+n>0$, then $K$ must contain $+1$; if $\beta+n>0$, then $K$ must contain $-1$.
3. If $n+\alpha+\beta+1<0$, then $K$ must contain $\infty$.

Show that with $\mathcal{F}$ so defined, $E^*(\mathcal{F})<+\infty$ and is attained at a unique $n$-tuple $X^*$, whose points coincide precisely with the zeros of $P_n^{(\alpha,\beta)}$.

Let $(M, \mathcal{F})$ be a compact foliated manifold, and let $E \to M$ be a Hermitian vector bundle. Consider the transverse pseudodifferential calculus on $(M, \mathcal{F}, E)$. Let $\overline{\Psi}^{0,-\infty}(M, \mathcal{F}, E)$ denote the completion of the algebra of transverse pseudodifferential operators of order $(0, -\infty)$ in a suitable operator-norm topology, and let $\overline{S}^{0}\bigl(G_{\mathcal{F}N}, \mathcal{L}(\pi^* E) \otimes |TG_N|^{1/2}\bigr)$ denote the completion of the associated transverse symbol algebra of order $0$, consisting of sections of the bundle of endomorphisms of $\pi^* E$ twisted by the half-density bundle of $TG_N$. The transverse calculus yields a continuous algebra homomorphism, the completed principal symbol map
$$\overline{\sigma} : \overline{\Psi}^{0,-\infty}(M, \mathcal{F}, E) \longrightarrow \overline{S}^{0}\bigl(G_{\mathcal{F}N}, \mathcal{L}(\pi^* E) \otimes |TG_N|^{1/2}\bigr).$$
Determine whether $\overline{\sigma}$ is surjective.

Let $(M,\mathcal{F})$ be a compact foliated manifold, and let $E\to M$ be a Hermitian vector bundle. Consider the algebra $\Psi^{*,-\infty}(M,\mathcal{F},E)$ of transversal pseudodifferential operators on $M$ that are smoothing along the leaves of $\mathcal{F}$, and its (suitably) completed version $\overline{\Psi}^{0,-\infty}(M,\mathcal{F},E)$. The symbol map identifies elements of $\Psi^{*,-\infty}(M,\mathcal{F},E)$ with sections in $C^\infty\!\big(G_{\mathcal{F}N},\,\mathcal{L}(\pi^* E)\otimes |TG_N|^{1/2}\big)$, where $G_{\mathcal{F}N}$ is the holonomy groupoid of the lifted foliation $\mathcal{F}N$ on the transverse cotangent bundle, $\pi$ is the natural projection, and $|TG_N|^{1/2}$ is the half-density bundle on the tangent groupoid.

Let $A\in\Psi^{m}(M,E)$ ($m>0$) be a transversally elliptic operator with positive transversal principal symbol, regarded as a positive self-adjoint operator. It is known that for any $Q\in\Psi^{l,-\infty}(M,\mathcal{F},E)$ with properly supported symbol, the function
$$z\mapsto \operatorname{tr}\!\big(Q\,A^{-z}\big)$$
admits a meromorphic continuation to $\mathbb{C}$ with an explicit residue formula.

Problem. Extend this meromorphic continuation and residue formula to operators $Q\in\overline{\Psi}^{0,-\infty}(M,\mathcal{F},E)$ whose symbol, viewed as an element of $C^\infty(G_{\mathcal{F}N},\mathcal{L}(\pi^*E)\otimes|TG_N|^{1/2})$, is not properly supported (for instance, in the case where the symbol is exponentially decreasing at infinity).

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact Riemannian manifold without boundary, let $\Delta_g$ denote the (positive) Laplace–Beltrami operator on $M$, and let $\sqrt{\Delta_g}$ be its self-adjoint square root. Let $\overline{\Psi}^0(M)$ denote the norm closure inside the bounded operators on $L^2(M)$ of the algebra $\Psi^0(M)$ of classical pseudodifferential operators of order $0$ on $M$; this is a unital $C^*$-algebra. Define a one-parameter group $\Phi_t$ of $*$-automorphisms of $\overline{\Psi}^0(M)$ by
$$\Phi_t(T) = e^{it\sqrt{\Delta_g}}\, T\, e^{-it\sqrt{\Delta_g}}, \qquad T\in\overline{\Psi}^0(M),\ t\in\mathbb{R}.$$
Let $S^*M$ denote the unit cosphere bundle of $(M,g)$ and let $F_t : S^*M\to S^*M$ be the classical geodesic flow, whose (Bowen–Dinaburg) topological entropy is denoted $h(F_t)$.

Problem. Define a notion of quantum topological entropy $h(\Phi_t)$ for the noncommutative dynamical system $(\overline{\Psi}^0(M),\Phi_t)$ in such a way that $h(\Phi_t)$ is meaningfully related to the classical topological entropy $h(F_t)$ of the geodesic flow (for example, by being equal to it, by bounding it, or by reducing to it on a natural commutative quotient).

Let $(M,\mathcal F)$ be a smooth Riemannian foliation on a compact manifold $M$, and let $N^*\mathcal F\subset T^*M$ denote its conormal bundle. The lift of $\mathcal F$ to $N^*\mathcal F$ gives the linearized foliation $\mathcal F_N$, which is transversally symplectic. Let $G_{\mathcal F_N}$ denote the holonomy groupoid of $\mathcal F_N$, and consider the convolution algebra $\mathcal A := C^\infty_{\mathrm{prop}}(G_{\mathcal F_N},|TG_{\mathcal F_N}|^{1/2})$ of properly supported smooth half-density sections, equipped with the noncommutative Poisson bracket coming from the Block–Getzler construction for transversally symplectic foliations.

Recall that on a (commutative) symplectic manifold, a Hamiltonian flow is the one-parameter group of automorphisms generated by $\{H,\cdot\}$ for a Hamiltonian function $H$. On the algebra $\mathcal A$ above, one obtains, for any homogeneous degree-one Hamiltonian $H$ on $N^*\mathcal F$, a "transverse Hamiltonian flow", that is, a one-parameter group of automorphisms of $\mathcal A$ associated with $H$ via the transverse geometry of the foliation.

Problem: Formulate a general notion of "noncommutative Hamiltonian flow" on an arbitrary noncommutative Poisson algebra in such a way that, when specialized to $\mathcal A = C^\infty_{\mathrm{prop}}(G_{\mathcal F_N},|TG_{\mathcal F_N}|^{1/2})$ with its Block–Getzler Poisson structure, every transverse Hamiltonian flow arising from a homogeneous degree-one Hamiltonian on $N^*\mathcal F$ is an instance of a noncommutative Hamiltonian flow in this sense.

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact Riemannian manifold equipped with a Riemannian foliation $\mathcal{F}$, and assume the metric $g$ is bundle-like with respect to $\mathcal{F}$. Decompose $g = g_H \oplus g_V$ into its components in the directions normal (horizontal) and tangent (vertical) to the leaves, and for $\varepsilon>0$ consider the rescaled family of metrics
$$g_\varepsilon = g_H + \varepsilon^{-2} g_V,$$
together with the associated Laplace–Beltrami operator $\Delta_\varepsilon$ acting on $C^\infty(M)$. The adiabatic limit refers to the asymptotic regime $\varepsilon \to 0$, in which spectral problems for $\Delta_\varepsilon$ on $M$ can be regarded as semiclassical spectral problems on the leaf space of $\mathcal{F}$. On the transverse side, the holonomy invariant transverse Riemannian structure determines a transverse geodesic flow on a suitable transverse cosphere/cotangent bundle of $\mathcal{F}$, which is a classical Hamiltonian flow on the leaf space.

Establish precise quantitative correspondences between dynamical properties of the transverse geodesic flow (such as ergodicity, mixing, hyperbolicity, complete integrability, or periodicity) and the asymptotic behavior, as $\varepsilon \to 0$ and/or as the spectral parameter tends to infinity, of:
(i) the eigenvalue distribution and clustering of $\Delta_\varepsilon$, and
(ii) the concentration and equidistribution properties (e.g. weak-$*$ limits of microlocal lifts) of the corresponding eigenfunctions.

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact Riemannian manifold equipped with a Riemannian foliation $\mathcal{F}$, and assume the metric $g$ is bundle-like with respect to $\mathcal{F}$. Let G be one of the three regular planar lattices: the square lattice, the hexagonal lattice, or the triangular lattice, embedded in the complex plane so that 0 is a vertex of G. A self-avoiding walk (SAW) of length n in G starting at 0 is a sequence of vertices v_0 = 0, v_1, ..., v_n with v_i v_{i+1} an edge of G and all v_i distinct. Call such a walk a half-plane SAW if every v_i lies in the closed upper half-plane H = {z : Im z ≥ 0}.

For each n ≥ 1, let μ_n be the uniform probability measure on the (finite) set of n-step half-plane SAWs in G starting at 0, identified with the corresponding piecewise-linear curves in H. Assume that the weak limit μ_∞ = lim_{n→∞} μ_n exists (as a measure on infinite half-plane self-avoiding paths) and let γ be a sample from μ_∞.

For s > 0, let sγ denote the rescaling of γ by the factor s. The chordal Schramm–Loewner evolution with parameter κ = 8/3 in the upper half-plane from 0 to ∞, denoted SLE_{8/3}, is the random curve generated by the Loewner equation driven by √κ B_t, where B_t is standard Brownian motion.

Prove that, as s ↘ 0, the law of sγ converges to the law of SLE_{8/3} in the upper half-plane from 0 to ∞. The convergence is to be understood either in the Hausdorff topology on closed subsets of the Riemann sphere, or in the stronger topology of weakly-uniform convergence of curves parameterized by half-plane capacity.

The conjecture that the scaling limit of the planar self-avoiding walk is SLE_{8/3} remains a major open problem. Lawler–Schramm–Werner proved that if the scaling limit exists and is conformally invariant, it must be SLE_{8/3}, but existence and conformal invariance are not established on Z^2, the hexagonal or triangular lattice. Strong numerical evidence supports the conjecture, and a related convergence has been proven for SAW on random quadrangulations to SLE_{8/3} on √(8/3)-Liouville quantum gravity (Gwynne–Miller), but the Euclidean lattice case is still open.
